Sister of Pakistan's ex-PM Imran Khan arrested
- Published
The sister of Pakistan's imprisoned former prime minister, Imran Khan, has been arrested ahead of next week's protests held in his support, his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party has said.
Aleema Khanum was detained in the eastern city of Lahore on Sunday afternoon, PTI officials said, calling it an "illegal detention". Her son is demanding her return.
The order for Khanum's arrest, which came from Lahore's deputy commissioner, alleged that she was mobilising Imran Khan's supporters "through social media and public meetings". It added that she will be detained for 30 days.
Khanum is a vocal critic of her brother's detention, regularly speaking to his supporters and the media.
A police official confirmed Khanum's arrest to the BBC. According to the order, she will be taken to Kot Lakhpat jail in Lahore.
Earlier in the day, her family said they had had "no contact or news of her whereabouts".
"We demand the government immediately disclose her whereabouts and ensure her safe return," Khanum's son Shahrez Khan wrote on X.
Many have linked her arrest to the protests that have been organised across the country on 27 September, when demonstrators plan to march to the Pakistani capital, Islamabad.
The arrest order said Khanum had been mobilising people to "create law and order situations" and "raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the Government."
Streets in Islamabad are already lined with shipping containers, ready to safeguard the city's government buildings.
Local media has reported Pakistan's interior minister as saying that the protests harm the country and that the government will do everything they can to stop them.
Khan has been detained since 2023, when he was sentenced to three years in prison for not declaring money earned from selling gifts he had received while in office.
He has faced charges in over 100 cases, ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts - all of which he has decried as politically motivated.
Last year, the cricket star-turned-politician was jailed for 14 years in a land corruption case - the longest sentence he has received.
While in prison, his health has being deteriorating, and last month Khan had to visit a hospital for an examination.

Tottenham bottom of Premier League despite £300m summer spend - where do they go from here?
Why have Tottenham regressed despite spending more than £300m on new signings in the summer? Spurs go into international break with two points and two goals from five games, sitting bottom of Premier League table after a 3-2 defeat by Aston Villa on Saturday
Monday 21 September 2026 17:59, UK
This time it was supposed to be different. After multiple false dawns for Tottenham Hotspur, the club had a manager with proven Premier League experience, and had handed him a £300m+ war chest - easily the biggest in its entire history.
Instead, Spurs find themselves bottom of the table after five games for the first time in 18 years, with their only goals a pair of consolation strikes on another dismal afternoon against Aston Villa at the weekend.
Things aren't quite as bad as the table suggests and had Tottenham taken any of a number of presentable first-half chances against Villa, they would have gone into the three-week international break silencing some of the noise around the club.
But instead, two points from five games and such a dismal record in front of goal has kept the spotlight firmly on them.

Though it is only five games, their struggles to find consistency have extended into a third consecutive season. Tottenham have now picked up just 18 points in 2026 and, since the start of 2024/25, still one fewer than a West Ham side who were relegated at the end of last season.
Roberto De Zerbi cannot avoid scrutiny forever, especially after a summer where he was given relative carte blanche in the transfer market and, a top-class left-winger aside, got most of what he asked for.
Speaking before the Villa game, he hinted he would have liked to have done things differently during the summer window, but the club had to respect Financial Fair Play and some players who had been earmarked for sale remained at the club.
That will not afford him much sympathy given the size of Spurs' spend. One of the outgoings who they were happy to let go, Luka Vuskovic, is thriving at Brighton. Meanwhile, the player he replaced, Jan Paul van Hecke, toiled in that Villa defeat and was dribbled past three times.
Regardless, Tottenham were always unlikely to be an overnight fix given money alone will not solve the sizeable task of changing course after finishing 17th in back-to-back seasons.
But fans still expected something more than this, especially from a head coach known for his man-management and getting the best out of limited resources, as he demonstrated across nearly two years on the south coast at Brighton.
Even one win would lift them out of the quagmire - and they will target a similarly under-pressure Man Utd side when the Premier League returns on October 10, live on Sky Sports. However, there are a number of issues of concern even after that mammoth spend.
The naive manner Spurs fell behind to Villa with Micky Van de Ven off the pitch injured and Andy Robertson inadvertently teeing up the opportunity, led De Zerbi to complain that "leaders have to be leaders" in such crunch moments. "We can't lose games in this way," he added.
But does his squad have enough of that kind of player? Van de Ven, Pedro Porro, Ben Davies, James Maddison and Archie Gray were named as De Zerbi's five-man leadership group last month, but none would be considered an out-and-out natural leader, who can hoist his team-mates up by their collars.
This is nothing new. Despite long-standing allegations of being 'Spursy', in the last two years, that nickname has truly taken on a new form. Tottenham have not won a league game when conceding first in approaching two years and have picked up only nine draws from losing positions since.
It was the right time for Cristian Romero to move on in the summer largely because his aggression could often overstep the mark, but it has left a void which has not been filled.
Instead, it has been compounded by the further loss of perhaps limited but unquestionably combative midfielder Joao Palhinha. In De Zerbi's defence, he made no secret of his desire to keep him.
More worryingly, it does not appear a problem the head coach has a solution to. "It is difficult to explain," he admitted after Saturday's defeat. "In my 14 years as a coach, I've never seen a team like us, so fragile and inconsistent."
He need only look to the home stands if he needs any filling in from a fanbase who are all too used to seeing exactly that over the past two years.
Even without Palhinha he cannot complain too loudly about his midfield given the near £200m sanctioned to sign Sandro Tonali and Matheus Fernandes.
Tonali in particular should be fresh after a summer off from the World Cup, but has yet to hit the heights which made him a fan favourite for much of his time at Newcastle and convinced Spurs to break their transfer record to sign him.
The bizarre sideshow of Richarlison's future has not helped matters either, despite his own limitations. That too is only compounded by Spurs' lack of goals while last season's top scorer watches on from his own, albeit partly self-imposed, spell in exile.
Dominic Solanke has still not returned to full fitness and De Zerbi was almost apologetic for his out-of-form striker after his latest performance against Villa, saying "he's much better than this Dominic Solanke".
But with the average xG of Spurs' shots the lowest across the Premier League and their overall total better only than Coventry's, the real Solanke needs to stand up sooner rather than later - or Omar Marmoush re-find his scoring boots.
It is still very early days in the latest iteration of the Spurs machine, and given the significant turnover in players in the summer - over half of Saturday's starting line-up were not at the club last season - no surprise there have been some teething problems.
But the sight of a Premier League table showing two points, two goals and Spurs holding up the rest of the league will feel like a lot more than that.
There is still a feeling things will come good - there is undoubted quality in the squad and no-one needs reminding of De Zerbi's abilities. But his spells elsewhere have a habit of ending on a sour note. The hope is that it hasn't already set in here.
Watch Spurs take on Man Utd at Old Trafford when the Premier League returns, live on Sky Sports Premier League and Main Event from 4.30pm (kick-off 5.30pm) on Saturday October 10.

You have to give points to DreamWorks’ latest animated feature, Forgotten Island, just simply for being an original from a studio system that rewards familiarity. And it comes from writer/directors Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado who proved with their own sequel, 2022’s Puss In Boots: The Last Wish that you could find clever ways to renew and energize existing IP, rather than just settling for what the audience expects.
I suspect this one though will have the most appeal to a teenage female audience as it is centered on the BFF relationship of two young girls, besties since grade school in the Phillipines, who have lived a life of memories (they have matching charm bracelets to prove it) since being little kids inseparable from each other. Now on the cusp of seeing life taking them down separate paths, they are about to embark on their greatest adventure together ever. But will they even be able to remember it? That is the hook here as the opening of the film introduces us to the wild and wacky Jo, and the more serious-minded Raissa with dreams of being a scientist one day.
At home in Manila they both dream of a mythical place that in their minds absolutely exists. During their lives they have been fed epic stories by the beloved elder Lola (Dolly DeLeon) which are vividly shared with her class by Jo. The film jumps ahead to the end of their high school years where Jo (the older version voiced by singer H.E.R.) and Raissa (Liza Soberano) are at that inflection point. Raissa is accepted into Caltech in America and is going to be leaving, while meanwhile Jo is stuck in a menial job at a fast food joint. This will be their last night and they are going to make the most of it when they come upon a magical portal on the beach, the portal it turns out to, Nakali, that Forgotten Island.
Watch on Deadline
Next thing you know they have landed there, with absolutely no idea of just how they got to the place of their imaginations. They are about to find out in this play on memory and the importance of it in all of our lives. With colorful new appearances (Raissa now has wings and half a head of hair) they have gone down the kind of rabbit hole that infamous characters like Alice and Dorothy have tread in literature and movies before, but this place is something else. In quick and whirring succession they meet some real doozies starting with Weredog, Raww (voiced with style and fun by Dave Franco), who claims he had just spent the previous 12 hours with both of them. He is a bit of a mess, embarrassed by his ever-changing appearance from human to dog and back again, mostly dog though. He will be their self-appointed guide thorugh Nakali, but he has competition from another new acquaintance, Bungi (Manny Jacinto) a cycloptic giant blue baby still stuck (literally) to his mother after all these years. We also meet the more restrained cave dwelling Batiba (terrifically voiced by Jenny Slate) who is agoraphobic to her core, but lives with a collection of knick knacks it turns out have been stolen from other peoples memories, just not her own since she is deathly afraid of venturing out into the world. She promises to help Jo and Raissa get back to their own world in return for their own memories.
Along the way we meet Daju (Jo Koy) leader of a tree brigade; King Truffle Wuffle (Ronny Chieng) lording over his own feifdom; and the impossibly vain and slick Prince Mermahn (Kevin McCann). As in every single cartoon aimed at kids there is also a villainess, and here it is The Dreaded Manananggal (Lea Solonga) who can magically divide herself down the middle and other horrific talents. She’s the wicked witch and evil queen of the piece but of course there is a reason she got to be so bad and we will find out in due time.
Jo and Raissa must navigate all of this in order to get back to where they came from in this uber frenetically-paced journey. Crawford and Mercado (who clearly has added the Filipino flavor to this story) pack way too much visually, especially in the first half perhaps sensing today’s younger moviegoers have a bit of attention deficit. I thought this thing, beautifully animated with different styles creeping in and out and as colorful as it could possibly be, would never slow down to take a breath. But finally in the second half when the girls’ own hopes and dreams come front and center, and the emotional elements take charge, it does cool its jets just enough to take it all in. The main theme of saving our memories, and keeping them close comes through loud and clear and there is nice resoloution to all of this. The busy soundtrack has lots of catchy tunes, old and new, including an original or two from H.E.R. herself.
Is this an animated movie I will keep in my memories? Not likely, but I think its younger (much) target audience will indeed be the ones who will find some cool things to remember and some sharp life lessons about the value of friendship.
Producer of the DreamWorks Animation production is Mark Swift.

Imagine a customer walking into a premium lifestyle store to buy a vase, but leaving with a dinner set, tableware, candles, and a few other pieces of décor for their living room. A few months later, the same customer is back, looking for a housewarming gift for family and friends. This is the loyalty that brands yearn for. Give more reasons for the customers to return and get a larger share of their wallet as well as their mind space. It’s never about one vase. This is exactly where the next leg of growth lies for the premium and mass-premium lifestyle market – not by abandoning what they are known for, but by finding more ways to bring the same customer back into their world. While some are simply moving from kitchenware into décor and gifting or from clothing into home and occasionwear, others are seeing an opportunity in new channels to reach those customers. The catch, however, is that every new avenue, be it physical retail, marketplaces, or quick commerce, comes with its own set of challenges. And there’s no channel that can be sacrificed. More stores mean more fixed costs More categories mean more inventory and operational complexity Wider distribution can bring reach but reduce control over the brand experience More discounting can move volume while making it harder to justify the premium tag The question, then, is not whether these brands can find new avenues for growth, but which of them can deliver growth without stretching their economics or diluting the brand. The Bar For Premium Is Rising From mass-premium homeware to more design-led and aspirational propositions, brands are carving out different positions to woo a crowded market. But the underlying challenge is: how do you give customers more reasons to buy? For Nestasia, the answer lies in making premium design accessible to a broader set of Indian consumers while expanding the occasions and categories around the brand. Cofounder Aditi Murarka Agrawal says the brand sees room to grow both its customer base and category presence. The mass-premium opportunity is therefore less about making premium products cheaper and more about widening the addressable consumer base without stripping away the attributes that justify the premium. Nestasia’s positioning sits around this balance of design, quality and accessibility, particularly for middle- and upper-middle-income consumers who may be trading up selectively rather than buying luxury across the board. “We see substantial room for deeper penetration. We already operate across D2C and marketplaces and have our exclusive brand outlets (EBOs). Meanwhile, trade and other offline channels remain relatively untapped opportunities that we are exploring to reach newer customer cohorts,” Agrawal said. Then, the customer is also changing. Products that once were bought purely for utility are increasingly being evaluated for how they look and what they say about the home. Kitchen tools, cookware, storage and dining products are becoming part of a broader design vocabulary. “The Indian consumer has become far more discerning. There is much greater exposure to international brands, and with that comes a sharper understanding of design, material and longevity. People are buying fewer things, but they want those things to mean something and to last,” said Rashi Sethia, the CEO of Nicobar, a modern Indian lifestyle and fashion brand. This shift changes the growth equation for premium brands. If consumers are becoming more deliberate about individual purchases, brands cannot rely on simply increasing product launches or pushing volume. They need to create more occasions in which the same consumer sees the brand as relevant, while retaining the design, material and craftsmanship cues that support the original purchase. While this creates an opportunity, it also raises the bar for many. Meanwhile, Kushal Bhagia, the founder and partner at All In Capital, sees repeat behaviour, full-price sell-through, contribution margins, customer acquisition costs and lifetime value as the more meaningful measures of demand. “For a premium consumer brand, I would want to see improving contribution margins, disciplined customer acquisition, healthy inventory turns and a credible path to EBITDA profitability. Growth can create value, but only if the economics improve as the business scales,” Bhagia added. The Cost Of Staying Premium Finding more customers is only one side of the equation, but serving them without diluting what made the brand attractive in the first place is another. For ellementry, a premium handcrafted homeware brand, expansion has meant moving beyond kitchenware and tableware into décor, furniture, soft furnishings and gifting. But founder Ayush Baid sees a clear limit to category expansion. “Our filter is fairly simple: does the category let us use the same design philosophy and manufacturing strengths such as our artisans, our materials, our craftsmanship, or does it require us to build an entirely new competency from scratch?” he said. This matters because premium positioning can make some conventional growth tactics counterproductive. A case in point is heavy discounting, which may accelerate sales but can also teach customers to wait for promotions. Similarly, wider distribution may create reach but can compress the experience through which a design-led brand communicates its value. The same tension is emerging with quick commerce. For ellementry, platforms such as Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart have created new impulse and gifting-led buying occasions that were not meaningful to the brand a few years ago. But the channel also changes the nature of discovery: a premium product can suddenly compete alongside convenience-led purchases and price-led promotions. Nicobar’s approach is similarly selective. Its expansion into gifting, eveningwear, menswear and home is being framed not as a way to increase the product count, but as an attempt to accompany the same customer across more occasions. “So, as we look at new categories and new markets, the first question is never: ‘How big is this opportunity?’ but ‘Does this feel genuinely right for Nicobar?’” CEO Sethia said. Physical retail creates another version of the same trade-off. A store can help a consumer experience materials, craftsmanship and the full product universe, but it also creates rent, staffing and inventory costs. The Next Growth Engine If premium brands cannot simply sell more of the same product to the same customer, the next phase of growth will depend on creating more reasons to buy. That need for growth becomes clearer when the scale of some of these businesses is put into perspective. Nestasia reported ₹115 Cr in revenue in FY25 but posted a ₹7.7 Cr loss, while Nicobar reported ₹174.8 Cr in revenue in FY25 and a ₹13.6 Cr profit. Aditya Birla Group-acquired Jaypore reported ₹93.5 Cr revenue in FY25, with a loss of ₹55.9 Cr. These are meaningful businesses, but they are still some distance from the scale of India's larger consumer franchises. Therefore, the next phase is less about proving demand for premium lifestyle products and more about finding the levers that can take a ₹100–200 Cr brand to its next stage of scale. Nestasia is eyeing adjacent categories and new channels; the company sees an opportunity in moving towards more elevated homes, better dining experiences and design-led kitchen spaces. For ellementry, the opportunity extends beyond India. According to cofounder Baid, the brand is seeing demand for Indian design and craftsmanship internationally, while digital channels are making premium products more accessible to consumers. “The key to making these opportunities commercially viable will be balancing design and craftsmanship with operational efficiency, consistent quality, and the right distribution strategy,” he said. Geography could become an equally important growth lever. The next affluent customer may not necessarily emerge from a traditional metro city. Consumers in smaller cities are increasingly exposed to global brands and design trends, while physical access to premium labels remains more limited. Nicobar sees physical expansion outside the metros as an inevitable part of the growth strategy. But the economics have to catch up with the aspiration: sensible retail costs, adequate demand and supply chains capable of maintaining quality. All in all, the broader opportunity for these brands lies not in India’s rising affluent population but in the premium that their customers can willfully cough up repeatedly. A larger category portfolio can increase wallet share, but only if the categories reinforce the brand. More stores can create discovery, but only if they eventually generate attractive returns. New channels can widen reach, but not if they train consumers to expect discounts. The brands that crack this equation well won’t just sell one vase but a reason to keep coming back. SPOTLIGHT | The Indian Puja Box Wants To Modernise Everyday Rituals Founded in 2021 by Maithili and Giresh Vasudev Kulkarni, the D2C startup offers curated puja kits and devotional products aimed at making everyday Hindu rituals more convenient and organised, building around the idea of a ‘masala dibba’ for puja essentials. Its flagship Puja Boxes bring together essentials such as agarbatti, dhoop, Gangajal, kumkum, haldi, chandan and ghee/oil wicks, packaged in premium wooden boxes priced upwards of ₹2,000. The brand sells primarily through its D2C website and also caters to gifting and bulk orders. The brand is tapping the shift towards convenience-led religious consumption, packaging traditionally fragmented puja essentials into curated, ready-to-use kits. By 2024, the startup was profitable and clocking ₹5.5 Lakh in average monthly revenue. The Deep Dive ECOMMERCE BUZZ RentoMojo’s Bumper Market Debut: The furniture and appliance rental company closed its maiden trading session 32.24% above the IPO issue price at ₹534.25 on the NSE, giving the furniture and appliance rental startup a market capitalisation of ₹5,548.8 Cr. Practo’s Leadership Reset: The healthtech startup has appointed former COO Jagnoor Singh as CEO, while cofounder Shashank ND will become the managing director and executive chairman as Practo prepares for a proposed public listing and Shashank shifts focus to his new venture ‘Cent’. Rebel Foods Narrows Losses: The foodtech unicorn cut its FY26 net loss by 16.3% to ₹281.8 Cr, while its revenue jumped 20.7% to ₹1,951.6 Cr. Its international revenue jumped 38.8% YoY to ₹283.81 Cr, while revenue from India grew 18%. UPI Gets Its First MDR Framework: NPCI has introduced a 0.4% MDR on P2M UPI transactions above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300, which is set to take effect on October 15. P2P payments and small merchants receiving up to ₹1 Lakh a month will remain exempt. The Operator Question With online customer acquisition getting expensive, how can a premium lifestyle brand use physical stores to attract new buyers without overspending? Share a practical playbook for choosing the location, store size and budget. We reached out to Rashi Sethia, the CEO of premium lifestyle brand Nicobar, to understand the playbook here. Here’s what she divulged: Turn Stores Into Brand Experiences: Nicobar sees its stores as more than points of sale. They are spaces where customers can experience the brand, its design and products, making physical retail an important way to acquire new customers. Let Digital Demand Guide Expansion: The brand uses online demand to identify cities and neighbourhoods where it already has customers but no physical presence. It also looks at locations where its target consumers already spend time, including areas around cafés, restaurants and other lifestyle spaces. Test Before Going All In: Nicobar does not believe bigger stores are necessarily better. Right-sized stores, pop-ups, exhibitions and dedicated gifting spaces can help the brand tell its story while testing demand before committing to a larger physical footprint. The focus is on keeping fixed costs such as rentals disciplined while investing in store design, product selection and frontline staff.

Imagine walking into a neighbourhood medical store with a prescription in hand. The pharmacist checks the medicine, packs it and hands it over. But what happens when there is no prescription? According to a nationwide survey, for a large number of consumers, the answer is that the medicine may still be sold. The finding comes as the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has proposed installing CCTV cameras at medical stores to make prescription-medicine sales traceable.
The survey, conducted by LocalCircles, saw about 1.06 lakh responses from consumers across 327 districts of India. Of the total respondents, 63% were men and 37% women. Besides, 52% of them were from tier-1 districts, 29% from tier-2 districts and 29% from tier-3, 4 and 5 districts.
The survey found that 64% of consumers said their chemist never or rarely asked for a doctor’s prescription before selling medicines in the past 12 months. Only 15% said their chemist mostly or always refused to sell medicines without a prescription. The survey also found that only 31% of consumers were able to get assistance from a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always, while 13% said they were assisted by someone who was not a qualified pharmacist.
The findings come as the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has floated a draft notification proposing mandatory CCTV surveillance at every medical store that dispenses drugs sold on a doctor’s prescription. Under the proposal, the supply, other than by wholesale, of any drug sold on the prescription of a Registered Medical Practitioner would have to take place under a CCTV surveillance system installed and maintained at the premises.
The proposal also comes against the backdrop of intensified enforcement in multiple States against chemists selling prescription medicines without valid prescriptions, operating without registered pharmacists and failing to provide proper bills.
Neighbourhood chemist remains the main source
The survey found that the neighbourhood chemist remains the primary source of medicines for most consumers. The question on how respondents had primarily purchased medicines in the previous 12 months received 16,822 responses. This revealed that 86% of the respondents primarily depended on local chemists, followed by 14% on ePharmacy apps.
Who is actually behind the counter?
The survey then looked at whether consumers were receiving assistance from qualified pharmacists when they needed help with medicine or disease-related queries. The question received 19,409 responses. 31% of the consumers said they were able to get assistance from a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always. 27% of them said they never or very rarely received such assistance.
Home delivery is not free of the prescription gap
The survey also examined prescription checks when medicines were delivered to consumers’ homes. The question received 15,473 responses. 41% of consumers surveyed said a prescription was never or rarely asked for during home delivery.
A missing bill can mean a missing trail
Consumers were also asked whether they received proper bills when buying medicines from local chemists. Of the 20,573 respondents, 26% said they were not provided a GST bill. “A bill is not merely a tax document. It carries the batch number, expiry date and identity of the seller and provides a record if a medicine turns out to be expired, defective or counterfeit,” it said.
The survey also sought to establish whether consumers had purchased medicines that later turned out to be counterfeit or ineffective. The question received 18,457 responses. 15% of consumers said they had bought medicines that were later found to be fake or counterfeit.

Watch: Six-year-old girl from China sets new Rubik's Cube world record
A young girl has broken the women's world record for the 3x3x3 Rubik's Cube twice in three days at the World Cube Association.
At age six, Lian Yunzhi has become the only female cuber in the world to have an average time under 4.5 seconds. She first broke the record with an average of 4.52 seconds and then 4.27 seconds at competitions in Wuhan and Guangzhou, China.
The young competitor from Sichuan Province has mastered more than 1,300 Rubik's Cube solving algorithms after vigorous training that involved spending two to three hours a day on the cube over the past year.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

PATNA: The main accused in the alleged molestation of a minor student in Jamui was shot and injured in a police encounter while he was being taken to the scene of the incident, police said on Tuesday.
The accused, identified as Nandan Yadav, had been arrested in connection with the case. According to police, Yadav was hiding near Madwa Hill, where the two students were stopped on September 19.
Police surrounded him and tried to apprehend him, but he allegedly attempted to flee. An encounter followed, during which police shot him in the left leg.
Yadav was subsequently admitted to Jamui Sadar Hospital for treatment.
ADG (Law and Order) K Suhita Anupam said Nandan Yadav had tried to escape while police were attempting to apprehend him, following which an encounter took place and he was shot in the leg.
According to police, Yadav was identified as the young man wearing a red scarf in the viral video. So far, six people have been arrested in connection with the case.
Three of the accused are aged between 35 and 40, while the other three are minors.
Earlier, police had arrested Ramashish Chaudhary for allegedly making the video of the incident viral on social media. Police identified and arrested Chaudhary after the video surfaced online.
The incident occurred around 7pm on September 19. Both victims are Class 10 students.
After attending tuition on Saturday, the students went to Madwa Hill in Jamui. While they were returning, some young men allegedly stopped them and subjected them to harassment and assault.
The two students were allegedly subjected to the harassment for around an hour and made repeated attempts to escape.
During the incident, Nandan Yadav allegedly chased one of the students and grabbed her from behind.
The viral video showed one of the accused forcibly assaulting the student. He allegedly grabbed her from behind and later lifted her onto his lap.
The girl's friend immediately intervened and tried to free her, leading to a scuffle between the students and the accused.
The student eventually managed to free her friend. However, the accused allegedly continued to harass them and attempted to prevent the two girls from leaving, while they continued trying to escape.
Police said all the accused identified so far had been arrested and further investigation into the case was underway.

భారత స్వాతంత్ర్య ఉద్యమ సమయంలో RSS కార్యకర్తలు బ్రిటన్ రాణికి గౌరవ వందనం చేస్తున్నారంటూ ఒక ఫోటో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారమవుతుంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: RSS కార్యకర్తలు బ్రిటన్ రాణికి గౌరవ వందనం చేస్తున్నప్పటి ఫోటో.
ఫాక్ట్: వైరల్ ఫోటో రెండు వేర్వేరు సందర్భాల్లో తీసిన ఫోటోలను జోడించి ఎడిట్ చేసి సృష్టించబడింది. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ ఫోటోలో RSS కార్యకర్తలు నిలబడి ఉన్న భాగాన్ని రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, దానికి సంబంధించిన అసలు ఫోటో (ఆర్కైవ్) లభించింది. ఈ ఫోటోను ‘డెక్కన్ క్రానికల్’ వార్తా సంస్థ తమ వెబ్సైట్లో 2016లో ప్రచురించిన ఒక కథనానికి ప్రతీకాత్మక చిత్రంగా ఉపయోగించింది. ఈ ఫోటోలో బ్రిటన్ రాణి లేరు.
ఇక వైరల్ ఫొటోలో బ్రిటన్ రాణి ఉన్న భాగాన్ని రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, దానికి సంబంధించిన అసలు ఫోటో ‘Getty Images’ వెబ్సైట్తో పాటు ‘History Ville‘ అనే ఎక్స్ (X) ఖాతాలో లభించింది. ఆ వివరాల ప్రకారం, 1956లో ఎలిజబెత్-II రాణి నైజీరియా పర్యటనలో నైజీరియా సైనిక దళాలను తనిఖీ చేస్తున్నప్పుడు ఈ ఫోటో తీయబడింది. దీన్ని బట్టి, సంబంధం లేని పై రెండు ఫోటోలను ఎడిట్ చేసి, RSS కార్యకర్తలు బ్రిటన్ రాణికి గౌరవ వందనం చేస్తున్నట్లుగా తప్పుడు ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారని స్పష్టమవుతుంది.
చివరిగా, RSS కార్యకర్తలు బ్రిటన్ రాణికి గౌరవ వందనం చేస్తున్నట్లుగా చూపుతున్న ఈ ఫోటో ఎడిట్ చేయబడినది.

A nine-second long video clip is has gone viral on social media, showing a man assaulting a puffed rice vendor. In the video, the man is seen overturning the box hanging from the snack seller’s neck and pouring all the food items onto the vendor’s face before they scatter onto the street. As this purported attack unfolds, the vendor stares at the man helplessly.
The video was posted by X user Alka Maurya on September 16 and has garnered more than 2,85,000 views and shared over 1,500 times till publication time. The caption of the post, translated from Hindi, reads: “(He) must be feeling so proud after doing something like this.” (Archive)
कितना गर्व महसूस कर रहा होगा ऐसे करके हैं ना …… pic.twitter.com/F6upi4I2ZD
— Alka Maurya (@MauryaAlka76391) September 16, 2026
Apart from Maurya, film actor Kamaal R Khan posted the same video with the caption: “How will you fix this mentality which has developed in last 10 years. India can’t be fixed now.” (Archive)
How will you fix this mentality which has developed in last 10 years. India can’t be fixed now. pic.twitter.com/o2T2AJzGoj
— KRK (@kamaalrkhan) September 17, 2026
Other social media users circulated the viral clip with similar captions, condemning the man seen purportedly attacking the vendor.
As a billboard visible in the video reads ‘Welcome to Patna Junction’, the Patna police was tagged in the comment section of certain posts, requesting them to take stringent action against the man who allegedly assaulted the vendor.
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the viral video clip, we ran reverse image search on several relevant keyframes. It led us to a video posted by content creator Sonu Paswan on Instagram. With 1,79,000 followers, he posts scripted videos highlighting the helpless condition of the working class people in India. Paswan has a social media presence on Facebook and YouTube as well. And according to his social media bios, he is from Darbhanga, Bihar.
In all of his videos, accessible on his Facebook page, Paswan himself can be seen playing different “poor characters” being harassed and attacked by others as he helplessly accepts his fate.
On September 18, Friday, Paswan posted a video on his Instagram page, where he clarified that he enacts emotional scenes on poverty as ‘content’ on his social media platforms. He clarifies that the viral clip does not depict a real attack on him, but is in fact a prepared skit. “I want to tell you that in the video you are seeing, the vendor is me and the man who is attacking me is part of my team. I want to let you know that we, as a team, make emotional videos on poverty. I request you to take this video purely as entertainment, and not believe that this is real,” he said.
The caption of this video reads, translated from Hindi, “Because we make emotional videos on the poor…You all give me so much love…but you guys have taken this clip to heart.
I know I have hurt you guys with this video. Please delete the video from your channel…I request you not to share this video any further.”
View this post on Instagram
After the clip started going viral and attracted significant backlash, on September 17, most of his videos on YouTube and all of his previous videos on Instagram had to be deleted. In the aforementioned video, Paswan urges audiences to not share the viral clip and excerbate his situation even further. “I request you to not share the clip on your personal profiles, please do this much for your brothers,” he said. He shared the same clarification on his YouTube page.
Moreover, Paswan posted videos of the guy who is acting as the attacker in the video, also clarifying the viral clip is indeed a skit, on his Instagram and YouTube pages. “The video you guys are watching and getting emotional and taking to heart is just our content…its not real…please stop roasting this video. Because of you [sharing the viral clip as real] all my efforts have gone to waste, all my videos, over 300 videos…I have had to delete them all. I request you to keep supporting and loving us,” he states in the video.
View this post on Instagram
Given that their skit went viral, misleadingly as a real incident, the content creators said they received backlash and trolling, compelling them to remove their previous videos. At present, Paswan’s Instagram page only features the two clarification videos and his YouTube page features the same. However, his Facebook still displayed his earlier content. The description of his Facebook page, translated from Hindi, also reads: “I make emotional videos on poverty.”
True to the description, Paswan’s Facebook page contains videos similar in theme to the viral video. In these videos, visibly destitute people or poor vendors are seen being humiliated or suffering at the hands of others, while accepting their fate.
Paswan can be identified acting in all of these videos, and a visual match can be established, indicating that he was indeed the person seen in the viral video. Thus, it can be concluded that a scripted video made by a content creator has gone viral, leading netizens to falsely believe that it depicts a real incident of attack on a puffed rice vendor.

Colombian authorities declared a public calamity as a wildfire burned through mountains surrounding one of the country’s best-known colonial towns in the north-east, scorching large swaths of vegetation and forcing evacuations.
Nearly 20 active fires are burning across the South American country. Dry conditions have increased fire danger in Colombia as it braces for the effects of El Niño, which can help wildfires spread.
The fire in Villa de Leyva, a popular tourist destination about 160km (100 miles) north-east of the capital, Bogotá, began Saturday on a mountain overlooking the town. By Sunday evening, authorities said about 290 hectares (717 acres) had been affected – an area roughly equivalent to 400 soccer fields – and the blaze was about 50% under control.
Strong winds have complicated efforts to contain the flames, which at times advanced toward populated areas. Local authorities declared an emergency, suspended in-person classes Monday and carried out preventive evacuations, including at hotels near the fire.
More than 400 firefighters, emergency workers, residents and volunteers took part in the response, while four helicopters dropped water on the flames. Carlos Amaya, the governor of Boyaca, where Villa de Leyva is located, said aircraft carried out about 170 water drops Sunday, releasing 240,000 liters (63,400 gallons).
Fabio Arjona, Colombia’s environment minister, said preliminary information from the disaster management agency suggested it may have been deliberately started, but authorities were still investigating.
Abelardo de la Espriella, the Colombian president, said Sunday on X the Villa de Leyva fire was about 50% controlled and contained on the ground.
Colombia’s national disaster management agency said in its latest nationwide update that authorities were monitoring 27 forest fires, with 19 still active and eight under control. Nine of the active fires were in Tolima, a mountainous region south-west of Bogotá, while others were burning across several parts of the country’s Andean region.
The weather agency said last week that 279 municipalities were under some level of wildfire warning, including 36 under its highest, red-alert level, with much of the risk concentrated in the Andean and Caribbean regions.
Between 16 June 16 and 6 August, Colombia recorded 438 forest fires in 191 municipalities, affecting about 7,153 hectares of vegetation, according to government figures.
Neighboring Ecuador is also battling a wave of wildfires. Ecuador’s national risk management agency said Sunday that 12 fires remained active across the country, while more than 21,800 hectares of vegetation have burned so far this year.
High temperatures and strong winds have helped flames spread rapidly in some areas. A fire on the slopes of Ecuador’s Imbabura volcano burned about 300 hectares before being brought under control Sunday after three days of firefighting.
El Niño is a periodic warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean that can reduce rainfall and raise temperatures in parts of the country, creating conditions that allow wildfires to spread more easily.
Disaster officials have said the period of greatest risk across the region from the developing El Niño is expected between October and April, with wildfires and water shortages among the main concerns.

Pope Leo XIV will meet with the French abuse survivors as critics demand action
Pope Leo XIV plans to meet with seven survivors of sexual abuse by Catholic clergy during his visit to France
PARIS -- Pope Leo XIV, during his four-day visit to France beginning Friday, will meet privately with seven survivors of sexual abuse by priests and other Catholic personnel. The outcome will be closely watched by critics who say the church has not done enough to confront the problem.
The meeting is scheduled for Sunday in Lourdes, one of Catholicism’s most important pilgrimage sites. Some survivors’ groups have criticized the decision to select individuals rather than representatives of established organizations.
The seven survivors said in a joint statement last week that they do not claim to represent all survivors.
“Engaging in dialogue does not mean endorsing,” they said. “Being received does not mean abandoning our demands.”
“Each of us is taking part in this meeting in our own name, free to express our own views, convictions and choices," they added.
The French Bishops’ Conference said the group includes people who were abused as minors or adults in Catholic schools, parishes and religious congregations.
In recent years, the French Catholic Church has established an independent compensation system for survivors and acknowledged the institution’s history of abuse.
A 2021 report estimated that 330,000 children in France had been sexually abused over seven decades by priests, other clergy members, church workers and volunteers.
One participant says he was abused at the private Catholic school Notre-Dame de Bétharram in southwestern France, where allegations span more than five decades.
Another was abused by Bernard Preynat, a priest who acknowledged sexually abusing at least 75 boys over several decades.
Preynat was sentenced in 2020 to five years in prison in one of France’s most prominent clergy abuse cases to reach trial.
Another participant is among those who have accused Abbé Pierre, a nationally revered priest and humanitarian who died in 2007, of sexually assaulting women.
Charles Mercier, professor of history and sociology of Catholicism at the Paris-based École Pratique des Hautes Études, or EPHE, said the main criticism concerns the group meeting with Leo "not being chosen by the victims but by the bishops and the institutions.”
That has left some advocates who have fought for survivors’ rights feeling they “are not recognized by the church,” he said.
Following the 2021 reckoning over the extent of sexual abuse, “bishops begged for pardon to the victims. And now they give the impression that they want to turn the page,” Mercier added.
Church leaders appear to be saying that “we have dealt with this crisis and now we are building the future,” he said.
Alain Esquerre, a spokesperson for a group of Bétharram school survivors, said words of compassion are “no longer enough” and called for a concrete plan to combat abuse.
“Receiving survivors’ groups would carry far too much symbolic and political weight, and it would require concrete action to be taken,” Esquerre said. “Because what we want is to move beyond simply hearing survivors’ testimony and potentially providing them with financial compensation."
During a visit to Spain in June, Leo met in Madrid with six survivors of clergy sexual abuse and vowed to consider their suggestions for improving the church’s response to the crisis, according to the Vatican.
In Lourdes, the façade of a basilica features mosaics by the Rev. Marko Rupnik that were recently covered entirely. Rupnik is on trial in a Vatican court on accusations of psychological, spiritual and sexual abuse involving more than two dozen women dating to the 1990s.
Last week, child protection activists protested near the home of Jacques Delfosse, a former Catholic priest suspected of sexually assaulting dozens of children.
Protesters denounced what they described as authorities’ failure to act against Delfosse, who served in northern France and the Paris region from 1964 until the 2000s.
Delfosse was convicted in 2007 of raping two girls younger than 15 during school holiday camps in the 1980s.
He was dismissed from the clerical state in 2025 after media reports prompted dozens to come forward with allegations. The Lille prosecutor’s office opened an investigation in August into the new allegations.
Arnaud Gallais, 45, president of the child protection group Mouv’Enfants, called on President Emmanuel Macron to raise the case during his meeting with Leo on Friday. He also urged the Lille diocese and the Vatican to open their archives.
Denouncing an “unbearable” denial of justice, Gallais cited a report by the Independent Commission on Incest and Sexual Violence Against Children, or CIIVISE, stating that only 3% of rapes and sexual assaults committed against children each year in France result in a conviction.
___
Associated Press journalists Jeffrey Schaeffer and Alexander Turnbull contributed to this story.

The Delhi High Court on Wednesday (September 16, 2026) asked the Centre to respond on whether it was contemplating formulating a policy to regulate addiction-causing design features on social media platforms like infinite scroll and autoplay.
A bench of Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Amit Sharma said it would hear a PIL seeking the constitution of an expert committee to examine engagement-maximising and addiction-causing design features on social media platforms after three weeks. It asked Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma to take instructions on the issue.
Mr. Sharma said that it would be in the domain of the policymakers to consider some of the issues raised in the plea and suggested that the petitioner could submit a representation to the government.
The counsel for the Centre and certain social media platforms also took objection to the maintainability of the petition in view of some orders from the Supreme Court and high courts which refused to entertain petitions on a similar issue.
Addictive architecture
Petitioner Vikas Kathuria, a professor of law, said the fulcrum of the issue is not what content social media platforms carry, but how such platforms are architecturally designed to cause addiction through infinite scroll, autoplay, algorithmically curated and personalised feeds, notification systems, and variable-reward engagement metrics, such as “likes”, to capture, retain and repeatedly re-stimulate the attention of the user.
The plea said the concern assumes significance in the Indian context as statistics reveal that Indian youths aged 18-24 spend more than an average of 120 minutes daily on social media.
It has been clinically proven that long hours on social media are linked to suicide and depression among adolescents, the petition said.
The plea sought the court’s direction to the Central Government and the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights to restrict, prohibit, or regulate the use of these features.

British prosecutors charge doctor in the 1994 Rwandan genocide
British authorities have charged a doctor living in London with crimes related to the 1994 Rwandan genocide
LONDON -- A doctor from Rwanda was arrested in London and charged Monday with crimes related to the 1994 Rwandan genocide, British authorities said.
Dr. Vincent Brown, formerly known as Vincent Bajinya, is the first person to be charged in the U.K. for taking part in the ethnic genocide in which an estimated 800,000 people were killed, prosecutors said.
Brown, 65, was arrested and charged with one count of conduct ancillary to genocide and six counts of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity. U.K. law allows British prosecutors to bring charges for some international offenses, including genocide and crimes against humanity, regardless of where they were committed.
“The charges relate to allegations that Dr. Brown took part in the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda in 1994,” said Frank Ferguson, head of the Crown Prosecution Service's counterterror division. “He is alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others."
Metropolitan Police war crimes investigators began looking into the case in 2019 at the request of the Rwandan government.
Brown is originally from Kigali but lives in London, where he once worked for a London-based charity assisting refugee nurses and midwives seeking to work in Britain.
He is believed to have entered the U.K. as an asylum seeker in 1998, former Rwandan Justice Minister Tharcisse Karugarama told The Associated Press in 2006.
Brown changed his name when granted British citizenship in 2004, attorney Philip Eldin-Taylor said at the time.
Brown is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Tuesday.
Police said they are continuing to investigate several other Rwandan genocide suspects living in Britain.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Michelle Gudiño Prestamo, a 41-year-old human resources manager at a major footwear company in Mississippi. The following has been edited for length and clarity.
I'm the distribution center human resources manager at a major footwear company. I started at the company in 2019. Before this job, I worked at a staffing and recruiting firm where I supported footwear and retail brands.
I don't want to work until I'm 80 years old. I'd like to retire around 65 and open a coffee shop because I have such a passion for it. Here's my plan to make that happen.
I was born in Venezuela
I came to the United States in 2009 on a cultural exchange program as an au pair. I lived with an American family in Germantown, Tennessee, for almost two years. I worked full-time as an au pair and studied English and human resources management.
I met my husband in 2010, and we got married in 2013. I became a US citizen in 2019. The US is a place where you have a lot of opportunities, avenues, and ways to access a home and a car. There's a lot of financial temptation.
Some people have a problem with alcohol, some with gaming. I had a problem with spending. My way of demonstrating love was by spending on gifts for family members and on souvenirs while on vacation.
At its highest, I had over $55,000 in credit card debt
At one point, I had 10 credit cards. I tried to pay off my debt on my own, but I realized I needed some help. Through my company's employee assistance program, I learned about resources available to me. Money Management International was one of the options.
Before I got help, my debt was not coming down; it was increasing because of credit card interest. With some help, I was able to redefine my budget and get out of the paycheck to paycheck cycle.
My monthly payment during the three-year program was $1,077. Some months, I paid more than the monthly payments with bonuses I received at work.
This April, I finally finished paying off my credit card debt.
My husband and I also have a mortgage
My husband owns a restaurant. He makes the mortgage payments with his restaurant income. My credit card debt was fully mine, as we don't share finances. My parents also live with us, and we have a son who will be 6 in December.
After renting for a while, I told my husband we should buy a place to live. We applied for a mortgage, were approved, and moved to Olive Branch, Mississippi, a suburb of Memphis, Tennessee, in 2018. The house is a few minutes from work. We're now building equity in our home.
I have a retirement account that my company matches up to 6% of my salary
Until April, I had been saving 2% of my salary in the company 401(k) plan, but I increased it to the maximum matched amount of 6% after I paid off my credit card debt. I may increase it more in the months ahead. I establish goals for myself all the time.
My next goal is to keep one month's salary in a separate "buffer" checking account and not use it. Ideally, I will have two months' salary in the account. I plan to use future bonuses to create this emergency fund. Because of my debt, I haven't been able to establish an emergency fund yet.
I eventually want to save six months' salary in my account with a local credit union. I need to start slow. I also set up a separate account for my son with the credit union.
You have to have a goal
I use vision boards for personal goals and professional goals. You have to be consistent and have a clear goal of what you want. I learn from my failures and my mistakes.
Right now, my goal is to build and maintain good money habits. I use an app to keep track of everything I spend, I have fewer credit cards, and I pay off the balance each month. Sometimes I'm scared. That fear pushes me to work harder toward my goals and to adjust them as needed.
I've been working at this company for seven years. I don't want to get back into debt again. I'm not getting any younger. I like my job, with its responsibilities, salary, and benefits, but I'm looking forward to retirement.

A techie's viral Reddit post highlighted the everyday struggles of the IT sector—surviving multiple layoffs, navigating a Performance Improvement Plan (PIP), and countering lowball HR offers. Documenting his career journey, an anonymous professional from Uttar Pradesh shared a candid account of how he grew his starting salary from ₹3 lakh per annum (LPA) to ₹20 LPA through persistence and aggressive negotiation. Growing up as an “above-average student” who eventually completed a BCA and MCA from a Tier-3 college, the techie admitted that programming never came naturally to him. At the time, his ambitions were incredibly grounded. “My biggest dream was to earn ₹30,000 per month,” he wrote. “I used to think, ‘That’s ₹1,000 a day. Imagine earning that much!’ That was my definition of success. I never imagined earning ₹1 lakh a month. I simply didn’t have that level of confidence.” But his corporate entry was turbulent. After facing 15 to 20 interview rejections, he said he secured his first job via campus placement, only to be laid off just two months later. Out of a team of nine freshers, he was one of three let go. Undeterred, he found another role, only to be laid off again when the COVID-19 pandemic struck. After spending 1.5 years at a smaller company, the techie shared that he capitalised on the pandemic-era tech hiring boom. The techie secured offers from industry giants like Genpact, TCS, Wipro, and Infosys before settling on Capgemini. The switch boosted his salary from ₹4 LPA to ₹9.5 LPA with just over two and a half years of experience. However, the transition was far from smooth. The techie noted that while his first project was manageable, a subsequent client assignment exposed his lack of experience. “I struggled badly. I lacked exposure, my confidence dropped, and I was even placed on a Performance Improvement Plan (PIP),” he recalled. “At that point, I had almost six years of experience, yet I constantly felt like I wasn't a good performer.” After spending nearly four years at Capgemini, battling stagnant wages, the techie shared he eventually left the company, earning just ₹10 LPA—a mere ₹50,000 increment over four years. Feeling stuck and constantly failing interviews, the professional eventually broke the cycle, but not without facing aggressive lowballing from HR departments. He recounted instances in which companies verbally promised higher figures, only to slash them in the final offer letters. The turning point came during his negotiations with HCL. Initially told the package would be ₹17 LPA, HR steadily walked the number down—first to ₹16 LPA, and then to ₹15 LPA plus a ₹1 lakh variable component. “When you don’t have many options, you often have to accept things you normally wouldn’t,” he explained. “That experience taught me an important lesson: always keep interviewing until you have the offer you actually want.” He did exactly that, eventually securing a competing offer for ₹20 LPA. When he informed HCL, they initially capped their counter at ₹17 LPA. He declined. Forced to compete, HCL eventually matched the ₹20 LPA offer. Ironically, after joining HCL, he received a ₹23 LPA offer from Tech Mahindra, but he chose to stay put. Reflecting on his progression from a ₹3 LPA fresher to earning ₹20 LPA, the techie acknowledged that while his college friends might be earning upwards of ₹30 LPA, his personal growth has been monumental. “When I look back at the boy whose biggest dream was to earn ₹30,000 a month, I realise I’ve already achieved something that once felt impossible,” he wrote. Leaving a final piece of advice for other struggling IT professionals, he said: “You don’t have to be the smartest coder in the room. You don’t need perfect communication skills from day one. You might get rejected, laid off, put on a PIP, or made to feel like you’re not good enough. Just don’t stop learning, don’t stop interviewing, and don’t stop believing that your next opportunity can completely change your career.” The candid post struck a chord with the online community, as many appreciated the techie's transparency about the industry's hidden struggles. “It's tough to navigate IT sometimes; sharing your experience can really help others feel less alone,” one social media user commented. However, the discussion also reflected broader anxieties about current tech hiring trends and global competition. Pointing to the changing landscape, another user argued, "The job market is completely oversaturated now. Unlike pre-COVID times, you can't just get a job without solid skills." The commenter also sparked a debate about wage stagnation by attributing the decline in salaries to a “massive influx” of IT professionals from India.
