India’s higher education policy framework increasingly talks about inclusion. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPwD Act) places obligations on educational institutions to promote inclusive education, while the University Grants Commission (UGC) has, over the years, developed guidelines and institutional mechanisms intended to ensure that students with disabilities (SwD) can participate in higher education on an equal basis.
Despite these measures, the dearth of remedial support makes them vulnerable to academic exclusion and widens existing educational inequalities. Limited digital access further restricts their access to online learning resources, digital libraries, academic databases, and other educational platforms, hindering participation in technology-enabled learning and limiting their ability to make full use of academic opportunities.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
Most recently, the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities listed the Accessibility Guidelines and Standards for Higher Education Institutions and Universities, issued by the Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education, on June 25, 2024. The UGC describes these guidelines as part of its effort to ensure equal participation and inclusion of persons with disabilities in higher education.
Importantly, the UGC states that every higher educational institution (HEI) is expected to develop an effective accessibility mechanism extending from the admission process through the completion of the course. The Commission issued fresh directions to universities to furnish a report along with statistical information in respect of students admitted, teaching and non-teaching recruitment, as well as fellowships/scholarships provided to PwD students through the Universities Activity Monitoring Portal (UAMP) by September 30, 2026. It calls for the need to form an Internal Committee comprising teachers, staff, students and parents to take care of the day-to-day needs of persons with disabilities.
Yet institutional attention to disability often becomes focused on admission, reservation, and physical infrastructure. The more difficult question of what happens to the student after admission receives considerably less attention.
“The national statistical architecture measures how many students with disabilities enter higher education but does not adequately measure what happens to them after they enter colleges and universities,” disability rights activist and Professor at University College of Medical Sciences, Delhi, Dr. Satendra Singh told The Hindu.
Students with disabilities may enter higher education with varying levels of exposure to accessible learning environments. Some may require additional academic assistance, remedial classes, note-taking support, assistive technologies, or additional time and flexibility to engage with coursework. A student who misses classes because of disability-related issues may not have access to a structured academic mechanism to navigate the backlogs. The result is a form of exclusion that is not visible in institutional statistics.
Supportive system needed
The RPwD Act itself points to Section 16, which requires not merely admission without discrimination, but reasonable accommodation, necessary support, and monitoring of participation, academic progress, and completion. The UGC’s own accessibility framework similarly speaks of an accessible mechanism covering the student journey from admission to completion. But the lack of adequate remedial support has a direct bearing on how students with disability perform academically.
“Majority of the HEIs do not have a rights-based understanding of reasonable accommodation. They are still stuck with ramps, braille and talking books,” Dr. Singh said.
Pointing to the 2023–24 AISHE data, he said, “Of the 4.50 crore students enrolled in HEIs, the reported 54,080 students with benchmark disabilities (SwBD) represent approximately 0.12% of total higher-education enrolment. This is about 12 SwBD per 10,000 students. The AISHE reporting does not provide a detailed disability-type categorisation. This is a significant data gap because ‘SwBD’ is an extremely heterogeneous category. A student who is blind, a deaf student who uses Indian Sign Language (ISL), a student with dyslexia, an autistic student, and a student with psychosocial disability can have completely different accessibility and academic-support requirements.”
Dr. Sanjay Kant Prasad, Director of the National Centre for Disability Studies at IGNOU and former Deputy Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities, echoes his views. He said, “Higher education must recognise that the 21 categories of disabilities identified under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act have diverse and often distinct educational needs. While some disabilities may require limited remedial support, students with blindness, low vision, hearing impairment, deafness, cerebral palsy, autism and learning disabilities, among others, may require specific forms of academic and assistive support.”
He stresses that inclusive education does not mean eliminating specialised support. Rather, it is about creating an accessible environment in which the same educational curriculum can be accessed by students with different needs.
“In higher education, teachers may not require specialised training for every disability, but they should at least be oriented to disability-related needs and know how to make classrooms, teaching methods and learning materials accessible. This could include tactile materials and Braille for students with visual impairments, appropriate seating and mobility support, hearing aids or visual aids for students with hearing impairments, and the use of assistive and digital technologies such as text-to-speech software,” Dr. Prasad said.
Citing IGNOU’s efforts to provide study material at students’ doorsteps, counselling through teleconferencing and facilities for submitting assignments using computers, while following government and UGC guidelines, Dr. Prasad feels students’ ability to remain in education depends on broader social and economic support, not just classroom accommodations. Housing, awareness of available services and support from disability organisations are important factors.
Progress has been made over the past several decades from exclusion towards inclusion, but implementation remains uneven, and continued awareness, teacher training, and institutional support are needed to navigate the barriers.
In schools, the structures for remediation are more readily available than in higher institutions. The multi-tiered systems of support are a comprehensive framework that help provide individualised support to students.
Under this tiered system, the first level of support is the universal support that is offered to all students to help them learn better; the second level is classroom-based strategies and only the third level involves intensive care such as remediation.
“Often, students who reach higher education come equipped with an understanding of their own needs, have developed learning strategies, and carry an arsenal of tools that have been offered to them since school. Therefore, not every SwD requires remediation; some might require accommodations and modifications. Here is where inclusive EdTech, digital access, and online learning resources come in handy,” Dr. Rajeshwari Muthukumaran, Assistant Professor at the Centre for Neurodiversity Research and Innovation at Christ (Deemed-to-be University), said. She runs a support group aimed at fostering a sense of belonging and building a community on campus with students with disabilities, and neurodiverse students.
Although SwD might already come with their specific digital tools/modified equipment, they may still need guidance and access to software and tech tools often used in their domain.
Significant resource gaps persist, including the availability of Braille-translated materials and books in accessible typefaces. These constraints make it more challenging to design and implement tailored remediation programmes.
Additionally, institutional resource limitations, including a shortage of faculty with both subject expertise and training in developing accessible curricula, pedagogical practices, and assessment methods, as well as limited spaces and opportunities for one-on-one student-faculty support, further compound the problem.
Drawing from experience, Dr. Muthukumaran said, “I have met students who often enter higher education with a mix of hope, anxiety, and anticipation, and are seeking a supportive and approachable guide/mentor/peer who can offer them a safe and understanding space and serve as a support system. While guiding them in classrooms, I often end up recommending students to mental health professionals/supportive online communities where they can exchange ideas and converse with individuals with similar experiences to help them deal with campus life overall.”
Evidently, more colleges have now started looking into strategies, establishing specialised cells and centres that further look into research and student support. “While there is a long way to go, this scattered chatter needs to grow louder, unanimously, to shape future education and move towards evidence-based inclusive practices,” Dr. Muthukumaran added.
The digital divide
Considering that higher education has become increasingly dependent on digital infrastructure, learning management systems (LMS), university portals, digital libraries, online journals, e-books, recorded lectures, online assignments, examination portals, email systems, and virtual classrooms are now integral to campus life. For many learners, this digital environment offers greater convenience, flexibility, and access to educational resources. But for students with disabilities, digital technologies can be either powerful enablers or, when accessibility is inadequate, can become significant barriers to participation and academic success.
A university website that cannot be navigated effectively with assistive technology can make admission and administrative processes more cumbersome. A PDF that is simply a scanned image may not be usable for a blind student. An online learning platform without appropriate keyboard navigation, captions, transcripts, or alternative texts can prevent students from participating on equal terms.
Digital exclusion can widen the educational divide even when the physical campus is accessible. This is particularly important because UGC’s own framework requires online programmes to meet accessibility standards for learners with disability. If education is delivered digitally, its accessibility must be inclusive.
The lack of adequate data makes it difficult to assess the enormity of students’ plight. “There is no AISHE, NAAC or NIRF indicator reporting the percentage of students with disabilities in higher education who have access to accessible LMS platforms, screen-reader-compatible material, captions, Indian Sign Language interpretation or accessible e-books,” Dr. Singh said.
Without such indicators, institutions may be able to report enrolment and infrastructure without demonstrating whether students with disabilities can actually access, participate in, and benefit from digital learning on an equal basis. The absence of systematic data also makes it difficult to identify gaps, assess institutional performance, or hold institutions accountable for meeting accessibility requirements.
“We need a stricter implementation protocol for higher education institutions as there is mostly a lack of awareness and enforceable rules that institutions should follow,” says Deepa Palaniappan, Disability Inclusion practitioner, highlighting the need for more discussions, training, and handholding, as well as forming national task forces and committees to track effective inclusion of students with disabilities in higher education institutions across the country.
Reality check
For Delhi University (DU) alumnus and disability rights activist Ashutosh Singhal (24), the challenges of being an undergraduate and later postgraduate student of Political Science were harrowing. ‘’I use a regular, mainstream computer with a screen reader that reads out the text and other information displayed on the screen. This means that questions appearing on the computer can be read aloud to me, enabling me to access and answer them independently,” Ashutosh said, who suffers from late-onset visual impairment (retinitis pigmentosa), a condition in which the vision can gradually deteriorate.
Beating the odds, he managed to use a computer to write his Political Science BA and MA exams in Hindi, which was the first instance of its kind.
“Initially, they gave me a computer that crashed. The computer instructor apparently knew that there were problems with the computer but did not inform me beforehand. A substitute computer was eventually provided, but by then considerable examination time had been lost. I was told that I would receive additional time to compensate for the lost time, but this was not implemented adequately. Since the examination authorities had to collect and pack the answer scripts at a fixed time, I was under pressure to finish and submit my answers immediately,” he added. Ashutosh was also made to sit in a computer lab during the exam where the constant noise made it difficult to detect the sounds of the screen reader, disrupting his flow of thoughts.
Ashutosh’s experience made him realise that the biggest difficulty for students with disabilities is often not the technology itself which is already available. It is about getting institutions to recognise and implement accessibility provisions consistently.
A student may have to repeatedly explain their requirements, submit applications, approach different departments, contact outside organisations, and persuade officials to make arrangements that should ideally be part of a standard accessible examination system. “For me, the computer and screen reader made it possible to access examinations independently. But the institutional process surrounding the technology created many obstacles. Accessible examination systems should be implemented proactively rather than requiring students with disabilities to repeatedly request, justify, and negotiate for accommodations each time they have an examination,” he added.
(Rajlakshmi Ghosh is a journalist with over three decades of experience in media houses and educational institutions)

In a move mirroring European indie producers’ look out for strong partners in an unstable market, Helsinki-filmi (“Tom of Finland,“ “The Summer Book,” “Codename: Annika”), one of the biggest content creators in Finland, and Glassriver (“As Long as I Live,” Black Sands”), one of the leading players in Iceland, have come together to co-produce a slate of films and series.
Kickstarting the initial three-title partnership is the Finnish crime show “Tango Metal” (“Rautamurhat”), to be pitched on Thursday at the Helsinki Intl. Film Festival’s industry sidebar Finnish Film Affair.
Based on an idea by showrunner Mia Ylönen, Helsinki-filmi’s head of drama credited for SkyShowtime’s “Codename: Annika,” the six parter reunites Ylönen with writer Tua Harno (“North 66 Precinct,” “Guts”) and AFI, NFTS graduate Jojo Erholtz (“Detective Mario Kallio,” “Living With My Ex”), both attached as well to Helsinki-filmi’s upcoming series “Dead Women Talking.”
Popular on Variety
The story turns on Finnish crime reporter and tango enthusiast Paula (38), sent to Reykjavik to investigate the ritualistic murder of her estranged brother. In her search for the truth, Paula is joined by detective Bjarki Haraldsson (35), her polar opposite. While the Finn’s life is at a standstill following the accidental death of her husband, the sunny Bjarki is a father, crime detective by day and metal band frontman at night. The investigation draws them close to each other, until the killer comes after them.
“Basically, Paula has lost everything, while Bjarki has seemingly everything. I wanted to oppose these characters and see how their worlds collide,” said Ylönen, who used to cover Heavy Metal gigs as a journalist.
The producing partners are currently in advanced negotiations with commissioners in Finland and Iceland, with the show in development and scheduled to start production later this year.
Ylönen, who approached Glassriver with the project, said tangoing with them on this series and other scripted content “makes total sense.”“They have an impressive track record, especially in crime, thriller series such as ‘Black Sands,’ ‘Cold Haven,’ and are very active in international co-productions, which is where we’re venturing into for our series. Financing is in decline in Europe. We have to stand on our own feet and be clever with financing,” said the former TV news reporter turned writer, showrunner and executive producer.
Ylönen also pointed at shared mindsets between the two Nordic nations. “We both come from small nations; we have a dark sense of humor and rely on trust. This is something that has been evident since we started working on this project.”
Glassriver CEO, producer Andri Ómarsson, concurred with her. “In Iceland, we’re on the outskirts of the Nordics and Europe. Today, all countries realize that international partnerships are critical to get a project off the ground. It makes sense on a creative and business standpoint to collaborate with Finland,” said the seasoned TV executive, who also underscored broadcasters’ and streamers’ flexi mindsets and shift towards co-commissioning.
“We did ‘Cold Haven’ as a co-commissioning between Síminn [Iceland’s leading streamer] and RTP in Portugal. That was Síminn’s first co-commissioning on a high-end show, and they got really excited about it,” said Ómarsson.
Other upcoming projects to be co-produced by Helsinki-filmi and Glassriver include a Finnish near-sci-fi adventure feature, and an Icelandic TV project based on an original story, to be majority shot in Iceland. Details will be announced when key financing is locked.
Currently on Glassriver’s active slate are Síminn’s crime series “Elma,” based on Eva BjörgÆgisdóttir’s best-selling book series, set to premiere next month. The co-production with Belgium’s Lunamine is repped globally by Mediawan, with a pre-sale to Finland’s MTV in place.
Also on Síminn’s list and set for a spring 2027 premiere is the climate disaster series “Avalanche,” co-produced with Finland’s Whatevergroup, currently in post in Finland. The prolific Erholtz is attached as editor.
Meanwhile, soon to start lensing in Tenerife is the comedy drama “Hot Stuff,” ordered by Iceland’s Channel 2 and co-produced with Romania’s IDEA Film.
On Helsinki-filmi’s slate is the Yle crime series “Dead Women Talking,” backed by the Nordic 12 pubcasters alliance. “That’s our biggest international co-production since “Codename: Annika,” stated Ylönen about the series currently lensing, which will have a podcast spinoff.
Then on the feature film front, Helsinki-filmi’s “Tell Everyone” by Alli Haapasalo (audience prize winner at Sundance 2022 for “Girl Picture”) is due to open domestically Oct. 9. The film bagged last year’s Finnish Film Affair best project award.

If you are a patient looking to join a clinical trial, a clinician advising one, or a researcher trying to understand the trials that have been conducted for a particular medication, you may have encountered ClinicalTrials.gov. The website serves as a resource for clinicians and patients interested in trial participation as well as for researchers who want to understand the body of evidence for different conditions, assess signs of publication bias, and explore trial composition and representativeness. Since late 2007, federal law has required companies and researchers to register most Phase 2 to Phase 4 drug trials. Over 600,000 studies are listed on the site, which draws more than 3 million visitors each month and can be easily filtered based on patient age, sex, diagnosis, and ZIP code.
However, pregnant patients can’t easily identify studies for which they are eligible. ClinicalTrials.gov lacks structured data on whether pregnant or lactating people were included or can join a trial.
We believe the website should add a field to the participation eligibility criteria module that flags whether a study enrolls pregnant and/or lactating people and, if eligible, how many enrolled. This straightforward step would make trials easier to find and enable simple, accurate tracking of studies that enroll pregnant and lactating people.
Over the past decade, we have seen increasing concern about the lack of high quality medical evidence in pregnancy, particularly around drug safety. The shift began with efforts to reframe pregnant people from a “vulnerable” group requiring protections similar to children to a “scientifically complex” one, and bioethics work arguing why we should protect pregnant individuals “through” rather than “from” research. The issue entered the public consciousness through writers like Emily Oster and controversies around the exclusion of pregnant people from Covid-19 vaccine trials.
More recently, Trump administration officials have criticized the lack of drug safety evidence in pregnancy, particularly around the use of antidepressants and acetaminophen. Even as their scientific conclusions have been disputed, it remains striking that a politically diverse group of Americans agrees that more pregnancy studies are needed.
There are signs of progress, most notably ICH E21, a draft guideline from the International Council for Harmonisation, which would shift drug development from a presumption of excluding pregnant participants to a recommendation that sponsors plan early during drug development to collect data in pregnant and lactating people. The Food and Drug Administration released the draft for public comment in July 2025 alongside regulators in Europe, Japan, and other ICH regions, and final adoption is expected around early 2028.
Even amid these reasons for optimism, progress is not a foregone conclusion. ICH guidelines allow for expanded inclusion but don’t require it. Past calls for inclusion have led to minimal change. In prior work, one of us found that fewer than 1% of drug development clinical trials enroll pregnant patients, a statistic that didn’t budge over 15 years of data.
And obtaining that figure was unnecessarily difficult. We parsed data in ClinicalTrials.gov from 44,160 randomized drug trials open to women ages 18 to 45. To do this, we used large language models to read through the unstandardized fields, checked a sample against records we coded by hand, and called some of the study coordinators when the text didn’t say. About 76% addressed “pregnancy” in their inclusion or exclusion criteria reported as open text fields in the ClinicalTrials.gov database (0.8% explicitly permitted pregnant participants; 75% excluded them, e.g., through contraceptive requirements). The remaining 24% left pregnancy unspecified, which typically implied exclusion when we examined trial documents or called coordinators (who were uniformly very kind).
If we could calculate these numbers using LLMs, why bother adding additional required fields? Even with current technology, the data processing is laborious and error prone. And busy clinicians and sick patients who access the website are unlikely to be looking for a technical project.
Several expert panels have also emphasized the need for better data. The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine’s 2024 report “Advancing Clinical Research with Pregnant and Lactating Populations,” to which one of us contributed, noted that they could not use ClinicalTrials.gov to measure the extent of pregnant and lactating trial participation. And both that committee and the Task Force on Research Specific to Pregnant Women and Lactating Women, established by Congress in the 21st Century Cures Act, recommended improving data sharing and infrastructure, with the latter calling for a user friendly website for listing registries.
Adding these eligibility data to ClinicalTrials.gov would make it easier to find, fill, and track trials including pregnant and lactating patients. Clinicians and patients could more easily search for trials open to them. Researchers could study how enrollment evolves over time. And advocates and regulators could understand the impact of ICH E21 or other shifts in guidelines and regulations.
Improving ClinicalTrials.gov isn’t a panacea for the gaps in pregnancy data. It won’t address ethical and institutional review board concerns, resolve liability fears, or fund new research. But it’s a straightforward and inexpensive improvement at a time when better evidence for pregnant and lactating patients has rare bipartisan support.
ClinicalTrials.gov should add the fields.
Alyssa Bilinski is the Peterson family assistant professor of health services, policy, and practice and of biostatistics at the Brown University School of Public Health. Haley Sullivan is a faculty fellow at the Brown University School of Public Health. Anne C.C. Lee is the Levinger family professor of pediatrics at the Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University.

WHO and Switzerland have announced the renewal of their cooperation strategy for the period 2024-2028. Francesca Moody Productions has unveiled further casting for Tim Crouch’s “An Oak Tree,” adding Juliet Stevenson, Olivia Williams, Sean Gilder, Brian Gleeson, Sophie Melville, Rhashan Stone and Ria Zmitrowicz to the roster of guest artists appearing opposite Crouch during the show’s run at The Other Palace from Oct. 7-Nov. 15.
“An Oak Tree” hinges on one rule: a fresh guest artist steps in alongside Crouch at every performance, with no prior look at the script and no rehearsal. First staged in 2005, the play has now been performed in upward of 19 countries, drawing on a pool of guest artists that has grown past 350 names, among them Frances McDormand, Geoffrey Rush, Peter Dinklage, Mike Myers, David Tennant and Phoebe Waller-Bridge.
The newly confirmed dates are Olivia Williams on Oct. 10, Rhashan Stone on Oct. 11, Juliet Stevenson on Oct. 18, Sophie Melville on Oct. 25, Sean Gilder on Oct. 27, Brian Gleeson on Oct. 30 and Ria Zmitrowicz on Nov. 8.
Popular on Variety
They join a previously announced group performing over October and November that includes Rosalie Craig, Clare Perkins, Tom Mothersdale, Gemma Whelan, Bessie Carter, Sacha Dhawan, Hammed Animashaun and George Fouracres.
Stevenson, an Olivier and Critics’ Circle award winner, has recently starred in “King and Conqueror” and “Professor T.” Williams’ television credits include “Dune: Prophecy” and “The Crown.” Dhawan currently appears in “Doctor Who” and “The Great,” while Whelan is known for “Game of Thrones” and “The Tower.” Carter stars in Netflix’s “Bridgerton.”
“An Oak Tree” is directed by Crouch, Karl James and Andy Smith, with music by Pete Gill and piano by Simon Crane.
The production is part of a new Francesca Moody Productions season at The Other Palace that also includes “Garry Starr: Classic Penguins,” running Oct. 22 through Jan. 3, 2027, and “Feeling Afraid As If Something Terrible Is Going To Happen,” running Nov. 19 through Jan. 10, 2027. FMP also produces Hannah Reilly’s “Roleplay,” transferring to Soho Theatre from Oct. 22-Nov. 21, and presents Shedinburgh at the Young Vic’s Maria Studio through Oct. 10.
Francesca Moody, whose credits include “Fleabag” and “Baby Reindeer,” is the company’s executive producer.

An Australian man accused of murdering a Thai teenager and putting her body in a suitcase pleaded not guilty on Friday in a hearing in the seaside resort city of Pattaya, a court official said.
Simon Peter Carman, 45, was arrested in June after 17-year-old Tunchanok Donhomla was reported missing in Pattaya City, about 150km south-east of Bangkok. A suitcase containing her body was found shortly after.
Police said she died of suffocation.
Carman appeared on Friday at Pattaya provincial court, where he pleaded not guilty to all charges, a court spokesperson said.
He had been charged with murder, concealing a body and taking a minor for indecent purposes. The next court date was set for 12 October.
Police previously said CCTV footage showed him entering a condominium in Pattaya with the girl in the early hours of 25 June, and leaving that evening carrying a large black suitcase.
In a police interrogation video shared online by Thai media, Carman has said he was acting in self-defence because the girl was threatening him with a knife.
The case put the spotlight on Pattaya, which is popular with foreign tourists for its beaches and nightlife, but also has a reputation for sex tourism.

Senegal job an 'absolute dream' for new boss Vieira
- Published
Patrick Vieira says it is "an honour" to become Senegal head coach, with the decision to take the job "one from the heart".
The 50-year-old was born in the West African nation but subsequently represented France as a player, winning the 1998 World Cup and the 2000 European Championship with Les Bleus.
The former Arsenal midfielder spoke of his "immense pride" to begin his first international job, following stints with New York City, Nice, Crystal Palace, Strasbourg and Genoa, at his unveiling by the Teranga Lions on Friday.
"Being head coach of the Senegal national team is an absolute dream," he told a news conference in Dakar.
"I was born here, my parents were born here, and it really is a homecoming.
"From the very first meetings I had with the [Senegal football federation] president, I accepted this challenge straight away, because there was also an exceptional generation of players.
"I realise the expectations of the people - all 20 million Senegalese. And I know that with the experience I have, with the determination I have, I'll be able to see this project through."
- Vieira named new Senegal head coach 
  - Published18 August
Taking over after the dismissal of Pape Thiaw, Vieira inherits a Senegal side which exited the 2026 World Cup in dramatic fashion in the last 32, throwing away a 2-0 lead after 85 minutes against Belgium before losing 3-2 following extra time.
Before that the Teranga Lions claimed the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) title with a 1-0 extra-time win over Morocco in January.
However, the ultimate destination of the trophy will be decided by the Court of Arbitration for Sport after a walk-off by some Senegal players and staff protesting against a penalty decision in the final resulted in the trophy being handed to the North African hosts instead in March.
"Today, Senegal is among the major nations in world football," Vieira said.
"Senegal's objectives aren't what they were 10 or 15 years ago. On the back of its recent results, Senegal has moved forward, has reached new levels.
"The demand for results has also stepped up. We need to lay solid foundations."
Vieira plans to build a side with "a very precise structure" which can play with "intensity and aggression".
"What matters to me isn't starting again from scratch," he added.
"It's about respecting what the federation has put in place over the last few years and building the next stage, opening a new chapter.
"A new chapter meaning my job isn't to tear everything down, it isn't to throw everything out of the window.
"It's about keeping this team's strength: its identity, its unity, its ability to suffer together.
"To make this project work, I'll need the whole nation united. I'll work heart and soul to restore the team's pride."
Starting with two away trips
Vieira has been thrust straight into competitive action in qualifiers for the 2027 Afcon with two fixtures in this international window, two more in November and the final two rounds in March 2027.
His stint in charge was due to begin with a home match against Mozambique on Friday, 25 September but the fixture has been reversed as Dakar is in the midst of preparations for the 2026 Youth Olympic Games.
"Of course, I'd have preferred to play the first match here in Dakar but unfortunately, with the federation, we all felt the best decision was to postpone the match and go and play in Mozambique," Vieira explained.
"Those are difficulties we're going to accept and deal with."
Senegal will be without several notable names for the trip to Maputo and the subsequent away game against Ethiopia on 29 September.
Long-time number one Edouard Mendy, 34, has retired from Teranga Lions duty and Vieira said talismanic forward Sadio Mane will be absent with "a bit of a physical issue".
Despite previous speculation that Mane, also 34, could follow Mendy into retirement, Vieira said the former Liverpool and Bayern Munich man will "surely" be part of his next selection, fitness permitting.
Right-back Krepin Diatta has been left out because he is currently without a club, while forward Ismaila Sarr, who is yet to feature for Crystal Palace this season because of transfer speculation and a groin injury, is also absent.
'No doubt' about his managerial ability
Vieira's career as a player was trophy-laden but he has found the same kind of success hard to come by as a manager.
He departed Palace in March 2023 with a record of 22 wins from 74 games in all competitions and, after a season at Strasbourg, has been out of work since being sacked by Genoa in November last year with the Italian club bottom of the table.
He had guided them to safety in Serie A in the 2024-25 campaign but was then dismissed after six defeats in nine league games at the start of last season.
"When you talk about my coaching career, or a certain amount of experience, I've always been someone who stays positive," Vieira said.
"That means you learn, and there are always positive things to take from it. I'm a better coach today than I was in my last spell at Genoa, because that experience helped me grow and made me realise certain things.
"Given the experience I have as a manager, I've got no doubt about my ability to meet the expectations of fans."
Vieira was warmly received when he arrived in Dakar on Thursday evening, with video clips posted on social media showing him holding a Senegal flag aloft while shaking hands with a throng of fans gathered at the capital's airport.
"I couldn't have been given a warmer welcome. I saw the supporters' enthusiasm and I thank them for it.
"Taking charge of this national team isn't just a new stage in my career - it's coming back home."

Hong Kong animal groups call for tighter pet laws after suspected fatal mauling
Former guard dogs may turn aggressive due to territorial instincts or past trauma, welfare advocates warn as government pledges review of policies
Animal welfare groups in Hong Kong have called for closing a legal loophole in pet ownership laws to better protect public safety, as authorities pledged to review stray dog policies following Sunday’s suspected fatal mauling of a woman.
The groups suggested that, based on their experience, the 27-year-old victim was likely attacked by former warehouse guard dogs rather than strays.
But existing legal provisions make it difficult to prosecute owners who fail to microchip or properly secure their animals, they noted.
Police suspect a pack of dogs attacked the woman, who was found unconscious beside a bicycle in Yuen Long on Sunday and later died, less than a month after a similar canine-related case.

It always creates apprehension because the sight is somewhat gory, but a nosebleed, in general, isn’t a cause for major concern. Occurring mostly in the under 10s and the over 45s, nosebleeds are very common: about 60% of the population is estimated to experience one in their lifetime. They can occur in one or both nostrils, but usually affect one. The medical term for a nosebleed is epistaxis.
How do they occur?
Our noses are lined with a moist, delicate tissue, the nasal mucosa. This lining cleans the air that we breathe in, and also warms and moistens the air. The mucosa is made of many tiny blood vessels, lying to close to the surface. These blood vessels can easily be irritated, injured and broken. When they break, they cause a nosebleed.
There are two types of nosebleeds: anterior and posterior. An anterior nosebleed, which is the most common type, starts at the front of the nose. These types of nosebleeds can mostly be treated at home. A posterior nosebleed takes place place deep at the back the nose, may cause heavier bleeding and could result in blood going down the back of the throat. This type of nosebleed requires medical attention.
Why do they occur?
Common causes include the inside of the nose becoming dry, usually due to a change in temperature, picking the nose, or blowing the nose too hard.
When the air is very dry, it causes the nasal mucosa, which is meant to be moist, to dry out, making it prone to crusting and bleeding. Dry air can occur in hot places with low humidity, areas of high altitude and in air-conditioned or heated spaces. People with upper respiratory infections, sinus infections, allergies or other ailments such as rhinitis may also sneeze, cough or blow their nose frequently, making them more prone to bleeds. The frequent use of medications such as antihistamines, nasal sprays or blood thinners, could also make people vulnerable to nosebleeds, as could breathing in strong fumes.
Nosebleeds can also occur due to injuries to the nose, the insertion of objects into the nose, a deviated septum, recreational drug use as well as less common causes such as having blood disorders, alcohol use, nasal polyps or tumours.
Being pregnant may also increase the chances of nosebleeds.
When to see a doctor
In general, nosebleeds aren’t serious and can be treated at home. In some circumstances, however, it is best to consult a medical professional. You should see a doctor if: the nosebleed has followed an injury or accident; if there is heavy bleeding or the bleeding lasts longer than 30 minutes; blood has been swallowed; if there is a feeling of weakness, dizziness, lightheadedness or if you have breathing difficulties, chest pain or a rapid heart rate. A doctor should also be consulted if the person with the nosebleed has other health issues such as a bleeding disorder, or high blood pressure, or if the person is a child under two years old.
How to stop a nosebleed
To stop a nosebleed, there are some first-aid measures that can be taken:
- Sit upright so the head is above the level of the heart, lean forward slightly
- Breathe through the mouth and gently blow the nose to clear it
- Use the thumb and index finger to pinch the both nostrils shut. Do this for 10 minutes.
- Use an icepack on the bridge of the nose at the same time as the pinching
- Check in 10 minutes, and if the bleeding has not stopped, repeat the pinching for another 10 minutes
- Once the bleeding has stopped, lean forward and clean the nose with lukewarm water
- See a doctor immediately if the bleeding does not stop in 30 minutes
Preventing nosebleeds
Using a humidifier in the house especially in dry air conditions, trimming children’s fingernails, managing allergies, using a nasal saline spray or petroleum jelly to keep the inner lining of the nose moist and avoiding smoke exposure can all help prevent nosebleeds.

The Climate 100 List: Erin Brockovich on her fight against ‘secretive’ data centres
Erin Brockovich’s work in helping win a $333m environmental lawsuit in the 1990s spawned a hit film starring Julia Roberts – now, Brockovich tells David Callaway, her attention has turned to the burgeoning issue of data centres
It’s been more than 30 years since Erin Brockovich made history – and had a movie made after her – for standing against one of America’s largest power companies and winning a $333m groundwater pollution suit for a small California town. People still email her with environmental concerns.
This past spring she noticed a spike in emails from a small Pennsylvania county concerned about the sudden growth of a large AI data centre in their community. Data centres are giant warehouses full of powerful computers used to run digital services from movie streaming to online banking. There are more than 4,000 across the US, the most in the world. The UK and Germany are next with more than 500 each.
There are concerns about the huge amount of energy and water the new data centres will consume, as well as the wastewater they produce that is funnelled out back into the environment.
Following those emails, Brockovich – who is recognised on this year’s Independent Climate 100 list of changemakers and activists working to save the planet – quickly built out a digital map of data centres across the country and within 72 hours had received email complaints from every state in the US. That has now become a dozen countries.
“What they all have in common is the secrecy, the lack of transparency to people about what is going on,” Brockovich says. “People’s water bills are going up. Their electricity bills are going up. Even their property bills are going up. They are changing zoning laws. Some people say local councils are trying to claim their property by eminent domain to lay transmission wires and cables.”
The Brockovich Data Center Map currently shows more than 9,200 complaints, coming from all 50 states.
Texas has the most complaints, followed by Ohio and Virginia. The complaints are tied to 112 operating data centres, 143 under construction, and 128 under proposal at the last count. Out of a total of more than 4,000 data centres across the country.
Brockovich, 66, is now at the centre of one of the most rapidly developing environmental issues in America; one that even threatens to upend the country’s midterm elections for Congress in November. “It’s bipartisan. It affects everybody,” she said. “Politics is definitely going to be involved.”
After months of growing anger, many city councils are starting to get the message. More than 500 moratoriums on new data centres are now in place, one of them declared by New York state governor Kathy Hochul. Some of the city councils trying to pause projects are being hit with multimillion lawsuits from the tech companies, however, Brockovich says. That makes it even harder for them to stand up.
Brockovich adds she has nothing against AI, arguing that the "genie is out of the bottle" on the new technology. She acknowledges she even uses it to get information from the tech and AI companies who rarely comment on their intentions beyond their growth plans. But she says the speed with which companies are building these massive operations is something every community should be concerned about.
Many of the data centres are being built in drought-restricted areas, meaning the threat to water rights and access is even more acute. The construction comes as AI companies – from Open AI to Meta and Google and Elon Musk's SpaceX – are racing to develop the technology, as investors throw money at them on the stock market and the administration of Donald Trump pushes them to achieve dominance before China does.
"I don't understand what the sudden rush is," Brockovich says. "It's as if these companies believe there is some sort of window that is going to close."
The phenomenon has been compared to the dot-com boom a quarter century ago, with many worried that it will also lead to a spectacular bust at some point, if the technology, and profits, don't develop as expected. As the AI arms race continues, many of these tech giants have resorted to using natural gas to power their data centres instead of cleaner, renewable energy, because gas is cheaper and more accessible.
Brockovich says her goals are to get companies and local governments to take a step back and assess what the actual environmental impact of building data centres might lead to before going forward.
For many people, climate change and global warming have always been vague terms, she says, which is why they probably never resonated in national politics before. But the data centres are "bringing it to life" for everybody.
"The stakes are too high for all of us," Brockovich adds. "People are mad enough. Maybe data centres are what unites us after all."

The 2026 Urban Local Body elections were held recently in Rajasthan for 309 urban local bodies and 10,244 wards, with polling held on 09 and 11 September and counting on 14 September. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) won 4,182 wards, followed by the Congress with 3,619, while Independents secured 2,273 wards. The results also saw the BJP secure majorities in several municipal corporations, while Congress and Independent candidates won in some others (here, here).
In this context, a video is circulating on social media (here, here, and here), claiming it shows a BJP candidate crying after receiving just one vote in the Rajasthan civic elections. The post also alleges that even his own family members did not vote for him. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows a BJP candidate crying after receiving just one vote in the 2026 Rajasthan civic elections.
Fact: It is true that a BJP candidate named Kailash Chandra received one vote in the 2026 Rajasthan civic elections. However, the viral video is unrelated to this incident. The man seen in the video is Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) leader Shivchandra Ram, who was seen crying during a press conference in June 2026 after being denied an MLC ticket in Bihar. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several media reports (here, here, here, and here) published in June 2026 featuring the same video. According to these reports, the person seen crying during a press conference is RJD leader and former Bihar minister Shivchandra Ram, who broke down in tears after being denied an MLC ticket. RJD’s Sunil Singh had filed the nomination for the Grand Alliance for one of the 10 seats in the Bihar Legislative Council, which reportedly angered Ram. He alleged that the party had promised to make him an MLC but had betrayed him, following which he announced his resignation from all RJD posts, while clarifying that he had not left the party. This confirms that the viral video is unrelated to the 2026 Rajasthan civic elections.
To investigate the claim that a BJP candidate received only one vote in the 2026 Rajasthan civic elections, we conducted a Google keyword search and found multiple reports (here, here). According to these reports, BJP candidate Kailash Chandra received only one vote in Ward No. 13 of the Parbatsar Municipality in Rajasthan’s Deedwana-Kuchaman district. Congress candidate Hina Khanam received 376 votes, while Independent candidate Rasheed Khan received 195 votes. The reports also state that Kailash Chandra was a voter in Ward No. 12 but was fielded by the BJP from Ward No. 13, meaning he could not vote for himself.
We then checked the election results available on the official website of the Rajasthan State Election Commission. The results for the Parbatsar Municipality show that Kailash Chandra, the BJP candidate from Ward No. 13, received one vote.
To sum up, an unrelated video of a Bihar RJD leader crying is falsely linked to the BJP candidate who received one vote in the 2026 Rajasthan civic polls.

EXCLUSIVE: Here’s a trailer for Doula – A True Crime, a Canadian doc series from The Walrus and the Whistleblower filmmaker Nathalie Bibeau about a bizarre criminal case of a woman who faked pregnancies.
The three-parter, which will premiere on Canadian pubcaster CBC on October 7, looks into the story of Kaitlyn Braun, who aged 24, reached out to more than 40 doulas with the same shocking story: that she had been sexually assaulted and was in her third trimester carrying a stillborn child.
We can reveal Boat Rocker Studios has acquired the international distribution rights to the Muse Entertainment-produced show and will launch it at MIPCOM Cannes next month.
The doc is notable for including the first interview with Braun, who was hit with 53 criminal charges after doulas, who had helped her and provided pro bono services such as hours of phone and video calls and round-the-clock in-person care, began to question her narrative.
Watch on Deadline
After piecing together the pattern that had formed over nine months between June 2022 and February 2023, many found others like themselves and started a grassroots campaign for to alert authorities through a viral TikTok counter-offensive.
In the trailer, we hear from several doulas shaken by their experience. “I can’t tell you I was assaulted, that’s not really what happened and I can’t tell that I was scammed, that doesn’t encompass what she did to me. I have to tell you the whole story so you understand,” says one. “I have no felt fear like that in my entire life,” says another later in the trailer.
The one-minute clip ends with a camera making its way up a porch, where it is met by Braun, who smiles as she opens the door and says, “Hello!”
The film was made over several years, and attempts to go beyond the sensationalist reporting that followed the story at the time. Braun conversed with Bibeau several times over extensive interviews and phone calls, offering insight into her actions and motivations.
“Everyone knew that Kaitlyn Braun had committed crimes. I wanted to understand why,” said Bibeau, writer, director and producer of Doula: A True Crime. “The deeper I went, the less the story yielded to easy conclusions. Kaitlyn’s deception played on empathy, and the harm it caused was real.
“But the very thing that made the harm possible was also what I needed to understand her. I’m drawn to the places where human behaviour resists a clean moral frame. And this story lives in one of those places – where empathy doesn’t get in the way of truth, but brings us closer to it.”
Jonas Prupas, Managing Director of Unscripted and executive producer at Montreal-based Muse, said the story “could easily be reduced to its more sensationalist elements,” but that Bibeau had made it “into something nuanced, surprising and deeply human.”
Mellany Welsh, SVP and Global Head of Distribution & Brands at Boat Rocker Studios, added the doc offered international buyers “a story they won’t find anywhere else.”
Muse – known for the likes of Sullivan’s Crossing, The Kennedys and Nose Deep – made the show for CBC and CBC Gem, with the series premiering on October 7 at 8am ET on CBC. Prupas and Courtney Dobbins are exec producers for Muse, with Michelle McCree overseeing production for CBC.
A CBC and BBC podcast titled Kaitlyn’s Baby launched last year.

Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in India, prompting authorities to investigate if they were trafficked into the country from south-east Asia.
The orangutans, native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra and known for their shaggy red fur, were found in Balasore district of Odisha state, thousands of kilometres away from their natural habitat.
Odisha’s environment minister, Ram Singh Khuntia, said wildlife investigators were trying to establish how the rare apes reached India.
“We suspect that an international racket might be involved in this,” Singh said.
International commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under Cites – a global agreement governing trade in endangered wildlife.
The five babies were found by forest department officials who were patrolling in the Jaleswar range in Balasore district.
Officials believed the orangutans had been in the area for just a few days, and they have now been placed in quarantine at a zoological park in Odisha.
According to the World Wildlife Fund, about 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago.
The Tapanuli orangutan (Pongo tapanuliensis), a third species, is classified as critically endangered, with fewer than 800 believed to survive in the wild.
In November, conservationists found the Tapanuli population had been reduced by 7% after severe flooding in Indonesia.
Between 33 and 54 Tapanuli orangutans were estimated to have been killed in widespread floods and landslides in North Sumatra province.
Previous research has suggested annual losses of 1% of the Tapanuli orangutan population would be sufficient to lead to eventual extinction.
The entire Tapanuli population dwells solely in the West Block of the Batang Toru, a forest threatened by mining, palm oil plantations and a large hydropower project.

Info Edge Ventures backed NBFC Ascend Capital’s profitability improved significantly in the fiscal year FY26, growing 6.25X to ₹10 Cr from ₹1.6 Cr in FY25. As per ratings assigned by ICRA, the Jaipur-based EV-focused lender’s total income for the fiscal jumped about 131% to ₹50.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹21.8 Cr in FY25. Its total managed assets (AUM) also expanded 46% to ₹238.6 Cr from ₹163.7 Cr during the period. ICRA noted that the cumulative collection efficiency from Ascend’s securitised EV loan portfolio, comprising of three-wheeler EVs like e-autos, loaders and L5 vehicles, stood at 97.5% as on July 2026, while the 90+ days past due (dpd) delinquency stood at 1.3%. Its gross non-performing assets (GNPA) increased to 2.6% in FY26 from 1.7% in FY25 while capital-to-risk weighted assets ratio (CRAR moderated to 34.8% from 41% a year earlier, though it remained well above the regulatory capital requirement. Despite the healthy pool performance, ICRA highlighted that the NBFC poses risks such as limited operational history and geographical concentration. As of September 2025, Ascend Capital was present across 60 cities in five states and UTs, although its top three states made up for 87.5% of the portfolio. Its total borrower base stood at 18,975 at the time. Tapping The Growing EV Demand Founded in 2019 by Lokesh Chandra and Gaurav Maheshwari, Ascend Capital extends loans of up to ₹2-4 Lakh to consumers looking to buy EVs and batteries for e-rickshaw and L5 vehicles. Ascend originates EV loans through its NBFC and funds its lending book through a mix of institutional debt and securitisation, where pools of EV loans are packaged into securities and sold to investors, allowing the lender to recycle capital into fresh loans. To overcome underwriting and collection challenges related to EV financing, the NBFC has developed an internal benchmark for valuing batteries and maintains a data repository covering OEMs, distributors and drivers. It started disbursing loans against e-autos and e-loaders in January 2024. The NBFC’s PAT stood at just ₹0.1 Cr in FY24, while income stood at ₹13.7 Cr, highlighting a notable acceleration in its scale over the past two years. It also raised ₹50 Cr in equity funding from Info Edge Ventures and Asha Ventures in 2024. The investors own a 24.8% stake in the NBFC as of now. The development comes as a growing set of specialised lenders targets the financing gap in India’s EV ecosystem. A record 24.5 Lakh EVs were sold in India in FY26, up 25% YoY, with electric three-wheelers accounting for 8.31 Lakh units, or 34% of total EV sales, as per Vahan data. E3Ws also crossed a 60% share of India’s overall three-wheeler sales during the year.

Virat Kohli-backed D2C fashion brand WROGN’s net loss surged 17.1% to ₹88.4 Cr in FY26 from ₹75.5 Cr in FY25. The youth-focused fashion brand’s loss increased despite an uptick in its top line performance during the fiscal year. The startup, which is a portfolio brand of Aditya Birla Group’s TMRW, recorded a 9% uptick in its FY26 operating revenue to ₹243.9 Cr from ₹223.2 Cr recorded in FY25. Including other income of ₹10.2 Cr, the startup’s total income for the fiscal year stood at ₹254 Cr. In a statement, the startup said that FY26 EBITDA loss for the fiscal year improved 34% to ₹38 Cr from ₹54 Cr, delivering an 8.5-point margin gain. It claimed to have opened FY27 on a strong note. It is targeting ₹600 Cr gross merchandise value (GMV) in the ongoing fiscal year after recording a 40% YoY uptick in Q1 GMV to ₹125 Cr. WROGN said its owned channels – D2C sales and exclusive brand outlets (EBOs) – grew 120% YoY in the June quarter. These channels will be a key focus for WROGN in FY27 as the brand is targeting 100+ EBOs by March 2027 to “strengthen owned-channel economics and customer experience”. It attributed this growth to a revamp of its store identity and operations as well as its sourcing and supply chain. “While denim and shirts remain strong anchor categories, WROGN has also expanded into new categories built on robust R&D, design, and sourcing capability – with WROGN Active and Footwear (₹60 Cr ARR) already seeing strong consumer traction and scaling up rapidly,” it said. Founded in 2014 by siblings Anjana and Vikram Reddy, WROGN is a men’s fashion brand which sells a wide range of casual wear, footwear and accessories. It sells the products via its own website, ecommerce platforms like Myntra, Flipkart, and Meesho, as well as the aforementioned offline channel. While cricketer Virat Kohli is cited as a key co-creator and stakeholder of WROGN, ABFRL, via its roll-up arm TMRW, invested ₹125 Cr in WROGN to acquire a 16% stake in the brand. TMRW later doubled down on the brand with further investment, taking its total stake in WROGN to 32.84%. Besides, VC firm Accel is also an early backer of the startup. Where Did WROGN Spend? WROGN’s total expenses for FY26 rose in proportion with its revenue, growing around 9.5% to ₹342.4 Cr from ₹312.6 Cr in the year-ago period. Here’s where the brand spent the most: Purchase Of Stock-In-Trade: Stock purchases increased 14.4% YoY to ₹141.2 Cr from ₹123.4 Cr in FY25, comprising its biggest expense. Changes In Inventories Of Stock-In-Trade: As this line item featured a negative amount, the brand earned ₹21.4 Cr due to inventory accumulation during the year under review, as compared to spending ₹2.3 Cr in FY25. Employee Benefits Expense: Employee related costs grew 13.6% YoY to ₹44.2 Cr from ₹38.9 Cr in the prior year. Finance Costs: Spending under this line item climbed 36.1% YoY to ₹16.8 Cr from ₹12.4 Cr in FY25. Depreciation And Amortisation Expense: Depreciation expenses surged 73.8% YoY to ₹14.5 Cr from ₹8.3 Cr in the year-ago period. Other Expenses: The company’s other expenses accounted for a significant portion of its total spending, rising 15.5% YoY to ₹147.2 Cr from ₹127.4 Cr in the previous fiscal year.

15 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న ఉత్తర అరేబియా సముద్రంలో భారత్, పాకిస్తాన్ నావికాదళాలకు చెందిన యుద్ధనౌకలు ఒకదానికొకటి ఢీకొన్నాయి. తమ నౌక సాధారణ నిఘా విధుల్లో ఉండగా పాకిస్తాన్ నౌక వేగంగా, ప్రమాదకరంగా దూసుకొచ్చిందని భారత్ పేర్కొంది. దీనిపై నిరసన తెలుపుతూ సెప్టెంబర్ 16న పాకిస్తాన్ దౌత్యాధికారికి భారత్ సమన్లు జారీ చేసింది. అయితే, పాకిస్తాన్ మాత్రం ఇందుకు భిన్నమైన వాదన వినిపించింది. తమ ‘SEASPARK-26’ నావికా విన్యాసాల్లో ఈ ఘటన జరిగిందని, భారత నౌక ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా తమ నౌక సమీపంలోకి వచ్చిందని ఆరోపించింది.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, భారత, పాకిస్తాన్ యుద్ధనౌకలు ఢీకొన్న దృశ్యాలంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: 15 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న భారత్, పాకిస్తాన్ యుద్ధనౌకలు ఒకదానికొకటి ఢీకొన్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో 15 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న భారత్, పాకిస్తాన్ యుద్ధనౌకలు ఢీకొన్న ఘటనకు సంబంధించినది కాదు. వాణిజ్య నౌక ‘ఎంవీ సూయజ్’కు భద్రతగా వెళ్తున్న సమయంలో 2011లో పాకిస్థాన్ నౌక పీఎన్ఎస్ బాబర్, భారత నౌక ఐఎన్ఎస్ గోదావరిని ఢీకొన్న పాత సంఘటనకు సంబంధించిన వీడియో ఇది. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియోని 16 అక్టోబర్ 2014న “mix” అనే యూట్యూబ్ ఛానెల్లో అప్లోడ్ (ఆర్కైవ్) చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియోలో పాకిస్తాన్ నౌక బాబర్ భారత నౌకతో పోటీ పడుతుందని పేర్కొనబడింది. ఏడెన్ అఖాతంలో (Gulf of Aden) ‘ఎంవీ సూయజ్’ అనే వాణిజ్య నౌకను రక్షించే సమయంలో తీసిన భారత, పాకిస్తాన్ నౌకల దృశ్యాలను ఈ వీడియో చూపుతుందని వివరణలో రాసి ఉంది. దీన్ని బట్టి, వైరల్ వీడియో సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నాటి ఘటనకు సంబంధించినది కాదని, అది దశాబ్దానికి పైగా పాతదని స్పష్టమవుతుంది.
దీనికి సంబంధించిన మరింత సమాచారం కోసం ఇంటర్నెట్లో వెతకగా, ఇదే ఘటన గురించి చెప్తున్నా 2011 నాటి NDTV వార్తా కథనం లభించింది. ఈ కథనం ప్రకారం, ఈ ఘటన 16 జూన్ 2011న జరిగింది. వాణిజ్య నౌక ‘ఎంవీ సూయజ్’కు భద్రతగా వెళ్తున్న సమయంలో, భారత నావికాదళానికి చెందిన ‘ఐఎన్ఎస్ గోదావరి’ నౌకను దాటి వెళ్లే ప్రయత్నంలో పాకిస్తాన్ యుద్ధనౌక ‘పీఎన్ఎస్ బాబర్’ దాని వెనుక భాగాన్ని ఢీకొట్టింది. సముద్రం అల్లకల్లోలంగా ఉన్న సమయంలో ఐఎన్ఎస్ గోదావరికి అతి సమీపంలోకి వచ్చిన పీఎన్ఎస్ బాబర్ రాసుకుంటూ వెళ్లిందని, దీనివల్ల భారత నౌకలోని హెలికాప్టర్ డెక్కు నష్టం వాటిల్లిందని ఆ కథనం పేర్కొంది. నౌకలు ఢీకొన్న తర్వాత పాకిస్తాన్ నౌక సిబ్బంది సంబరాలు చేసుకుంటున్న దృశ్యాలను కూడా ఆ కథనం చూపించింది.
18 జూన్ 2011న భారత విదేశీ వ్యవహారాల మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ ఒక పత్రికా ప్రకటన విడుదల చేసి పాకిస్తాన్ తీరుపై నిరసన వ్యక్తం చేసింది. పీఎన్ఎస్ బాబర్ చేసిన ప్రమాదకరమైన విన్యాసాలు ఐఎన్ఎస్ గోదావరి నౌక, దాని సిబ్బంది భద్రతను ప్రమాదంలో పడేశాయని అందులో పేర్కొంది. అంతేకాకుండా, పాకిస్తాన్ చర్యలు అంతర్జాతీయ సముద్ర భద్రతా నిబంధనలను, అలాగే సైనిక విన్యాసాలకు ముందస్తు సమాచారం ఇవ్వాలనే 1991 నాటి ఇండో-పాక్ ఒప్పందాన్ని ఉల్లంఘించాయని భారత్ స్పష్టం చేసింది.

Apple is preparing to open a new “state-of-the-art” live music venue in the UK, a 600-capacity space for hosting performances, recording sessions, and video broadcasts. The venue, called Apple Music Hall, is located underneath Apple’s European headquarters in London’s iconic Battersea Power Station, and is set to open next week on September 28th. Details about the opening show have yet to be announced.
Apple’s first live music venue is opening beneath its UK headquarters
Apple Music Hall is a new performance and recording space located in London’s Battersea Power Station.
“Apple’s deep love for music dates all the way back to the very beginning, from the launch of the iPod to the long-running iTunes Music Festival to the debut of Apple Music,” said Oliver Schusser, Apple’s vice president of Apple Music and International Content. “Today, with the opening of Apple Music Hall, we are once again taking an unprecedented step further in our commitment to artists and fans by supporting live music in ways only Apple can do.”
The limited capacity and layout is “designed intentionally to close the gap between intimacy and production value,” according to Apple’s announcement, with seating that feels close to the performer while providing artists with a 38-foot-wide stage that can be reconfigured to their needs. Apple Music Hall has a 48-speaker spatial sound system positioned around the audience, is hardwired for 16 or more broadcast cameras, and includes two dedicated recording and mixing studios behind the stage that allow it to operate as a full production facility.
The performance space is opening alongside new Apple Music radio studios in Battersea, with Apple announcing that all of its London-based hosts and shows will now broadcast from the facility. “We’re always looking for new opportunities to connect the artists and the fans because we are fans,” said Apple Music’s global creative director, Zane Lowe. “Great music and memories will be made at Apple Music Hall.”
Apple Music Hall marks the company’s return to London’s music scene, having previously run the iTunes Music Festival in England’s capital city for a decade — hosting acts like One Direction, Lady Gaga, Elton John, and Adele at intimate local venues — before its cancellation in 2017. Battersea Power Station, a decommissioned Art Deco facility that reopened in 2022, also has its own roots in music history, having appeared on the cover of Pink Floyd’s Animals album.

Mahanadi water dispute likely to be resolved soon: Chhattisgarh CM
The dispute over sharing of Mahanadi waters has continued for more than a decade, with Odisha objecting to the construction of barrages by Chhattisgarh
The long-standing Mahanadi water-sharing dispute between Chhattisgarh and Odisha is likely to be resolved soon through discussions and technical consultations between the two states, Chhattisgarh chief minister Vishnu Deo Sai said on Monday.
Speaking to reporters at Swami Vivekananda Airport after returning from a two-day visit to Odisha, Sai said he discussed the issue with Odisha CM Mohan Charan Majhi and stressed that there was no scope for conflict between the two states over the river water.
“The Mahanadi water issue is going to be resolved very soon. Both states have BJP [Bharatiya Janata Party] governments and there is an NDA government at the Centre. There is no situation of dispute anywhere,” Sai said.
He said the matter, which was earlier being heard by the Mahanadi Water Disputes Tribunal, has now been referred to the Central Water Commission (CWC).
The dispute over sharing of Mahanadi waters has continued for more than a decade, with Odisha objecting to the construction of barrages by Chhattisgarh in the upstream areas. Odisha has maintained that these structures affect the flow of water into the downstream areas, particularly during the lean season.
Odisha approached the Union water resources ministry in 2016, raising objections to the construction of six barrages in Chhattisgarh for industrial purposes and alleging reduced downstream flow during the non-monsoon period.
Following a suit filed by Odisha in the Supreme Court, the Mahanadi Water Disputes Tribunal was constituted in 2018 to adjudicate the dispute.
The issue gained renewed attention in recent months, with both states signalling their willingness to find an amicable solution through dialogue and technical consultations.
On July 30, the Centre facilitated a meeting between Sai and Majhi, chaired by Union Jal Shakti minister CR Patil, as part of efforts to find a mutually acceptable solution to the dispute.
The Mahanadi is considered the lifeline of Chhattisgarh, with around 78% of the state’s population living in its basin. The state is also part of the basins of five major rivers — Mahanadi, Godavari, Ganga, Brahmani and Narmada.

Texas mom arrested for giving away her baby to a stranger at a bus stop, cops say
The teen mom left her newborn with the stranger in San Antonio and fled in an Uber
An 18-year-old Texas mom has been arrested after giving away her one-month-old baby to a stranger she met at a bus stop, police said.
Karla Ibarra was carrying her infant at a bus stop in downtown San Antonio September 13 when she approached Jennifer Benavides and asked to use her cellphone, KSAT reported.
Benavides was fawning over Ibarra’s baby when the teen handed him over — along with all his federal ID documents — and asked if she wanted to take him.
“She’s like, ‘Well, do you want him? I’m going to give him away. I’m going to give him to somebody,” Benavides recalled.
“She begins handing me his birth certificate, his Medicaid, his Social Security card,” she said.
Realizing Ibarra was being serious about giving her baby away, Benavides brought her to the home of a friend who lived nearby — but the teen mom quickly left the house in an Uber without her son.
Benavides called 911 and she and her friend cared for the baby while they waited for police to arrive.
Ibarra later returned to the home, where she was arrested. The teen mom is charged with abandoning and endangering a child with intent to return.
“It’s upsetting to know that, with even all the resources that we have out there, that somebody would just do this,” Benavides said.
Following Ibarra’s arrest, her child was placed with other relatives, Child Protective Services confirmed.
Texas has the Baby Moses Law, which allows a parent to legally and anonymously surrender their newborn at designated locations without facing any criminal penalties.
The infant must be 60 days old or younger to be left at locations, which include fire stations and hospitals. The baby must be physically handed to an employee or placed in a Safe Baby Box.
The Independent has contacted the San Antonio Police Department for more information.
A judge set Ibarra’s bail at $7,000.

An Islamic State group member was sentenced on Wednesday to 20 years in prison for aiding the terrorist organization that took credit for a suicide bombing that killed 13 US service members and about 160 Afghans at the Kabul airport five years ago during the US military’s chaotic withdrawal from the country.
A federal jury in Virginia had convicted Mohammad Sharifullah in April of providing material support to the IS affiliate known as Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP). But jurors could not agree whether he bore some responsibility for the airport bombing on 26 August 2021.
US troops were conducting an evacuation operation at the airport when a suicide bomber detonated an improvised explosive device near an entry point known as Abbey Gate. Sharifullah’s role in the attack was scouting a route to Hamid Karzai international airport, prosecutors said.
Sharifullah, 28, received the maximum sentence for his one-count conviction in an international terrorism case that Donald Trump heralded last year during a speech to a joint session of Congress.
Sharifullah did not testify at his trial and declined to address the court before the US district judge Anthony Trenga imposed the sentence. The judge said the defendant was a “dedicated terrorist” who expressed no remorse for the “unfathomable” grief and suffering that he had caused.
Trenga heard victim impact statements from several parents of US service members. From a podium only a few feet from where Sharifullah sat, they took turns paying tribute to their children’s sacrifices and describing how the attack has shattered their families.
Mark Schmitz of Missouri asked Sharifullah to turn and look at him as he spoke about the life and death of his 20-year-old son, Marine Corps L/Cpl Jared Schmitz.
“They may have taken his life, but they’ll never take his legacy,” Mark Schmitz said. “A bomb killed my son. It did not kill what he stood for.”
Paula Knauss-Selph, whose son, army SSgt Ryan Knauss, was killed in the Abbey Gate bombing, said the family was “forever changed” by the attack.
“No justice will ever be enough to mend my broken heart,” she said.
Sharifullah requested a 17-year prison sentence, while prosecutors sought 20 years. His lawyers said he was never an ISKP leader and had not been convicted of any conduct related to the airport suicide bombing.
“He was brought here because the government believed he participated in the Abbey Gate attack, a theory which it was unable to prove at trial,” defense attorneys wrote.
Prosecutors said in their sentencing memo that “from his teenage years, when he pledged an oath of allegiance to [ISKP], Sharifullah’s carnage was driven by hate. Hate towards Americans.”
Jurors convicted Sharifullah of providing material support to ISKP. They deadlocked on whether any deaths at the airport “resulted from” that conspiracy. Sharifullah could have faced a possible life sentence if the jury had unanimously decided that question.
According to prosecutors, Sharifullah told a journalist that he wanted to “catch and kill the crusaders” from the United States for invading his country after the attacks of September 11. They said Sharifullah was involved in dozens of other attacks, including a March 2024 assault on a Moscow concert hall that killed roughly 140 people.
Defense lawyers argued that prosecutors failed to present any evidence tying Sharifullah to the Kabul bombing besides his own words during hours of FBI questioning. His team said Sharifullah told FBI agents what he thought they wanted to hear, possibly because he was afraid of being tortured in Pakistani custody before he was brought to the US.
A review by US Central Command found that the Abbey Gate bomber was Abdul Rahman al-Logari, an IS member who had been released from an Afghan prison by the Taliban. According to an FBI affidavit, Sharifullah recognized the alleged bomber as an operative he had known while incarcerated.

Officials are investigating the death of Presley Gerber, the son of supermodel Cindy Crawford, as a suspected overdose, Santa Monica police said on Monday.
The 27-year-old model died at a rehab facility on Sunday, according to Los Angeles County Medical Examiner records. The exact cause of death has not been determined, police said, adding there was no indication of foul play.
Allie Jenkins, a representative for Crawford and her husband Rande Gerber, told the BBC's US partner CBS News: "The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time."
Gerber had been a model like his mother and younger sister Kaia, making his catwalk debut for Italian label Moschino aged just 16.
He went on to model for brands including Burberry, Dolce & Gabbana, and Bottega Veneta.
His father Rande Gerber, a well-known businessman, co-founded the Casamigos tequila brand with George Clooney.
In recent years, Presley Gerber had spoken openly about his mental health challenges and drug use.
In 2023, he told the Studio 22 podcast: "Having struggled with mental health, depression and some other things that come along with that, I think that whether I help one person or a hundred people get out of that place that I was in at one point in my life, that's all I need to do."
And in this month's American Vogue, external, Kaia discussed her brother's struggles with addiction. She said: "When something like that happens in a family, it kind of levels everyone.
"I think that's also why I started to self-identify as the easy one and never wanted to ask for help."
She added: "My parents for most of our lives were very, very private and didn't share anything - and now we have this absolute teacher, my brother, who says, 'I'm gonna be very human for everyone.' There's only so much you can hide from the world. And trying to put a lid on something just makes the person feel like you're ashamed of them."
Gerber had previously spoken of his close relationship with his family, including Kaia, who he appeared alongside in a campaign for Calvin Klein in 2018, and whose name he had tattooed on his arm.
He told People Magazine that year: "We're a close family, especially me and my sister, so it's definitely cool.
"We get to travel together half of the time, so it makes it a lot less lonely."
Gerber also starred alongside his mother in Pepsi's 2018 Super Bowl commercial, 26 years after Crawford first appeared in her famous 1992 advertisement for the brand.
"We're a really tight family, so it was just like going to work with one of your friends. It was so fun, and easy," he told People Magazine at the time.
In July, Crawford shared two childhood photographs of her son on Instagram to mark his 27th birthday.
"I'm so proud of the man you've become, but I'll always see you as my little boy! Love you," she wrote.

An orange alert issued by the India Meteorological Department (IMD), Amaravati, has brought renewed hope of good rainfall across north coastal Andhra Pradesh. Several places from Srikakulam to Anakapalli have received steady showers since Monday (September 21, 2026) evening.
The well-marked low-pressure area over the Bay of Bengal has intensified into a depression and is expected to strengthen further on its way towards the north Andhra Pradesh-south Odisha coast.
The IMD expects the system to continue moving west-northwestwards and reach close to the coast by Wednesday (September 23, 2026) morning. It has forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall at isolated places on Tuesday and Wednesday, and thunderstorms with lightning at isolated places over Coastal Andhra Pradesh and Yanam and over Rayalaseema. Winds of 40 to 60 kmph are likely at isolated places in both regions.
Visakhapatnam has had steady rain since Monday evening, a relief to residents after several days of hot weather. The rain has also raised hopes of better water levels in reservoirs and of recharge for groundwater sources, which have depleted during the city’s water crisis.
Several areas recorded good rainfall on Tuesday (September 22, 2026) morning, according to rainfall data on government websites: Madhurawada, Gambhiram, Sheela Nagar, Pendurthi, Butchirajupalem (NAD Junction), Padmanabham, Akkireddipalem, Maharanipeta, Kapuluppada and Seethammadhara were among them.
The rain disrupted the morning commute, and motorists struggled to reach offices through waterlogging and slippery roads. Schoolchildren went to school under colourful umbrellas and in raincoats, a bright touch on a gloomy morning. The showers also brought the city’s pothole-ridden roads into focus.
Districts on alert
The Vizianagaram district administration has set up a control room (08922-236947) in the Collector’s office to monitor relief measures during the rain. Collector S. Ramsundar Reddy, Joint Collector S. Sedhu Madhavan and other senior officials directed all district and mandal officials to be vigilant for the next three days.
Srikakulam District Collector Swapnil Dinakar Pundkar reviewed the preparedness of officials in his district, which has a 190-km coastline from Pydibhimavaram to Ichchapuram on the State’s northern border and is expected to receive more rain. On Tuesday night, he visited several low-lying areas of Srikakulam town, including the APSRTC complex, which is inundated every rainy season, and directed the municipal authorities to clear the drains.
“We directed all revenue and irrigation officials to have coordination in all mandals and provide information to the district administration over the situation in their respective areas. The people living in low lying areas will be shifted to safe places if needed,” Mr. Pundkar told The Hindu.
Rivers such as the Nagavali and the Vamsadhara are likely to receive large inflows from rain in their catchment areas between Andhra Pradesh and Odisha. The rain would be welcome in the north Andhra districts, which have a rainfall deficit of about 50% this kharif season.
