Because you are over the age of 12.

Mira Murati was trying to speak. Women swished around in evening gowns, men in tuxes. Giant piles of carved meat rested like sleeping babies on banquet tables draped in linens as red as a handmaid’s robe. Bartenders served up a cocktail named Zero to One, a nod to the philosophy of Peter Thiel.
It was a recent Saturday night in a converted church in San Francisco, and the Foundation for American Innovation, a center-right think tank, was hosting a black-tie affair to hype the new religion of AI.
Murati, the founder and CEO of Thinking Machines Lab, was talking about the history of revolutions to a crowd of more than 350 people. The Albanian-born executive had for several years kept a relatively low profile as a VP and then CTO of OpenAI before participating in an unsuccessful coup against Sam Altman and then launching her own $12 billion AI startup. Now, with chatter bouncing off the church walls, Murati’s efforts to get her points across were about as successful as that coup: No one seemed to be listening. The woman interviewing Murati asked more than once for people to stop talking or take their conversations outside.
I whispered to the friend sitting next to me that this was the second time in a week that I’d seen a woman getting drowned out. She sighed. Both of us were there to actually hear what Murati had to say. I tried to restrain myself from what I said next, but I sensed my friend was holding back too. “Her hair is amazing, though,” I hissed. “Oh my God, I know,” she replied immediately. Murati’s hair has achieved AGI. Her jaw cuts glass.
Soon after, President Donald Trump’s top science adviser, Michael Kratsios, took the stage. The crowd quieted down. We are all part of the problem.
Over the past three months, I’ve been asking anyone and everyone about the most powerful women in Silicon Valley, a club to which Murati clearly belongs. Ask who the most powerful man in tech is and many quickly say “Elon.” Or “Jensen.” Or “Sam.” Wait a beat and you might hear the name of a billionaire VC whose financial capital has been broadly and ruthlessly deployed to advance an agenda, like “Peter” or “Marc.” Ask who the most powerful woman is, and most people respond with a thoughtful pause. A thinking-face emoji. “Gwynne?” “Lisa?” “Daniela, maybe?”
An astute observer of the Valley might posit that the most powerful woman has to jet-set between SV and DC, like Ruth Porat, the president and chief investment officer of Google, or Dina Powell McCormick, Meta’s president and vice chair. WIRED’s top editor—a woman—said at one point, “Isn’t it obviously Gwynne Shotwell?” Then a Silicon Valley CEO told me that whenever she mentions the SpaceX president and chief operating officer, her friends say “Gwynne who?”
Some people seemed allergic to my question. They don’t view tech as gendered, they told me, or didn’t have much to say. Who cares? Just put your head down and do the work.
Still, the question provoked reactions. My conversations—which took place on the phone and Zoom, in boardrooms, in San Francisco coffee shops, in a Palo Alto home where my source dozed off on the couch—produced a wealth of options, ranging from founders and CEOs to venture capitalists and philanthropic ex-wives. Some of those women, both CEOs and those who call bullshit on CEOs, spoke to me at length.
I realized that the real question is not who is most powerful, but why this question is still, in 2026, so difficult to answer. What’s missing from their lives or résumés? Why is there no woman Elon? Why don’t we have our own all-powerful heroine or supervillainess?
In June, a friend and former Slack executive suggested to me that power in Silicon Valley contains multitudes of capital—financial, intellectual, political, and social or cultural.
We agreed that the mononymous men score high in all categories. Their influence has been stunning, alarming even, in its contagion. They write blog posts that are referenced for decades. They dox people with a single post on X. They sway elections. They deliver sermons. They are asked to sign a woman’s breasts at a trade show in Taiwan, like some ’80s hair-metal frontman. They suggest that a young woman trying to save the planet is the antichrist.
Does any woman in tech come close to achieving this cult of personality, to spreading the seeds of their capital in this way? There is no “Time to Build” manifesto that the women of the Valley are rallying around. The last time women in tech had a manifesto, things didn’t go as planned.
On a recent drive to Lake Tahoe, I downloaded the audiobook of Sheryl Sandberg’s Lean In. I’d read the book when it came out in 2013, and I wanted to see how its ideas had aged. By the third chapter I had heard enough.
My brief listen reminded me, though, of why the book had been influential for nearly a decade. Sandberg, who clocked 14 years as chief operating officer of Meta, put words to a lot of bad workplace patterns. Women were treated as second-class at the office. We were prone to self-doubt and backed away from opportunities that seemed incompatible with family life. And for God’s sake, we should be paid as much as men.
But Sandberg’s book suffered from too many unrelatable anecdotes and simplistic solutions. It largely put the onus on women to sit closer, speak louder, marry better. Perhaps most crucially, what began as a guidebook for a select group—relatively privileged women clawing their way up the corporate ladder—was marketed as the answer to a whole host of women’s issues. Start a “Lean in Circle.” Create a hashtag, like #BanBossy. Run for office. Small actions can, of course, catalyze movements, but in a post-pandemic world, legions of frustrated working women opted to lean out instead.
Aileen Lee, a prominent VC who often hosts private gatherings of women in the industry, said she “appreciates” what Lean In brought to the foreground. It presaged a series of events that led Silicon Valley to examine its bro-topia. There was the Ellen Pao trial in 2015, in which Pao alleged gender discrimination and retaliation by her former firm, Kleiner Perkins. (A superior court jury eventually ruled in favor of the firm.) Then came Susan Fowler’s revelatory 2017 blog post about the way she was treated while working at Uber. And, later that year, reports emerged that a male VC had made unwanted sexual advances toward half a dozen women he interacted with while doing business.
Tech firms responded by hiring investigators and crisis comms squads and suddenly found high-profile roles for the women in their ranks. But “the 2010s was the era of lip service,” says Timnit Gebru. “‘Look at how many women we have on our team!’ And if there was one woman on the team, that woman got advertised to death.”
She would know. In 2018, Google hired the Ethiopian-born Gebru to colead a project on ethical AI. Gebru did what she was hired to do: She called out biases in AI via a now-infamous research paper that Google said didn’t meet its standards. Her subsequent termination caused a firestorm. Now she heads a group called Distributed Artificial Intelligence Research that investigates some of the harms caused by tech giants and AI.
Gebru noted that the 2010s weren’t all a wash. Women were forming networks behind the scenes. Ifeoma Ozoma, who left her job at Pinterest due to pay disparities and racial discrimination, successfully cosponsored California’s Silenced No More Act, which protects employees who speak out about workplace discrimination.
But then came the backlash to the backlash. Some men had been itching to declare their sacred workplaces free of distracting social politics. When Elon Musk bought Twitter in 2022, the app morphed into a platform where men in tech were more emboldened to share their rightward beliefs, while Musk himself became even more of a “hardcore” icon. Once Trump was reelected in November 2024, all bets were off.
“The industry focused so much on the topic of ‘women in tech’ for a few years that it backfired along with a broader backfiring against DEI,” said one founder, speaking anonymously. She observed that it’s not only men who avoid discussing identity and gender. “Women don’t want to talk about it, either,” she said.
Fortunately, I managed to find exceptions to that rule. Which is how I ended up on the front stoop of a home in Palo Alto, ringing the doorbell for 18 minutes, wondering if I was at the right place. A yellow wooden W on the stoop indicated that I was. Then Anne Wojcicki, in athletic shorts and a tank top, rolled up to the house on one of those bizarro outdoor elliptical bikes and waved at me.
“Is my mom not home?” she asked.
This was where Anne and her two sisters grew up; where a young Ruth Porat came over to swim in their backyard pool. The Wojcicki matriarch, Esther, was a well-known journalism teacher at the local high school. She later wrote a book about raising her immensely successful daughters: Anne, the founder and CEO of 23andMe; Janet, an epidemiologist; and Susan, who was the CEO of YouTube before passing away two years ago from lung cancer.
Anne welcomed me in, offered me a glass of water, and kicked off her shoes, revealing mismatched fluorescent socks. Then she plopped down on the floor of the living room. I followed suit.
Esther arrived soon after and took a regal seat on the couch. I asked them both if anything had gotten better for women in the Valley over the past 15 years.
“I do think it has improved,” Esther said. “Men don’t shake their heads and say ‘My God, what a ridiculous idea’ if a woman heads up a company. But there’s still hesitancy.”
She continued, “I remember all of the battles that my poor daughter Susan went through when she moved from Google to the head of YouTube.”
Anne spoke up. “Look, Susan took over YouTube, and she was very comfortable with herself. She had a strong vision, and she was a tough negotiator. You’re always going to have different groups that make your life difficult. Susan was really good at just powering through … Whenever I would complain about something, Susan would tell me, ‘Just ignore them and move on.’”
Anne may have had her sister’s mantra in mind when she hit a recent road bump. In 2025, her genetic testing startup, 23andMe, went bankrupt, and Anne stepped down as CEO. Customers deleted their accounts, concerned that their genetic data would end up in a new owner’s hands (23andMe had experienced a major data breach before). But she managed to buy the company back, a power move if there ever was one. It’s now controlled by a nonprofit public benefit corporation that Anne runs.
Many of her earlier investors declined to support her, Anne said. Someone like Adam Neumann can whittle his commercial real estate company down to a fraction of its peak value and still raise hundreds of millions for his next act.
But there’s more to power than money, Esther said firmly. You need cultural capital. “You have to be on X. You have to be out there,” Esther said. “If you can’t get a word in …”
Anne disagreed, calling X a distraction. She does post on Instagram; lately, her Stories have centered on lung cancer research, in honor of her sister. But she dismisses X as “male-dominated.”
“Do you have to be out there creating a lot of noise versus just using social media to show a little bit of what you do?” Anne said. “Gwynne Shotwell is powerful because she’s the leader of this incredible company, but a lot of people don’t know who she is. She’s not always out there on the conference circuit. She’s heads down, executing.”
Some of what Anne said struck me as true. Over twenty-plus years Shotwell grew SpaceX into an $800 billion business prior to its IPO this year. To the public she’s elusive, but not to the world’s power brokers: She zips around the globe to try to obtain regulatory approval for her technology. On SpaceX’s first earnings call in August, she took the lead on answering questions about Starlink, the company’s cash cow.
What she doesn’t do, except rarely, is post on X.
I got the sense that the Wojcickis were antsy to get back to their work. As I made my way out, I noticed the family portraits and framed magazine covers on almost every surface of the home. Many photos featured the three sisters, now just two. Social capital, financial capital, old media, new media were all on display; a stunning collage of power and a sobering reminder that no amount of it can control certain outcomes.
It’s impossible to talk about power in Silicon Valley without talking about venture capital. Anne Wojcicki was clearly haunted by her attempts to raise enough of it to buy back her company.
In July I headed to an event on the San Francisco waterfront for women entrepreneurs and VCs. When I arrived, I found hundreds of well-heeled women and a handful of men grazing on prosciutto skeins, dried apricots, and cubes of cheese, swanning around an airy space misnomered Shack15.
Event sponsors had set up tables with goodies. An experiential marketing firm offered a K-beauty snail mucin sheet mask to anyone who followed the firm on its socials. The event’s swag bag included a pack of Popo Band, a “gentle mouth tape” meant to encourage nasal breathing during sleep. I imagined future historians asking why we women tucked ourselves into bed glistening with snail slime, our mouths taped shut.
The soiree, titled Funded Female Founders, was the brainchild of a man named James Gee. He was appropriately brief and charming in his intro speech, joking that he’d just learned what K-beauty was. Mabel Chan, the founder of an events company called Superconnected, reminded attendees that the goal was to increase deal flow. “Our ethos is high-signal rooms, not performative panels,” Chan said.
Then the evening’s emcee, AJ Thomas of Good Trouble Ventures, took the mic. She asked the crowd to snap their fingers and began belting out a revised version of “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough”:
“Ain’t no startup hard enough,
Ain’t no valley low enough,
Ain’t no founder strong enough,
To keep us from running the world, babe …”
The singing portion of the evening was brief, for better or worse. The panel conversations that followed were lively and instructive; you might even say they were high-signal. Libby Leffler, who founded a legal tech platform called First, said she was giving discounts on prenuptial agreements. Literal cheers.
The belief that the tech industry has entered a brave new AI world was palpable. But most of the entrepreneurs speaking that night emphasized that fundraising is still hard for women, particularly when they pitch VCs who have “preconceived notions.” Capella Kerst, who has a PhD in mechanical engineering and runs an adhesives company, told the room that a potential backer once suggested she take business classes.
The financial data platform PitchBook has tracked VC fundraising trends since 2007. This year, it reported that female-founded or -cofounded startups had raised “a record $73.6 billion in 2025—even exceeding pandemic-era highs—capturing an unprecedented 27.7 percent of total US venture deal value.” In 2022, the firm estimated that solely woman-founded companies raised 2 percent of VC capital for US startups.
Yet despite the gains since then, the overall deal count for women declined last year, PitchBook noted. The companies in its dataset might have had male cofounders who led the fundraising. And a huge fraction of last year’s VC funding went to two startups with women cofounders, Anthropic and ScaleAI. Alas: Despite the record high, it’s not clear that those billions mark progress.
In the gap between the two panels, a lawyer named Dobrina Ustun stepped up to give a short talk on immigrant visas. The audience seized the moment to migrate to the back of the room, where they replenished their wine, scored some K-beauty, and struck up conversations. The noise reached a fever pitch. Thomas, the emcee, asked the crowd to quiet down and listen to Ustun. They declined. How rude could we be to our own? Very, it turns out.
Venture capital is not Silicon Valley’s only currency, but it is a signifier. It’s status. “It’s definitely not 2013 anymore, where someone raises a round and it’s on the front page of Fast Company,” Catherine Bracy told me over the phone. “But there’s still real cachet in raising funding, and it would be better for women if they could raise more.”
Bracy is the CEO and cofounder of an activism group called TechEquity and the author of a 2025 book on venture capital titled World Eaters. She noted that VC is typically an “alpha male” game. Its “testosterone” culture lends itself to a high-risk, high-reward investing style: VCs are OK with a 90 percent failure rate, provided the remainder pays off big time. It’s often the overconfident founder, with an outlandish story of potential success, who gets backed. And those founders, she said, tend to be men.
“If VCs were more willing to set up smaller funds, where you can still make market-beating returns but at smaller margins across 30 to 40 percent of your portfolio companies, you would naturally see more women and founders of color in those cohorts,” Bracy theorized. “It would open up the industry to more risk-averse founders and a totally different set of companies.”
Aileen Lee told me that her firm, Cowboy Ventures, receives hundreds of inbound notes and pitches each month from AI entrepreneurs. Only a fraction are coming from women. “It’s really low,” Lee said. She told me she sometimes jokes with friends that they should create a “World Wildlife Fund” for the endangered species of women entrepreneurs.
“You did this,” Sarah Guo said across the table at Tartine Bakery, down the street from her VC firm, Conviction.
Guo drank two glasses of water, while I downed coffee and ordered a toast that turned out to be half a loaf of bread. She broke off a small piece. “The entire problem with the last era of tech is that you made women out to be a special thing. You made a generation of people take an entire class of people unseriously.”
“Do you mean ‘you’ as in the media, or—,” I began.
“Yes!” Guo said. “But also, the people writing … those books,” she said, waving her hand.
I had been chasing Guo for months, trying to schedule a meeting. People kept telling me she was someone I should know. And now she was basically telling me off. (I later told Guo that I was terrified to compliment her appearance, like her sparkling tennis bracelet or collared navy midi dress, fearing that I was reverting to old tropes.)
“The girlboss era aesthetically did not appeal to me,” she said. “I’m not embarrassed about being female. I also think it has absolutely nothing to do with what I’m trying to achieve.”
Guo belongs to a class of women at the intersection of capital and internet culture. She’s hyper-energetic, extremely online, obviously wealthy, politically astute, and pals with the guys. She doesn’t pretend that traditional power structures don’t exist, she told me. She just honestly believes that anyone can win in Silicon Valley.
She invests in defense tech companies. She hosts a podcast, No Priors, on which tech legends like Jensen Huang appear. Her husband is a prominent venture capitalist, though that does not define her. (Guo told me a story in which she and her husband, Pat Grady, showed up at a private opera event, hosted by Huang. “Are you two together?” Huang asked them. “Only for the past 10 years and four kids,” Guo replied.)
“Look, my firm is majority women,” Guo said. “And if you publish that I’ll be so annoyed with you. Because it doesn’t matter. I don’t know if you noticed, but we’re fucking winning.”
Guo’s fund has raised over $330 million and invests between $1 million to $25 million in early-stage AI companies. Its portfolio includes Harvey, Mistral, and Sierra—buzzy AI startups with multibillion-dollar valuations. It’s a hugely impressive group.
Guo told me several times that she didn’t believe she was the person to ask about powerful women. Yet during our meeting she fired off a list of names and sent more later via WhatsApp. Two were from Anthropic: Daniela Amodei, cofounder and president, and Ami Vora, chief product officer. Jayshree Ullal, chairperson and CEO of Arista Networks. Fidji Simo, most recently the CEO of AGI Deployment at OpenAI, and before that, the CEO of Instacart.
“Fidji is amazing. Very mission-driven,” Guo told me. “She’s a girl’s girl.”
“She seems well liked throughout the industry,” I said, then caught myself. “And there you go. ‘Well liked.’ Is Elon well liked?” I mused aloud.
“No, Elon is revered,” Guo corrected me. “But Fidji is both.”
Knowing of Guo’s connection to Huang, I opened an email on my iPhone and slid it across the table. In July I’d emailed Huang, asking who he thought was the most powerful woman in tech. Huang replied an hour later: Dina Powell, Ruth Porat.
“How often (if at all) do you interact with Ruth and Dina, and what impresses you most about them?” I wrote back. “See them when I’m in DC,” he replied. I tried again: “What about Gwynne Shotwell?”
“Oh my gosh, absolutely. I forgot! My bad. You are right,” Huang responded, as though a Jensen AI had wrested control of his inbox.
“Oh yeah,” Guo said when I showed her the email. “Gwynne Shotwell is amazing. Dina, too.”
“Is Gwynne powerful partly because she’s juxtaposed with Elon?”
“What does it matter?” Guo shot back.
I asked her whether spending significant time in Washington, DC, had become more essential to tech power. It’s hard to miss the parade of executives jetting to the White House. Guo said she has traveled to DC more in the past three years than in the decade prior. So yes: Politics is part of the game.
“I can’t make the US government do anything. What person has that power? I think it’s a nonsense concept,” Guo said. I decided not to interrupt her with “Elon” once again. “However, I can ask questions, and I can influence if it makes sense for me to do so,” Guo continued.
A recurring theme in my interviews is that the most powerful women are cultivating allies in DC—on behalf of their companies. When I spoke to AMD’s CEO and chairperson Lisa Su last year, she told me she doesn’t weigh in on social issues, because that’s not her “value add,” as she put it. “But when it comes to technology policy and where semiconductors are in the world, yes, we have to participate.” (Su declined to participate in this article.)
Another woman I spoke to pointed out that Mary Barra, the CEO of General Motors, introduced Trump at a rally at the GM Proving Ground in Milford, Michigan, in July. “She needs the company to survive,” this person said. “Now is definitely not the time to use your dry powder.”
A decade ago some large tech companies did wade into social issues; Salesforce, for example, threatened to pull back from states where LGBTQ+ rights were under fire. Now, if you’re one of the many tech companies in Texas, it’s of no concern that rates of pregnancy-related sepsis and maternal deaths have spiked since the state essentially banned abortion in 2021. You cannot stick your neck out and be a suffragette for women broadly. You have thousands of people to employ. You have deals to make.
Guo stood up to leave, and I indicated I was staying behind to work. To my surprise, she offered me a hug. “I don’t know if any of this was helpful,” she said.
I thanked her and assured her it was. “I do love your outfit, by the way.”
“Thanks! It’s vintage Fendi,” Guo said, and floated out the door.
Here’s a non-exhaustive list of powerful women, sourced largely from other women in tech: Gwynne Shotwell, Lisa Su, Michelle Zatlyn, Fei-Fei Li, Safra Catz, Meredith Whittaker, Melanie Perkins, Fidji Simo, Jayshree Ullal, Reshma Saujani, Tekedra Mawakana, Aicha Evans, Ruth Porat, Dina Powell McCormick, Sarah Friar, Amy Hood, Colette Kress, Rachel Whetstone, Liz Reid, Sarah Guo, Theresia Gouw, Timnit Gebru, and Mira Murati. Laurene Powell-Jobs, MacKenzie Scott, Melinda Gates, and Cari Tuna, if you consider the origins of their immense wealth. Kara Swisher, if you count lambasting tech bros.
And one name that came up more often than most: Daniela Amodei.
Amodei is arguably the most important person at Anthropic, the nearly $1 trillion “startup” that has created some of the most powerful large language models. She’s also one half of the Amodeis. Her brother, Dario, is CEO and a cofounder. His novella-length encyclicals on AI and nutty-professor mannerisms have captivated people in the industry and the press that covers it. Either he or the savvy communications professionals behind the duo have positioned the Amodeis as cherubic foils to a Machiavellian Sam Altman.
Given tech’s long record of power imbalances, I was curious how the benefits of the AI future will be distributed across genders. Amodei was more than happy to discuss this with me over Zoom in early August. The number one thing she tells people, she said, is: “Do not let AI become a tool that’s just for the guys. It’s our job, and the job of other model providers, to not make this technology gendered, right?”
Anthropic has a remarkable number of women in its leadership ranks. Its chief product officer, chief people officer, head of public policy, head of design for Claude, head of platform engineering, head of product for coding, head of product for research labs, and head of “personality alignment” for AI models (yes, that’s a thing) are all women.
(More recently, another woman close to Anthropic has emerged as something of a power player. According to The Information and The Wall Street Journal, Dario’s longtime partner, Cami Clark—who reportedly tried to get Jeffrey Epstein to invest in her porn company—was instrumental in connecting him with some of Anthropic’s early financial backers.)
In a June interview with Bloomberg’s Emily Chang, the Amodeis revealed that Dario largely sidesteps having direct reports, while Daniela runs the day-to-day operations. All of the leadership team reports to Daniela. “That sounds like a pretty sweet job,” Chang said to Dario, her brows raised. “It’s incredibly freeing,” Dario replied, with his trademark enthusiasm. “It lets me do all the things that I do, much more easily than I would otherwise.”
“And she does all the work?” Chang replied. Dario faltered in his response.
I asked Daniela what she makes of Chang’s points and the responses they elicited. (“I saw that interview, and it just showed me how much Dario thinks he’s a special boy,” a friend in one of my group chats fumed.)
“Dario and I very much run the company together,” Amodei insisted. “I think everyone who knows the company really well or works here knows it’s a two-person ship.” She believes it would be hard for one person to run a company at the “level of consequence” of Anthropic.
Daniela has amassed considerable financial, intellectual, and cultural capital. She is not, however, the face of Anthropic’s political agenda. That’s her brother and, more recently, Anthropic cofounder Tom Brown.
“I worked on Capitol Hill before, and I know enough to be dangerous,” she told me. “I do go to Washington, and I think it’s a matter of what’s happening in the headlines versus behind the scenes.” She engages on topics like trust and safety or how AI will impact future generations—things viewed “not necessarily as the most sexy,” she explained.
And who arbitrates the “most sexy” issues in artificial intelligence? We already know the answer to that.
With her fleet of women executives and her stated ethos of non-gendered AI, Amodei may emerge as a historic figure in Silicon Valley, depending on the fate of her company. What she’s built may signal a new era of corporate culture and achievement for women. But when I asked other people if the AI boom presents ample opportunities for women, their outlook was less rosy. Bracy, who wrote World Eaters, flatly said, “No.”
Gebru told me that “the AI industry is worse for women than whatever the tech industry was in the 2010s.” People still don’t want to listen to women, she said, and many of the most hyped companies are still led by men.
She is correct. Outliers like Amodei and Shotwell are the industry’s high-
profile heroines. They’re also complex examples of power. They are operational masterminds and the steady hands guiding the men in charge, much like Sheryl Sandberg was.
I thought about the powerful figures now schlepping to DC on a regular basis to try to bend the ear of a man and his army of acolytes who regularly minimize and degrade women. A few names on that non-exhaustive power list jumped out at me as women who aren’t afraid to say exactly what they’re thinking, consequences be damned. Significantly more women told me it’s not worth it to post their politics on X or to say the spicy truth in interviews or to try to be a podcast bro. It would compromise their focus on the work.
Women now possess all kinds of capital, which is in itself remarkable. But they are choosing not to fully enter the matrix. And really, why would they? What awaits them on the other side?
Gebru was still going, and now she flipped my question on its head. “How successful women are in AI is not my measure of power or success for women. Why do women have to join the terrible thing men are doing? They’re accelerating harm. They’re talking about littering the world with data centers. The kinds of arguments I thought were fringe, like AGI, they’ve mainstreamed.”
“What does power mean? Does it mean you have to trample on your own people in a terrible system in order to succeed in your career?” Gebru said to me over the phone.
She was sitting somewhere outside, in Boston, and kids were shrieking in the background. At one point she apologized for the noise and asked if I could hear her. I assured her I was listening.

Russia's elections had few surprises - but how the Kremlin uses the results will be crucial
- Published
Many things about Russia are hard to predict.
The result of this election wasn't one of them.
In a political system tightly controlled by the Kremlin, the party of power – United Russia –had been widely expected to remain the largest in parliament by a large margin.
There were no upsets. No surprises. No other party came close.
Preliminary results suggest that United Russia, which is supported by President Putin, is on course to retain its constitutional majority in the State Duma - with even bigger numbers than last time round.
And that's after more than four-and-half years of war on Ukraine, which have resulted in massive battlefield losses for the Russian army, economic difficulties and, most recently, widespread petrol shortages due to Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities.
Those parties trailing far behind, but which have cleared the 5% threshold and made it into the new Duma, featured in the previous parliament, too: a Duma that was fully behind the Kremlin and the so-called special military operation.
One party that didn't make it into parliament was Yabloko.
Yabloko had been the only anti-war political party permitted to take part in the election - permission that was short-lived.
Just twelve days after being registered for the vote it was removed from the ballot (the party list) by the Supreme Court, an indication of Kremlin concern that Yabloko's pro-peace message was gaining too much traction with the public.
The party isn't surprised that the new Duma looks like being as pro-Kremlin as the previous one.
"What other result can there be if there were ten parties on the ballot and they all support the policies of Putin?" Yabloko party chairman Nikolai Rybakov tells me.
"I don't think the Duma will change. They'll vote 100% for the policies of Putin just like they did."
Although Yabloko had been struck off the party list, around a hundred of its candidates remained in individual constituency races. According to preliminary results, none have won seats. The party claims it has come under sustained pressure.
"Some of our candidates, who should have been running, are in jail, many were barred from running and some of our election observers weren't registered and were unable to keep an eye on the voting," Nikolai says.
Ahead of the final day of this three-day election, Ukraine launched a large-scale drone attack on the Moscow area. Three people were killed in Moscow Region, while in the capital the city's oil refinery was hit.
At a polling station near the oil refinery, I spoke to voters about the attack.
There was no sense of surprise. More a quiet resignation. With Russia's war on Ukraine now in its fifth year, Muscovites have grown used to their city periodically becoming a front line.
"People in the Donbas, as well as in Bryansk, and Belgorod near the Ukrainian border, hear this kind of thing every day," a voter called Viktor told me.
"And they just get on with their lives."
The outcome of this election was predictable. What happens next is less clear.
The Kremlin is likely to use the result to claim that most Russians have rallied behind the president, and to justify future policies and subsequent decisions on the course of the war.
The key question: what will those decisions be?
President Putin recently ruled out another wave of mobilisation.
"There is no scenario today that would require it," he declared.
Not today, then. But what about tomorrow?
Despite official denials, in Russian society there remains deep anxiety about the possibility of a new round of mobilisation.
At the very least, the Kremlin is likely to treat the election result as a 'mandate from the people' to continue the war.

New book by Princess Diana's brother prompts war of words with King Charles III
LONDON — A new book published Tuesday by the brother of the late Princess Diana has made headlines around the world with its damning allegations about Diana's ex-husband, now King Charles III, and reopened decades-old wounds within Britain's royal family.
In "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," Charles Spencer alleges that he argued with the then-Prince Charles over palace plans for Prince William and Prince Harry, then 15 and 12, to walk behind their mother's coffin during her 1997 funeral procession.
Spencer says he told Charles that Diana, who was killed in a car crash in Paris at the age of 36, would not have wanted her boys to undergo the ordeal. He claims the prince "went ballistic" during the argument, and told him: "Rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough." Spencer also accuses Charles of having "contempt" for his ex-wife and of sounding "elated" after her death.
After excerpts of the book were published last week, Buckingham Palace responded with a strongly-worded statement that's rare by the measured standards of the royal household.
"His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," it said.
Spencer has stood by his claims, insisting to the BBC that he is telling the truth. On the royal rebuttal, he asked: "Is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"
War of words draws renewed attention to Charles and Diana's stormy history
Charles, then 32, married 20-year-old Lady Diana Spencer in a lavish ceremony at St. Paul's Cathedral in 1981. The couple divorced in 1996, and a decade later Charles married Camilla Parker Bowles, now Queen Camilla.
Charles Spencer, the 9th Earl Spencer, has long clashed with the royals over their treatment of his older sister.
Tensions between the palace and the Spencer family following her death were dramatized in the film "The Queen" and the Netflix series "The Crown."
In a searing eulogy at his sister's funeral, Spencer vowed that her "blood family" would carry on her "imaginative and loving" legacy in raising her two sons. The speech was widely considered a swipe at the royal family.
At the time, many in Britain and beyond felt Queen Elizabeth II and the royals were too slow to acknowledge the global outpouring of grief over Diana's death and that the monarchy was deeply out of touch with the public mood.
Charles Spencer says press treatment of Harry echoes that of his mother
The royals have spent decades putting that period of crisis behind them. The warmer, more personable approach of William and Harry — and, in recent years, the king — is a legacy of that time.
In his book, Spencer also criticized the royals for what he described as a "lack of obvious care" for the then 12-year-old Harry.
He recounted how "tiny, and slight, and bereft" his nephew looked after the funeral. "He needed Diana's hugs, of course, and they would forever be denied him," he wrote. "But instead of calm and nurture, he was allowed to spin out of control."
Some critics have questioned why Spencer felt the need to revisit the pain and trauma 30 years on.
The aristocrat said he wanted to write down his own thoughts and memories about Diana, "once and for all, rather than having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others, many of which are based on untruths."
Asked if the relationship between the press and Harry and his wife, Meghan, mirrors the way the media treated his sister, Spencer told the BBC: "(Diana) was really brought low by all that criticism. I suppose it's a pity when I see echoes of that now."
Penguin Press said the book will be published globally and translated into 12 languages.

Another Marineland beluga has died after being moved to Chicago aquarium
Whale was 4th to die after being moved from the Niagara Falls, Ont., park in July
A fourth whale that was moved out of Marineland in July has died after struggling with its health since arriving at her new home in Chicago, Shedd Aquarium said Monday.
The park said 26-year-old Osiris died Monday morning. The female beluga was one of 10 that came to Shedd from Marineland, the shuttered tourist attraction in Niagara Falls, Ont.
It was part of the world's biggest collective move of captive whales. Marineland had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for its animals.
Over a series of moves beginning in July, Marineland moved 30 belugas and four dolphins to five aquariums abroad: Shedd in Chicago, SeaWorld locations in San Antonio, Texas, and San Diego, Calif., Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta and Oceanografic Valencia in Spain.
Osiris was "not a consistent eater" but had improved recently after receiving fluids and medication, Shedd said.
"Our care team observed sudden changes this morning in both Osiris's behaviour and respiratory patterns," Shedd said in a statement.

"Respiratory rates are one of many measures we track closely and continuously, as changes can signal that an animal may need additional support. The team moved Osiris to the medical habitat, so immediate care could be provided if needed. Her condition declined rapidly, and Osiris passed away despite lifesaving efforts by our veterinary and animal care teams."
The park will conduct a necropsy to try to better understand what happened.
Two other Marineland whales, Rain and Peekachu, died at Shedd within weeks of the move. One longtime Shedd resident beluga, Beethoven, also recently died.
All are being investigated, but the results have not yet returned, Shedd said.
Another Marineland beluga, Jelly Bean, died at Oceanografic in Spain last week.
The whales were cleared by veterinarians at Marineland and the other parks to move and Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson also signed off on the relocation.
Last week, Shedd said it is concerned about the health of another recently moved whale, Secord.
"Secord has not yet been consistently taking in the amount of food teams would like to see, even as they try different feeding approaches and offer different types of herring to gauge her preference," Shedd said in a blog post last week.
Marineland originally sought to move the whales to China after securing a deal to sell all 30 of its belugas to Chimelong Ocean Kingdom, which has a Guinness Book of World Record for the largest aquarium in the world.

Thompson blocked that move, saying it was not in the best interest of the whales and inconsistent with a 2019 federal law. That law banned whale and dolphin captivity and performances, but grandfathered in Marineland's whales. It also banned breeding, which forced Marineland to separate its whales by sex.
Marineland turned to an American-led consortium to house the world's biggest pod of captive belugas, but they needed five aquariums to house them all.
There are no breeding or performing restrictions at the belugas' new homes.
Marineland's whales had struggled in recent years. Nineteen belugas and one killer whale died at the park between 2019 and 2025.
The park blames some of those deaths on the new federal laws.

The Centre has told the Delhi High Court that an adult can nominate a partner, including one in a non-heterosexual relationship, to make medical decisions if they become incapacitated, potentially opening the way for same-sex partners to act for each other despite existing rules not clearly recognising such arrangements.
The submission comes in a case filed by Arshiya Takkar, who has been in a relationship with her partner since 2015 and married her in New Zealand in 2023. Her plea highlighted that in the event of a medical emergency, she could be left without any legal mechanism to make critical decisions for her partner, despite the couple having lived together in Delhi since 2018.
Responding to her plea, the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the National Medical Commission said that allowing a competent adult to nominate a partner, including one in a same-sex relationship, to take medical decisions in the event of incapacity was “substantially capable of being accommodated within the existing legal and ethical framework”.
“Permitting a competent adult to nominate his/her partner, including a partner in a non-heterosexual/same-sex relationship, to take medical decisions on his/her behalf in the event of incapacity would constitute a logical and tailored extension of the same principle,” the affidavit said. It added that such a nomination could be subject to appropriate safeguards and the applicable law.
The Centre said decisions concerning an adult patient who is unable to make or communicate a decision must be considered in light of the nature of the treatment, the circumstances requiring the decision, the patient’s own wishes, and the legal framework governing such representation.
It further submitted that where a competent adult has nominated or otherwise authorised their partner to act on their behalf in the event of incapacity, “there appears to be no medical or ethical rationale for excluding such person merely on account of the sex, gender or sexual orientation of the partners or because their union does not fall within the conventional understanding of marriage...”.
The Centre also said it recognised and respected the constitutional guarantees of dignity, privacy, autonomy, equality and individual choice available to all persons, including members of the LGBTQIA+ community.
The petition is likely to come up for hearing on Thursday (September 17, 2026).
Ms. Takkar, in her petition filed last year through advocates Manjira Dasgupta and Bhargav Ravindran Thali, highlighted the lack of a clear legal framework or common law recognising “partners in a union”, making it difficult to provide consent during medical treatment or emergencies.
The plea stated that the existing regulation, Clause 7.16 of the Indian Medical Council (Professional Conduct, Etiquette, and Ethics) Regulations, 2002, mandates consent for medical procedures or treatment from a “husband or wife, parent or guardian in the case of a minor, or the patient himself”.
“This lack of explicit recognition of partners in a union renders the petitioner effectively powerless to make critical medical decisions for her partner, or vice versa, a right readily available to heterosexual partners under the current regulations,” it stated.
The petition contended that despite the Supreme Court directive for a high-powered committee to address entitlements of LGBTQIA+ couples, including their recognition as “family” for medical decision-making, the authorities have failed to take expeditious measures.
“This inaction leaves the petitioner and other same-sex couples vulnerable and unable to exercise the fundamental right to care for each other in medical emergencies,” the plea said.

Fiji has declared an HIV national emergency after data showed one in 60 people in the South Pacific island nation is now estimated to have the bloodborne virus.
The country says it is boosting testing and treatment efforts to fight a surge in new infections, which have increased 12-fold over the last 15 years, according to the Joint United Nations Program on HIV and Aids (UNAIDS).
Latest figures showed there was about 9,000 people living with HIV in 2025 in a country which has less than a million people, according to the UN agency. It said only 39 per cent of patients knew their HIV status and just 22 per cent were receiving antiretroviral treatment.
Fiji said that one in every 60 adults in the country has HIV, compared with one in 167 five years ago.
"This means HIV is now a national crisis and the government is treating it like one. No more business as usual," Fiji's Health Minister Antonio Lalabalavu said in a video statement on Facebook. “More people in Fiji are living with HIV than ever before.” The government said it was finding more cases because its testing efforts are reaching more people. It will provide more free testing, clean needles for drug users and free treatment for people who test positive.

War, runaway AI and climate shocks to take center stage as world leaders meet at UN
World leaders are meeting under a global cloud of wars and bitter divisions for their annual meeting at the United Nations this week
Under a global cloud of wars and bitter divisions, world leaders meet at the United Nations this week facing new fears that runaway artificial intelligence could threaten humanity even as climate shocks and escalating prices are already making life much tougher for hundreds of millions of people.
The annual high-level gathering at the U.N. General Assembly will also be consumed with major wars in Iran, Gaza, Ukraine,Sudan, Congo and Myanmar and a persisting question: Can the leaders do anything to end them?
And what can they do about the relentless rise of global warming threatening the future of the planet, the growing inequalities within and among nations, and shocks to the global economy as blocked shipping routes and supply chains increase the cost of living and slow growth?
The future of the United Nations will also definitely be on the agenda. At 81, its powers are still the victorious nations from World War II, not the 21st century’s major global players. The U.N.’s 193 member nations have agreed to a wide-ranging reform package that includes updating key institutions such as the powerful U.N. Security Council, where the U.S., Russia, China, Britain and France hold inordinate sway because of their veto power. Reform, however, is easier said than implemented.
Behind the scenes, there will be speculation about who will lead the United Nations next. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ second five-year term ends Dec. 31 and no clear successor has emerged.
This meeting is still pivotal
There is still no question that the U.N. remains THE gathering place for its 193 member nations and their leaders. Some 130 heads of state and government are expected to speak at the General Assembly starting Tuesday along with dozens of ministers.
Among the headliners will be U.S. President Donald Trump and French President Emanuel Macron. Both will speak Tuesday after Guterres’ opening “state of the world” address. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian speak Wednesday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu — whom New York Mayor Zoran Mamdani wanted arrested for his treatment of Palestinians in Gaza until he learned he has no such authority — will address the assembly on Thursday. For a second year, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas won’t be coming to the U.N. because the U.S. has refused to give him a visa. He will nonetheless address the assembly by video the same day.
The United States, under its agreement with the U.N. to host the organization, is required to allow diplomats from all member nations to attend meetings.
Equally telling is who else isn’t coming. China’s President Xi Jinping is meeting Trump in Washington on Wednesday, yet he is skipping — some diplomats say snubbing — the U.N. gathering and sending a vice president instead. Russian President Vladimir Putin isn’t coming either, and Indian President Narendra Modi has backed out.
France's U.N. ambassador, Jerome Bonnafont, said it is “extremely critical” for world leaders this week to support the U.N. as the place where the world’s nations meet — especially at a time of such polarization.
“We believe in multilateralism," he said, "and we believe that the high-level week is the occasion for countries in the world to reaffirm that they prefer cooperation and dialogue to confrontation.”
United Nations has not had a great year
There is no doubt it’s been a tough year for the world body. It has been pushed to the sidelines when it comes to its key responsibility of ensuring international peace and security and trying to end major conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine. The U.S. failure to pay billions of dollars in outstanding arrears has left the organization’s finances in rocky shape.
But veteran U.N. watcher Richard Gowan, the International Crisis Group’s global issues and institutions program director, says 2025 was even worse.
A year ago, he said, people were contemplating that Trump would use his U.N. speech to announce that the United States would leave the world organization. Trump didn’t announce a pullout last September and the U.N. muddled through the past 12 months with financial troubles that forced cutbacks to its peacekeeping operations and humanitarian aid.
In recent days, the U.S. paid $725 million of its dues to the U.N.’s regular operating budget for this year, enough to keep the Trump administration from losing its vote in the General Assembly. The payment was a strong indication Trump will keep the U.S. in the United Nations.
The U.N. is no longer “in freefall,” Gowan said, but it “is stuck in an open-ended or permanent crisis.” Put more graphically, he said, “The U.N. may not be in emergency care like it was last year, but it does seem to be trapped in a trauma center for the foreseeable future.”
Former U.N. deputy secretary-general Mark Malloch-Brown, a United Nations Foundation board member, said, “While the world still trusts the U.N., the global public is eager for change."
AI is pushing toward the center of the agenda
The future of artificial intelligence has pushed to the forefront of global concerns, with its speeding advances and the dawning recognition that there are no industry controls, let alone any global guardrails for a technology that has many advantages but also many disadvantages and unknowns.
Days before the global gathering, leaders of three major AI companies warned about the technology getting out of human control and called for a pause, but Trump dismissed their concerns as “a hoax,” and urged continued advances to keep the U.S. ahead of China.
The U.N. Security Council added a high-level meeting on AI to its agenda on Wednesday afternoon, a sign of the growing apprehension and need to address the issue. It was already slated to hold a high-level meeting on Ukraine with Zelenskyy on Wednesday morning.
For the U.N. chief, this will be his last assembly meeting with global leaders. He previewed his speech last week, telling U.N. reporters that power is shifting in “an era of deep uncertainty."
“At a time when the world faces three existential threats," he said, “international cooperation is more necessary than ever.”
Others will be vying for the spotlight on issues from rising sea levels and funding education to the fight for gender equality. Hundreds of private meetings will also convene in U.N. cubicles, hotels, diplomatic missions and restaurants.
Esther Brimmer, a senior fellow in global governance at the Council on Foreign Relations and former U.S. assistant secretary of state for international organization affairs in the Obama administration, said in-person meetings can help countries hash out ideas that get implemented months later.
She called the situation in 2026 “much more serious and complex than in decades past."
“With that said, I’m also not without hope as well,” Brimmer said. “Over the past decades we’ve learned a lot about international cooperation.”
___
Edith M. Lederer has covered international affairs for The Associated Press for more than a half century.

Srinagar, Sept 22: Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Tuesday said Jammu and Kashmir’s tourist destinations should be developed according to their individual character and potential rather than replicating the Gulmarg model everywhere.
“Every tourist destination should have its own identity,” Omar said in the Assembly while responding to questions on tourism development.
“We cannot make every tourist destination Gulmarg,” he said, adding that the success of the Gulmarg Gondola did not mean similar projects would work equally well at every destination.
“Just because Gulmarg’s Gondola runs, it does not mean that gondolas will be equally successful everywhere,” he said.
“So repeatedly saying that give us a gondola because tourism will revive through a gondola, that is not correct,” Omar added.
He said the government would instead develop tourism products suited to individual destinations. “We should look at something different for every destination and promote it,” he said.
Jammu tourism push
Omar said the Tourism Department was pursuing a “comprehensive and multi-pronged approach” to develop and diversify tourism in Jammu, including pilgrimage, heritage, adventure, eco, nature, rural, cultural, wellness and leisure tourism.
The government has begun identifying new destinations and assessing their tourism potential in consultation with local stakeholders and the Revenue and Forest departments.
Adventure tourism, including skiing, has been introduced at Dhopa Pathri since 2023, while a drag lift became operational in 2026. The proposed Gondola cable car project at Godda 3 is under consideration.
Dood Pathri transit hub
The government has identified around 25 kanals of state land near the sheep farm at Kral Pathri for a proposed tourist transit hub and 400-car parking facility at Daud Pathri.
A ₹75-crore detailed project report has been submitted to the Union Tourism Ministry under Swadesh Darshan 2.0.
The government has also approved ₹50 lakh for wayside facilities at five locations along the Ariyam-to-Rearch stretch, with the works at the tendering stage.
Omar opposes blanket power amnesty
On power-bill amnesty, Omar said the government was examining the issue on merit but opposed repeatedly extending blanket waivers.
“I think repeatedly extending amnesty is an injustice to those people who pay their bills,” he said.
“You are incentivising people not to pay their bills on time,” Omar added.
He said consumers genuinely unable to pay, particularly those below the poverty line, could be considered individually.
“For those for whom amnesty is really necessary, and who genuinely live below the poverty line and do not have the ability to pay these bills, we will definitely consider them on merit,” he said.

Salt, as an essential electrolyte, sits at the centre of human well-being, but being most prone to overuse and misuse, the condiment remains at the heart of illness as well. When Tamil Nadu Health Minister K.G. Arunraj took salt to the floor of the Assembly, he dragged it willy-nilly into public discourse. He announced plans to launch a multi-pronged mission to reduce salt intake, turning attention to the right quantities and forms that must be consumed. The Minister’s speech made it clear that the government’s plans were not merely about a dietary tweak, but instead, a recalibration of how wellbeing is perceived.
Salt, in the right proportions, facilitates hydration, nerve signalling, muscle function, and digestion and also has a role to play in stress physiology. However, in excess, or in ultra-processed foods, it can have a deleterious impact on health, increasing the risk of stroke, heart disease and kidney strain over time. On the other hand, very low salt intake can contribute to hypotension, fatigue, dizziness and brain fog, as well.
The health difference comes from the quantity of salt consumed and the overall diet patterns, undergoing rapid changes in favour of ultra-processed, packaged foods, and fast foods, that tend to be high in salt. The Indian diet itself, with its pickles and spicy curries, lends itself to tilting the salt cellar over a little too often. Surveys by the Indian Council of Medical Research show that in India, men consume an average of 8.9 gms daily, while women consume about 7.1 gms. Urban areas tend to consume higher amounts of salt, averaging around 9.2 gms a day. The WHO, which recommends keeping the intake under 5 gms of salt per day, released a set of guidelines in January 2025, recommending the use of lower-sodium salt substitutes, essentially including potassium chloride, and reducing the percentage of sodium chloride in table salt.
In Tamil Nadu, hypertension is a major public health concern. A 2024 study by Selvavinayagam T.S. et al., published in PLOS 1, showed adult prevalence of hypertension hovering around 33.9%, much above the national average of 28.5%. There is a direct link between consuming excess salt and hypertension — eating too much salt causes the body to retain extra water, which increases blood volume and puts higher pressure on the artery walls, leading to clinical hypertension.
Action plan
The Tamil Nadu government’s plan is appropriately comprehensive. For the first time, a statewide survey using urine samples will scientifically measure salt consumption. Salt will be gradually reduced in government-run kitchens, including the Nutritious Meal Programme, ICDS centres, government hospitals and hostels. The feasibility of introducing a low-sodium salt substitute will be examined.
This will be backed by a state-wide awareness campaign on how to read labels on packages, tasting before adding salt and using natural flavour enhancers. Researchers of a randomised, double-blind, controlled trial reported in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, in 2021, wrote that the replacement of salt with a reduced-sodium, added-potassium salt substitute is an acceptable and effective dietary intervention for lowering systolic blood pressure in persons with hypertension in rural India.
The State also intends to step up its hypertension control activities through its community health outreach programme ‘Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam’ and other public health care institutions. People diagnosed with hypertension will receive systematic counselling and anti-hypertension drugs. There is evidence that such closely-monitored health interventions succeed. A study published recently in Nature, Archana Ramalingam et al., studying the cascade of care between 2019-20 and 2023-24 in Tamil Nadu, showed that overall, hypertension care in Tamil Nadu improved, with increased use of public health facilities for treatment.
The Sapiens Health Foundation has welcomed the new salt reduction campaign of the Tamil Nadu government. Founder Rajan Ravichandran says: “This is a wonderful surprise; we have been knocking at many doors to bring in awareness of salt reduction in the public health sector. It can be very powerful in changing the way people consume salt. We just have to go back to 2005, when the campaign initiated by Graham MacGregor of the World Action on Salt, Sugar and Health resulted in a reported 30% reduction of salt in bread in the United Kingdom,” Dr. Rajan adds.
G. Sengottuvelu, senior interventional cardiologist, Apollo Hospitals, explains further: “Excess salt is one of the most important and preventable contributors to high blood pressure, heart attack and stroke.” His argument is that Indians’ preference for salty food is largely an acquired habit, often beginning in childhood, and the palate can adapt when salt is gradually reduced. Cutting down salt is a simple change that can make a major difference to cardiovascular health — less salt today can mean lower blood pressure, fewer heart attacks and fewer strokes tomorrow.
Incidentally, the regulator Food Safety and Standards Association of India’s submission of guidelines for ingredient labelling on packaged food has grabbed eyeballs. While experts point to lacunae within the labelling guidelines, it does seem that momentum is growing towards building a society that is aware of the importance of salt and regulating it, and reclaiming the kitchen staple as a transformative touchstone for improved public health. As Tamil Nadu rolls out its programme, hopefully with scientific vigour and cultural sensitivity, other States will do well to watch and emulate. If it is possible to cut down hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and kidney disease with adjusting the size of a single pinch, then, the question is why not?

BepiColombo has been on a bit of an Odyssey. The space probe—named after an acclaimed Italian scientist who developed the “gravity assist” trick that enables interplanetary journeys today—was originally scheduled to arrive at Mercury last year. However, after a malfunction with the propulsion, the probe was forced to change course so it could reach Mercury at reduced power. As a result, the arrival date was pushed back by nearly a year, and now after eight years in space, BepiColombo is beginning its descent to low orbit around Mercury.
On September 3, ground control confirmed that the propulsion module had successfully separated from the rest of the craft, marking the final phase of the joint mission between the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). After a bumpy journey—reaching more than 200 million kilometers from Earth—transmissions from the probe indicated all went smoothly.
Mercury has only been explored twice before, both times by NASA probes. Because even without propulsion mishaps, Mercury is especially challenging to reach due to it’s position as the closest planet to our sun. When traveling towards the center of our solar system, a spacecraft is essentially “falling” from Earth towards the much greater gravity of the sun. That’s the easy part. The hard part is to not keep falling. Getting to Mercury therefore requires a lot of fuel not to travel there but to engage rockets to put on the breaks.
Spacecraft can also use the gravity of other planets as a means of slowing down, but that involves taking a more convoluted path, looping between celestial objects. To-date, BepiColombo has traveled approximately 6 billion miles (9.9 billion kilometers), swinging around Earth once, Venus twice, and Mercury six times for a total of nine gravity assist maneuvers to control its velocity.
Furthermore, being so close to the Sun, Mercury’s surface can be intensely hot—over 800 degrees Fahrenheit or about 430 degrees Celsius. And because the small planet has essentially no atmosphere, temperatures drop to -290 degrees Fahrenheit (-180 Celsius) at night. BepiColombo therefore needs to survive not just these extremes, but the daily swings between them.
Once in position, BepiColombo will break into two separate spacecraft: the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), which will study Mercury’s surface and internal structure, and the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (dubbed “Mio”), which will investigate the planet’s magnetic field and tenuous atmosphere. This is the first time multiple probes will orbit Mercury simultaneously, with the goal of gaining a more comprehensive picture than any single probe could capture on its own.
Mio will enter a higher elliptical orbit oriented to circle across the poles. MPO will then lower its altitude further and is scheduled to reach its final orbit in March of 2027. Even after the probes take their positions, full-scale observations will not begin immediately. The probes must go through a series of procedures—such as the deployment of Mio’s essential sunshield—before conducting scientific observations, which are scheduled to begin in April 2027.
The two probes will attempt to uncover answers to much that remains unknown about the swift planet. Some key questions include why Mercury has an extremely large iron core relative to its size; why ice exists in permanently shadowed craters at the poles despite the scorching heat; why it’s the only rocky planet other than Earth to possess its own magnetic field; and the true nature of the mysterious depressions known as “hollows” that dot its surface.
Answers to into these questions are expected to provide crucial clues for how terrestrial planets—including Earth—formed and evolved within the solar system. Astrophysicists also plan to use precise orbital data from the mission to test Einstein’s general theory of relativity, because—due to its proximity to the sun—Mercury is an ideal testing ground for verifying the gravitational distortion of spacetime.

The Reserve Bank governor said AI could be a bubble and there was no evidence it is making the economy more efficient, as the Albanese government claims the technology will solve Australia’s economic malaise.
Ahead of an expected interest rate rise next week Michele Bullock also said the slump in house prices was deeper than others in Australia’s recent history.
Resurgent oil prices and inflation are weighing on markets but US tech stocks surged on Monday after Facebook owner Meta debuted its new Muse AI agent and saw its shares rise 11%.
Bullock said a messy slump in tech values could hurt economic activity, speaking at a CEDA event in Sydney.
“All central banks are a little bit worried about that,” Bullock said.
“Some people think it’s a bubble, some people don’t. I don’t have a particular view one way or the other, but it’s a risk that I think we’re watching.”
Bullock said the RBA and its overseas colleagues believed AI was “the great white hope” to make economies more productive but had seen little sign of any effect yet, with rapid adoption and investment in datacentres adding to inflation instead.
She cited research from the RBA’s South Korean counterpart that found employees adopting AI tended to produce the same output but work 1.5 hours less each week.
“[While] people fiddle around and try and figure out what to do with this new technology, productivity actually can decline,” Bullock said. “But once we reimagine our business processes… then you might see productivity take off.”
The Australian government’s intergenerational report, released on Tuesday, relied on the potential “profound” boost from AI in its projection that Australians’ inflation-adjusted per-person economic activity would rise from $99,200 today to $157,300 by 2066.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, told the Guardian’s Australian Politics podcast: “It’s the most transformative thing that will happen in our lifetime.”
The report assumed productivity would return to its long run level of improving by 1.2% a year, which economists have said appears unlikely. If productivity only rose by 0.8%, per-person activity would only hit $136,600 by 2066.
Bullock said on Tuesday: “Many have put it, ‘well, it’s an unrealistic assumption, we’re not going to get that.’ I guess the way I’m trying to think about it is, ‘OK, that’s what we’ve got to aim at.”
Housing downturn
As the government defends Australia’s easing rate of immigration, Bullock said immigration was almost entirely responsible for Australia’s economic growth in the last year.
Bullock said new arrivals did not add to inflation as they typically worked as well as spending money. She said the exception was the housing market, as new immigrants did not immediately generate new housing supply.
“Where it bites is the housing market, because the housing market can’t respond,” she said.
One Nation has called for more migrants to leave Australia than arrive over three years, including reducing the number of temporary migrants by more than 750,000.
Labor has instead planned to tighten the existing immigration intake, which home affairs minister Tony Burke said would be “part of the solution for the housing crisis” – but Burke warned more severe cuts could “trash the economy”.
House prices have fallen 3.1% over the past three months after the RBA lifted interest rates three times and the government reformed property investor tax breaks. Bullock said home loan approvals had slumped, in her most explicit public comments on the budget to date.
“They’ve dropped for everyone but they’ve really dropped a long way for investors, so it has changed the dynamic for investors, whether it’s worth investing in housing or not,” she said.
Bullock said housing had become “pretty unaffordable” before the decline, which she described as “a slight dip down after a very long run up”.
“The downturn is sort of in the lower range … but it’s certainly not out of the ballpark of the sorts of downturns we’ve seen in the past,” she said.
She declined to say whether she would recommend an interest rate increase next Tuesday. Traders are betting on more than a 90% chance rates will rise from 4.35% to 4.6%, which would be a 14-year high.

Former Tottenham midfielder Yves Bissouma is on the verge of joining Ajax on an initial deal that runs until the end of the season.
