The Book Claiming to Teach Couples How to Select Their Baby’s Sex
The Babydust Method features advice debunked decades ago. Why have tens of thousands of people bought in?
When Christina Kattula, a 31-year-old yoga teacher in Michigan, was ready to start a family in 2024, she hoped for a son. Her husband “wanted a boy to bond with,” she told me. “And if we had girls later, he thought it would be cute to have a protective-big-brother-type thing.” Kattula decided to try something she’d heard about on a podcast: the so-called Babydust Method. The theory, which was first laid out in a self-published book from 2016, claims, contrary to scientific evidence, that couples can influence their baby’s sex by precisely timing when they have intercourse. Why not try it? she thought. What’s the harm if it doesn’t work? Kattula and her husband followed the book’s advice, and she became pregnant with a boy.
During her pregnancy, Kattula posted a TikTok to her few hundred followers recommending the book to other couples. “Blessed either way,” she said in the video. “But it worked for us. If you’re on your last kid and you’re really, really trying for something, read The Babydust Method.”
She’s one of many women on TikTok and elsewhere on social media who credit Babydust with helping them conceive a child of their preferred sex. Some acknowledge that the method is scientifically unfounded, while other posters are more credulous: In one video, Julie Wise, a mom of two in Massachusetts, said that it’s “not like a fact; I’m pretty sure it’s just like a theory,” but that she is nevertheless “kind of a believer.” In Wisconsin, a day-care owner and mom of four named Courtney Raspor said the method has something like a “90 percent success rate.” Some go a step beyond what the book recommends, into the realm of the woo: In Australia, Faye Briotti said that in addition to timing when she had sex, she also kept pink crystals and salt by her bed, and painted her nails pink. A woman named Reagan, who’d had two boys and was hoping for a girl, said that she got rid of all her baby boy clothes, “because I really wanted to put out into the universe that I wanted a girl.”
The rise of TikTok and other social-media platforms has given audiences ready access to folk-science life hacks of all kinds. People can now more quickly find vertical videos about scientifically suspect practices such as mouth-taping and cortisol-lowering than they can make a doctor’s appointment to address snoring or weight gain. Conceiving and carrying a pregnancy—high-stakes experiences that are full of uncertainty—seem to make some women unusually susceptible to dubious strategies.
Kathryn Taylor, the author of The Babydust Method, got the idea when she was preparing to conceive her first child. She wanted to see if she could increase her odds of having a boy—she thought her husband would be more excited about the baby if it was. She is not a medical doctor and doesn’t have a Ph.D.; she has a bachelor’s degree in microbiology, immunology, and molecular genetics, and now works in pharmaceutical sales. But she knew that an embryo’s sex is determined by the sperm that takes part in creating it: If the sperm carries a Y chromosome, the embryo will be a boy; if it has an X chromosome, the embryo will be a girl. And so she wondered if she could encourage a Y-bearing sperm to fertilize her egg.
She read studies about reproduction on PubMed, a medical database, and came away believing that, after a man and woman have sex, Y sperm undergo an activation process called capacitation faster than X sperm do, but that they also deteriorate sooner. Therefore, she posited, having sex as close as possible to the day the woman ovulates should give boy sperm the best chance of getting to the egg first. By the same logic, having sex a few days before ovulation would allow the boy sperm time to die off before the egg arrives, and increase the likelihood that an X sperm will fertilize the egg.
Sandra Carson, an ob-gyn and reproductive endocrinologist at Yale who has written about sex-selection efforts since the 1980s, and Michael Zinaman, a reproductive endocrinologist in New York, told me that X and Y sperm don’t move or activate at different rates, that one doesn’t live longer than the other, and that the timing or frequency of intercourse does not determine the fetus’s sex.
Taylor told me she was “100 percent” sure the method was going to work for her. As she writes in her author bio, she had “a boy first and a girl second, just like she planned.” She decided to write the book, she told me, after a few moms who had “three boys or whatever” asked her how she had managed to get one child of each sex, and after she shared her tips, she said, they were successful too. She set out to create a short, readable guide—the Kindle version of Babydust is 82 pages long—to help other women. Taylor has claimed that the method works about 87 percent of the time; more than 50,000 people now belong to a Babydust Method Facebook group, which requires proof of book purchase—$10 on Amazon—to join.
When I asked Taylor about Carson and Zinaman’s research, she stuck by her theory. She told me that doctors might not understand the method because they work with patients rather than researching sperm. (Carson has researched sperm extensively.) Taylor emphasized that she thinks a crucial difference between X and Y sperm is their capacitation, and even if that’s proved wrong, she said, it “doesn’t debunk the theory.” It would just mean, she believes, that male and female sperm are distinct in a way “that’s microscopic, that’s genetic, and it’s deep inside the cell.”
Attempts to naturally influence a baby’s sex have a long history. Hippocrates believed that having intercourse immediately after a woman’s period would increase the odds of conceiving a son; doing so “a good while” later, he thought, would favor a girl. In the 1960s, an ob-gyn named Landrum Shettles hypothesized that Y sperm are faster but more fragile, and that to conceive a boy, a couple should have sex as close to ovulation as possible. The following decade, a public-health researcher named Elizabeth Whelan proposed entirely different advice: that couples seeking to conceive a boy should have sex four to six days before ovulation. Babydust is the updated, Millennial-pink gloss on some of these old ideas. In her book, Taylor argues that although the essence of the Shettles method is correct, the science behind it was wrong.
The reality is that none of these ideas are proved to work, and neither is Babydust. At least, they don’t have a better success rate than the 50 or so percent chance a couple has of conceiving either a boy or girl anyway. Zinaman said that if techniques such as Babydust were sound, ob-gyns and fertility doctors would tell patients about them. But, he said, “we don’t have anything we can use to assist patients that way.” The only process that can guarantee having a boy or a girl is in vitro fertilization, which allows parents-to-be to choose the sex of the embryo that gets transferred into the mother. (American doctors are allowed, but not encouraged, to offer IVF for non-medically-necessary sex selection.)
This is now such settled science that the most recent definitive study on the topic is from 1995, when researchers recruited 221 women who wanted to become pregnant, tracked their hormones and dates of intercourse, and found that “the timing of sexual intercourse in relation to ovulation has no influence on the sex of the baby.” The author of that study, Allen Wilcox, who once led the Reproductive Epidemiology Group at the National Institutes of Health, told me that no further studies have been conducted about these methods because “you can’t get a paper published saying there’s no association, because every scientist knows that.”
One reason some people might believe that Babydust is worth trying, despite the lack of evidence, is that it offers a sense of control. All the stages of bringing a baby into the world—trying to conceive, being pregnant, delivering the child, caring for a newborn—can inspire magical thinking in some parents, precisely because so much is out of their hands. One study of hundreds of women undergoing fertility treatments found that 40 percent of them performed a good-luck ritual on the day of their procedure; another, of pregnant Jewish women in Israel, found that they scrupulously avoided buying baby furniture before the baby’s birth in order to avoid “tempting fate.”
When my son was still breech at 37 weeks of pregnancy—when most babies have already flipped into the head-down birthing position—my ob-gyn recommended a website of the most batty methods imaginable to get him to rotate. This is how I, a skeptical science writer, found myself standing on my head in a swimming pool one morning and having a “heart to heart” with my fetus about the importance of turning. (This did not work.) It doesn’t help that the first question people typically ask a mother-to-be—Are you having a boy or girl?—is something she has no power over.
Many Babydust adherents with whom I spoke and whose videos I watched didn’t seem to believe in Babydust as much as they wanted to believe in something. “People are hoping to alter fate,” Zinaman said, “and half the time it alters fate and they’re happy, and the other half, Oh well, it was never 100 percent anyway.”
It can’t hurt to try was something I heard often. Raspor, the Wisconsin day-care owner who used Babydust to conceive a girl, told me, “There’s no way to know whether it was the method or simply chance,” but, “I personally don’t see the harm in giving it a try, as long as you understand that there are no guarantees.”
At other points in history, and in certain cultures, many parents hoped for a boy rather than a girl. Today, though, that broad preference seems to have shifted. The Economist reported last year that American and some European couples who have a girl first are more likely to stop at one child than couples who have a boy first, and that adoptive parents are willing to pay a premium for a girl. Taylor told me that, according to nonrepresentative surveys she’s conducted, two-thirds of her method’s practitioners are hoping to conceive a girl. Thus, another factor likely playing a “huge role” in this trend is sex preference, Brittany Stahnke Joy, a social-work professor at East Tennessee State University, told me. Although precise numbers aren’t available, Stahnke Joy estimates that 30 to 40 percent of expectant parents at some point experience a strong desire for a certain gender and some sadness if they find out they’re having the other.
The women I spoke with seemed to sense that they’re not supposed to have sex preferences. Wise, the mom and content creator in Massachusetts, used Babydust when conceiving her daughter three years ago, after learning about it on a pregnancy-app discussion board. “Obviously, a healthy baby is the main goal,” she told me, “but we can’t deny that we do have preferences sometimes.” Kattula, the Michigan yoga teacher, expressed misgivings about the concept of trying to influence a child’s sex, even though she was pleased to be having a boy. “Is it effed-up to pick and choose what you think the gender of your kids should be?” she said. “I don’t know.”
A number of desires might motivate sex preferences and gender disappointment, Stahnke Joy said: With their child, a parent might hope to recreate themselves, or a relationship with their father or mother; or they might look forward to certain activities that they can imagine doing only with either a daughter or a son. Most of the time, she said, these feelings resolve once the baby is born, but “some people have a lot more children just to try to get the girl.”
This is partly why, as much as I know Babydust doesn’t work, I also understand wanting to believe. When I was pregnant, I initially wanted a girl. I thought girls were smarter and more verbal, their games were more imaginative, and they were better behaved, even though intellectually I realized this was not always true. I wanted to play Fairy Princess Unicorns instead of Garbage Trucks.
Two and a half years later, I do play an awful lot of Garbage Trucks. I sometimes get jealous when I see a toddler girl sitting patiently at storytime while my son, Evan, runs wildly around the room. But Evan has also upended some of my expectations about gender: He is very talkative, has a great sense of humor, and is extremely smart. He loves stories and singing, and even getting dressed up occasionally. I sometimes wonder if, had I gotten my wish and conceived a girl, my hypothetical daughter would have any of those traits or interests. I realize that I don’t care, because I love my son exactly the way he is. Maybe the true magic dust of parenthood is that your baby will surprise you, no matter what their sex turns out to be.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed making CCTV surveillance mandatory at licensed premises selling prescription drugs, as part of proposed amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945.
The draft notification, G.S.R. 791(E), issued on September 8, proposes inserting a new provision in Rule 65 requiring the supply of drugs on the prescription of a registered medical practitioner, other than through wholesale dealing, to take place under a CCTV surveillance system installed and maintained at the licensed premises. The recordings would have to be preserved for at least three months.
The proposal follows deliberations by the Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC) and subsequent consideration by the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB). The DCC had earlier recommended that CCTV cameras be made mandatory at medical stores and that they be positioned so that drug sales could be verified.
The move is aimed at strengthening oversight of the sale of prescription medicines and providing a mechanism to verify transactions in cases of suspected unauthorised sale. Under the existing Drugs Rules, medicines covered by Schedules H, H1 and X cannot be sold at retail without a prescription from a registered medical practitioner, with additional record-keeping requirements for certain drugs.
The draft, however, is not yet a final rule. The Ministry has invited objections and suggestions from affected persons and other stakeholders for 30 days from the date the Gazette was made available. The proposed rules will be considered after the expiry of this period.
The Ministry has said submissions may be sent to the Under Secretary (Drugs), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, U-6, Work Hall-C Wing, First Floor, Kartavya Bhawan-1, New Delhi, or emailed to drugsdiv-mohfw@gov.in.
“The draft does not merely propose CCTV for Schedule H, H1 and X medicines by name. Its wording is broader — it covers any drug supplied on a registered medical practitioner’s prescription, except wholesale transactions,” said a senior health official.

Reading for pleasure is linked to better mental health, greater empathy and a lower risk of dementia, Cambridge University scientists said on Tuesday.
As part of a National Year of Reading tie-up with the Queen's Reading Room, a charity founded by Queen Camilla to highlight the benefits of reading for pleasure at any age, the scientists argue that it doesn't matter what or how we read.
In a review published in 'Psychological Medicine', Professor Barbara Sahakian and Christelle Langley said reading for enjoyment can bring huge benefits and reading with others, whether it's as part of a book club or a parent reading with their children, can bring even greater rewards.
"Reading is a great way to support our brain health, develop important cognitive skills and boost our wellbeing. It's something we ought to be encouraging from an early age, given the increasing evidence of its benefits, particularly to children, but really, it's never too late to start, and it can bring benefits throughout our lives and into old age,” said Sahakian.
Some of the strongest evidence of the benefits of reading for pleasure comes from a study by Sahakian, Langley and colleagues of more than 10,000 young people, which found that children who began reading for pleasure in life showed benefits including: better attention, memory, and executive functioning, greater academic achievement, fewer mental health problems, and healthier lifestyles, including more sleep and less screen time. Langley said: "Given how beneficial reading for pleasure is at a young age, we should be doing everything we can to introduce children and young people to reading.
"The important thing is to find something they really enjoy – it might be a TV programme or a game – and use this as a way in. Reading comics and graphic novels could also be a helpful introduction as they might be seen as less intimidating, maybe less boring, than novels.”
In ‘Reading and associations with brain health, cognition, well-being, and mental health’ published this week, the experts draw on subjective surveys and objective studies using longitudinal, neuroimaging, and behavioural methods to highlight converging findings that link reading engagement with improved brain and mental health, better cognitive performance, and reduced risk of cognitive decline.
"Shared reading groups and book clubs appear to provide additional benefits through social interaction. They can help people feel less isolated and more connected to others, which has been shown to reduce the risk of dementia,” said Sahakian.
“While these clubs can be fun and beneficial at any age, they're perfect for older people who may be not so mobile – they might not be able to go out as an exercise group or a cycling group, but a reading group is something most people can enjoy,” she added.

Ferrari’s two-seat sports cars might be the brand’s identity, but the Italian automaker has always catered to customers who want to bring more than one passenger along for the ride. It started building cars with back seats in the 1960s with the 250 GT 2+2; as the name suggests, the second row was more for occasional use, something that was true all the way through to the 612 in the early 2000s. Ferrari followed with its first true four-seater, the all-wheel drive FF, which adopted “Breadvan” styling. Its first hatchback was still a three-door, though, and slightly more practical for carrying cargo rather than humans in the rear. That was true for the GTC4 that followed, too. But with the Purosangue, the rear passengers have been given something of an upgrade.
For one thing, there is an extra pair of doors, rear-hinged ones that provide direct access to the pair of rear bucket seats. There’s still a rear hatch, so this is technically a five-door. But there’s an immovable firewall between the cargo area and the passenger cabin, and the rear seats do not fold flat. So unlike the 21st century breadvans we have previously reviewed, a Costco run in the Purosangue might be possible, but you’re probably going to want a roof rack if you plan to go skiing, cycling, or anything else that requires bulky equipment. It’s also probably accurate that Ferrari says the Purosangue is not an SUV but an FUV—a Ferrari Utility Vehicle.
Underneath that long hood lives a 6.5 L naturally aspirated V12, but mounted back in the chassis such that this is technically a front-mid engined layout. That contributes to the 49:51 front-to-rear weight ratio, as does the use of a transaxle gearbox for the rear wheels (an eight-speed, dual-clutch box); a separate power transfer unit at the front of the engine drives the front wheels, for this is an all-wheel drive Ferrari. But make no mistake, it’s a substantial one, too, befitting that massive 715 hp (533 kW), 528 lb-ft (716 Nm) engine: 195.8 inches (4,973 mm) long, 79.8 inches (2,028 mm) wide, 62.6 inches (1,589 mm) tall, with a 118.1-inch (3,018 mm) wheelbase and a 4,784 lbs (2,170 kg) curb weight.

Despite that size, it doesn’t take very long for the car to shrink around the driver; earlier this summer, I spent a couple of hours driving another Purosangue around Rome on the eve of Ferrari’s Luce reveal, where it coped quite ably with millennia-old streets. It’s an easy car to drive slowly or in traffic despite its size and power output. The stop-start system works even from cold and is unobtrusive, and your speed is easy to modulate thanks to plenty of pedal travel for the throttle and an engine with sufficient torque that you’ll rarely see more than 2,000 rpm on the digital tachometer if you’re in Comfort mode and letting the eight-speed transmission shift for itself.
Which is something, considering the fact that the engine doesn’t redline until 8,250 rpm. You’ll probably want to be in Sport to experience that; it’s the most extreme of the Purosangue’s settings, for you won’t find a Race mode on the steering wheel-mounted manettino dial that toggles through drive modes, although you will find one for Ice instead. Regardless of the mode, you can choose to change gears for yourself using the large and tactile paddle shifters, either to temporarily override the auto function or in true manual mode, selectable via a switch on the center console, where you’ll also find reverse.
The steering is heavier than something like a 296 but still feels very direct, with good feedback of the road conditions as the front wheels are experiencing them. In Sport, you can feel the chassis control systems and the electronic differentials doing their thing to tighten your line if you’re steering and adding power at the same time. And because there are four seats, you can share the experience with three passengers: The squeals of delight from happy young neighbors getting their first ride in a Ferrari were a real high point of our time with the car.

Twist, tap, and swipe
The somewhat complicated UX, on the other hand…
At least the multifunction steering wheel uses actual physical buttons for most of its controls rather than the near-unusable capacitive touch version that we experienced in the 296. Real buttons that you can use without taking your eyes off the road make it possible to do things like control Apple CarPlay while on the move—this appears in the main instrument display directly in front of the driver, and in doing so replaces the digital Ferrari dash with its central tach. Things get more complicated when you want to adjust the seats or the climate, though.
You do this via a rotating controller that pops out of the dash, swiping or tapping its touchscreen display to select the temperature, fan speed, ventilation, or massage for each individual seat. Not so difficult while stationary, but considerably more difficult if you’re on the move, given the small size of the targets your finger needs to aim for. A second dial is found between the rear seats with the same functionality.

While there isn’t a central infotainment display, there is a full screen for the front-seat passenger. Because the screen is heavily polarized (or otherwise filtered), though, I couldn’t ever see what my passengers were doing with it. They can interact with the native media apps, but they can’t project CarPlay onto this screen.
Painted in lustrous Rosso Portofino paint that glittered in the August sun, the Purosangue was something of a head-turner; certainly more striking than the yellowy-green metallic example I drove briefly around Rome earlier this summer. But this is a Ferrari, and between the standard colors and various customization programs, like Atelier and Tailor Made, the sky (and your ability to pay) is the limit when it comes to exterior and interior finishes. It’s certainly a Ferrari you could daily-drive, although at 12 mpg combined (19.6 L/100 km) that is perhaps a better task for the battery-electric Luce. But it’s a good way of sharing a V12 with as many people as possible, and I reckon on the right tires it would make quite an effective winter car.
It’s a huge amount of money for a car, but the Purosangue does feel adequately special when you drive it or ride in it.

Starting at $393,350, a Purosangue is significantly less expensive than the EV Ferrari, although our test car’s $576,544 price tag gives you some idea of how quickly the options list can start to add up. It’s also a lot more than you would pay for similarly powerful SUVs from Ferrari’s traditional rivals, like the Aston Martin DBX or Lamborghini Urus, but that’s the way that Maranello likes it.

Srinagar, Sep 22: Jammu and Kashmir Bank will soon issue a recruitment notification for appointments to the posts of banking assistants and officers in Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh, J&K Bank Managing Director and CEO Amitava Chatterjee said on Tuesday.
Speaking at the bank’s 88th Annual General Meeting at SKICC in Srinagar, Chatterjee said the recruitment process was being taken up after 2021 and that the bank had completed negotiations and signed an agreement with the agency that would conduct the examinations.
“The bank will come out with a notification for recruitment for Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh. After 2021, the bank is going for a recruitment of both assistants as well as officers into the bank,” Chatterjee said.
He said the agreement with the examination-conducting agency had been finalised and the recruitment notification would be issued within a few days.
"The negotiations and the signing of the agreement with the agency which will conduct these examinations are over. Our bank will come out with a notification in a few days,” he said.
On recruitment outside Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, Chatterjee said the bank would broadly follow its earlier practice, with the possibility of hiring a limited number of employees based on local language requirements.
He said the bank has a presence in 22 states outside Jammu and Kashmir and requires employees with proficiency in local languages to serve customers in those areas.
“The bank may decide in future to hire only a few number of employees to support our existing staff strength, specifically on the language issue,” he said.(KNS)

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on Friday said it has initiated legal action against Nestle India Ltd for alleged non-compliance with food safety norms in three infant nutrition products.
According to FSSAI, it examined NAN Excella Pro Stage 1, Lactogen Pro 1, and a follow-up formula along with their promotional material available on e-commerce platforms.
In NAN Excella Pro Stage 1, the regulator flagged claims relating to "5HMOs" and "Whey Protein," while in Lactogen Pro 1, it observed a claim describing "Whey Protein" as easy to digest, the regulator said in a social media post.
FSSAI said it had sought clarifications from Nestle India on these claims.
Both the products were found to be in contravention of Regulation 4(2) of the Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020, which restrict promotional claims or material aimed at increasing the saleability of infant foods, as well as Section 3 of the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1992, which bars the advertisement or promotion of such products.
Separately, a sample of a follow-up formula manufactured by Nestle India was found sub-standard for Biotin content during laboratory analysis. The sample was sent for re-analysis, and the referral laboratory also found it non-conforming with the Biotin requirement prescribed under the 2020 regulations.
In light of these findings, FSSAI has filed three separate adjudication cases against Nestle India in respect of the three products, it added.
At 1.10 p.m., shares of Nestle India were down nearly 2% at ₹1,345.45 on the BSE.

The Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) government in Keralam on Tuesday (September 22, 2026) ordered a police inquiry into the politically charged CMRL-Exalogic payoff controversy centring on Leader of the Opposition and former Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan, his daughter T. Veena, and son-in-law and former Minister P.A. Mohamed Riyas.
Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala signalled to reporters that “legal prerequisites, and not politics” as alleged by the Communist Party of India (Marxist), shaped the government’s decision.
“In the Vijay Madanlal (Choudhary) versus the Union of India case, the Supreme Court ruled that law enforcement could not but act on the information shared on record by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) under Section 66 (2) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). Neither the government nor the police have any latitude in the matter as per the legal advice proffered by the Advocate General”, he said.
However, Mr Chennithala said the Supreme Court ruled in Lalita Kumari versus the State of Uttar Pradesh in 2013 that registering an FIR in a suspected commercial fraud or corruption case depends on whether the mandatory preliminary inquiry reveals a cognisable offence, tempering the demand for immediate registration of a case on the receipt of allegedly inculpatory third-party information.
“I conferred the matter with Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan. The government has tasked the State Police Chief (SPC) with deciding the nature of the preliminary probe and the investigating agency. The government will issue the requisite order soon”, he added.
Mr Chennithala refused to state whether the Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) or the State Police Crime Branch would conduct the preliminary inquiry. “That is the prerogative of the SPC”, he added.
When asked whether the impending inquiry would be preliminary, Mr Chennithala replied: “I can only state that there would be an inquiry”.
ED’s charges
The ED had charged that CMRL, a chemical company in which the Keralam government has a minority stake, had camouflaged backhanders to Mr Vijayan, when he was Chief Minister, as retainers to Ms Veena’s now-defunct software firm Exalogic Solutions during 2017-2021 for consultancy services allegedly not provided.
Last month, the ED had sent a 25-page report to the State Police Chief, Ravada Chandrasekhar, seeking Mr Vijayan’s prosecution under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1985 (PCA). The ED had also claimed in the report that it had confiscated a diary detailing the allegedly illicit financial transaction during a raid at Mr Vijayan’s house in Thiruvananthapuram in May.
Mr Vijayan had disputed the existence of any incriminating entries in the diary. At the same time, Mr Riyas maintained that the personal journal contained scribblings about Ms Veena’s business plans in the Gulf, which, he claimed, had yet to materialise.
At a press conference last week, Mr Satheesan flagged an allegedly inculpatory discrepancy between the two CPI(M) leaders’ statements. He also stated that the ED’s report contained serious allegations against the former Ministers.
