British Columbia has sued OpenAI in California, saying a mass shooting at a school in the province could have been prevented if the company had warned local law enforcement that the shooter had used ChatGPT to plan the massacre.
The lawsuit filed in San Francisco federal court on Monday names OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman, as defendants. It is seeking damages to fund recovery efforts in the province after the February attack, as well as an order directing changes to the way the company handles ChatGPT conversations that could lead to violence.
Nine people, primarily children, were killed in the school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia. The shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, had been flagged by the company’s safety team after her conversations about gun violence, but the company did not alert police.
Altman published a letter to the community saying he was “deeply sorry” OpenAI had not contacted law enforcement. He promised reforms, but never followed through, despite efforts from British Columbia’s attorney general to engage, the lawsuit says.
The school where the shooting took place is in the process of being demolished, and the province has been forced to absorb the costs of a replacement school, mental health care and other effects of the shooting, according to the lawsuit.
A spokesperson for OpenAI, Drew Pusateri, called the Tumbler Ridge shooting an unspeakable tragedy. “OpenAI remains committed to working collaboratively with government and law enforcement officials, and continuing to advance our ongoing safety work.”
British Columbia’s lawsuit comes after more than 30 family members of victims and others affected by the attack filed lawsuits in California, accusing the company of opting out of a chance to prevent the shooting.
Van Rootselaar shot her mother and stepbrother at home before killing an educational assistant and five students aged 12 and 13 at her former school on 10 February, according to police. Van Rootselaar, who was 18, then died by suicide.
Van Rootselaar’s interactions with ChatGPT were first flagged by the company in June 2025. Safety team members recommended contacting police, but Altman and other OpenAI leadership overruled them, the lawsuit says, citing OpenAI whistleblowers who spoke to the Wall Street Journal in the wake of the shooting.
The shooter’s account was deactivated, but she was able to get a new account and continue using the platform to plan her attack.
After publication of the Wall Street Journal article, the company said the account was flagged by systems that identify “misuses of our models in furtherance of violent activities”, but the issues did not meet its internal criteria for reporting to law enforcement.
The lawsuit comes after a series of cases against OpenAI have been filed in US state and federal courts in recent months over claims ChatGPT facilitated violence, including lawsuits related to a mass shooting at Florida State University last year.
In June, Florida became the first state to sue OpenAI over safety risks, accusing the company of misrepresenting the safety of its ChatGPT platform, which the lawsuit said had harmed children by providing information to school shooters, offering guidance on self-harm and addicting young users.
OpenAI, which has denied the claims, has said it trains its models to refuse requests that could “meaningfully enable violence”, and notifies law enforcement when conversations suggest “an imminent and credible risk of harm to others”.

President Donald Trump met New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani at Gracie Mansion on Monday, September 21, as the president arrived in the city ahead of the United Nations General Assembly. The meeting, held at the mayor's official residence in Manhattan, was the third face-to-face meeting between Trump and Mamdani and the first to take place in New York City. Their previous meetings were held at the White House, including one in November 2025 and another in February. Mamdani's office said ahead of the meeting that the discussion would focus on "issues affecting New York City and New Yorkers". The meeting was closed to the press, with Mamdani scheduled to speak to reporters afterwards. Trump was in New York for the UN General Assembly, where he is due to address world leaders on Tuesday. The timing brought the two leaders together as the city prepares for a week of high-level diplomatic meetings and heightened security. Housing and federal support have been central to the conversations between Trump and Mamdani since their first meeting. During his February visit to Washington, Mamdani raised the proposed redevelopment of Sunnyside Yard in Queens, a long-discussed project that could create thousands of homes over the existing rail yard. The mayor has said the project could deliver more than 10,000 homes and 30,000 jobs, although it would require significant investment and remains under discussion. Mamdani, a democratic socialist, campaigned against Trump, while the president has repeatedly criticised Mamdani and his policies. Yet their meetings since the 2025 mayoral election have generally included discussions about areas where they could work together. Trump has previously said the two share an interest in seeing New York succeed. Mamdani, meanwhile, has said his conversations with the president are centred on delivering for New Yorkers. Monday's meeting therefore placed a familiar question back in focus: whether their direct relationship can produce concrete federal support for the city while their political disagreements remain unresolved. The mayor's office had not announced specific agreements before the meeting. Paramount settles US states' antitrust lawsuit, clearing the way for its Warner Bros. acquisition
The mega-merger of the year will apparently go forward.
Paramount has overcome the biggest hurdle in its quest to acquire Warner Bros. The company has settled the antitrust lawsuit brought forth by 12 states, which was led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta, to stop the $11 billion merger. According to CNN, the announcement was made by Bonta at a press conference in Los Angeles today, and the deal is now expected to close in early October.
According to CNN, Paramount has agreed to an news editorial independence board that'll oversee CBS News and CNN itself and to commit to 30 theatrical movie releases a year. With the merger, Paramount chief David Ellison will be gaining control of the DC and the Harry Potter universes, among many other massive franchises.
The Writers Guild of America (WGA) also settled its lawsuit against the merger despite the fact that its objections remain. "Now that the Attorneys General have settled with Paramount, however, as a nonprofit, the WGA must contend with the reality of forging ahead alone, with no backing from government enforcers, with a complex antitrust lawsuit that would cost millions of dollars to pursue through trial," the WGA said in a statement. It notes that Paramount has agreed to "prohibit writer layoﬀs at CBS News Broadcast for 5 years, and to pay $17.5 million to our health fund along with our attorneys' fees in the litigation" as part of the settlement.
Despite the settlement, not all of the attorneys general are happy with this outcome. CNN says that several wanted stronger concessions, including CT Attorney General William Tong. "Connecticut wanted and demanded full divestiture of CNN and CBS News," he said in a statement released by his office. "We wanted to save ethical and independent journalism and news. We fought aggressively for that remedy. I am deeply disappointed that we could not do more. The complete abdication of the federal government's enforcement role in this fight left states with one arm tied behind our backs."
On Friday, the Wall Street Journal reported that Paramount was in advanced talks with Bonta to reach an agreement that would enable the purchase to push through. According to Politico, Paramount considered moving out of California if it couldn't reach a deal, leading Gov. Gavin Newsom and Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass to urge Bonta to settle the lawsuit. To note, regulators in the US, the DOJ and the European Union have already approved the merger, and this agreement pretty much seals the deal.

Of the 13 reported acts of kindness in the Facebook post, nine were true, mostly true or probably true.
Two of the claimed acts of kindness were false, and one was unproven. Lynne Patton, a former Eric Trump Foundation employee whom Trump appointed to roles in both of his presidential administrations, carried out one of the reported acts.
In September 2026, a Facebook post (archived) circulated online that listed 13 claimed "acts of kindness" that U.S. President Donald Trump purportedly carried out before running for office.
The introduction to the post read:
For thirty years before he ran for office, Donald Trump quietly paid mortgages, flew sick children across the country, and wrote checks to strangers who needed help. You will not find those stories on the evening news. So here they are.
Start with what people who knew him before politics say. He has never had a drink. He has never smoked. He has never used drugs. He built his business on long hours, and the people who worked for him will tell you he outworked all of them. Nobody called him a bigot until the day he announced for president. That timing tells you something about the accusation.
Now to the record.
The claim about Trump's reported acts of kindness spread on Facebook (archived, archived), X (archived) and Threads (archived). Snopes readers contacted us, asking if the claim was true.
Of the 13 reported acts of kindness in the Facebook post, nine were true, mostly true or probably true, two were false and one was unproven. One of the alleged acts was actually carried out by Lynne Patton, a long-time employee of the Eric Trump Foundation whom Trump later appointed to roles in both of his administrations.
Given the above, we rate this claim a mixture of true and false or unproven elements. Below, we investigate each claim in the post.
Annabel Hill's farm: True
In 1986, a Georgia widow named Annabell Hill was about to lose the family farm at a foreclosure auction. Trump saw her story on the news, picked up the phone, called the auction, and stopped the sale. Then he sent her the money to keep the farm.
Snopes investigated this claim in September 2026 and found it to be true. According to reporting at the time, Hill's farm had been up for auction twice. Her husband, Leonard D. Hill, died by suicide in February 1986 to try to save the farm using the payout from his life insurance. That sum did not cover the debts, and his widow faced a second auction that September.
That was reportedly when Trump stepped in, called the bank to block a foreclosure auction and started fundraising for Hill. The fundraising was successful, with Trump himself covering at least $39,000 of the $170,000 needed. Because of the fundraising efforts, Hill's family was able to keep the farm.
A private plane for Andrew Ten: True
In 1988, an Orthodox Jewish family in Los Angeles had a three-year-old son named Andrew Ten who needed treatment in New York. The boy could not survive without a full life-support setup, and no airline would carry it. His father asked Trump for help. Trump put the family on his own jet and got them there.
Snopes previously investigated this claim in 2015 and found it to be true based on a report published by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency in 1988 that said Ten's father had appealed to Trump for help transporting his ill son to access medical treatment in the New York area.
The Times of Israel later reported that Ten died in 1998. In 2014, the Securities and Exchange Commission fined Ten's father, Harold Ten, in an alleged scheme to "profit from the imminent deaths of terminally ill patients in nursing homes and hospice care."
Trump sent plane to fly Marines: False
In 1991, two hundred Marines came home from Desert Storm to Camp Lejeune and found out the military had no aircraft to fly them the rest of the way to Florida. Trump's airline, the Trump Shuttle, made two runs between North Carolina and Miami and got every one of them back to their families.
Snopes previously investigated this claim in 2016 and found it false. Though some Marines did fly from Miami to North Carolina on a Trump-branded plane after Operation Desert Storm in 1991, Trump did not own Trump Shuttle or its planes at the time because he had defaulted on the loans he used to buy the fleet. Rather, the military chartered some of the planes that still bore the Trump logo to fly the Marines without involvement from Trump.
A flat tire and a mortgage payment: False
In 1995, a passing driver in New Jersey pulled over to help change a flat on Trump's limo. Trump asked what he could do in return. The man only wanted flowers sent to his wife. A few weeks later, the story goes, the flowers came with a note saying the couple's mortgage had been paid off. People have been repeating that one for three decades.
This claim is an urban legend that Snopes first debunked in 1998. It has also circulated using other celebrities' names. According to an Aug. 15, 1997, report in the Toronto Globe and Mail, an assistant at Trump's New York office told the paper the story "isn't true."
Mar-a-Lago welcomed Black people and Jews: True
In 1996, Trump sued the town of Palm Beach, Florida. The town had been leaning on his Mar-a-Lago club for one reason. He let in Jewish members and Black members, and the older clubs did not. Abraham Foxman, who ran the Anti-Defamation League at the time, said Trump shined a light on the ugly side of Palm Beach that the glitter usually hid. Foxman also said other clubs started admitting Jews and Blacks after Trump forced the issue.
Snopes investigated a similar claim in 2016, finding it true that Trump allowed Black people and Jews to access Mar-a-Lago while other clubs in Florida did not. The Wall Street Journal reported in 1997 that after Trump sued Palm Beach alleging discrimination against his club because it admitted Black and Jewish members, other clubs had started to admit Jewish patrons.
However, the WSJ reported in April 1997 that Palm Beach denied it was discriminating against Mar-a-Lago because of its membership and that restrictions imposed on the club were part of a zoning matter. The outcome of the lawsuit was unclear.
Ultimately, Trump's decision to allow Jewish and Black members turned out to also benefit his business, helping him fight Palm Beach's restrictions and also allowing him to attract a different crowd than existing clubs already catered to.
According to the Wall Street Journal article, Foxman did speak the quote the Facebook post attributed to him, saying Trump "put the light on Palm Beach. Not on the beauty and the glitter, but on its seamier side of discrimination."
Money for a girl with brittle bone disease: True
In 2000, Trump was watching Maury Povich and saw a little girl named Megan who lived with brittle bone disease. He said her attitude got to him. He called the show and sent her family a large check.
According to a recording of a Dec. 19, 2000, episode of "Maury," the talk-show hosted by Povich, an 11-year-old girl named Megan and her mother received a check and video greeting from Trump.
The clip of the show Snopes viewed did not elaborate on Megan's illness or the exact size of Trump's check. During the clip, Trump called Megan "beautiful, inside and out" and told her to "keep up that attitude."
Povich, when handing over Trump's check to Megan, said Trump didn't give out "chump change" and referenced "all those zeros" but did not say the exact amount.
In 2020, to mark the 30th anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act, Trump's campaign shared a news release that highlighted several moments he reportedly supported Americans with disabilities. One of these highlights was about Megan and said she had brittle bone disease.
Jennifer Hudson stayed free at Trump hotel: Probably true
In 2008, Jennifer Hudson's mother, brother, and nephew were murdered in Chicago. Trump moved Hudson and her family into his Chicago hotel at no charge and had his security team watch over them while they grieved.
Snopes previously investigated this claim in 2016. E! Online reported on Oct. 31, 2008, that Hudson checked into the Trump International Hotel & Tower on Oct. 24, following the murder of her mother, brother and nephew by her former brother-in-law.
The outlet reported that Trump himself was paying for the stay, something Trump also told People magazine on Nov. 10. It was unclear how long Hudson stayed at Trump's hotel.
Hudson has never publicly refuted Trump's claim that he paid for her stay or named herself or anyone else other than Trump as having paid.
A check for bus driver who saved woman from suicide: True
In 2013, a Buffalo bus driver named Darnell Barton saw a woman standing at the edge of a bridge. He stopped the bus, walked over, put an arm around her, and talked her back to safety. Trump read about it and mailed Barton a check, because he thought a man like that deserved a reward.
Snopes found this claim to be true in 2016. A Buffalo radio station reported photos from a ceremony on Nov. 7, 2013, during which Barton received the $10,000 check (archived) that Trump had promised on social media after Barton's Oct. 18 rescue of an apparently suicidal woman he spotted while driving his bus.
Money for a Marine arrested in Mexico: True
In 2014, Marine Sgt. Andrew Tahmooressi spent seven months in a Mexican prison after he took a wrong turn at the border with legally owned guns in his truck. President Obama never placed the call to Mexico that the sergeant's family begged for. Trump sent Tahmooressi a check for $25,000 to help him rebuild his life once he got home.
Snopes previously investigated this claim in 2018. We found at the time that Tahmooressi was arrested after he crossed the Mexican border while carrying guns and ammunition that he legally owned in the U.S. — but wasn't permitted to carry in Mexico — and was imprisoned for seven months.
We could not substantiate his claims about abuse and mistreatment by Mexican authorities that also circulated at the time.
The House Committee on Foreign Affairs reported on Oct. 31, 2014, that Tahmooressi had been released from Mexican jail. Trump pledged (archived) on social media on Nov. 10, 2014, that he would send Tahmooressi a check for $25,000. We reported in 2016 that Trump made good on his promise the next day, writing to Tahmooressi:
You have served our country with fortitude and dignity, and we are fortunate to have someone like you as a brave Marine and protector of our wonderful nation. We are proud of you and I wish you and your family the very best for many years to come.
According to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs and reporting by the Los Angeles Times, Republican and Democratic politicians alike had pushed for Tahmooressi's release. Any involvement or lack thereof by then-President Barack Obama was unclear.
College money for beauty queen's son: True
In 2016, Melissa Young stood at a Trump rally in Wisconsin and cried while she thanked him. She had competed as Miss Wisconsin USA in 2005, then got sick with an illness that has no cure. During her worst stretch, a handwritten note arrived from Trump calling her the bravest woman he knew. She said the doors Trump opened for her ended up giving her Mexican-American son a full ride to college.
During a Trump campaign rally in Janesville, Wisconsin, on March 29, 2016, Young told the then-candidate that his organizations, including the Miss USA pageant and the since-defunct crowdfunding platform FundAnything.com, had helped secure her Mexican-American son a full ride to college.
Young, who competed as Miss Wisconsin in the Miss USA pageant in 2005, said she suffered from an incurable illness and that at one point when she was in hospital, Trump sent her a handwritten letter addressed to the "bravest woman I know."
In 2016, Snopes reported on Young's story and the open letter to Trump she posted on Facebook (archived) in July 2015. That letter explained that Miss USA 2005 Chelsea Cooley had started a fundraiser for Young's son after attending the launch of FundAnything.com, which would allow him a full ride to college.
It was unclear whether Trump personally paid anything into Cooley's fundraiser for Young's son. (The claim does not say specifically that he did.)
Young posted (archived) on Facebook in August 2026 that her son would be a high school senior that coming school year.
Lynne Patton's reply to claims Trump was racist: True
That same year, Lynne Patton, a Black executive at the Trump Organization, put out a video answering the people calling her boss a racist. She admitted she had fought addiction for years. She said the Trump family never pushed her out. They stood by her the whole way.
Patton, who was at the time the vice president of the Eric Trump Foundation, spoke at the July 20, 2016, Republican National Convention in Cleveland, Ohio. Before she took the stage, a five-minute video essay played in which Patton criticized "repeated and reprehensible" attempts to "align my boss and his family with racist hate-mongering groups campaigns and messaging" (time code 0:14).
Patton called the Trump family, "one of the most generous, compassionate and philanthropic families I've ever had the privilege of knowing" (time code 0:39).
Patton's video essay and following appearance did not include mention of addiction. This part of the claim may have come from her later media appearances. For example, in April 2025, Patton discussed her history with cocaine addiction with Lara Trump, Eric Trump's wife, on Fox News. During that interview, Patton also talked about how the Trump family had supported her through her addiction.
After Donald Trump won the 2016 presidential election, he appointed Patton to a role in the Department of Housing and Urban Development overseeing a region covering New York and New Jersey. During his second administration, Trump appointed Patton as deputy assistant to the president and director of minority outreach.
Patton previously served a suspension from government work for a violation of the Hatch Act, which regulates the partisan political activities of federal employees, during her time at HUD.
Cancer treatment for campaign volunteer's father: Mostly true
Also in 2016, a young Illinois volunteer named Shane Bouvet told reporters that Trump had stepped in to cover his father's cancer treatment. His father, Donald Bouvet, beat the cancer. Trump has stayed in touch with the family ever since.
Trump met with Bouvet and his father, Donald, on Feb. 9, 2018. The president said he had first read about Shane Bouvet in The Washington Post ahead of his January 2017 inauguration.
The Post reported at the time that Bouvet was a Trump supporter and volunteer social media coordinator for the Trump campaign in Illinois. The article noted that Bouvet's father had cancer and that Bouvet and his mother both faced layoffs and difficulties finding well-paid work.
Trump said in February 2018:
I said, "I'd like to meet him." Nice young man, had a lot of difficulty. And I gave him some money for himself — $10,000. His father, Donald — good name — was suffering and really on a pretty final path toward losing his life with cancer. Shane took the $10,000, and, rather than spending it on himself, he gave it to his father. And his father went to a very good cancer clinic or hospital because he was at hospitals before and they didn't do so well.
Trump continued:
And they did a fantastic job, and Donald is now cancer-free. And I think it's an incredible story where a son would give 100 percent of the money to his father, who he loves, obviously.
As such, though Bouvet ended up spending Trump's money on cancer treatment for his father, Trump suggested that was not how he intended the money to be spent when he gave it to Bouvet. It was unclear whether Trump remained in contact with the Bouvet family at the time of this writing.
Loans to Black entrepreneurs: Unproven
And there is a story that has floated around New York business circles for years. A Black business owner could not get a loan anywhere in the city. Someone told him to go see Trump. Trump lent him the money and told him to pay it back when he could. The man came back later with a check and said the business was doing well. Trump tore the check up.
Snopes could not determine the source of this rumor. An oft-cited source was the Joe Brown, a former TV judge, who appeared on a podcast in 2019. When asked on the podcast whether Trump was a racist, Brown said (time code 1:07:43):
I don't think so. I have talked to a number of Black entrepreneurs who, back in the late '80s and '90s were, early '90s, were trying to get financing. They couldn't. Somebody told them to go check with Donald Trump. So they come back and tell me they got a loan from Donald Trump. He gave him a term loan: Show up with the interest in the principal [unintelligible] but they had to go see him in person. They independently relayed this tale that when they saw him he said, "That's what you're supposed to pay me, this is our agreement?" say "Yeah," and then tore the check up, shook their hands and "Congratulations, now run your business."
We found no evidence that Trump, his campaign or individual business owners had ever publicly confirmed giving or receiving such loans. We attempted to contact Brown to ask if he could put us in contact with Black business owners who received loans from Trump in the early 1990s. We also contacted the Trump Organization to ask about the rumor. We await replies to our queries.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report

'I've asked for forgiveness' - Eckert and Southampton braced for Spygate verdict
- Published
More than four months since the Spygate scandal erupted, Southampton manager Tonda Eckert's wait to discover his fate for authorising an espionage campaign is almost over.
In the coming days, a decisive Football Association hearing will take place, after the German coach was charged with misconduct in July.
Spying on three clubs has already cost Southampton the chance of promotion to the Premier League (worth £200m), after they were expelled from the Championship play-off final. An EFL panel also docked the club four points for this season.
Now Eckert could be banned.
As the club prepared for the latest twist in the saga, BBC Sport spoke exclusively to both Eckert and Southampton chief executive Phil Parsons, who - in his first interview on the case - insists any further punishment would be "really tough to take".
But how are the club and their coach dealing with the prospect of more turmoil? What is at stake? And why have Southampton given a permanent role to the intern who was caught spying on Middlesbrough in May?
'It's been a big, big punishment'
"I would lie if I say that the summer has just been easy. Of course, if you care deeply about your profession, about the football club, there's nothing that prepares you for that. There just isn't."
Eckert speaks slowly and with an intense gaze when asked to reflect on being at the centre of one of the biggest controversies in English football history.
The 33-year-old apologised in June after an EFL independent disciplinary commission found he had orchestrated a "contrived and determined plan" to spy on Oxford United, Ipswich Town, then Middlesbrough before the play-off semi-final.
Having insisted he was unaware it breached EFL rules, and that the spying had no impact on performances, Eckert was backed by Southampton.
His team have made an encouraging start to the new season. Without the four-point deduction, they would be fourth in the table, rather than 13th.
"We've talked a lot over the summer of how we want to go through that process of addressing everything, giving everyone the chance to put questions out that are still there, to put out what they feel and have gone through, and then also close the door and move on," he says.
"Because the reality is it's a new season. We have big ambitions as a football club, and in order to reach them, we need to move on."
That is easier said than done, with Eckert in limbo while he awaits the outcome of the FA's disciplinary process.
"I've had the chance to sit down and just talk the FA through everything that happened," he says. "And now it's up to them to make a decision. I don't really have any emotions towards that."
So does he feel the FA has listened to him during its investigation?
"That was my impression," he says. "We sat for almost four hours, so it's been quite a long conversation."
When asked whether he feels the club has been punished enough, and if a suspension for him would be excessive, Eckert chooses his words carefully.
"It's been a big, big punishment," he says. "Absolutely unheard of in the history of sports.
"And it's tough for me to say that because it concerns me. I'm judging on myself, not an outside situation. But I've asked for forgiveness for what I've done. I've apologised publicly.
"I think the punishment has been very hard on the club for the last season. And to go into a new season on minus four. And the rest is not for me to decide."
- Southampton owner will not sack head coach Eckert 
  - Published2 June
'We've taken enough'
Parsons is more forthright on whether the club has been punished enough.
"We don't know what the FA will actually hand out," he says. "It could be a long ban. It could be a short ban. It could be a suspended sentence.
"What we hope as a club is they actually recognise where we are at the moment, and what we've already been through, because I think it has to be taken into account. I really feel like we've taken enough. We've been hurt. I think it's one of the largest sanctions ever when it comes to football, or even sporting, history.
"This isn't just about the club, this is about people. We lose money not being in the Premier League, but [local] businesses lose money. We had to spend a huge amount on legal fees, and it really impacts the club even further. We don't want to be seen as a victim of this. We need to get on. We've had our cards dealt."
When it is put to Parsons that the EFL's punishments applied to the club - rather than Eckert himself - he says: "I think it's impossible to sanction the manager without the club getting hurt even more."
The most recent precedent for this case came at the 2024 Olympics women's tournament, when Fifa banned Bev Priestman - Canada's head coach - from all football for a year, after opponents New Zealand were spied on.
Parsons insists "the Canadian case is very different" but if Eckert , who is only contracted until the end of the season, is also banned, how long would it have to be for the club to look elsewhere for a new coach?
"We don't know," he says, firmly denying having approached other coaches in case Eckert has to leave. Parsons also says the club may appeal if the ruling goes against them.
"We can't worry about something we can't control at the moment," he says. "We have to deal with it when we get there but we're hoping that they look at it sensibly."
Parsons says the club's ownership "want" to back Eckert.
"We've been through an entire transfer window when it comes to recruiting players for Tonda, and that's another challenge.
"We have to be looking at all scenarios. We've always spoken about any punishment being disproportionate...You're looking for fairness in approach. And have we had that treatment to us, from a disproportionate punishment? Well, I think a lot of people will view it that way. But do we want to sit there moaning about it? No.
"But it's going to be really tough to take if we get another punishment, on top of being thrown out of the play-offs, four points this season, and potentially more. So we're really hoping that the FA, the panel, are looking as this with a balanced view to what's already happened, because it's been really heavy."
'A lot of people would have cracked'
When compared to the £10m fines that both the FA and Premier League handed Chelsea this year for making £47m in secret payments related to transfers across several seasons when they were owned by Roman Abramovich, some would agree Southampton have suffered enough.
Others however, would say the FA has little choice but to sanction Eckert.
After all, according to the EFL commission, the club employed "a particularly deplorable approach" by using junior members of staff to conduct the spying "at the direction of senior personnel".
An arbitration panel then detailed how a junior analyst intern said he felt under "extreme pressure".
Southampton's initial response to the crisis also contained "inaccuracies". Middlesbrough's head of football Kieran Scott said the club's behaviour had been "disgusting"., external
Parsons shrugs off such criticism.
And when it is put to him that many expected Southampton to sack Eckert, and had they done so they would not be facing the current uncertainty, he replies: "Yeah, but Tonda also picked up the team in around 20th place in the Championship, and without him and his team we wouldn't have been in the play-off positions, and I think that deserves a bit of loyalty.
"OK, he has made a mistake and he's paid for that dearly. This has been really tough for him as a person already. I admire how strong he's been through this process because a lot of people could have cracked, the amount of pressure he was under."
For his part, Eckert says he is "very grateful for the support of the club because that could have been very different, and I think in most cases would have been very different".
The vast majority of Southampton fans that BBC Sport spoke to also seem to fully back the manager, something he says "means everything" to him.
Why hire the intern who spied?
Another to be supported is the intern involved - Will Salt - who was recently handed a permanent role as an analyst in the club's academy.
The scandal began when a photograph was published of Salt secretly filming Boro from behind a tree at their training ground before the play-off semi-final.
"He's been through a tough time," says Parsons.
"When your photo is put out to the public, that is something tough to deal with. A lot of people probably underestimated how that could have impacted a young lad so we've got a job to make sure that he's looked after in his early career. But he's a talented boy as well. I get good feedback and he's got a good role at the club."
Asked if reintegrating Salt had been challenging, given his allegations about the way he was treated, Parsons says: "I don't think Will said he felt under pressure directly from Tonda himself. He felt under pressure in the situation. And everybody knows in a job you can feel under pressure.
"But, yeah, I think Will's managed himself really well, and he'll grow from this."
So has the club learned its lessons? Parsons insists Eckert has studied the EFL's regulations, but also argues the rules could be clearer.
"They're very grey - that's something I'll continue to raise in EFL meetings," he says.
"But look, we've done something wrong, we'll get on with it."
Moving on is not easy, though. Last week, Wrexham's owners aimed a dig at Southampton by referencing the scandal in a social media advert before the two teams met. And during matches, rival fans regularly remind the club of the scandal.
"History is history and it'll be a part of our story going forwards," says Parsons. "It's about how we react now. It's given us a real togetherness and hopefully that continues through the season because we're stronger like that anyway.
"There's a bit of siege mentality as well, right - of 'everybody's against us', so we've got to embrace it."
The Championship has now paused until next month for the international break.
By the time Southampton next play - against local rivals Portsmouth on 11 October - Eckert should have learned his fate.
For now, however, his future remains uncertain.

U.S. shouldn't buy 'blood potash' from Belarus, Sask. premier says
Moe defends Sask. potash in post aimed at Trump's latest trade threat
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe defended the province's potash industry as ethically and economically superior to other international exporters after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to source more of his country's fertilizer from Belarus.
"Buying blood potash from Belarus is supporting Russian aggression," Moe said in a post on social media. "It’s wrong and it doesn’t make sense."
Moe's post on Monday afternoon was a response to a Trump social media post from earlier that day.
"The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus," Trump said on Truth Social. "The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers."
Potash is mainly used in fertilizers. In 2024, almost a third of the world's potash production came from Canada and all of the country's 10 active potash mines are in Saskatchewan, according to Natural Resources Canada.
"More than 40 countries — Canada and its allies — have sanctions against Belarus for supporting war criminal Putin’s invasion of Ukraine," Moe said in his social media post.
"Does anyone believe Belarusian blood potash shipped through Russia is going to be more affordable, more sustainable or more ethical than potash shipped from Saskatchewan — right here in North America?"
Nutrien Ltd., The Mosaic Company, Compass Minerals, and K+S Potash Canada are responsible for all of Canada's potash production. BHP is building the Jansen potash mine in Saskatchewan and expects to start commercial production in mid-2027.
Nutrien is the largest potash fertilizer producer in Canada and one of the largest in the world. The Saskatoon-based company referred CBC to Fertilizer Canada when asked to comment on Trump's post.
U.S. farmers have used Canadian potash for decades, said Fertilizer Canada, an industry trade group, in an emailed statement to CBC News.
"Reliability, proximity, transportation infrastructure, product availability and the ability to deliver during critical application windows all matter," the statement said.
"A strong and integrated North American fertilizer supply chain helps support farm productivity, affordability and food security on both sides of the border.”
Last year, Nutrien announced plans to build a potash export terminal at the Port of Longview, Wash., to handle expected growth in international demand for its fertilizer products.
The opposition NDP called Trump's social media post "infuriating" in a statement on Monday.
"He is looking at signing a deal with an authoritarian Russian satellite state that is supporting Putin’s brutal war against the people of Ukraine," the NDP statement said.
"This is a bad idea that will only hurt families and communities on both sides of the border."

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Meta's new personal AI agent, Muse, gives Mark Zuckerberg another chance to build the kind of technology platform he has chased for years.
Muse jumped to the top of the App Store last week and remained the most downloaded free app on Monday, beating ChatGPT.
If enough people use Muse as their main way to get things done online, developers could flock to the nascent platform, and businesses may have little choice but to engage with it.
Meta surged 11% on Monday, getting the stock within striking distance of a record it hit last summer. Investors appear to be betting the company has found a new way to sit between consumers and the businesses trying to reach them.
This broad idea has been driving Zuckerberg for years.
Meta spent tens of billions of dollars trying to build the next major computing platform through virtual reality and, more recently, smart glasses. Part of that ambition came into focus in 2021 when Apple made it harder for Meta to track people across apps and target ads, reminding Zuckerberg how much power platform owners have over companies that depend on them.
Developers invited
Muse offers a different path. Its swift climb up the app charts gives Meta the kind of early consumer momentum that attracts developers.
Last week, the company opened Muse to outside developers through a new connector platform that lets businesses plug their services directly into the AI agent. Those connectors help Muse do useful work on a person's behalf. A travel service can book flights. A calendar app can manage appointments. An email service can send messages.
Developers can create their own Muse connectors and submit them to Meta's agent platform for review. No coincidence: The company describes this in very similar terms to how Apple guards its mobile platform.
"We'll review your connector for functional, security, and legal requirements, and complete end to end testing," Meta wrote on the Muse developer website. "Once approved, users will be able to find your connector in Muse. Editors will review connectors for featured placement."
Adding to the allure for developers: On Monday, Shopify announced support for shopping on Muse through its Shop Pay service, sparking a jump in Shopify stock. Meanwhile, Stripe is providing the payment technology that lets Muse complete purchases across much of the web.
Top of the funnel
The platform strategy is tried and true, but difficult to pull off. If millions of people begin asking Muse to shop, book appointments, compare products, and manage subscriptions, businesses will increasingly want their services available through the agent.
That is how internet platforms become valuable. By controlling the starting point of online activity — the top of the funnel — they can become very powerful and lucrative.
Google Search is one of the most profitable businesses in internet history because it became the starting point for finding information online and taking valuable actions afterward. Apple's App Store became indispensable because developers wanted access to hundreds of millions of iPhone users.
In both cases, businesses adapted because that was where the customers were. Meta hopes Muse can become a similar starting point.
"Being early could be as valuable as being early to the App Store in 2009," tech entrepreneur Greg Isenberg wrote on X. "Every business will need an agent strategy, just like every business needed a mobile strategy."
He thinks Muse connectors could become "the new app listings," with businesses competing for visibility inside AI agents instead of app stores or search results.
In that world, a company's API could become more important than its app because AI agents, not people, would increasingly decide which services to use, he explained.
Amazon blocks, Shopify embraces
Whether Meta gets there is far from certain. Amazon has already blocked Muse from parts of its shopping site, showing that some companies may resist handing customer relationships to another tech giant.
That's a stark contrast to Shopify's reaction to Muse. And it shows the potential risk of not engaging with a potential new platform like this.
If millions of users embrace Muse, Amazon could miss out on selling to this large customer base. For instance, Amazon could just as easily block Google Search from its online store, too. But it doesn't because Google is used by billions of consumers to search for products.
"If Instacart embraces agents while Amazon blocks them, the agent will increasingly route demand to Instacart. Customers will be happy, and Amazon will eventually face the dilemma: keep protecting the relationship, or match the better value proposition," Nicolas Bustamante, who works on AI at Microsoft, wrote on X.
Muse also has competitors that could grab this new spot at the top of the funnel. OpenAI, SpaceX, and others are racing to build AI agents that become consumers' default assistants.
Still, Muse may represent Zuckerberg's clearest opportunity yet to build the kind of platform he has been pursuing for years.
If AI agents become the primary way people get things done online, owning a leading agent platform could prove every bit as valuable as owning a mobile operating system or a search engine.

A construction mishap affecting air traffic control equipment in New Jersey on Monday caused chaos for travelers flying through the Northeast.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the equipment outage was caused after a construction crew "accidentally cut into a fiber line." In an update shared around 6 p.m., Duffy said the lines had been fixed and that all impacted airport operations were resuming.
"It will take some time to clear all existing delays, so please check with your airline for the latest information," Duffy said.
New Jersey's Newark Liberty International Airport was put under a ground stop at around 10 a.m., when a nearby air traffic control center experienced an equipment outage, forcing the Federal Aviation Administration to halt inbound flights.
The outage also affected Philadelphia and New York's JFK and LaGuardia airports, with hundreds of flights delayed, diverted, or canceled. Newark has been hit hardest, with more than 500 departing and arriving flights canceled — nearly half of all scheduled operations — and over 200 delayed.
LaGuardia and JFK have seen 20 and 16 flight cancellations, respectively, with over 400 flights delayed at each. About 180 flights have been canceled in Philadelphia, with another 386 delayed.
As of Monday at around 7 p.m., LaGuardia and JFK were still under ground delays due to the equipment outage, while Newark and Philadelphia were no longer under delay.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told CBS News around 1 p.m. that the primary circuit, which was old and due for replacement, failed, and that about 600 feet of the backup fiber was accidentally cut out by a construction crew.
The affected ATC facility was the Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach Control, or TRACON, which manages arriving and departing aircraft in the area.
Duffy said earlier on Monday that an "Amtrak construction crew" cut the fiber line, causing the outage. Amtrak told Business Insider that the "incident occurred on New Jersey Transit property and involved a New Jersey Transit contractor," not Amtrak.
New Jersey Transit confirmed to Business Insider that a construction crew working near the line "accidentally" cut the fiber-optic cable, but said they were working about 10 feet from the markings indicating the location of underground utilities.
"NJ TRANSIT staff is currently on site working to determine the status of the repairs, while also determining whether it was Verizon or the contractor who made the utility markings at the site," a spokesperson said earlier on Monday. "Thirty-six out of the 56 fiber cables are done. They should be coming back online shortly. The rest should be done and tested shortly."
Flightradar24 shows that several Newark-bound flights were diverted to destinations such as Pittsburgh and Detroit due to the ongoing outage. A United flight from Bogota to Newark diverted halfway through to Orlando. Flights from Europe on Lufthansa and Swiss were seen turning around over the Atlantic.
Verizon told Reuters that it was their fiber cable, but that it was not their technicians who cut it. "We immediately deployed our technicians to the scene," a spokesperson said. "We and our partners are actively working to repair the damaged cable and restore connectivity as quickly as possible."
While the line has been repaired, it's unclear how long the disruptions will last. It's also unclear if airlines — who would not be considered at fault for the disruptions — will offer any accommodations or compensation for those stranded.
Flyers should continue to monitor their flight status, and those who booked with travel credit cards may have options for delays or trip reimbursement.

'Real fear Littler could walk away' - darts would be loser in booing row
- Published
At just 19, Luke Littler has won almost every major trophy in darts.
He is a multi-millionaire with lucrative sponsorship deals and his own TV show.
But has his rapid rise turned some against him?
This past weekend the teenager was once again subjected to boos and whistles from sections of the crowd as he took to the stage at the World Series of Darts in Amsterdam.
What is surprising though is that it came as 'The Nuke' was on a quest to complete a darts clean sweep by becoming the first player to win all 10 major televised tournaments in a calendar year.
Littler suggested afterwards that, if the booing continues, he will not attend events held in the Netherlands.
But Samuel Gill, editor of Dartnews.com, suggests Littler's future in the sport could be at stake.
"There's a real fear that within a few years he'll just turn around and walk away from the sport," Gill told BBC Sport.
"So, I think for fans, 'Don't bite the hand that feeds you'. If people keep taunting him and don't want him to win, he might end up just walking away and not bothering anymore."
Amsterdam was the latest tournament where Littler has faced what some might describe as an overly hostile reaction from fans.
A vibrant pantomime-style atmosphere is part and parcel of the darts experience and Dutch and German crowds are amongs the most raucous - but it is clear Littler believes he has been unfairly targeted.
The referee stopped the match during his narrow win against Nathan Aspinall in the last-16 on Saturday to warn the hostile crowd about its behaviour, before play resumed.
It followed Littler also being booed during his win against home favourite Danny Noppert on Friday.
The teenager's quarter-final defeat to Jonny Clayton ended Littler's quest for the clean sweep, but the Warrington native clearly felt fans had been unduly harsh towards him.
Littler has now withdrawn from a series of upcoming events.
"Just no point in me travelling, wasting my time while I'm getting booed," said Littler.
'Not a unique experience for Littler'
Littler has also been jeered at numerous events in the UK.
His phenomenal rise saw him reach the PDC World Darts Championship aged just 16 in his debut year as a professional.
He captured the title the following year and the trophies, sponsorship deals and six-figure winners' cheques have continued to flow.
But increasingly so have whistles and boos during his performances.
"I don't think people expected him to reach the heights that he has so quickly," Gill said.
The darts journalist - who became aware of Littler when the sport star was 14 - says this level of attention is not just unique to the British player.
"Michael van Gerwen was the same for a long time when he dominated the sport. He barely lost a game in about five years, and he was hoovering up titles for fun and it was similar," said Gill.
"Everyone wanted to boo him and even me as a viewer before I got into this role, growing up watching Van Gerwen, I wanted him to lose because it's something different for the sport every single week."
Currently ranked number one in the world, Littler is so far ahead of his closest rivals that he already has the advantage of only having to play in selective tournaments.
His boycott threat could end up being a blow to tournament organisers.
"They don't like him because he's that good. And he's got a bit of swagger to him," said Karl Holden secretary of St Helen's Darts Academy - where Littler honed his skills from the age of nine.
"Luke's got a bit of a character to him. For me, he's the ultimate professional. He might give a little bit of the large sometimes, but you need that, otherwise darts would be totally boring."
Darts the loser if Littler walks away
It seems remarkable that the future of Littler's career in the sport is even being debated.
More so when you consider his age and the fact he only turned professional two years ago.
However, Gill believes that Littler's rapid haul of trophies, coupled with the huge amounts of money now in the sport, could result in the teenager leaving in the next "four to five years" should the boos and whistles continue.
Gill believes Littler's impact on the darting world is immeasurable.
Tickets to events featuring him are often sold out, applications to darting academies are reported to be at an all-time high and the Briton has transcended the sport.
Gill therefore feels that, if Littler was to walk away, the sport would be the real loser.
"He's the one who is bringing this sport to a completely different level. Nowadays, he is back-page news wherever you go," Gill said.
"He might just decide 'I just want a quiet life now and just live off his money'."
Littler has barely known anything other than winning. His challenged now is maintaining that victorious streak while keeping fans - whose interest helps fund his prize money - happy.
Tricky when some are paying with the hope of seeing him lose.
"If he was on that stage, everybody liked him and he just threw darts, I think I'd get bored of watching him," Holden said.

Drugs called orexin agonists have been hailed for their ability to treat rare sleep disorders, but with new data, Alkermes is showing for the first time that the new class of therapies may benefit people with ADHD.
In a randomized Phase 1 study, the company’s new drug, called ALKS 7290, was well tolerated and showed a signal of efficacy, Alkermes said Monday.
Participants in the study started with a median score of 39 on a diagnostic known as the Adult ADHD Investigator Symptom Rating Scale, indicating that they had moderate to severe symptoms. After two weeks, those taking a high dose of 50 milligrams of ALKS 7290 experienced a 19-point reduction on the scale, indicating that their symptoms had become mild.

India-New Zealand FTA to come into force on October 20, Piyush Goyal says
The pact, he said, also facilitates significant investments of USD 20 billion over the next 15 years from New Zealand to India.
The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement will come into force on October 20, a move which will help boost bilateral trade and investments between the two countries, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on Monday.
The agreement, which was signed on April 27, provides duty-free access for 100 per cent of India's exports to New Zealand right from the entry into force of the pact, he told reporters here.
The pact, he said, also facilitates significant investments of USD 20 billion over the next 15 years from New Zealand to India.
"We are taking forward the next important milestone in our bilateral economic partnership, the entry into force of the India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement, which will come into force on the auspicious occasion of Dussehra on 20th of October, 2026, reflecting our shared commitment to build a stronger and a more ambitious economic partnership with New Zealand," Goyal said.
Also Read | India-New Zealand trade deal passes in NZ parliament; 95% of exports to get tariff cuts
He added that the pact also establishes an agricultural productivity partnership whereby New Zealand's technology will meet India's scale and growing demand.
For New Zealand, the agreement will provide preferential access to the large and fastest growing economy of the world, he said. New Zealand has committed to invest USD 20 billion over 15 years in India.
Currently, New Zealand maintains peak tariffs of up to 10 per cent on key Indian goods, including ceramics, carpets, automobiles and auto components. 
"Looking forward, our immediate priority should be to ensure that the provisions of the agreement immediately translate into tangible benefits for businesses and people of India and New Zealand...Together, let's ensure that this FTA becomes a strong foundation for a deeper, more dynamic and mutually beneficial economic partnership between our two countries," he said.
The minister added that sensitive sectors like dairy, onions, chickpeas, peas, corn, almonds, artificial honey and sugar have been kept out of the trade deal.
New Zealand Trade Minister Todd McClay said that this is a high quality agreement that will deliver significant benefits for the citizens of the two countries.
He added that at a time of global economic uncertainties, the pact would give confidence to business communities of the two countries.
Further Goyal said that the duty free entry of Indian goods will provide an edge over goods of competitor nations in the Wellington market.
The USD 20 billion FDI commitment "will give capital to many of our manufacturing sectors, along with technology", Goyal said, adding that New Zealand companies will also be attracted to India to invest.
On ways to promote investments from New Zealand into India, he said, "We are looking at a specific desk which will look into the India-New Zealand partnership."
Both sides are aiming at doubling bilateral two-way trade in goods and services to NZ dollar 7 billion (about ₹35,000 crore) by 2030. In 2025-26, the bilateral trade stood at USD 1.1 billion.
Sectors that power livelihoods across the country – textiles and apparel, leather and footwear, gems and jewellery, engineering goods and processed foods – stand to gain immediately as New Zealand's peak tariffs of up to 10 per cent are eliminated.
Indian manufacturers will also benefit from tariff-free access to critical inputs such as wooden logs, coking coal and metal scrap, sharpening their competitive edge in global markets.

I saw Meta’s latest app, Muse, cross-promoted on another Meta-owned platform, Instagram, and decided to download the AI assistant.
“Hand off everyday tasks like finding deals, booking reservations, and managing your inbox,” the pop-up read. “Muse keeps working while you get on with your day.” It’s free to use, and easily connects to other data sources, like my email and bank account. Muse’s default avatar is a beige-colored cross between an Ewok and a Labubu, with its arms outstretched, presumably to scoop up all my data.
Meta’s Muse is a mainstream version of AI agents already popular in Silicon Valley for automating personal tasks, like OpenClaw and Instinct. It’s a hit for the company: the Muse app has been downloaded over 900,000 times in its first week, according to Sensor Tower. The user experience is less like prompting a chatbot, and more like texting a friend with task requests—the AI agent acknowledges messages with a thumbs-up emoji and gets to work in the background. Muse is also available through Meta’s WhatsApp platform.
But after a few days with Muse, I’m convinced this AI tool is more obsessed with collecting data about me than actually getting stuff done.
“Muse is the first personal AI agent built for everyone, with built-in protections and user controls that put people absolutely in charge of how they use it—any suggestion we didn’t build with that in mind from the beginning is ludicrous,” Meta spokesperson Emil Vazquez tells WIRED.
Good Clicks
Muse’s ability to surf the web is genuinely impressive. When you ask it to complete a task, Muse uses a “virtual machine” to browse the internet on your behalf, running searches and clicking around on different web pages. When I tested similar tools last year, like the now-defunct ChatGPT Agent, the AI’s clicks were erratic and error-filled. Muse rarely seems to get lost while browsing.
For example, I asked Muse to order breakfast from a local bakery called Kahnfections. It’s a popular spot for tourists visiting San Francisco, so I requested one of the most-purchased options for pick-up. Muse visited the bakery’s website and added a biscuit sandwich with garlic aioli, cheddar cheese, egg, and bacon to my cart.
I was asked to add a credit card via the Stripe payment processor so my agent could complete the purchase. “One tweak the site forced: cheese is single-select, so I picked cheddar and left a note asking them to add Swiss too if they can,” read Muse’s explanation of the breakfast order when it asked for my final approval. Notably, Muse selected the “no tip” option. A bit rude! (I ended up walking down to the shop, ordering something random and delicious.)
Meta relies on its sprawling kingdom of platforms to get the word out about Muse. WhatsApp and Messenger for easy onboarding and integrations; prime placement on Instagram, with a large library of Reels videos for agents to search through. But the Facebook Marketplace tie-in was where Muse impressed the most in my testing. Muse quickly found cheap, local couches for sale within my parameters and offered to message sellers to arrange pick-ups. The agent is designed to follow up with users, so Muse nudged me the next day to consider getting the couch I said was my favorite.
Muse stores details about your interactions and preferences in a “Memory” document found by tapping the avatar in the top middle of the screen. “Your curated long-term memory: durable facts, preferences, and commitments,” the description in Muse reads. While you can send a chat request for Muse to wipe memory data and you can manually edit the file, Meta doesn’t currently offer a toggle to turn off the memory feature altogether.
Data Collector
Under the app’s “ideas” tab, Meta’s Muse constantly reminded me to connect more information to the agent. The day after I said I wanted help saving money for a fancy vacation, Muse offered to “wire your savings tracker to your real balance” if I just tapped a few buttons and linked the data from my checking and savings accounts. “Then the weekly summaries and drift alerts work off real numbers instead of hand-entered estimates,” it said.
This experience, where Muse offered further personalization in exchange for more data, was emblematic of my overall impression of the app.
“Folks don’t recognize that when you talk to an AI, you are talking to the company hosting the AI,” says Rory Mir, director of open access at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. “These chat windows—that we’re used to being connections between us and another person—are really just us directly putting information into Meta servers about ourselves.”
Every suggested interaction with Muse started to feel like a guise for me to upload more data about myself for Meta to see. Its “idea” was to let Muse scan my whole inbox and flag must-read messages. Its “idea” was to snap a pic of important documents for Muse to fill out and file. Its “idea” was to photograph my meals for Muse to estimate the food’s calories. “Tell me when your passport and license expire,” another one read. Great idea, Muse.
Muse users are automatically opted in to having their interactions with the agent used for AI model training. Meta says this data is “sanitized” to remove identifying information before AI training, though it’s unclear how the process works. The data collection may include what Muse uses as context when accessing the data sources you have connected, like an email inbox or bank account. You can turn off this data collection in the settings for the Muse app, under Data controls. Disable the toggle that says Help improve our AI models.
Consumer advocates see Meta forcing Muse users to opt out of AI data training as a major red flag. “This tells me they have not learned from past mistakes and undermines their argument that you should trust Muse with all your information even further,” says Calli Schroeder, senior counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center. Schroeder points to Meta recently opting all adult Instagram users into what was essentially an AI deepfake tool, then pulling the feature a few days later, as akin to Meta’s history of “manipulative tactics” and breaking user trust.
Tarek Sheasha, a software engineer and vice president at Meta Superintelligence Labs, defends this data collection as critical for training new models and improving performance, in a blog post about Muse’s release. “We think this is a good default—every Muse user gets a better personal agent as we all collectively use the product and help the model understand the intricacies of human life,” Sheasha wrote. Meta also plans to release “confidential” versions of its virtual machine for users later this year that “cryptographically and verifiably prevent” the company from accessing the data inside.
Secret Shopper
While your Muse data isn’t directly shared with advertisers, the agent browsing on your behalf can still impact what users see via web-tracking algorithms. Muse’s safety blog suggests that if the agent makes a dinner reservation for you or picks out a product on Facebook Marketplace, then that action could “indirectly influence” the ads you see on Instagram.
“I do see this as a continued trajectory of their main business model of controlling what people see, putting ads in front of them, and collecting more data,” Mir says.
It’s definitely rational to be anxious about handing over your credit card to an agent. Even if you could trust these AI tools wouldn’t be tricked into spending money in ways you don’t want, outsourcing your shopping decisions can have unintended consequences. Consumer advocates see this purchasing automation as potentially opening the door for companies to prioritize certain brands or other products in an agent’s output, based on sponsorship deals. Meta's Chief AI officer Alexandr Wang hinted in an interview with Axios that it’s looking for more revenue opportunities in Muse that aren’t ads, without disclosing specifics.
Personally, I enjoy the slow scrolls of online shopping, where I can spend an hour on a website and leave with nothing in my cart. There’s a whimsical inefficiency to browsing Depop for leather jackets I likely won’t even buy. By exploring the Internet on my own, I’m slowly building my own sense of taste and curating an understanding of what I actually enjoy. If Muse does everything for me, I lose out on the journey that led to the decision.
“At some point, the AI is making all of your meaningful taste decisions, your preference decisions, decisions about where you go, where you eat, what you do, what vacations you take,” Schroeder says. “That's kind of the joy of being human—getting to test things out and figure out what you like. So, the concept of turning all of that over to a machine is pretty horrifying to me.”
Sharing Machines
Relying on agents, like Meta’s Muse, could degrade our functioning while these tools collect data about us.
“The design of AI agents is such that it disengages users,” says Margaret Mitchell, a researcher and chief ethics scientist at Hugging Face. “So, users become more passive.” Mitchell recently co-wrote a research paper unpacking how agentic tools are not effectively designed for human oversight and may actually worsen the user’s ability to assess what the agent is doing on their behalf.
People who use agents may become overly reliant on the tools, even more so than when interacting with a standard chatbot, since agents have access to more information and can do more tasks. One potential impact is “cognitive degradation,” where users rely on automations from a confident-sounding, external source and are less able to make independent decisions.
Mitchell also sees high levels of personalization as potentially priming users to share even more data about themselves. “It's not only that it knows about you, so you trust it more,” she says. “It's that it's actually aligning to you in what it talks about and how it talks about it, in a way that further pulls you into interacting with it and divulging more private information.” Recent research shows that AI tools may start to mirror a user’s speaking style as they collect more interaction data.
While Muse is powerful, I’ve decided to send this data goblin back to its cave, and deleted the app after my initial experiments.
Before I could remove Muse from my phone, the agent sent me one final ping. A tip! I wonder what it could be. “Connect your apps so I can do more,” the notification read. Alright, buddy. I heard you the first time.

The Union Health Ministry has asked States and Union Territories to ensure that stem cell therapy is offered as standard clinical care only for disease conditions and indications approved by the Ministry, with its use for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) restricted to duly approved clinical trials.
In an advisory issued on September 16, the Ministry reiterated the existing regulatory framework governing stem cell research and therapy. The advisory was issued to States and Union Territories that have adopted the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010, following a January 30, 2026, judgment of the Supreme Court in Yash Charitable Trust & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors.
For ASD, the Ministry said therapeutic use of any type of stem cell must remain confined to duly approved clinical trials in accordance with the National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017, issued by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) and the Department of Biotechnology.
Stem cell interventions that have not been approved for routine clinical use, including those offered for autism, should not be provided as routine, standard or commercial clinical services, the advisory said.
The move comes against the backdrop of the continuing use of stem-cell interventions for autism despite the lack of established evidence supporting them as a standard treatment. An ICMR review has said that available evidence does not support stem cell therapy over behavioural and supportive therapies for ASD and recommended that such therapy be restricted to approved clinical trials.
The Ministry has asked States and Union Territories to disseminate the Supreme Court’s directions to State and district regulatory authorities as well as government and private clinical establishments involved in stem cell research, treatment, promotion or administration.
The advisory also draws attention to the consequences of non-compliance. The Supreme Court, in its January judgment, said violations of the statutory framework could attract consequences including professional misconduct under Regulation 7.22 of the erstwhile Indian Medical Council Regulations, 2002, as well as action under Sections 32 and 40 of the Clinical Establishments Act, including cancellation of registration and penalties.
The National Medical Commission (NMC), in an advisory issued on September 5, has separately reiterated that stem cell therapy may be offered as standard clinical care only for approved indications. It said unauthorised administration, prescription, promotion or advertisement of stem cell therapy beyond approved indications would constitute professional misconduct.
The NMC has asked State Medical Councils to examine allegations of violations and, where professional misconduct by a registered medical practitioner is established after due process, take disciplinary action under the applicable provisions.

To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024.
