An AI tool is set to start advising air traffic controllers on managing air traffic in the congested airspace above the Washington, DC, area. The expected launch would be the first step toward a planned nationwide rollout covering the 29 million square miles of US national airspace overseen by the Federal Aviation Administration.
The FAA describes the SMART system as using AI models to predict air traffic flows and identify potential conflicts based on operational factors like airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, and airspace conditions. US government and industry officials told The Wall Street Journal that SMART could debut for the three major airports in the Washington, DC, area as soon as Monday, September 21.
The decision to launch SMART in limited scope before going nationwide is the “right call,” said Philip Mann, principal consultant at Vector Strategic Consulting LLC, where he advises on aviation safety and AI governance. Mann previously worked at the FAA in multiple roles for 17 years.
“SMART’s risk was never any single prediction—it is a national-scale system with AI components carrying more unknowns than anything the FAA has fielded,” Mann wrote in an email to Ars. “Every cut in scope shrinks the unknowns.”
The AI-driven forecasts and recommendations are meant to give the FAA, airlines, and aircraft operators the same shared view of operational conditions so that they can agree on the most efficient routes and departure times. The goals of SMART include reducing aircraft fuel burn, improving on-time performance for flights, and speeding up recovery from weather and air traffic congestion events.
However, the airline industry was reportedly confused for weeks about the agency’s plans to deploy the AI tool, according to Politico. Anonymous airline officials told Politico that their concerns only eased after the FAA said the SMART AI tool would not change any procedures for air traffic controllers or airlines, and would instead produce “alternative route information” that is made available through existing FAA systems.

You entered your profession because you wanted to teach, code, write, create, or design. But thanks to AI — and the immense pressure to use it — you now spend less time practicing your craft and more time managing the technology that's doing the work you wanted to do.
For many professionals, that means supervising agents: tools designed to perform tasks autonomously but that, in practice, require workers to set expectations, delegate assignments, evaluate performance, demand revisions, and intervene when things go wrong. Others manage a steady pipeline of AI-generated work, reviewing the output and taking responsibility for what ultimately ships.
Congratulations! You're a manager now. You just won't be receiving the title or the raise.
The idea that AI will turn everyone into a manager has been floating around for a while. Now companies are building around that premise. Salesforce unveiled earlier this month "job-ready agents" designed to do work in sales, customer service, e-commerce, and internal operations, while giving human employees tools to teach agents about their companies, coordinate them, and improve their performance. Meanwhile, Wipro, an Indian IT services company, has increased productivity through AI by the equivalent of 20,000 workers, according to chief technology officer Sandhya Arun, who envisions "the same engineer managing a bunch of agents." At Daytona, a 30-person AI startup, each of the company's 16 engineers manages an average of five AI agents, CEO Ivan Burazin recently told Business Insider. It's to the point where he says no one at the company writes code anymore.
For some workers, managing a digital workforce has become a new kind of workplace flex. I'm not being replaced by AI; I rule over AI. But plenty of others never asked to become the boss of the bots. That includes software engineers who pursued the principal or staff track because it offered career advancement without becoming a supervisor, only to find themselves becoming de facto managers of machines anyway.
Sinda Khenine became a software engineer because she wanted to build things. Now, as a software and AI engineer at appliance maker Electrolux who is simultaneously building her own AI business, she spends much of her time managing the systems that do the building.
Agents have allowed Khenine to produce far more code and build a company by herself — something she says would have been "10 times harder" in the past. Now she spends less time doing the engineering work that drew her to the profession. Instead, she chooses models, supplies context, sets boundaries, reviews the work, and coaxes the output of multiple agents into a finished product.
"The effort is more focused on the coordination itself rather than the engineering problem that we are solving in the first place," Khenine says.
Khenine, who also leads a human team at Electrolux, says managing agents can be more complicated than managing people. They require a lot of setup, and the oversight doesn't stop once they begin working.
"It's like a loop," she says. "You need to monitor the results. You need to see the progress. You need to decide if you need to rerun or finish the job."
Khenine considers that managerial work part of being a software engineer these days and doesn't believe it entitles her to a raise. But she says people outside the AI industry may overlook how much labor agent orchestration requires.
Mari Nnanna, a freelance technical writer and backend developer, estimates that she now spends 20% to 30% of her working time managing agents.
"It's suddenly becoming a skill you need to have," Nnanna says.
Agents can help her work faster, particularly by searching documentation or explaining unfamiliar material, but they need a lot of handholding. Otherwise you'll end up with "so many mistakes."
Although Nnanna would prefer to remain an individual contributor, supervising AI has become part of her work — and is unavoidable when she uses it if she doesn't want to sacrifice accuracy.
The shift extends beyond techies.
Patricia Diaz-Hymes, a product marketing consultant, estimates that she now spends about 30% of her time supervising AI.
"It does feel like management," she says. "I give my agents names. I have their configurations. I try and talk to my agents in a very human way."
I'm trying to avoid my judgment from living just in my head and instead — at least partially — for it to live in my agents.
That means giving them defined jobs, familiarizing them with her business, and explaining why their work falls short rather than simply asking them to try again. Recently, her strategy agent, "Atlas," drafted questions for an initial conversation with a prospective client. The questions sought agreement rather than a diagnosis of the client's problems, so Diaz-Hymes rejected them and explained why. Atlas hasn't made the same mistake since.
"I'm trying to avoid my judgment from living just in my head and instead — at least partially — for it to live in my agents," she says.
Diaz-Hymes builds similar knowledge systems for her consulting clients. She thinks marketers' larger role will be defining what good work looks like and building that judgment into AI systems. "Supervising is just this funny middle we're in right now," she says.
Not everyone taking on this management work has chosen it — or feels equipped to do it.
An American professor teaching at a university in China tells me she has been made responsible for managing AI in her classroom, despite having no special training in the technology and being deeply skeptical of it. She asked not to be named for fear of repercussions from her employer.
"I'm being asked to train my students to use it," she says. "I'm also asked to make sure they don't use it for assignments. A fun contradiction."
She is also expected to teach students to use AI "ethically," though she says no one has clearly defined what that means. Telling students that using AI may itself be unethical risks making her seem insufficiently "technology forward," she says. Focusing too much on its environmental impact can similarly be treated as ignoring the technology's inevitability.
At the same time, incoming students are being told AI is "the future" and that they will learn about it in their classes — leaving professors like her to figure out what that instruction should actually look like.
"So then that's dumped on me to manage because no one knows how to use it, why it's useful, or what it's actually going to do," she says.
These examples reflect a much broader change in how work is being divided between people and machines. In a global survey of nearly 12,000 employees, 47% say they spend more time managing and directing AI than doing the work themselves, according to Boston Consulting Group. Sixty-seven percent say AI has taken over simpler tasks, leaving them with more complex work.
In other words, AI may be doing more of the execution, but it is leaving humans with more of the judgment, responsibility, and oversight.
David Martin, leader of the People & Organization practice at BCG and coauthor of the report, says the managerial shift is particularly pronounced among certain career types like software engineers and marketers, who can face an overwhelming amount of agent oversight, leading to AI "brain fry."
These are "people who historically weren't managers, who are now feeling like they have to manage," Martin says. They must tell agents what to do, judge their work, and own the outcome. "That is a new muscle that historically they might not have had to build."
The new responsibilities are also arriving faster than the training required to handle them. In the BCG survey, 72% of respondents say AI has considerably changed the skills expected of them, but only 36% believe they have received adequate upskilling — a figure Martin says has remained unchanged across BCG's successive surveys, even as more workers have begun using AI.
If you are a manager of people, you have the financial advantage. If you are managing agents, nothing changes for you.
Martin says much of the training companies provide is classroom-oriented and generic. Employees instead need to use AI on real assignments, compare what worked with colleagues, and develop the judgment to evaluate its output.
And while workers are taking on more managerial responsibilities, their titles and pay often aren't keeping pace.
According to data from an upcoming survey from the workforce analytics company Visier, 54% of full-time US employees surveyed say their roles or careers have significantly changed due to AI in the past two years. Of those whose roles changed, only 17% have been promoted.
Andrea Derler, principal researcher at Visier, says individual contributors are increasingly doing "managerial activity" without the formal recognition that traditionally comes with management.
Previous research by the Kellogg School of Management based on Visier's data found that individual contributors earn about 33% less on average than team leaders at the same firm.
"If you are a manager of people, you have the financial advantage," Derler says. "If you are managing agents, nothing changes for you. You still have the same role."
Maria Colacurcio, CEO of compensation software company Syndio, says she is "100%" seeing individual contributors take on what she calls "management light" responsibilities governing agents.
"If I'm responsible for assigning work to five agents, evaluating their performance, correcting them, being accountable for what they produce, what exactly makes me an individual contributor anymore?" Colacurcio says. Workers may benefit from the additional output their agents produce. But that doesn't always translate into greater recognition: Managers can devalue employees' contributions when they know AI was involved.
Companies are largely layering agents onto existing organizational structures and expecting workers to absorb the additional responsibility without much preparation or recognition, she says. After recently asking compensation leaders at large companies how they are addressing the shift, Colacurcio heard responses across the spectrum: Some are exploring ways to reward employees who manage agents effectively while others have barely considered the question. One adjacent effort: Ernst & Young is giving out $100 million in bonuses for employees who demonstrate the human skills needed to make AI work.
If companies begin rewarding agent management, Colacurcio expects the money to come through bonuses and other incentives rather than higher base pay.
"Managing an agent is its own skill set," Colacurcio says. "Companies aren't training for it or paying for it yet. And I think they should be."
For now, workers are getting more responsibility — and little else.

In March this year, the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and the American Heart Association (AHA), both globally recognised premier organisations in cardiovascular medicine, handed down their newest dyslipidemia guideline, and gave universal Lipoprotein(a) screening in every adult a ‘Class I’ recommendation -- the strongest tier there is. The High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hsCRP) test got a lighter endorsement: checked selectively, alongside coronary calcium scoring, to sharpen risk estimates when they’re uncertain. These two long-debated biomarkers, were both freshly blessed by the field’s governing societies.
Then arrived the irony. On July 31, pharma major Novo Nordisk’s ziltivekimab — a drug built to block the inflammatory pathway behind elevated C-Reactive Protein (CRP) — fully hit its target in a Phase 3 clinical trial and still didn’t move the needle on heart attacks or strokes. Five weeks later, pelacarsenm, a drug that lowers high levels of Lp(a) failed the same way. Within six months of the guideline telling every clinician to start checking these numbers, the two flagship drugs built to act on them came up empty.
It’s a familiar shape for cardiology. Heart disease mortality fell almost every year through the back half of the last century — statins, blood pressure control, smoking cessation, better acute care — and that decline has visibly slowed this past decade, even as the drug arsenal has never been more sophisticated. LDL (’bad cholesterol’) is already driven remarkably low in anyone on a serious statin; medicine needed a new lever, and reached for the two candidates the guidelines had just endorsed. Neither has delivered yet.
What actually happened
On September 4, Novartis announced pelacarsen missed the primary endpoint of Lp(a)HORIZON, the first cardiovascular outcomes trial ever run for a drug built to lower lipoprotein(a). Pelacarsen is an antisense drug — a short, lab-made strand of genetic material injected monthly, designed to intercept the liver’s instructions for building Lp(a) before it’s ever made, rather than mopping up what’s already circulating. In 8,323 patients with established heart disease, it cut Lp(a) by roughly 80%. And yet, there was no reduction in heart attacks or stroke.
What we were taught
Lp(a) was drilled into me in medical school as one of the ‘unfair’ risk factors — a number you’re essentially born with, indifferent to diet or willpower, and loaded disproportionately onto South Asian patients, who as a population carry some of the highest mean Lp(a) levels of any group studied. It helped explain a pattern every cardiology rotation eventually shows you: South Asian patients with premature, multi-vessel disease and normal LDL numbers. That teaching isn’t wrong, and this trial doesn’t overturn it — Lp(a) is a real, heritable, biologically active risk factor. What it disputes is narrower: whether lowering it, this late and this fast, changes what happens next.
What Lp(a) actually is
Here’s the plain version of how a heart attack builds. LDL particles, commonly known as ‘bad cholesterol’ work their way into the artery wall and get stuck there. Once trapped, immune cells chemically alter them and swallow them up, ballooning into fat-filled ‘foam cells.’ Over years, those dying cells pile up into a fatty core, and the artery seals it off with a cap of scar-like tissue. When that cap eventually cracks or wears thin, a blood clot forms on top of it — that’s the heart attack.
Statins, ezetimibe, and the newer PCSK9-inhibitor injections all lower LDL through different mechanisms, but the trial data lines up the same way every time: about a 22% drop in heart attacks and strokes for every 39-point drop in LDL, no matter how you get there.
Lp(a) is an LDL particle with one extra piece stuck to it — a protein called apolipoprotein(a), built from the same molecular parts as the protein your body uses to break up blood clots. But it’s a decoy, not a copy: it fits into the same docking spots on a forming clot, without carrying the working part that actually gets activated into a clot-dissolving enzyme. So instead of helping to break clots down, it crowds out the real thing and makes clots a little harder to clear. That’s what makes Lp(a) different from LDL: it builds plaque the same way LDL does, but it also nudges the body toward clotting rather than away from it. And unlike LDL, your Lp(a) level is almost entirely set by your genes at birth — diet, exercise, and statins barely move it.
Why did the trial fail?
A floor effect: Mean background LDL in the trial was 66 mg/dL as most patients were already on aggressive therapy. Whatever risk Lp(a) adds on top of that may be smaller than older, less-treated cohorts suggested, offering little room for an 80% reduction to matter.
Too late in the game: Every patient entered with 50-plus years of Lp(a) exposure already built into their arteries. Lowering the level for three or four years in someone’s sixties, after a cardiac event, may be too late to undo a lifetime of exposure the genetic data actually measured.
This isn’t cardiology’s first time at this wall. The CANTOS trial suggested a decade ago that quieting the immune system could work, independent of cholesterol reduction. Hitting the biomarkers still doesn’t seem to be enough: Lp(a) may just be writing the newest chapter of the same story.
Back to basics
The interventions with the deepest trial evidence are still the boring ones: eat well, move, don’t smoke, stay lean. LDL, blood pressure, glucose, and tobacco remain the pillars with decades of reproducible data behind them.
Lp(a) will likely still matter — as a flag for who needs those basics enforced hardest, and maybe eventually as a target that is treated decades earlier than this trial tried. But for now, the fanciest number on the panel failed its biggest test, and the oldest advice in medicine didn’t.
No antisense drug, no anti-inflammatory antibody, has found a way around the same wall. In Greek mythology, Icarus didn’t fall because he was foolish — he flew exactly as high as anyone reasonably could, and the sun turned out to be closer than he’d been told. Despite everything medicine can now measure, alter and silence, the quest for a healthy long life perhaps rests on the same principles it has rested on for centuries: eat well, move well, sleep well.
(Dr. Dinesh Arab is director, interventional and structural cardiology, AdventHealth Daytona Beach and clinical assistant professor of medicine, Florida State University. dinarab@yahoo.com)

Retired Bombay High Court Judge Justice RC Chavan resigned as a member of Maharashtra’s Uniform Civil Code (UCC) committee, the Indian Express reported on Tuesday. He reportedly submitted his resignation on September 19, hours after the committee held an online meeting. The state government accepted it on Monday.
In July, a seven-member committee, headed by retired Supreme Court Justice Ranjana Desai, was formed to draft a Uniform Civil Code for the state. The other members of the committee include Former Bombay High Court Judges Justice RC Chavan and Justice SG Mehare.
Maharashtra's former Chief Secretary DK Jain, and former Advocate General of Maharashtra Virendra Saraf, Padma Shri awardee and Constitution expert Ramesh Patange, and Educationist and social activist Suvarna Rawal were also part of the committee, according to PTI.
Born on April 12th, 1952, (retd) Justice RC Chavan joined judicial service as Civil Judge (Junior Division) and Judicial Magistrate First Class on March 1, 1976.
He was promoted as Civil Judge (Senior Division) in July 1985 and as an Additional District and Sessions Judge in March 1987, according to his profile on a government website.
Justice Chavan served as an Additional District and Session Judge at Jalgaon and Thane and Joint District and Sessions Judge at Nashik.
He was appointed as Joint Director, Judicial Officers Training Institute in Nagpur and served as such from 1990 to 1994.
He also worked as District and Sessions Judge in Nanded, Aurangabad, Daman and Diu and Pune.
He served as Additional Registrar, Registrar and the first Registrar General of Bombay High Court and was elevated to judge of the Bombay High Court on June 22, 2005, and served till 2013.
Justice Chavan also pioneered the e-court system in India and is known for insightful judicial contributions, according to Pravah Foundation.
He was appointed as a Judge of the Special Court (TORTS), Bombay on November, 19, 2012. He joined as Chairman of Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission.
After his retirement as a high court judge, he entered into the field of literature and authored two books “Cries in Wilderness” and “More Cries in Wilderness,” expressing his candid views on various aspects of law and judiciary.
He has recently authored a novel “Yes My Lords, It’s You In The Mirror”, which is a tale of four friends’ journey in Judiciary. Currently, he is working on his next literary title – “Who Killed Rule Of Law”.
Justice (retd) RC Chavan's resignation came after Maharashtra’s Uniform Civil Code (UCC) committee held its second meeting on September 19.
In his email to the committee, Justice Chavan said, as per the Indian Express, that one of the agendas of the meeting was to finalise the questionnaire for public feedback on the UCC.
He reportedly wrote, “Three members tried to articulate their views, such as respondents being required to answer only in yes or no, or the need to have the questionnaire quickly examined professionally by professors under the supervision of member Dr Suvarna Rawal."
"The honourable chairperson had already circulated the questionnaire finalised by her and stated that it would be uploaded once the website was ready. Thus, the third and the last item on the agenda of today’s meeting was over. Therefore, to save time and internet, I logged out," it read, as per the Indian Express.
“My attempt to put forth my views, even though the questionnaire finalised by the honourable chairperson had already been mailed, was due to my misunderstanding that our exercise was aimed at gathering the views of the people of Maharashtra, and to generate a consensus to remedy the issues of late marriages, perversions, infertility, unstable marriage, time-consuming dispute resolution mechanism, etc," he reportedly said.
"Now that it is removed, I realise that the aim is to just provide an opportunity to people who may care, to share their responses in a yes or no to the questions posed so that analysis of data becomes easy,” he said.
The email also alleged that a non-member attended the meeting. The non-member said the website prepared by the state officials needed further modifications, and the committee chairperson directed the authorities to make the necessary changes within a week, Justice Chavan said.
He said he did not know where the person fit, and added that the non-member’s suggestion made him speculate that the state’s officials may feel they are not competent. “To solve this problem, I am vacating my seat on the committee by resigning now, so that the government can fill in the blank promptly,” he said, adding that as a free citizen, he would be free to air his views. “It was a great learning experience on a subject close to my heart,” he said.
The meeting’s three-point agenda included confirming the minutes of the previous meeting held last month, and discussion on the website for feedback and opinion on the UCC.

ICE quietly wipes thousands of detainees from public tracking system, advocates say
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has stopped publicly revealing where it is holding most detainees who are subject to final deportation orders, in a move that has made it harder for lawyers and relatives to find them
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has stopped publicly revealing where it is holding thousands of detainees who are subject to final deportation orders, an unannounced move that has made it far more difficult for lawyers and relatives to find them, according to current and former officials familiar with the practice.
ICE removed those detainees from its online detainee locator system on Sept. 15, according to three current and former ICE officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the change. Several lawyers contacted by The Associated Press confirmed their clients vanished from the system this week, and the American Immigration Lawyers Association warned its members about the situation Friday.
The move represents a stark departure from previous practice and highlights the hardline nature of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, leaving thousands of detainees exceedingly hard to trace and potentially unable to exercise all of their legal options.
The practice, which applies to detainees who have received final orders of removal from an immigration court, could speed deportations by making last-minute legal challenges harder to pursue, immigration lawyers said. Nearly 16,000 people who were arrested and booked into ICE detention in July were subject to final removal orders, more than a third of the overall bookings, according to ICE data obtained by the Deportation Data Project based at U.C. Berkeley and UCLA.
The practice does not apply to detainees held at a detention facility in Adelanto, California or at temporary holding facilities in Minneapolis, New York City or suburban Chicago, the sources said. Judges have ordered ICE to list detainees in those facilities in the online locator promptly upon their arrival, as part of litigation over their detention practices.
Quiet policy change leaves families in the dark as federal officials ramp up deportation pressure on detainees
Immigration officials have increased pressure on detainees to accept deportation and forgo appeals, with the concealment of their locations creating another obstacle for individuals and their families under the Trump administration.
ICE did not publicize the policy shift and neither confirmed nor denied the change in a statement to the AP. The agency noted that it prioritizes detainees with final removal orders for deportation, even as it contends with a "historic number of injunctions" from courts halting individual removals.
This lack of disclosure has left lawyers and families unable to track loved ones without explanation. This is especially troubling because detainees are frequently transferred to new facilities prior to removal, said Greg Chen of the American Immigration Lawyers Association.
"Families are freaking out because they think the person has been deported and they don’t know where the person might be," he said. "On the attorney side, this has serious implications for the ability to contact their client. It certainly has implications about how it will interfere with the attorney-client relationship."
The Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent agency, maintained that individuals subject to final removal orders have received complete due process. This typically means an immigration judge ordered removal following a hearing, including cases where individuals missed court, and the decision was affirmed or left unappealed.
Over 65,000 individuals going through due process violations, advocates say
Individuals in detention still possess legal mechanisms to challenge their custody and deportation, including requesting to reopen their cases or submitting habeas petitions asking federal judges for release on constitutional grounds. To date, federal courts have issued thousands of rulings granting bond hearings or ordering detainees released.
According to the most recent data from early July, ICE facilities housed more than 65,000 people. Approximately 30 percent of those individuals likely face final removal orders, Michelle Mendez, the legal director at the National Immigration Project, noted. Mendez explained that more people have received final removal orders in recent months after failing to appear for hearings, as immigration courts have implemented policies that make participating in proceedings or reopening cases significantly harder.
"To me, it’s just another iteration of disappearing people," she said. "Why would we do that in the United States of America? It’s something we’d hear about in another country and be concerned about individual rights and due process."
A portion of those with final removal orders maintain legal protections against being sent back to their home nations due to credible threats of torture or persecution. Attorneys caution that many are instead facing deportation to third-party countries where they lack any ties, adding that their disappearance within the ICE network will make subsequent legal challenges far more difficult to pursue.
ICE online locator wipes detainees with final removal orders, lawyers say
Launched in 2010, ICE's online detainee locator system was created to enable relatives, attorneys, and the public to search for individuals in custody. Previously, tracking people down required making direct phone calls to individual detention facilities or ICE regional offices.
Lawmakers and advocates have long complained that the online tool updates far too slowly and contains inaccurate or missing data, effectively allowing ICE to obscure detainee locations for days or weeks. Minors, individuals being transported, and people held by U.S. Customs and Border Protection for under 48 hours are among those excluded from the system.
However, immigration attorneys point out that no clear precedent exists for excluding detainees who have received final removal orders. Atenas Burrola Estrada, a deputy program director with the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, said 17 clients were affected as of Monday, noting that "every single one of our clients who has a final order has disappeared from the locator,"
Those absent from the database include eight Somali men currently detained at the U.S. military base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, according to My Khanh Ngo, an attorney representing them from the American Civil Liberties Union. Ngo warned the modification could render it "nearly impossible" for people to challenge their removals in specific instances.
"If you can't find your client, don't know what's happening to your client, you can't get that information to the court to stop their removal," she said.

Keralam rail funding rose 10-fold under PM Modi: Rajeev Chandrasekhar
Rajeev Chandrasekhar accused the UPA of shortchanging Keralam on railway funds despite strong representation. He used the latest allocation figures to argue that the NDA is delivering faster rail development in the state.
Keralam BJP chief Rajeev Chandrasekhar on Tuesday criticised the then Congress-led UPA government at the Centre, saying the state received inadequate railway investment during its tenure despite having eight Union ministers. He said railway funding for the state had risen sharply under the Narendra Modi-led government.
In a post on X, Chandrasekhar said Keralam received Rs 372 crore for railway development in 2014 during the UPA rule, when the government was supported by the CPI(M). He said the allocation had gone up to Rs 3,795 crore in the 2026-27 financial year, even though the BJP has only one MP from the state.
Calling it a "10-fold increase", Chandrasekhar said railway projects worth more than Rs 20,000 crore were currently under way across the state. "Modiji does not just promise development, he delivers it," he said.
He also accused the Congress and the CPI(M) of continuing "vote-bank politics" and claimed that the BJP-led NDA government was delivering development while safeguarding the interests of all Malayalees.
His remarks came a day after Union Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said the allocation for development of the rail network in Keralam had increased 10-fold, from Rs 372 crore in 2014 to Rs 3,795 crore in the 2026-27 financial year. The minister said the higher allocation showed that there was a clear roadmap for the development of the railway network in the state.
"We also discussed the development of the railway network in Keralam. Hon'ble PM Shri @narendramodi Ji has increased the allocation for Keralam 10 times to Rs 3,795 crores in FY26-27. This amount was just Rs 372 crores in 2014. I also discussed the matter with Hon'ble CM @vdsatheesan Ji," Vaishnaw had said in a post on X.

Herpetologists first discovered in 1933 that rattlesnakes are immune to their own venom. Native to the Americas, rattlesnakes are pit vipers, a family of vipers with a heat-sensing pit organ between each nostril and eye.
Venom resistance in snakes comes in two forms: either the targets in their bodies have evolved such that the venom doesn’t attack them, like in cobras, or they possess specific molecules in their bloodstream that serve as “toxin sponges”, like in vipers, Sean B. Carroll, chair of biology at the University of Maryland, U.S., said.
In 1972, Japanese researchers discovered the first example of a so-called toxin sponge — a serum protein dubbed Fetuin-A — from Okinawa habu (Protobothrops flavoviridis), a pit viper endemic to the Ryukyu Islands. Fetuin-A could inhibit metalloproteinases, a class of venom toxins that could cause haemorrhage, damage tissue, and disrupt the coagulation system.
Metalloproteinases are the most abundant toxin family in rattlesnake venoms, and researchers have studied metalloproteinase inhibitors such as Fetuin-A in great detail. However, only recently did they discover that Fetuin-A belongs to a larger family of FETUA proteins.
In a 2022 paper, Dr. Carroll and his team identified four FETUA proteins from the western diamondback rattlesnake (Crotalus atrox).
Curiously, understanding the principles of venom resistance from C. atrox led the researchers to leverage these antitoxins, which had evolved over millions of years, for human benefit.
In a new study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team at Maryland has shown that specific combinations of C. atrox FETUA proteins can fully neutralise rattlesnake venom lethality in mice, with roughly 10-times the potency of commercial antivenom.
‘String of surprises’
On discovering metalloproteinase-inhibiting FETUA-2, 3, 4, and 5 proteins from C. atrox, the research team studied their antivenom potency. By injecting various protein combinations preincubated with C. atrox venom into experimental mice, they found that some combinations successfully blocked haemorrhaging, while some even staved off death.
“Rattlesnake venoms have 10-15 different kinds of toxins,” Dr. Carroll said. “So it was entirely unexpected that just blocking metalloproteinases would block the lethality of the venom.”
The test results that followed were a “string of surprises”. Encouraged by the success of FETUA proteins against C. atrox venom, the team tried them against the eastern diamondback rattlesnake (Crotalus adamanteus), which proved successful. Then they tested them against two Asian snakes: the Malayan pit viper (Calloselasma rhodostoma) and the Chinese moccasin (Deinagkistrodon acutus). The proteins could protect against those as well.
The team then moved to candidates outside of pit vipers. Of the two true vipers they tested against, the proteins protected significantly against the Sochurek’s saw-scaled viper (Echis carinatus sochureki) — but none against the puff adder (Bitis arietans).
“Our surprises ran out, you could say,” Dr. Carroll said.
According to him, an antivenom needs potency and broad reactivity. And not only could these proteins recognise and neutralise the venom of a spectrum of distant species, when tested against CroFab, a commercial antivenom obtained from animals immunised with four pit viper venoms, including C. atrox, the proteins proved tenfold more potent.
The findings are a “real advance” for antivenom development, according to Kartik Sunagar, an associate professor at the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru; he was not involved in the study. “The paper shows convincingly that a combination of naturally evolved FETUA proteins can fully neutralise rattlesnake venom lethality by inhibiting metalloproteinases alone.”
However, Dr. Sunagar also pointed out that the study did not exactly measure clinical capacity.
“Every efficacy experiment premixed venom and inhibitor before injection,” he said. “So the study measures neutralising capacity, not treatment of an animal already envenomed, which is the clinically relevant scenario.”
Next-generation antivenom
According to Dr. Carroll, unlike lab-made compounds, FETUA proteins have been tested in nature.
“Rattlesnakes have evolved these proteins for 50 million years, with remarkable specificity and potency to inhibit their own venom, which gives me the sense that it is worth exploring,” he said.
Manufacturability and purity are added advantages, he added: “We can make recombinant FETUA proteins in the lab in unlimited quantities — whereas traditional antivenom requires animals to be immunised, and then the obtained antibodies have to be purified.”
Dr. Sunagar also shared the view that the recombinant and defined nature of FETUA proteins will help sidestep the low purity of animal-derived products.
While the study showed that these proteins can protect experimental mice from venom lethality, toxins other than metalloproteinases will have physiological effects on humans, Dr Carroll said: “What we don’t know is what else we will have to use in conjunction with these proteins to make an antivenom” for humans.
“FETUAs do nothing for the neurotoxins that dominate many medically important venoms,” Dr. Sunagar said. “The honest reading is that these proteins form the metalloproteinase-neutralising component of a next-generation antivenom, but it is not yet a standalone therapy.”
Dr. Carroll also said his team has found a new component that could aid human antivenom development, but did not elaborate on ongoing research.
Implications for India
In countries like India, which host both vipers and elapids such as cobras, FETUA proteins alone cannot provide a complete antivenom solution, Dr. Carroll said.
Although the study revealed partial protection against saw-scaled vipers (Echis carinatus sp.), one of India’s ‘Big Four’ and a major cause of death and disability, partial cross-reactivity need not translate into clinical protection, Dr. Sunagar added.
But India’s bigger takeaway is the strategy: “The logical path for India is to identify and test FETUAs from our own vipers rather than relying on rattlesnake versions, and to pair them with agents covering the neurotoxic elapids the FETUAs cannot touch,” according to Dr. Sunagar.

Trump’s new arch plan: snipers and drones
If you give the president his national security ballroom, he’s going to ask for his national security arch.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s proposed triumphal arch is going in a new direction: drone port and sniper platform.
What’s happening? Trump has been pushing to build a 250-foot-tall “triumphal arch” near the National Mall since at least this January. Relative to some of his other projects, however, it’s been slow going, and now he has a new plan.
Trump announced the updated design in a Sunday morning post, writing, “At the strong request of the United States Military, and for National Security purposes, I have agreed to convert” the arch into “a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch.”
In addition to drones, Trump said, the new arch will have “snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage.”
Really? Maybe. We don’t yet know if this version of the arch will happen, or even if the military actually requested it.
For that matter, we don’t know if the arch will get built at all — though the administration appears prepared to move forward, despite a National Park Service determination that the arch would harm nearby historical sites, including the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.
What’s the big picture? Trump’s plan for a “Military Complex/Triumphal Arch” sounds an awful lot like his “Ballroom/Military Complex,” which got a stamp of approval from the Supreme Court last month after multiple lower courts ruled against its construction without permission from Congress (which Trump also does not have for his arch).
Like the arch, the ballroom acquired its “military complex” label after running into obstacles (though unlike the arch, there’s a clear connection: The ballroom does in fact sit on top of a secure bunker).
The unifying theme, though, is Trump’s instinct to reach for “national security” as a cudgel whenever he’s thwarted. He also accused the media of being a “threat to our National Security” on Monday amid backlash to his press ban.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

Indian Institutes of Management mull over common UG entrance test, MBA counselling amid other changes
Changes were discussed at the Coordination Forum of IIMs meeting chaired by then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The Indian Institutes of Management (IIMs) are considering major changes to admissions and student mobility, including a common entrance test for undergraduate (UG) management programmes, a centralised counselling platform for MBA admissions, a uniform fee-refund policy, and inter-IIM transfers, according to official documents accessed by HT.
Directors and representatives across the IIM system, including IIM Ahmedabad director Bharat Bhaskar, who is also mentor director of the newly established IIM Guwahati, the 22nd IIM , discussed “critical issues”, including aligning UG entrance examinations with the “futuristic requirement of the country”, developing standard operating procedures (SOPs) for MBA admissions, and policies on inter-IIM student migration and fee refunds, according to minutes of the Coordination Forum of IIMs meeting chaired by then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan in Ahmedabad on May 14, 2026. The education ministry circulated the minutes to IIMs on June 17, and HT obtained them through a Right to Information (RTI) application on September 15.
Under the Indian Institute of Management Act, 2017, the forum is an “advisory body”, unlike the IIT Council, whose decisions are binding on IITs. The forum held its first meeting in eight years in September 2025.
Also Read I IIM CAT 2026: Registration date extended, apply at iimcat.ac.in
Common test for UG admissions
During a discussion on the “advantages and disadvantages” of having more than 10 entrance examinations for UG and Integrated Programme in Management (IPM) courses and whether these could be merged to “reduce students’ stress”, Pradhan said multiple UG entrance tests should be “avoided”. “He clarified that this should not be perceived as government interference, but rather as a reflection of the government’s role as a stakeholder in the process,” the minutes said.
The IIMs, however, were divided. IIM Indore, which launched the first IPM in 2011, said multiple tests provide “multiple opportunities” and accommodate different programme requirements, while acknowledging the financial burden of multiple application and admission processes. It proposed that IIMs planning to offer IPM join the existing IPMAT framework, backed by IIM Rohtak.
IIM Bodh Gaya, Jammu, Amritsar and Ranchi supported a “common entrance test”, with Jammu and Bodh Gaya favouring one conducted by the National Testing Agency (NTA).
IIM Kozhikode favoured “minimal regulation” and flexibility for individual IIMs, while IIM Udaipur suggested using existing JEE, CUET and CLAT scores instead of another test.
To be sure, the IIMs themselves conduct a common entrance test, CAT for post graduate programmes.
Currently, 13 of the 22 IIMs offer UG programmes. Seven — Indore, Rohtak, Ranchi, Jammu, Bodh Gaya, Amritsar and Shillong — offer five-year IPMs, but use three admission mechanisms: IPMAT, JIPMAT and IIM Rohtak’s own aptitude test.
Newer four-year programmes have further diversified admission routes. IIM Lucknow’s BS in Artificial Intelligence & Business Analytics uses JEE Advanced, while IIM Mumbai’s BS in Digital Science and Business Management uses JEE Main. IIM Sambalpur and IIM Sirmaur use IPMAT; IIM Kozhikode conducts its own BMS Aptitude Test; IIM Bangalore uses the IIMB Undergraduate Admissions Test; and IIM Udaipur admits students to its BBA without an entrance examination.
“Our UG program requires students with a strong mathematical background. We admit students through JEE Advanced because it aligns with the academic requirements of the programme,” IIM Lucknow director MP Gupta said, adding that programmes with different academic objectives may need different admission pathways.
IIM Indore director Himanshu Rai said the “broader consensus idea was to avoid creating new entrance tests and instead leverage credible examinations that already exist.”
Then higher education secretary Vineet Joshi, in the meeting, said such a “significant decision” could not be finalized in a single meeting and required analysis of students’ test-taking patterns and socio-economic backgrounds.
Common MBA counselling
The forum also discussed a common counselling mechanism for MBA admissions. The minutes noted that candidates often pay non-refundable seat-booking amounts at multiple IIMs before choosing one, causing financial losses and blocking seats.
Members discussed a common digital platform modelled on the Joint Seat Allocation Authority (JoSAA) system for IITs, allowing candidates to freeze, slide or float choices. IIM Mumbai was tasked with developing a prototype.
“We had sent the prototype of a common digital platform to the education ministry by the end of July. The ministry might be reviewing the platform and will update us accordingly. The final decision is yet to be taken. The platform will ensure smooth and timely counselling in IIMs,” said a senior IIM Mumbai official, requesting anonymity.
The Union education ministry did not respond to HT’s queries.
Also Read I IIM Jammu students threatened with ₹500 fine for missing ‘mandatory’ Modi birthday event
While IIM Lucknow’s Gupta called it “a good” idea, IIM Indore’s Rai said: “Unlike engineering institutions, IIMs have different missions, pedagogies and admission processes. The concern raised by newer IIMs was that seats sometimes stay vacant when students leave after receiving offers from older IIMs. One of the suggestions was that older IIMs could stop admissions after a defined date and share information with newer IIMs so they can better manage waitlists and admissions. The objective is to improve coordination across the system and minimise vacancies.”
Fee refund policy
The forum also discussed complaints over non-refund of fees after withdrawals before classes began, “citing potential shortfalls in batch size and consequent financial loss”, or after migration to another institute.
While most IIMs follow a standardised refund policy modelled on UGC guidelines under which students withdrawing before classes commence would receive a refund of the admission confirmation amount with only ₹1,000 deducted.
The forum called for framing a “standardised policy” modelled on UGC guidelines, to be implemented from the academic year 2026–27.
However, several IIMs continue to follow different refund rules. For instance, IIM Udaipur allowed withdrawals after classes began with a ₹30,000 deduction, IIM Visakhapatnam barred refunds after the start of Term-I, IIM Mumbai prescribed forfeiture of the admission amount in certain cases, while IIM Calcutta’s policy for some programmes stated that “fees paid are not refundable under any circumstances”.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday that Iranian airlines will be shut down globally by 23 September while he threatened countries that allow Iranian aircraft to land or use any of their facilities with secondary sanctions.
In an interview with CNBC, Bessent said, "On September 23, all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world." He warned that any airport that services Iranian aircraft could face consequences from the US.
"If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets or you will be knocked out of the dollar system," he said.
The comments were made after Bessent concluded his talks on Sunday night with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.
Bessent also said that Washington was having productive discussions with Beijing's financial authorities, which includes the People's Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng, on compliance with its sanctions on Iran.
He also said that Chinese officers were "very engaged" in the economic pressure that the US has been putting on Iran.
US sanctioned 27 Iranian airlines earlier this month
Earlier in September, the United States' Department of the Treasury placed 27 Iranian airlines on its Specially Designated Nationals List, which targetted all commercial carriers in the country as part of its pressure campaign.
In a press statement, the department had then claimed, "Iran's commercial airlines have long supported the Iranian regime's destabilising activities."
It also added that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps IRGC) has been routinely using private airlines to procure and transfer weapons as well as ferry personnel.
The measure was also aimed at "covert front companies, foreign intermediaries, and deceptive transhipment routes that Iran relies on to obtain US-origin aircraft and sensitive technology," the Treasury release noted.
The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated four entities based out of Türkiye, Malaysia, and Kazakhstan for operating as cargo service providers and general sales agents for Mahan Air.
The OAFC also suspended authorisations that earlier allowed overflights and also let non-US airlines to operate US-origin or controlled commercial flights to Iran.

A top engineer for Big Tech asked for a demotion at the peak of his career.
Philip Su, who reached the prestigious "distinguished engineer" or IC9 level at Meta and OpenAI, said on "The Peterman Pod" podcast that promotions lost some of their shine as his career progressed.
"The thrill of the promotion itself was no longer the same as when I was younger," Su told show host Ryan Peterman. "When I was younger, because I sought after those grades, those measurable metrics, I very much felt great every time I got promoted."
By level seven, however, advancement no longer felt like an unqualified win.
"It wasn't all roses to me anymore, the idea of getting promoted, because I realized that each promotion also came with much higher expectations," Su said. "Expectations that I was no longer positive that I was going to deliver well."
Su, now the CEO and founder of Superphonic, an AI-powered iOS and iPadOS podcast player, ultimately sought a demotion at Meta from IC9 to IC7. He said that operating at a higher level left him exhausted and like the "Eye of Sauron" was constantly scrutinizing his performance.
"The higher level you are, the more that you feel that intensity all the time," Su said, adding that companies are entitled to question whether highly paid employees are delivering enough value.
At Meta, an IC9, also known as level E9, is one grade above a Principal Engineer and one promotion away from being a Meta Fellow. According to Levels.fyi, a compensation estimate platform, an IC9 engineer at Meta can earn roughly $4.3 million annually, including about $404,500 in base salary, $3.8 million in stock grants, and a bonus of at least $110,000. By comparison, Levels.fyi estimates that an IC7 Meta engineer could make around $1.63 million a year in total.
Stepping down was not painless. Su said it was difficult watching people who had once been below him rise past him. Still, he said had come to recognize that a lower-level role could offer work he enjoyed without requiring him to perform indefinitely at the edge of his abilities.
Su said people chasing a major career goal should ask themselves a simple question: What will they do once they achieve it?
"Now pretend you've just reached it. What do you do next?" Su said. "If you have a good answer for that, then you're fine."
Su's reversal reflects a broader retreat from the traditional corporate ladder. A late 2024 Randstad survey found that 42% of US workers would decline a promotion if offered. An Apple engineer also previously told Business Insider that she burned out and needed a career break after being promoted to a manager role.
For Su, he said the lesson was that every career has an upper limit, and reaching it need not be the goal.
"You know what?" Su said. "Like maybe this ultimately is my final level."

Why Cardiff is set to win race to host Fury-Joshua
- Published
The long-awaited heavyweight fight between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua is expected to take place at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on Friday, 11 December.
While BBC Sport understands final details are still being hammered out between Netflix, Saudi Arabian organisers Sela and both fighters' camps, Cardiff has firmly emerged as the frontrunner, with an official announcement expected this week.
It marks another dramatic twist in a saga that, only weeks ago, appeared destined for New York. A date at Madison Square Garden was so close to completion that plans were already being drawn up for a Manhattan news conference.
Instead, after Joshua and promoter Eddie Hearn refused to budge on their contractual right to stage the fight on British soil, the Welsh capital has taken centre stage.
BBC Sport takes a look at how Cardiff became the leading candidate to host what would arguably be the biggest event in British boxing in the 21st Century.
Joshua and Matchroom stood firm on Britain
Wembley Stadium was long assumed to be the natural home for a meeting between the two defining British heavyweights of their generation. However, the path to making the fight was complicated by Joshua and Fury having signed separate agreements with Sela rather than a joint contract.
Joshua's deal explicitly stipulated that the bout must take place in the United Kingdom, whereas Fury's contained no such restriction.
That distinction proved critical when organisers and broadcast partner Netflix began lobbying to move the show to the United States.
Hearn acknowledged that virtually every other party involved preferred New York, with Matchroom even exploring what compensation would be required to waive the UK clause.
For a moment, that stand-off threatened to scupper the entire event. Fury publicly accused Joshua of stalling and briefly floated the prospect of a trilogy fight with Oleksandr Usyk.
But once Fury relented, organisers needed to find a British venue capable of satisfying the broadcast demands without leaving fans exposed to the British winter.
Cardiff, almost by process of elimination, became the answer.
The roof solves the December problem
The fight had initially been discussed for November but, with negotiations over the venue dragging on, it now looks set for December.
Staging an open-air stadium fight in the UK at that time carries immense risk.
While Wembley offers unmatched prestige, exposing tens of thousands of fans and a massive international broadcast operation to potentially freezing temperatures, wind and rain was deemed unacceptable.
Moving the event indoors to an arena like London's O2 would eliminate weather risks, but at the cost of sacrificing tens of thousands of ticket sales.
The Principality Stadium's retractable roof allows organisers to capture the immense scale, atmosphere and gate revenue of a stadium show while offering full protection from the elements.
The venue's official seated capacity is just under 74,000, but boxing configurations allow for even larger crowds.
Joshua has already proven he can sell out the venue, having defended his WBA and IBF titles there against Carlos Takam in front of nearly 80,000 fans in 2017 before adding the WBO belt against Joseph Parker five months later.

A US-friendly start time is easier to accommodate
Perhaps the most difficult hurdle has been aligning the event with Netflix's preference to broadcast during prime-time hours in the United States.
A projected UK ring walk of about 01:00 GMT - 20:00 on the US east coast - created a logistical headache for London. Wembley operates under a strict 23:00 event curfew.
While Mayor of London Sadiq Khan offered his support and Wembley officials were open to discussions, securing the necessary approvals from Brent Council and local safety advisory groups for a 01:00 start presented an administrative hurdle.
Cardiff offers a far smoother path. The Welsh Rugby Union, which owns and operates the Principality Stadium, previously indicated it would be delighted to host the fight and confirmed a late-night finish would not be a dealbreaker.
While early-hours finishes still require extensive coordination around transport, policing and crowd management in the city centre, the venue already holds a clear precedent for late-night boxing. In 2007, Joe Calzaghe's super-middleweight unification victory over Mikkel Kessler did not start until 02:00 local time to satisfy American television network Showtime.
Delivering a true stadium super-fight
For all the delays and frustrations that have plagued this rivalry over the past decade, Fury against Joshua remains the pinnacle of domestic boxing. Downgrading to an indoor arena would diminish the magnitude of the occasion.
Crucially, taking the fight to America would have deprived domestic fans of a generational spectacle. British supporters have driven the commercial value of this rivalry for years, filling stadiums for both fighters' respective careers and following every collapsed negotiation.
Staging the bout on home soil serves as a long-overdue reward for that loyalty, even if both men are now former world heavyweight champions.
A stadium fight of this magnitude dominates the national conversation in a way a 04:00 New York or Las Vegas broadcast simply cannot, and local amateur boxing clubs could see a surge in interest when the country's biggest stars compete on home soil.
Wales also has history of staging a huge fight between two British heavyweights: In 1993, Lennox Lewis defended his WBC title against Frank Bruno at Cardiff Arms Park - the venue that the Principality Stadium replaced.
When the demands surrounding the event are broken down, Cardiff's emergence becomes easier to understand.

'I don't even know if my parents are alive' - the war heroes jailed 25 years ago
- Published
Hanna Petros Solomon breaks down in tears as she recalls how she and her siblings effectively became orphans 25 years ago when their father was arrested in Eritrea and jailed without trial. Their mother was subsequently detained - and no-one has heard from either of them - or of them - since.
"He had a towel on his shoulders like a sportsman," she tells the BBC about the last time she saw her father when she was 10 years old, and he had gone out for a jog.
"He used to work out every morning."
Her parents met when they both fought in the long liberation war that saw Eritrea gain independence from Ethiopia in 1993.
Her father Petros Solomon had been one of the senior leaders during the war and is regarded by many as a national hero for his critical role.
After independence, he had served as defence minister, then foreign minister and had been heading the fisheries ministry when his troubles began.
That was in May 2001 when he and 14 other high-profile politicians signed an open letter to President Isaias Afewerki calling for the implementation of a constitution that was ratified after independence and demanding national elections. They became known as the G-15.
Isaias, the leader of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) which had fought against Ethiopia, did not take the criticism well.
Unbeknown to Hanna, her father had been dismissed as a minister, though he still went out early to get some exercise each day.
It was not until a few days after 9/11 - when the world was distracted by the al-Qaeda attacks on the US - that the country was to discover the full extent of Isais's displeasure in what became a watershed moment in Eritrea's history.
In the early hours of 18 September, the security forces positioned themselves outside the homes of 11 senior government officials in the capital, Asmara, on the president's orders.
Petros was picked up by security agents as he left in his tracksuit.
The family had no idea what had happened to him. Hanna and her three siblings went to stay with their paternal grandmother as their mother, Aster Yohannes, was away studying in the US.
It was only some days after Petros had disappeared that things became clearer, says Hanna about the painful memories.
"My classmates told me that my father sold out his country.
"That is when I understood how serious the situation was, and how people framed my dad and his colleagues who fought for the independence of their country. I was hurt."
In the US, Aster was shell-shocked by what had happened - and was in a very bad way. She asked government officials if they could issue the children with passports - but they refused, telling her to come home.
After agonising about the situation for two years and reportedly receiving assurances from government officials, she packed her bags to return.
Hanna and her siblings desperately wanted her back - but they were also worried.
"I told her on the phone: 'What if they arrest you?'" Hanna remembers.
"She insisted nothing would happen to her, saying: 'I haven't done anything wrong, and am only coming to raise my children.'"
Hanna says she learned later that President Isaias himself had promised Aster that she would be safe. But while the family waited at Asmara International Airport on 11 December 2003, she failed to emerge through arrivals with the other passengers.
Their hopes began to wilt along with the flowers they had brought: "It was a long, long wait. Eventually we gave up and went back home.
"First we called to the US, friends and relatives told us they saw her off at the airport."
Then ominously an official called from the airport asking Aster to collect her luggage. That is when they realised she had arrived in the country but would not be coming home.
All pleas and requests for information fell on deaf ears in the months that followed. Instead Hanna's grandmother was warned by authorities to stop inquiring.
The family later heard that Aster was being held in the infamous jail known as Karshelli in the heart of Asmara.
Hanna's father is believed to be detained, with the others arrested on 18 and 19 September 2001, in the remote, hostile and highly secretive prison known as Ela-Ero, located in eastern lowlands north-east of Asmara. Accused of treason, none of them has ever been brought to trial or allowed to see their relatives.
At around the same time, the government also shut down all the fledgling independent newspapers and detained their editors and journalists - also believed to be imprisoned in Ela-Ero.
The Eritrean government - including its embassy in the UK - has not responded to the BBC's request for comment regarding the whereabouts of the prisoners or whether or not they are alive.
Hanna, like many thousands of young Eritreans fleeing conscription and in search of better opportunities, left the country - travelling secretively over the border without a passport.
Now 35 years old, she is married and lives in the US, working as a trauma specialist - but still feels traumatised herself by how she lost her parents.
As she stares at old pictures of her parents, she worries her memories will fade of the happy times before their arrest - the laughter, the family gatherings, the birthday parties: "My dad always wanted to gather people in the house, they were good days."
She also hankers after her mother's "unmatched" egg and potato sandwiches.
On trips down to the coast when her father was the minister of fisheries, Hanna remembers him organising singing competitions in the car: "He would ask us to sing one by one and whoever won would get a present."
One of his favourite songs included the lyrics: "I had a sweater, a blue sweater, that my sister took" - which reminded him of his sister who was also a freedom fighter and had been killed during the war.
She also has memories of her mother loving music - playing and singing hits by Abba, Dolly Parton and Whitney Houston.
Until her father's arrest, Hanna remembers September as being full of hope with its three big Orthodox Christian festivals, including the Geez New Year. Now the month brings her no joy.
Ibrahim Sherifo knows exactly how she feels. Both his parents, who were senior members of the ruling People's Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ), were among the G-15 people arrested 25 years ago.
He was 13 years old at the time
"For me 18 September 2001 is a dark day, but not only for me, it is a dark day for Eritrea and its people, because it is the day when law and democracy was detained," he tells the BBC.
He is now 38 and living in exile in the Netherlands, where he was granted asylum, and is pursuing an MA in political science - following in his father's footsteps.
His dad Mahmoud Ahmed Sherifo was the local government minister and de facto deputy president before his detention.
Ibrahim was with his mother, Aster Fissehatsion, staying with her sister when he remembers security agents knocking on the door early in the morning and taking her away in her pyjamas.
Worried about his father, Ibrahim immediately ran to his nearby house but was told he had already been picked up when he had gone out for exercise.
Both Hanna and Ibrahim say they are forever grateful to the friends and family who offered them care and supported them as they grew up without their parents, despite the risks.
They are also proud of what their parents stood for and daring to call for reforms.
"They had conscience and couldn't observe idly while what they fought for what had been hijacked by Isaias and his coterie," says Ibrahim.
"As a family, we should be informed whether they are alive or not," he adds, accusing the government of wanting to erase all memory of the political prisoners.
Hanna also wants the plight of the many others whose relatives have disappeared over the years to be heard too.
Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down"
Human rights groups, including the UN, consider the G-15 prisoners of conscience and have been calling for their release.
President Isaias, now 80, has still not implemented the country's first constitution - approved in 1997 - and remains in power without ever holding an election.
Hanna recalls that on the eve of her father's disappearance, she had a "bad feeling" - and had crept into his bed and tied his legs to her own with string while he slept.
"In the morning he woke up to find he was tied up and to release himself he pulled my legs and I woke up. I begged him not to leave but he assured me that he would return [after his run]."
Describing the years of sorrow since, she says it is like living in the deep sea.
"Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down.
"Sometimes you lose hope and you are out of breath."
Asked what she would say if she could get a message to her parents, she replies: "Don't worry about us.
"Like you survived the struggle through sheer steadfastness, we hope you can pull through this too and return to us."

Did a hidden phone cause a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy murder case?
Lawyers for Lindsay Clancy are asking a judge to investigate the conduct of the lone juror who wanted to convict her of murder in the deaths of her three children
Defense lawyers for Lindsay Clancy are targeting the lone holdout juror who blocked her acquittal, asking a judge to probe whether he secretly used a cellphone during deliberations in the prosecution of the Massachusetts mother accused of strangling her three young children.
In court filings unsealed Monday, defense attorney Kevin Reddington requested a formal inquiry into juror Michael Desronvil. The defense wants the court to question Desronvil regarding his alleged phone use during deliberations—a violation of state court rules—and to scrutinize his honesty on a pre-trial questionnaire and during a judicial inquiry held the day before the trial concluded.
The filings request subpoenaed phone and text records for Desronvil between 8 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. for every day the jury deliberated.
The high-profile trial ended in a mistrial on Sept. 4 after the panel declared an irreparable deadlock. Eleven of the 12 jurors favored finding Clancy not criminally responsible, believing the defense’s argument that she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis when she killed her children. Desronvil stood alone in siding with prosecutors, who argued Clancy acted with intent and understood the wrongfulness of her actions.
In a separate motion filed Monday, Clancy’s legal team made the rare request for the judge to throw out the murder indictment altogether rather than permit a retrial. Defense lawyers argued the mistrial was improperly declared, saying the judge should have replaced Desronvil with an alternate after the jury foreperson reported that one panelist refused to follow instructions on reasonable doubt.
The court has not formally charged Desronvil with misconduct, though fellow jurors reported he remained unyielding in his belief that Clancy was guilty. In a statement released through his attorney, Edward Paltzik, Desronvil maintained he had "no doubts" Clancy was fully aware of her actions.
Spokespersons for Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz declined to comment on the defense motions. Prosecutors have not yet announced whether they intend to retry Clancy, who remains committed to a psychiatric facility pending the resolution of her case.
On Sunday, Clancy’s ex-husband revealed why he forgave her for killing their three children, in his first interview since her mistrial.
Her former partner, interviewed alongside his new wife Rachel Danis, explained he did not know how to handle the condition.
“I could piece together what it was like to be really, really anxious or depressed, but I didn’t know how to manage a postpartum illness,” he said. “I think mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive. So I’m sure there are things that I didn’t see.”
He went on to address the media and social media's perception of his ex-wife, revealing he decided to forgive Clancy.
“I saw headlines that said, you know, ‘Killer Mom,’ and ‘Baby Murderer,’ ‘Monster.’ And none of them were accurate,” he continued.
“I believe that it was her mental illness that caused that. So I shared those words. And I think when it comes to forgiveness, I also felt that if I didn't get there, I would be eaten up inside forever.”
He also revealed that he and Danis, an infertility specialist, are starting a family and planned on sharing the memories of his lost children with their future brothers or sisters.

The strengthening El Nino weather pattern has matched the highest intensity recorded on a widely used measure, with its effects already being felt across parts of Central America and Indonesia.
Zeke Hausfather, a climatologist at Berkeley Earth and co-author of United Nations climate change reports, said the sea surface temperature anomaly in the tropical Pacific had reached 3.07C. That matches the level recorded during the 2015-2016 El Nino.
Hausfather said September was also likely to become the month with the highest anomaly on record, unless there was an unexpected change during the final week.
His figures, published through the Climate Brink dashboard, use sea surface temperature data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), collected through satellites and buoys.
The figures are based on daily sea surface temperatures in the Nino 3.4 region of the Pacific and compare them with a 30-year average.
NOAA has also introduced a newer measure known as the Relative Oceanic Nino Index, or RONI. Instead of looking only at warming in the Nino 3.4 region, RONI compares it with warming across the wider tropical belt.
That adjustment is intended to account for the broader warming of the world's oceans caused by climate change.
Using RONI, the current El Nino remains below the previous record, although scientists expect it could eventually surpass it.
El Nino is the warm phase of the El Nino-Southern Oscillation, a natural climate cycle in the tropical Pacific. It develops when the trade winds that usually move from east to west weaken, allowing warm water that normally gathers in the western Pacific to move towards the east and rise to the surface.
When unusually warm surface temperatures persist for several months, they can alter rainfall, storms and atmospheric circulation far beyond the Pacific.
The resulting weather changes can bring hotter and drier conditions to some regions while producing cooler and wetter conditions elsewhere.
Climate change can also intensify some of the effects associated with El Nino. A warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, potentially making El Nino-related rainfall heavier. At the same time, increased drying can worsen drought conditions in regions already receiving less rainfall.
Scientists remain divided on whether climate change directly makes El Nino events stronger. However, a recent study using coral skeletons found what researchers described as a “striking amplification” of El Nino events over the past 40 years compared with the pre-industrial period.
The current event is already affecting communities and ecosystems.
In Central America, drought linked to El Nino has contributed to the deaths of animals and damage to crops. Water shortages are also creating problems for the Panama Canal, a key route for international shipping.
Around 5% of global trade passes through the canal, which relies on reservoir water to operate the locks that raise and lower vessels. Authorities have therefore had to reduce the number of ships able to pass through the waterway.
In Indonesia, meanwhile, El Nino-linked drought has contributed to conditions that have fuelled wildfires across the archipelago.
