Trump’s constant-presence aide Natalie Harp fueled his decision to ban CNN, MSNow and Politico: report
Harp, known as Trump’s ‘human printer’ for pulling together clips for him from news reports and videos, was described by her brother as having an ‘unhealthy obsession’ with the president
President Donald Trump’s decision to ban news outlets from the White House reportedly came hours after he was shown unflattering and critical clips by Natalie Harp, one of his closest aides known for putting news reports about his administration in front of him.
Trump banned MSNOW, CNN and Politico from the White House on Friday without notice, stripping journalists of access to the grounds with immediate effect after he accused them of writing “fiction and lies.”
The president did not point to any specific reports that triggered the ban, but it came hours after Harp — dubbed the “human printer” — showed Trump the clips of MSNOW anchors criticizing his administration, according to The Wall Street Journal. An unfavorable Politico graphic was among the content that angered Trump, according to CNN.
“It’s really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it,” Trump said when asked what prompted the decision.
A regular presence alongside Trump, Harp is known to carry a portable printer to produce hard copies of favorable news articles and social media posts. The president is also known to dictate posts out loud to Harp, who often manages his day-to-day social media output on Truth Social.
Harp’s proximity to the president was thrust into the spotlight in recent weeks after she was one of only a few staffers the president took with him during a secret plane swap in Turkey after Iran made a threat against his life and Air Force One.
The ban on news outlets comes as the president’s frustrations over media coverage reached boiling point last week amid his plummeting approval rating ahead of the midterm elections, according to the Journal.
Trump also reportedly complained to White House aides that there were not enough of his allies defending him and touting the achievements of his second term on television.
The president’s ban caught White House officials by surprise and happened while chief of staff Susie Wiles was out of town, according to the Journal.
The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.
CNN, MSNOW and Politico have filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration to “protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” a statement on behalf of the news organizations said Monday.
Trump doubled down on the ban Monday in a Truth Social post, citing national security.
“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America,” the president said. “It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”
He previously warned that other outlets would follow, including The New York Times and The Washington Post.
The revelation about Harp’s reported role in the media ban is the latest in a series of reports regarding her influence with Trump.
Stephen Miller, deputy chief of staff and the architect of Trump’s anti-immigration agenda, has reportedly put content he wants the president to see in front of Harp. He has used Harp’s position with the president “at least a couple” of times to get his message to the president without speaking to him directly, a source previously told Zeteo.
The insider revealed that after Miller showed Harp videos, they quickly appeared on Trump’s Truth Social account.
And another person who wanted to give a physical message to Trump told Politico they texted the material to Harp, who replied, “printed.”
The White House previously criticized media coverage of Harp’s relationship with the president, touting her as “one of the most loyal and hardest-working aides on President Trump’s team” in a statement to The Independent.

'Alarming' - does WSL have a homegrown problem?
- Published
When London City Lionesses beat Manchester United on the opening night of the 2025-26 season, it suggested times were changing in the English women's game.
For some, that had become clear about an hour before kick-off in Bromley when the team news revealed a starting XI without any English players - the first time a Women's Super League side had done so on the first day of the season.
Two days later it happened again, when Scotland striker Kirsty Hanson was the only British player to start for Tottenham in their win over West Ham.
Both instances speak to the increasing ability of WSL clubs to attract top talents from across the globe, creating a league many now view as the world's best.
But, with the Women's Champions League returning this week, is what's good for the WSL good for homegrown players, and by extension the home nations?
Or is it, as The Guardian's Tom Garry puts it, "alarming" for the hopes of the home nations?
Arsenal v HB Koge, Women's Champions League
Tuesday, 22 September, 20:00 BST
Listen to BBC Radio 5 Live commentary and follow text updates of the matches featuring English teams on the BBC Sport website as the Women's Champions League returns
The changing make-up of the WSL
Ten years ago when current champions Manchester City last won the WSL title, they did so with an all-British starting line-up.
Much has changed since.
In 2018, the WSL went fully professional, the subsequent success of the Lionesses in the 2020s rapidly grew the game's audience and revenues have increased accordingly.
As a result, clubs have expanded their scouting pool and been able to attract players from a wider variety of nationalities - with transfer fees exploding since the turn of the decade.
Over recent windows, WSL clubs have recruited heavily from Germany and Sweden, while two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas exchanged the trophies of Barcelona for big-spending London City this summer.
The proliferation of players from Japan and Australia also highlights the WSL's attractiveness for those at the top of the game as those clubs with the deepest pockets pack their squads with players from across the globe.
"Our league has grown significantly and attracted world class athletes from all over the world," says Birmingham City manager Amy Merricks. "Unfortunately that blocks some of the pathways for the youngsters coming through.
"We need [this] talent in our league because our league is growing, but at the same time we have got to try and address this issue."
Looking at the proportion of homegrown players (English, Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish) to start 11 or more matches, half of a WSL season, the data shows a steady decline over the past three seasons to under a third.
The first three weeks of 2026-27 have offered a bump on last season, but that can partly be attributed to the WSL's expansion from 12 teams to 14 teams and the greater proportion of homegrown talent in the promoted trio of Birmingham City, Crystal Palace and Charlton Athletic.
It is a downward trend that is not mirrored across other major European leagues.
For 2025-26, 61% of those to start half or more of Premiere Ligue matches in France were French, 63% of those in Frauen Bundesliga games were German, and 69% of Liga F players in Spain were Spanish.
And, while WSL managers say they appreciate the importance of cultivating homegrown talent, the reality of the job ensures it is not their first priority.
"The club has a responsibility to raise young players, give our own talents possibilities to be in the squad and compete every week," says Manchester City boss Andree Jeglertz.
"But when it comes to team selection, I always need to pick the team that gives us the best chance of winning the game. If that contains eight young and promising English players or zero, I don't care. I just want to win the game."
What is the potential impact on the national team?
1 of 4
It feels like a crossroads has been reached between clubs wanting to be competitive, the WSL continuing to grow, and the need to regenerate an England squad that has not changed much over the past three major tournaments.
After all, England are the two-time European champions but seven of the team that started against Spain in June also played in the Euro 2022 final against Germany - while two of the remaining starters in this year's game were on the bench four years ago.
Sarina Wiegman's side were outclassed in Majorca, losing 4-0 to miss out on automatic qualification for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil. They must now navigate two rounds of play-off matches, starting against Greece next month.
Discussions on England's future is pertinent given the biennial Women's Under-20s World Cup is ongoing in Poland.
Last Thursday, Lydia Bedford's young side were dismissed 3-0 from the last 16 by Nigeria, albeit with the caveat a number of players such as US-based Erica Meg Parkinson and Laila Harbert were not released by their clubs to play.
Nevertheless, in 2022 and 2024, like the other home nations, they did not even qualify.
It is a far cry from the class of 2018 where the likes of Alessia Russo, Lauren Hemp and Georgia Stanway led the Lionesses to third place in the Under-20s World Cup, setting the tone for the incredible subsequent success.
Wiegman has handed debuts to 21 players since her arrival in September 2021, but only Lauren James, Hannah Hampton and Lucia Kendall have become established starters.
When England kick off in Crete on Friday, 5 October (20:00 BST), it is likely to be the same faces once again.
- Young Lionesses win European trophy 
  - Published17 April
To try and facilitate the pathway to top level football for young academy players, Football Association rules require WSL sides to include eight homegrown players in their squad lists.
The quota for WSL 2 clubs is higher and works on a sliding scale depending on squad size.
Former England striker Ellen White told the Women's Football Weekly podcast this was insufficient, saying: "We should be updating that quota of eight players, tweaking it to best help and complement our international structure, our homegrown talent."
"I would love to see them go much further - something mandated, a minimum on the pitch at any one time," the Guardian's Garry told BBC Women's Football Weekly. "London City's line-up was alarming.
"It's great for the product over here, but will we see pain in 15 years' time if England are struggling to go deep in major tournaments because we're not developing players?"
Last month, the FA approved a controversial plan to allow some WSL academy sides to play in the National League from 2027-28, saying it would "strengthen the women's football pyramid, raise standards across the league, and improve the development pathway for young players".
The FA believes this reform will address the relative lack of competitive minutes young English players receive.
Chelsea have already confirmed they plan to enter an academy side in the third tier and Manchester City women's managing director Charlotte O'Neill has previously said she would want to enter a team too.

Pope to retrace missionary footsteps in Peru and finally visit Argentina in November
Pope Leo XIV is set to return to Peru in November, retracing his steps as a missionary priest
ROME -- ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV will retrace his steps as a missionary priest when he returns home to Peru in November in his longest trip to date that will also take him to Uruguay and Argentina, where his Argentine predecessor Pope Francis never returned.
The Vatican on Monday published the detailed itinerary for Leo’s first visit to Latin America as pope. The Nov. 6-17 trip will be a homecoming for the U.S.-born pontiff who also has Peruvian citizenship and spent two decades there as a priest and bishop.
As he showed during his four-nation Africa trip in April, the 71-year-old Leo has no qualms about covering vast distances and working late into the night when he’s on the road. In all, he’ll clock just over 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles) of flight time during the trip, nearly double the 17,000 kms (10,000 miles) he traveled in Algeria, Cameroon, Angola and Equatorial Guinea.
The visit begins in Uruguay to put Leo in place to mark an important Catholic feast day Nov. 8, associated with the country’s patron saint, of Our Lady of the Thirty-Three. The small statue of the Madonna dates from the 18th century Jesuit missions in the area and currently is housed in the city of Florida, where Leo will celebrate Mass at the National Shrine.
Leo will also honor Argentina’s patron, Our Lady of Lujan, on the second, Argentine leg of the trip. The statue of the Madonna, located in the city of Lujan in the province of Buenos Aires, was particularly dear to Francis.
Francis, who died in 2025, confounded friends and foes alike by never returning to his native Argentina, after he left for Rome for the 2013 conclave that elected him pope.
He had been a divisive figure back home, both as Jesuit superior and archbishop of Buenos Aires, and apparently wanted to avoid fueling the country’s polemics by not giving the ruling party at any given time the political benefits that come with a pope visit.
But Leo seems keen to finally grant Argentina’s faithful a papal visit for the first time since St. John Paul II came in 1982 and 1987.
In Buenos Aires, Leo will visit the capital’s federal prison, perhaps a nod to Francis’ legacy of prison ministry that he developed first as a “slum priest” in Buenos Aires.
The highlight of Leo’s trip will certainly be his return to Peru and especially his diocese of Chiclayo. The former Robert Prevost was bishop of Chiclayo from 2014-2023, when Francis brought him to the Vatican to head the office for bishops.
On the night of his election, Leo gave a shoutout in Spanish to his “beloved diocese of Chiclayo,” from the loggia of St. Peter’s Basilica. He praised its faithful for having “walked alongside their bishop, shared their faith, and given so much to continue being a faithful Church of Jesus Christ.”
Leo is spending the bulk of his visit in Peru, arriving in Lima on Nov. 11 and leaving the afternoon of Nov. 16 after a final Mass in Callao, outside Lima, where he served as a temporary administrator. In between, he’ll spend time in Chiclayo, including having a special private dinner with the diocese’s priests.
He’ll meet with popular groups in Cusco, in the Peruvian Andes, to celebrate the city’s rich history. Cusco was the capital of the Inca empire, an important city of Spanish colonial rule and today remains an important cultural destination with ruins including Machu Picchu.
That same day, Nov. 15, he’ll also honor Peru’s Indigenous peoples by traveling to Pucallpa, deep in Peru’s Amazonian forest, to celebrate Mass.

Just past 6 pm on a recent Wednesday night, half a dozen pet owners logged into a Zoom meeting to confess something they’re afraid to talk about in public: They’re fed up with their dogs.
Before discussion began, Louise Crane, the president and cofounder of Dogs Anonymous, the organization hosting the meeting, recited the seven acknowledgements participants must agree to, the first being, “I admit that life with my dog is not what I imagined.” Crane wore a black T-shirt exclaiming “Abolish ICE” in thick white lettering.
“I may need to be talked off a ledge,” one attendee said as conversation kicked off, mentioning that she wasn’t sure how to handle her dog’s mood swings. Her family had been through a series of new changes: Their other dog died and they were also fostering one, and now their boxer was “unsettled” and “grumpy” to the point he was doing more “demand barking, which has never been like him.”
Other attendees confessed their private shames: a shepherd mix had started engaging in more intense “resource guarding” when around other dogs—the term for when dogs aggressively protect something they value. “He got into it with my sister’s little weiner dog the other day because they both were begging for food.” One woman, who lives in a busy apartment complex, needed advice on how to better handle her dachshund’s constant barking at strangers. (In the spirit of anonymity, Dogs Anonymous asked WIRED to leave out the names and identifying characteristics of its participants.)
Shame is the emotion attendees struggle with the most in these meetings. “The embarrassment of having a dog that’s losing its shit, especially as a woman,” is difficult for some people, Crane tells me when we speak a few days before.
Crane launched Dogs Anonymous, a nonprofit focused on training and emotional support by animal behavior experts, in 2025 in an attempt to help people vocalize their shame.
“We wanted to give people not just a space they could trust for advice on behavior issues or if they are having a crisis with their dog, but also a place where they don’t feel judged to ask questions and admit that maybe it’s a little bit too much for them,” Daphne Mendoza-Tervanis, a cofounder, says.
Sessions are held weekly and span first-time and experienced dog owners, adopters, foster caregivers, and occasionally trainers seeking tips on how to work aggression cases. The meetings are primarily attended by US residents, though previous sessions have attracted dog owners from Singapore, Costa Rica, and beyond.
Jerri Scherff, a cofounder who is 13 years sober, had first-hand experience with recovery programs, and it was important to her that Dogs Anonymous also include some of the same traditions as Alcoholics Anonymous. “We wanted to create something that was repeatable, sustainable, and eventually autonomous, which is the way that recovery groups work,” she says. The most important one was anonymity—what is discussed in the group stays in the group.
The founders say the effectiveness of the group doesn’t necessarily stem from the advice they impart during meetings but comes from members bonding over shared struggles. “The magic of AA the community is that you are going through something that somebody else has either been through or they’re going through the same thing,” Crane adds. This approach, called “sharing your experience, strength and hope,” is a core part of the 12-step recovery program and encourages members to analyze their experience in a way that makes them feel less alone.
According to a survey published in the scientific journal Pets in June examining guilt, burden, and wellbeing among owners of dogs with behavior problems, 53 percent of respondents reported feeling alone, and 78 percent reported “elevated caregiver burden,” a term for the emotional and financial strain of being a caregiver.
During a meeting in August, the group took a beat to dig into the particulars of why shame was the first emotion owners often experience when their dog reacts aggressively. One attendee said it threatened their sense of belonging in a neighborhood they already felt out of place in. Another mentioned how it made them feel judged because others wouldn’t think they were a capable owner. “There’s so much shame when you don’t get Lassie,” Crane says of the fictional TV dog that, for many Gen Xers and millennials, represented the ideal companion.
“I just broke down crying on the way home from my dog’s reactivity training,” one owner in New Orleans posted on Threads last month, writing that she signed up for classes after a woman threw coffee at her “anxious pit” for reacting badly. Dog reactivity is the number one issue most owners deal with. A 2026 study by researchers at the University of Lincoln shows that behaviors group into three main categories—oral attacks, frustration, and posturing—with lunging and barking reported as the most frequent symptoms.
“After three sessions it seems like the main lessons are to avoid triggers and anticipate my dog’s reactions,” the New Orleans owner continued. “As someone who has spent my entire life anticipating human volatility, I’m exhausted. Is there no other way?”
Another Threads user suggested she attend Dogs Anonymous, replying, “Part of what you’ll do here is grieve the dog you thought you would have as you grow closer to the one you have.”
No Dogs Anonymous meeting is the same. Some weeks attendees might discuss what it’s like dealing with their dog’s anxiety issues or ask for advice about going through the euthanasia process. Other weeks, they might vent about life. “The other day we were talking about random things that our dogs had pooped,” Mendoza-Tervanis says. “It was a lot of money and tampons.”
Unlike other support groups for owners of dogs with behavioral challenges, DA prioritizes the owner first. “Why we’re in the problem that we are right now is because we are putting dogs before people,” says Mendoza-Tervanis, who has worked in pet care for 15 years. According to the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, 2 million dogs were adopted from shelters in 2025, but Mendoza-Tervanis believes the problem is that most owners do not have the actual support they need, especially when the dog doesn’t meet their expectations. “A lot of services are becoming financially inaccessible”—hourly rates for private dog trainers in Los Angeles, for example, can cost up to $300 an hour—“so when someone comes to us the question is not, how much can you pay, but how are you feeling about what happened.”
Social media has also warped the expectations people have around dogs, where colorfully-curated pages of petfluencers @_violasnow, the Husky with 5.8 million Instagram followers, and @tikatheiggy, the Italian greyhound Vogue once called “a new fashion it girl,” can often make owners feel like they are not doing enough. It’s why organizations like DA have become a refuge.
In March, after Scherff’s American bulldog passed, weekly meetings became her safe space to process what happened away from the judgments of social media. Scherff has 283,000 Instagram followers “but with the group, I knew that whatever I said, it was going to stay there and they weren’t going to think anything of me.”
Before Wednesday’s session wrapped, one attendee in Puerto Rico expressed gratitude for the gathering. “I’m just glad we all ended up here through the magic of the internet. It can be such a dark place sometimes. It’s just nice to hear these conversations.”
More than anything, the founders want the weekly Zoom meetings to be a forum that keeps the “toxic outside noise out,” Crane says. “This is a place where you can come and say, I fucking hate my dog today. And there are people who are going to be like, yeah, that was me last Tuesday. Sometimes they drive us crazy and that’s OK.”

Workers came across human remains – and unearthed a mass grave of 572 people
- Published
When a mass grave was unearthed in northern Sri Lanka last February, it was not by design.
Workers were digging to extend a cremation ground in the Chemmani area of the Jaffna region when they suddenly discovered human remains, prompting an investigation.
By August, archaeologists had completed the third phase of the excavation at the site, during which they found the skeletal remains of 572 people, including children and infants.
Among the dead were artefacts from their lives – bangles, a school bag, a milk bottle.
It is believed to be the largest mass grave site ever uncovered in Sri Lanka.
There had been whispers of its existence before - a soldier on trial for the rape and murder of a young woman during the country's devastating civil war, had spoken about a mass grave which contained hundreds of bodies. Rights groups said they were disappeared civilians
But there was no proof - until now.
And while the discovery is devastating, it has offered hope to people like Jeyaruby Jeyabalan, whose father was among thousands of people who disappeared during the decades-long war. Jeyabalan and families like his hope that answers about what happened to their loved ones lie among the bodies.
Many Tamils believe the grave holds the victims of extrajudicial killings carried out during the civil war. They are calling for an investigation – and for justice.
But the excavation process at Chemmani has moved slowly, testing the patience of families searching for answers about their disappeared loved ones.
The discovery of hundreds of remains near a previously identified mass grave has fuelled anger among the Tamils, who have long-demanded a thorough inquiry into disappearances.
Many fear the mass grave will eventually fade from public attention because of a lack of political will to pursue the truth – and so the grave has become a rallying point for renewed protests in Sri Lanka's north.
Two decades waiting for answers
Sri Lanka, particularly the Tamil-dominated north and east, suffered decades of conflict. The war, which lasted from 1983 to 2009, divided the island-nation along ethnic lines. Tamil Tiger rebels fought for an independent state in the north-east of the country due to what they called systematic discrimination by the Sinhalese-dominated government.
The conflict lasted 26 years and the fighting killed an estimated 100,000 people. It also left about 23,000 – mostly Tamils – missing.
Both the security forces and Tamil Tigers are accused of atrocities and crimes.
In 1995, after a bloody conflict, the Sri Lankan army wrested control of the Jaffna Peninsula from the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE). It was seen as a key turning point in the war, which ended with the defeat of the Tigers in 2009.
As they extended control in the late 1990s, the entire Chemmani region became part of a high-security zone and was dotted with army camps, check points and security posts. There was an army camp in Chemmani close to the cemetery as well.
Some at that time described the Jaffna region as an "open prison" - and the security forces were accused of causing the disappearance of thousands of civilians, something Sri Lankan governments have always denied.
"I was 12 years old when my father was picked up by the Sri Lankan army at a checkpoint close to Chemmani area in September 1996. We still don't know what happened to him," Jeyaruby Jayapalan, who now lives in Jaffna, tells the BBC.
She recalls how, after learning of his disappearance, the family panicked and visited military camps and police stations across Jaffna in a desperate search for information without any luck. He never came back.
Her father, Kandaiah Jayapalan, was a government employee who also ran a roadside café not far from Chemmani.
"I went to Chemmani mass grave with many others hoping that I will find some answers. But we didn't find any material evidence. We want a detailed forensic analysis of the human remains," says Jeyaruby.
Two weeks before Kandaiah Jayapalan vanished, an 18-year-old Tamil school girl, Krishanthi Kumaraswamy, disappeared in the same area.
In 1998, a court in Colombo sentenced five soldiers to death for the rape and murder of Kumaraswamy and for killing three of her family members. The case drew global attention at that time. Their bodies were later found buried in Chemmani area.
It is among the most infamous cases from the conflict – and the grave currently under investigation is within 100 metres of the remains of Kumaraswamy and others were found.
In a startling court testimony, one of the convicted soldiers, Somaratne Rajapakse, alleged that between 300 and 400 people who had been killed in the mid-1990s were buried in Chemmani.
His claim led to the first excavation at Chemmani a year later, during which investigators unearthed more than 10 human skeletons. Human rights activists believed those remains were linked to people who had disappeared during the civil war, but there was little judicial follow-up.
Activists say that because the war with the Tamil rebels was ongoing, the then government didn't pursue the investigation and did not explain why.
The discovery of another mass grave in the same area has revived calls for accountability.
"Preliminary inspections suggest this was not a normal burial site and not consistent with ordinary Hindu burial practices," says Gehan Gunatilleke, a commissioner with Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka, which conducted inspections at Chemmani last year.
Activists and experts say that while a few dozen bodies appeared to have been formally buried, the vast majority told a different story.
Most of the human remains were found without clothing, packed tightly together and, in some cases, stacked on top of others. The graves were shallow, with bodies buried just one to two metres below the surface.
"There is a reasonable likelihood that the burials were unlawful and pursuant to extrajudicial killings," the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka said in a report last year.
Past investigations haven't led to prosecutions
The families of those disappeared during the conflict have responded to the discovery by holding protest meetings and remembrance ceremonies.
Among them is Suseela, a 65-year-old woman who is looking for her son, Gnanaseelan Ravi, who was picked up by the Sri Lankan military in 2007, when he was 24.
"He was my only son, and I keep crying every day remembering him. My life is empty without him," she tells the BBC.
She went to Chemmani grave but couldn't find any evidence, likes clothes or personal jewellery, that suggested her son was buried there. DNA tests on the human remains are yet to be carried out.
All the remains recovered so far from Chemmani have been kept in the Forensic Department of the University of Jaffna campus under court custody.
"We are preparing an interim report, and it will be submitted to the court by the end of September," Prof Raj Somadeva, the chief archaeologist of the mass grave told the BBC.
Some of the samples are expected to be sent abroad for detailed examination to help determine the age of the remains. Separate medical analyses will be needed to establish the possible causes of death.
More than 20 mass graves have been found across Sri Lanka in recent decades, but none have been conclusively linked to enforced disappearances or alleged extra-judicial killings in the north and south of the country – and none have led to prosecutions.
Given the failure of the authorities to investigate previous mass graves, there is scepticism among many Tamil people over what the new investigation might achieve.
They point out to the outcome of the investigation on another mass grave was unearthed in the north-western town of Mannar in 2018 in which more than 350 skeletal remains were found. Investigations proved inconclusive, leaving many families disappointed.
They want Sri Lanka to be referred to the International Criminal Court.
The government of President Anura Kumara Dissanayake insists that it is fully cooperating with the investigation.
After coming to power in September 2024, Dissanayake promised to work towards justice and ethnic reconciliation. But his government vehemently opposes any international mechanism to investigate alleged war crimes committed during the ethnic conflict, disappointing Tamils.
"We will continue with the excavation work at Chemmani," Harshana Nanayakkara, Sri Lanka's justice minister told the BBC.
"We need to analyse the skeletons and find out how these people died. Then we have to carry out DNA tests," he said.
The government, he insists, has also asked the families to give their DNA so that it can be analysed later with the remains.
During his inspection at Chemmani in June, the minister promised investigations to find justice and truth to bring an end to the matter. He also promised that necessary funding will be allocated for the excavation.
The Sri Lankan army spokesman, Brigadier Waruna Gamage rejects allegations that security forces buried civilians after massacring them.
"All the allegations should be proved in court," he told the BBC.
Calls for international assistance
The delays in investigating past crimes have attracted stringent criticism from rights groups.
After years of international pressure, in 2018 the government set up an independent body, the Office of the Missing Persons (OMP), to investigate the disappearances. But those affected say it hasn't made much progress in finding their missing relatives.
"Many cases of forced disappearance, torture and killing remain stalled, while families of victims and human rights defenders face threats and intimidation," Human Rights Watch said in a report earlier this month.
The United Nations has urged Sri Lanka to seek international help in identifying the victims, to find out how they died, and who is responsible.
"This is a situation where victims are deeply frustrated, have lived with pain for decades, have come to distrust past investigations," Rory Mungoven, the Asia-Pacific chief at the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights tells the BBC.
"I think involving international assistance would help to bolster confidence in these investigations," he points out.
Successive Sri Lankan governments have strongly resisted calls for international investigations into alleged wartime atrocities.
During earlier reporting trips to Sri Lanka, I met parents and family members of the disappeared who campaigned for decades to the search for truth. Some have since passed away without ever discovering the fates of their loved ones.
Human rights groups say that President Dissanayake's government now has an opportunity to break from a long-standing pattern of delay and denial and deliver accountability for grave abuses committed during the conflict.
Suseela is determined to know the truth.
"I don't know how long I will live with such uncertainty, but I want closure," she says.
Additional Reporting by: Ranjan Arun Prasadh, BBC Tamil Service in Kandy and Kumanan Kanapathippillai in Jaffna.

There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.
Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.
The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?
Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.
In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.
“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”
In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.
Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)
Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.
But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.
The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.
Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.
Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.
That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.
The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”
What else we’re reading about
Lollapalooza | British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.
The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.
Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
4,756,000
One-third of the electorate in Delhi, about 4.76 million voters, have been deleted from the draft voting list as the Election Commission carries out a contentious revision of its rolls across states. So far, about 130 million names have been dropped from draft rolls in 30 states and union territories, the Indian Express reported.
Vibe check
Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).
It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.
It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.

Amnesty accuses M23 of abuses amounting to war crimes at Congo mines
Amnesty International has accused M23 rebels in eastern Congo of abuses and unlawful killings of miners while trafficking minerals to Rwanda, in what it said could amount to war crimes
DAKAR, Senegal -- Amnesty International accused M23 rebels in eastern Congo of carrying out abuses and unlawful killings of miners while trafficking critical minerals to neighboring Rwanda, in what it said could amount to war crimes.
The Rwanda-backed rebels control dozens of artisanal mines in Congo's eastern North Kivu and South Kivu provinces, where tens of thousands of miners dig for minerals critical for much of the world's electronics, including mobile phones.
Amnesty International said in its report on Monday it interviewed 26 people to document the crimes allegedly committed from January 2025 to March 2026, particularly at a coltan mine near Rubaya in North Kivu and a gold mine in Lomera in South Kivu.
Sixteen of the interviewees, including miners and civilians, said the M23 rebels or security guards at the rebel-controlled mines had tortured or mistreated them, the report said.
The rights watchdog said it documented abuses by the rebels that likely amounted to crimes under international law, including “summary killings” — a term used to describe killings outside of any legal framework — torture, arbitrary detention, forced labor and pillage.
The report detailed the killings of 18 artisanal miners at the Rubaya and Lomera mines. “Witnesses and family members reported that 10 were beaten to death, two were shot dead and six abducted miners were later found dead."
Amnesty International also said it found evidence that gold was trafficked out of M23-controlled areas of eastern Congo into neighboring Rwanda through smuggling routes.
The M23 and Rwandan authorities did not immediately respond to requests for comments.
United Nations experts, the United States and Congo's government have in the past accused Rwanda of profiting off Congo’s minerals in exchange for its support to the rebels, which Rwanda denies.
Eastern Congo, the mineral-rich part of the Central African nation, has for decades been ripped apart by violence from government forces and different armed groups, including M23, whose recent resurgence has escalated the conflict, worsening an already acute humanitarian crisis.
The Rubaya mine is a major coltan mining site that has seen numerous tragedies, including a mine collapse in March that killed at least 200 people, and a landslide in January, which left around 200 people dead.
The Lomera gold mine suffered a collapse last year, trapping numerous miners.
Last year, Congo produced more than half of the world’s tantalum – an ore derived from coltan used in smartphones among other products – with the Rubaya mine pumping out about 15% of global production, according to Amnesty International.
The country also exported more than 28 tons of gold that year, the group said.

A trip to Switzerland had been my mother's dream long before it was mine. She'd seen the destination in movies and travel videos for years and always said she wanted to see it in person someday.
Every few years, my family would talk about going, compare flights, and then let the idea go. The timing was never right, and the cost was hard to justify for a family of four from India.
When we finally planned a trip for December 2024 as a gift for my mom's birthday, I knew I wanted to make the most of it. It was one of the most expensive vacations we'd ever taken, so I spent a lot of time thinking about where we'd stay, knowing our base would shape the whole trip.
I had to make some tough decisions when it came to where to stay and what to do to make sure the trip was worthwhile and met all of our expectations, especially my mom's. I'm happy with the choices I made, especially when it came to which town to stay in.
We didn't want our dream trip to feel rushed
Like most first-time visitors, I started by looking at tourist hubs like Interlaken and Lucerne. Both seemed like obvious choices — close to the attractions we'd planned to visit and easy to build an itinerary around.
But we were going to spend most of our days out exploring, not sitting in our hotel, and I wasn't sure it made sense to pay high rates to stay in such a busy tourist town.
We looked for a quieter base without giving up convenience
Through travel articles, Reddit threads, and Instagram, I discovered Thun, a lakeside town in the canton of Bern that many visitors recommended as a day trip from Interlaken.
I mapped out how easily we could reach the places we'd planned to visit from Thun. We had a week in Switzerland, with the final two days already set aside for Zurich, so I wanted to make sure we weren't losing too much time commuting.
Thun fit our itinerary perfectly.
It turned out to be the more affordable choice, too. We found a hotel overlooking the Aare River, which runs through the historic town, with two rooms for around CHF 1,500 (around $1,800 USD) for four nights — almost half what similar places cost in Interlaken and Lucerne at the time.
Thun gave us the same access, just at a slower pace
Interlaken is the main hub for the Bernese Oberland region, and many places we wanted to visit were easiest to reach from there. From Thun, it only took us 30 minutes to reach Interlaken by bus.
We'd bought the Swiss Half Fare Card in advance, which gave us 50% off most public transportation, which also saved us some money. Our hotel also provided a local travel card with free transportation to Interlaken, making day trips even easier.
One day, we were up in the mountains, riding the world's steepest cableway from Stechelberg to Mürren; the next, we strolled through the tiny village of Wengen. We also explored Lauterbrunnen Valley, a familiar backdrop from many Bollywood films we'd grown up watching. Seeing these places in person felt surreal.
Thun offered plenty beyond being a convenient base
During our stay, we wandered through the old town, walked along the Aare, and made our way up to Thun Castle. A small Christmas market right beside our hotel meant our evenings often ended with a walk through the stalls before heading in.
One rainy afternoon, we visited the St. Beatus Caves above Lake Thun. The path through the forest followed waterfalls rushing down the cliffs beside us. Despite the rain, we stayed much longer than planned, stopping along the way to take in the views of the Bernese Alps.
Later, we took a two-hour cruise on Lake Thun, passing historic lakeside towns and castles along the shore. My family still talks about that afternoon, it ended up being one of the highlights of our trip.
By the end of our stay, I understood why Thun had felt like the right choice. We saw the Switzerland we'd imagined for years, but Thun gave us the time to slow down and enjoy it together. After waiting so long for this trip, we wouldn't have wanted it any other way.
Nearly two years later, my mom still watches videos of Switzerland. She'll recognize a village or a lake we'd seen on our trip and immediately start talking about that day. It seems the trip gave her exactly what she'd wanted all those years: not just a picture of Switzerland, but memories of being there.

How will clubs train during three-week international break?
- Published
The first international break of the season is under way - and this one is longer than fans will have become accustomed to.
For the first time, the Premier League and the Championship will come to a halt for three weeks rather than the usual two.
Football fans tend not to love international breaks, but this change has been done with good intentions.
It merges the four games played in the old September and October breaks into one slot.
So the domestic game stops for three weeks, rather than four weeks across two windows. Club football is actually getting a week back.
But for players not on international duty, three weeks is a long time for finely tuned athletes not to play competitively.
So how are clubs going to deal with this change?
Here's how different teams plan to balance the international break.
Brentford's remaining players given week off
Most squads in the Premier League these days are packed with international players, and Brentford are no different.
Most of the Bees' squad are away, with about 12 players - including Callum Wilson and Igor Thiago - left at their training facility, including five who are coming back from injury.
Brentford have a longer break than almost every other team, given they hosted Chelsea on Friday evening.
Boss Keith Andrews has given his first-team players a week off with individual training programmes to follow. Those players will not have restrictions on leaving the country, but it is unlikely long-haul flights would be sanctioned.
The squad will reconvene on Saturday, 26 September to begin training again, before playing a behind-closed-doors game against another English club on the weekend of 3 October.
That friendly could potentially give the likes of Nathan Collins and Sepp van den Berg a chance to return to action, with the rest of the squad made up of under-21 players.
The second international break will look very different, with the Bees playing Brighton on Sunday, 8 November and back in action against Everton on Saturday, 21 November.
Players may be given the odd day off, but in general it will be a normal training programme with no friendly before the usual preparation for the fixture against the Toffees.
Liverpool, meanwhile, will carry on training with the small number of players that remain, with a few days off.
Manager Andoni Iraola says he will be left with "no more than three days probably to prepare" for the home game with Manchester City on 11 October.
Aston Villa have a very different international break planned.
Unai Emery will return to former club Sevilla, where he won the Europa League three times on the bounce.
Sevilla and Villa will face off in the 15th edition of the Antonio Puerta Trophy on Friday, 2 October.
The game is played in memory of the 22-year-old Sevilla wing-back, who died on 28 August 2007 after having multiple cardiac arrests on the pitch during a La Liga game against Getafe.
Blackburn glad to get injured players back
While Premier League teams see their squads decimated by international call-ups, it is not quite as dramatic in the Championship.
Many clubs will only have a handful, such as Blackburn Rovers with just four call-ups.
For Rovers boss Tony Mowbray this break will be a positive for a couple of reasons.
Mowbray has had to contend with an injury crisis in the early part of the season, with more than 10 players ruled out in the opening weeks.
The break gives Rovers the chance to ease some of those players back into action, such as Gady Beyuku and Moussa Baradji who recently made their comebacks, and others close to a return like Scott Wharton.
After the trip to Portsmouth on Saturday, Rovers headed back to Lancashire and will have a few days on the training ground this week.
After such a busy start to the campaign, with league fixtures and the Carabao Cup, it also gives Mowbray - who returned to the club in the summer - a chance to properly work with his players.
But it will not all be training.
Mowbray intends to give the players a few days off from the end of the week. Players such as Yuri Ribeiro will be able to return home to Portugal, if they so wish.
The cycle will then be repeated the following week, training the first half with a short break over the weekend. Then for week three, it is back to the usual pre-match routine before the home game against Cardiff.
Mowbray is also looking to find a Premier League or League One team to play in a behind-closed-doors friendly.
It will help those returning from injury to get minutes in the bank, and keep other members of the squad ticking over.
In the two-week break in November, players may still get a short spell off while matches are more likely to be in-house affairs with teams made up of senior and under-21 players.
Games off in League One, but no long break
The three-week international break might have posed a unique situation for a couple of clubs, whereby they could have a full squad and no games to play.
League One carries on playing unless clubs get three call-ups which meet the EFL's criteria, then a postponement can be requested.
Only four of the 12 matches have survived on each of the two weekends.
Yet many clubs prepared in advance by scheduling Football League Trophy fixtures during these three weeks.
Clubs tend to rotate in this competition anyway, so the games still go ahead even if league games are postponed.
Twelve teams will play two trophy ties, with 10 clubs playing once.
That left just Leyton Orient and Reading at risk at not having a game to play. Both have only had one league match called off, so will not have all three weeks vacant.

How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships
- Published
Kenya's President William Ruto says the World Athletics Championship will be "coming home", with Nairobi set to make history after being selected as the first African city to host the event in 2029.
Ruto hailed the winning bid as a "victory for generations of athletes" who have made the nation "synonymous with excellence" on the track and road.
Nairobi beat London and Rome to the hosting rights, with Munich selected to stage the 2031 edition.
After missing out on the 2025 World Championships to Tokyo, a series of factors helped Kenya see off its European rivals this time around.
A sport 'woven into the fabric' of the nation
When World Athletics president Lord Coe announced the decision in Budapest on Tuesday, he described Kenya's bid as "compelling and emotional".
The East African nation is the second-most successful nation in the history of the World Championships with 72 gold medals, placing it behind the United States.
The vast majority of those glories, alongside 38 Olympic gold medals, have come in middle- and long-distance running.
Lord Coe said that athletics is "woven into the fabric" of the nation and that Kenyans have helped "shape the history" of the sport.
He name-checked several runners including two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge - who was involved in the lobbying for Kenya's bid - men's 800m world record holder David Rudisha and multiple world and Olympic medallist Faith Kipyegon.
A passionate fanbase is also one of the country's great strengths.
Some 68% of Kenyans surveyed by World Athletics rated their interest in athletics as high, compared with a global average of 39%.
Athletics is the country's second-most followed sport, behind only football, and when World Athletics assessed its social media channels, Kenya was the fourth-highest nation in terms of followers.
Upgraded facilities
Kenya's previous bid for the 2025 edition fell down largely on the facilities which the country possessed.
This time around, the Kasarani Stadium will have gone through a complete structural upgrade well before the world's top athletes descend on Nairobi.
The 48,000-capacity venue will be used when Kenya co-hosts football's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) next June and July alongside Tanzania and Uganda.
"We learned from the 2025 bid because there were areas that we did not score well," Barnaba Korir, who worked on the successful bid, told the BBC World Service.
"Because of that, we managed to improve on those areas.
"I'm happy that the infrastructure that we have already developed will also meet the standards that we have seen all over the world."
Hotel space is one area not expected to be a problem, with Nairobi a regular host for large conventions.
"Kenya is also known for its very dynamic hospitality, the tourism sector," Elijah Mwangi, principal secretary at the State Department for Sports, told the BBC.
"It has a game park within the city, so we are waiting to welcome everybody."
President Ruto made financial and security guarantees in order to secure the Championships.
"We thank World Athletics for the confidence it has placed in Kenya," Ruto said.
"We will honour that confidence by delivering an unforgettable championship worthy of our athletes, our country and our continent."
Expanding athletics
Lord Coe became president of World Athletics (then known as the IAAF) in 2015 and has pledged to grow the sport around the globe.
During his time in office the World Championships have been hosted in Qatar (2019), the United States (2022) and Tokyo, while China's capital Beijing will stage them in 2027.
Kenya has successfully hosted age-grade events in Nairobi and the World Cross Country Championships in Mombasa, while the World Athletics Relays were held in Botswana's capital Gaborone in May.
With Coe's third term in office coming to an end next year, one official involved in Kenya's bid, speaking before the host announcement, said it was "unthinkable" that Nairobi would not succeed.
"With this decision we continue to fulfil our mission of growing athletics worldwide," Coe said.
"It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances.
Coe hailed the "quality, ambition and commitment" of all four bidding cities.
London, Munich and Rome have all previously held the Olympics, with the World Championships in London as recently as 2017, but the chance to break new ground in Africa was clearly compelling.
UK Athletics chief executive Jack Buckner said his team was "deeply disappointed" to see London miss out.
What is needed next?
Kenya now faces logistical and organisational challenges over the next three years as it prepares to deliver Africa's first World Championships.
With the 2027 Afcon looming large on the horizon, Nairobi will have a chance to test-run getting fans in and out of the Kasarani Stadium, which lies about a half-hour drive from the city's central business district.
The venue does not have any rail connections but Korir says World Athletics officials were "very satisfied" by Kenya's transport plan.
There were instances of overcrowding when the stadium hosted Kenya games at football's African Nations Championships last year, which led to the capacity being reduced for some matches.
Delays in preparations for Afcon have raised concerns, and the funding for the World Championships will come entirely from the Kenyan government.
Mwangi revealed that $78m (£58.5m) is the current estimate for the government's contribution, with sponsorship deals also playing a role.
"We are prepared to ensure that whatever is expected to be paid, it is paid in the due time," he added.
Presidential elections are scheduled for next year, but Korir is confident organisers will secure the "huge" and "legally binding" figure earmarked even if there is a change in government.
"Whatever the government assigns now will be observed by the next government. It is an international agreement," he said.
Then comes ticketing, first to make sure the local population are not priced out and then to ensure the stands are filled.
The cheapest tickets for the Under-18 World Championships in 2017 were priced at 200 Kenyan shillings ($1.15, £1.14) but attendances were low until entry was made free.
World Athletics generated $522m in revenue from Tokyo 2025, with a total of 619,000 tickets sold over the nine days of competition, while London sold a record 705,000 tickets in 2017.
In passing up the opportunity of returning to the British capital, World Athletics has chosen expansion over guaranteed ticket sales, but attendances will be scrutinised - especially after the sparse numbers seen in the stands in Doha in 2019.
Korir, however, is confident the Kasarani Stadium "will be full" on "every day" of competition, including morning sessions, if sales begin early enough.
Meanwhile, Kenya has endured a spate of doping scandals in recent years, with 11 individuals banned by the Athletics Integrity Unit so far this year alone.
The pressure is now on the East African nation to deliver on its promises in the build-up to Nairobi 2029 and ensure the Championships pass off without any major issues.

Lithuania ready to 'fight back' but has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM tells BBC
- Published
Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrender" if attacked.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told Newsnight that Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.
He told Newsnight if his country was attacked, "we will fight back... we will engage". But he said there were plans for a "variety of scenarios" and used an example of getting elderly citizens out of cities "smoothly" and avoiding traffic jams.
Lithuania, a Nato member, shares a land border with the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad.
"We're thinking about a variety of scenarios, not all of them are being discussed very much publicly," Sinkevičius told the BBC.
"We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us."
Sinkevičius also said the UK needed a "shift in the mindset" in terms of its approach to defence, but noted that Lithuania was "closer to the border and closer to [the] threat".
It comes just a week after Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace.
Though the origins of the drone have not been confirmed, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Newshour that it came from the direction of Belarus, Lithuania's neighbour and a key Russian ally.
The UK's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace.
"We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory."
Moscow did not comment on the incident.
Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine.
Residents in Lithuania's capital Vilnius were also forced to take shelter in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel.
Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into fellow Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.
Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.
Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against all members".
