Rows of hardware and car-part shops line Garstin Bastion Road, with faded signs crammed together above their shutters. By day, the street is one of Old Delhi’s busiest commercial thoroughfares. But as dusk falls, GB Road, as it is known locally, transforms into one of the city’s most notorious red-light districts.
An estimated 2,800 sex workers live and work in brothels that occupy the upper floors of the dilapidated buildings, their entrances tucked behind narrow stairways and unmarked doors. Women sit on plastic stools beneath the stairways, calling out to men passing on the street, while others watch from windows above, their eyes following the movement below before customers are directed upstairs.
The challenges the women of GB Road face are numerous and well documented – from health risks to abuse, debt to poor sanitation. Now they face a new struggle: India’s controversial electoral reform process. The Election Commission’s special intensive revision, or SIR, is a nationwide exercise in which electoral rolls have shrunk by more than 58 million voters across the 13 states covered in the first two of three main phases. In Delhi, covered in the third phase, the scale of exclusion is the highest recorded as a percentage: 4.76 million names – 33% of the city’s previous electorate – do not appear on the city’s draft roll published on 31 August.
The government says SIR is meant to “purify” the electoral rolls by removing ineligible voters, including alleged undocumented migrants, but critics have accused Narendra Modi’s government of using it to target minority voters and reshape electoral rolls in ways that could benefit his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
On GB Road, the proportion of those excluded is even higher. Data shared by officials overseeing about 1,300 voters in the area show that about 650 were sex workers on the previous electoral roll. Of these, at least 500 have either been marked as “shifted”, meaning they have moved home or location, or have been unable to establish their eligibility because of missing documentation – more than three-quarters of the sex workers on the local roll.
One of them is 36-year-old Beauty*, who has lived on GB Road for more than two decades. She got her first voter ID in 2008. At the time, the address where she lived and worked as a sex worker and verification by a government official called a booth-level officer (BLO) were enough to put her on the electoral roll. She voted in previous elections.
But under the new rules, voters had to establish eligibility by proving their link to the relevant previous electoral roll or by producing prescribed documents such as a passport, birth or education certificate – a paper trail Beauty struggled to reconstruct. Trafficked at 16 and brought to the brothels of GB Road, she has no contact with her family. She does have an Aadhaar card, India’s biometric identity document used widely to establish identity and access government services, with her GB Road address. But Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship and does not, by itself, establish eligibility to vote under the SIR process.
She tried to get a copy of her matriculation certificate, which is evidence of schooling, from the village in Rajasthan where she grew up. One of her regular customers of the past 10 years – a man she refers to as her husband, agreed to help track down the old record but failed.
“If I had the papers to show my father’s birth certificate, or even my own matriculation certificate, then I could prove who I am,” she says. “But how can I go back to my village to ask for these things when my trafficking has brought so much shame to my family that they no longer accept me?”
Now Beauty has lost hope – and, for now, her vote. Her name was left out of Delhi’s recent draft electoral roll. For her, the voter ID had meant more than a piece of identification. Sex workers, she says, are accustomed to being treated as immoral, degraded and less worthy than others.
“We all shit. That is what makes us equal as human beings. Voting is the same in the realm of rights. When I stand in that queue, nobody is more or less than me. It reminds me that whatever people think about my work, I am still equal to everyone else.”
Beauty is not alone in struggling to prove her eligibility. The SIR requirements have exposed the precarious paper trails of women across GB Road, a roughly 1.5km stretch running between two of Delhi’s historic landmarks, Ajmeri Gate and Lahori Gate.
Of the nine sex workers interviewed for this story, none had successfully completed the SIR process: six said they had never received the enumeration form distributed by BLOs to verify voters’ details and collect information for the electoral-roll revision, while the remaining three were unable to meet the documentation requirements.
According to Kiran Deshmukh, a sex worker and coordinator at the National Network of Sex Workers (NNSW), many have spent years, even decades, in Delhi but possess few documents establishing their family histories or links to earlier electoral rolls. “Some were trafficked as children and lost contact with their families; others never attended school or have moved between rooms and brothels without leaving a stable documentary trail,” says Deshmukh. “It is impossible in such circumstances to prove such rigid eligibility requirements under SIR.”
The process is so cumbersome that even people who are literate and have institutional and organisational support can struggle to establish their eligibility. “The process of receiving the enumeration form, knowing when you have not received it, reaching out, then trying to create a paper trail is so daunting that the entire burden of proving your eligibility is placed on the citizen to protect their own constitutional right,” says Deshmukh.
Sagrika Rajora, a researcher and member of Voter Adhikar Manch, a citizens’ collective, argues that the burden falls particularly heavily on people whose lives do not fit neatly into the categories used by the verification process. “To identify people of such marginality is a tedious task. These categories of ‘shifted’ become an easy way forward for booth-level officers, when finding people on the ground is already time-consuming.”
BLOs are often drawn from occupations such as auxiliary nurses or health workers, adding electoral duties to already demanding jobs. Some have raised concerns about the workload and unrealistic timelines of the exercise. Yet, Rajora says, there has been little effort to streamline the process to ensure that “no eligible citizen is left out”, the aim outlined by the Delhi chief electoral officer, Ashok Kumar.
“There is so much discretion vested in one BLO. Even if you leave citizenship aside and talk only about voter rights, the entire process of delivering and collecting these forms depends on that one person. There are no grounds for entrusting one person with such a huge responsibility without any accountability at all,” Rajora says.
“It is not surprising that sex workers are among those being excluded. When people have lives that are so complex and mobile, you are going to be untraceable, absent from the system. These are the people for whom such a verification system is simply not designed to work.”
The gaps also cause problems for workers’ children when they reach adulthood. “Children may not possess documents establishing parentage in the manner expected for verification. Some are raised by relatives, guardians or members of the community, while others grow up in institutional care, making conventional family records difficult to establish,” says Deshmukh.
For 23-year-old Dinesh*, whose mother was a sex worker, the problem is not abstract. His mother died three years ago, but she never had a birth certificate. Without one, obtaining her death certificate became nearly impossible, leaving Dinesh with little documentation through which to establish his maternal lineage.
When Dinesh submitted his enumeration form, he relied on his matriculation certificate as proof of his identity. But the booth-level officer pointed out that it did not have his father’s name. “If my mother gave birth to me, why do I need a man’s name on any official certificate?” he asks.
Dinesh says his name is missing from the draft electoral roll. He is still unsure why, but suspects the absence of his father’s name may have been a factor.
The NNSW has written to the chief electoral officer seeking special measures to ensure that sex workers and their children are not excluded from the SIR. But the joint chief electoral officer, Balram Meena, told The Hindu there was no separate process for sex workers. “If their mapping can’t be done and there are no documents either, their names will be removed as per the process.”
The fear of losing the vote is not only about voting rights. In West Bengal, where the SIR has already been completed, the BJP government has used lists of voters deleted during the exercise to scrutinise eligibility for welfare schemes. The BJP chief minister, Suvendu Adhikari, says welfare programmes will continue under a “transparent process”, but adds: “No deceased person, illegal infiltrator, or non-Indian individual will be allowed to avail benefits meant for citizens of the state.” The government has excluded about 3 million beneficiaries from its new Annapurna Bhandar welfare for women scheme, using SIR deletion data in its verification process.
In Delhi, the next stage of the SIR process – issuing notices to those whose eligibility or previous electoral-roll details could not be established or matched, and dealing with claims and objections – has now begun and will continue until 29 October. Those excluded from the draft roll can challenge their omission. But Dinesh says he does not intend to.
After years of being asked to produce documents that his family never had, he is unsure what more he can submit to prove that he exists.
“Even if my mother were alive today, I don’t think that would be enough to prove anything. She never had the documents they are asking for. So how am I supposed to get those documents now, especially after her death?”
* Names have been changed. Workers and residents did not permit any photography during the Guardian’s visit

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.
Molly McCann Sanders has a lot in common with many of the other women who helped Donald Trump win a second term as president. A pro-life Catholic who lives in Texas, she has staunchly conservative opinions on immigration and a fierce hatred of eminent domain—the practice of the government taking private property for public use.
Sanders, the president of the Eagle Forum Education & Legal Defense Fund, which was started by Phyllis Schlafly, also describes herself as “a crunchy MAHA mom”—and says she’s been paying particular attention to data centers.
“I'm alarmed by the idea that these data centers can move in and pollute,” she tells me. “I'm not a data center expert. I'm not a tech expert. But I’m suspicious and wary, and want to move slowly.”
She loves Trump, “but I think he’s wrong about data centers,” she says. And she sees the GOP’s effort to court what she calls “the laptop class”—young men who are enthusiastic about technology—at the Republican midterm convention earlier this month as a huge misstep with midterms nearing.
McCann Sanders isn’t alone. More than 60 percent of Americans, including 47 percent of Republicans, say they are opposed to the construction of data centers in a poll released by The New York Times last week. In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee sent a private memo to AI companies sounding the alarm on how voters perceive data centers, warning that “campaign or party committees can not fix the toxic brand of an entire segment of the economy.” Last week, GOP strategist Tony Fabrizio issued a memo to the party’s candidates claiming that “unqualified support for building more AI data centers is a losing position.”
But the GOP is facing one big hurdle: Trump himself. In recent weeks, facing mounting scrutiny on his policies and support for the industry, Trump has doubled down on his defense of both data centers and AI. In late August, he wrote in a Truth Social post that only communities that wanted to be “backwards and poor” would refuse data centers coming to town.
Last week, he issued yet another series of posts boosting AI data centers. Users on his own Truth Social platform pushed back. An analysis from The New York Times of thousands of responses found that anti-data-center and anti-AI comments—including from staunch MAGA accounts—outnumbered positive comments by four to one.
Sanders says she sometimes “looks past” the wilder things Trump says, but she can’t fully overlook his pro-data-center rhetoric.
“That is not the right way to go about this,” she says of the “backwards and poor” post. “We do have legitimate concerns. There are real problems.”
My colleague Hugo Lowell, who covers the White House and writes our Inner Loop newsletter, says he’s not surprised by Trump’s attitude. “He’s bullish on AI,” he tells me. “He’s been told that restricting data center development means restricting compute, which means the US loses to China.”
The China competition angle is being publicly echoed by tech accelerationists and White House allies, including former White House AI czar David Sacks and investor and Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale. The latter debated Steve Bannon’s tech editor Joe Allen—whom I profiled last month—at an auxiliary event during the convention. That conversation between Lonsdale and Allen, Sanders says, was the only time she heard data centers brought up during the entire midterm convention.
There’s some evidence that voters haven’t quite made up their minds on how heavily to weigh the issue—and which party to trust. The New York Times poll found that AI and data centers rank far down the list of voters’ priorities, and almost 20 percent say they don’t know which party would handle the issue better.
And candidates otherwise aligned with Trump may just decide to ignore cues from the White House. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee for governor in Wisconsin, has scored Trump’s endorsement. But he’s also attacked his Democratic opponent David Crowley for what Tiffany claims are pro-data-center views.
But despite breaks like Tiffany’s and concerns like Sanders’, Trump “thinks MAGA at the end of the day will back him—on Epstein, on Iran, on AI,” Hugo says.
What We’re Writing
Haven’t you always wished that data centers were a little more cuddly? You’re in luck! My colleague Boone Ashworth wrote about a new server-shaped plushie with gangly limbs and a little smiley face, called Bezzy. (Adorable!) When you squeeze him, he emits a terrible droning noise—real audio recorded by people living next to a data center in Virginia.
Bezzy is part of a larger project designed to raise awareness about data center expansion in the US. The plush toy is one of the many ways the data center backlash is taking shape.
“Personally, I love Bezzy and want to adopt one,” Boone says. “Also, it makes me very grateful I don't live near a data center. I really feel for people who do.”
What We’re Reading
The Washington Sun reports that the Interior Department is considering at least 12 data center proposals across at least 17,600 acres of public land—far more than had been previously reported.
Writer Natalie Fertig traveled to a swing district in Pennsylvania to take the political pulse of anti-data-center organizers there. Despite their success in blocking a big data center project, many of the folks she interviewed in both political parties felt like politicians didn’t care about them.
Amazon admitted this week that it had permanently lost customer data that was stored in data centers hit by Iranian drone strikes earlier this year. Reuters broke the story.
Virginia governor Abigail Spanberger signed an executive order on Friday that creates a state AI task force and may limit data centers. The latter is particularly notable given that the state is home to Data Center Alley, a global hot spot for the facilities. Read more about the order in The Verge.

You can get Google Pixel’s Rambler AI voice typing on many Android phones without root by patching a supported Gboard version with Morphe. Once enabled, Rambler can clean up speech, remove filler words, fix grammar, add punctuation, and format dictated text using AI.
If there is one feature that truly revolutionized because of AI, it is voice typing. Voice typing did exist way before AI, but it was very basic. It only converted the spoken audio directly into text, which included all the filler words, missing punctuation, grammar mistakes, and more. It basically turned whatever you spoke into text.
But with AI, voice typing goes through one extra step, where all your typing is fed to the AI models, which remove all filler words and format the sentence structure. It fundamentally eliminates the need for you to copy text into multiple apps, fix the grammar and sentence structure, and then copy it again to wherever you need it.
Third-party voice dictation apps went ahead and also included support for different formatting styles based on the app you are using, and they support almost every app.
However, the AI voice dictation feature truly gained traction after Google introduced the Pixel 11’s Rambler feature, which is very similar to AI voice dictation apps that use AI to refine the speech-to-text output.
However, currently, this feature is officially available on Pixel 11 series devices. You can see the full requirements here. But with a single patch for your Google Gboard, you can get this feature on a supported Android device. In this video, you are going to learn exactly how to get the Google Pixel’s Rambler feature on another Android device without root.

How to Get Pixel 11 Rambler Voice Typing on Any Android Without Root
Before we get started, here are the prerequisites
Download the supported Gboard 18.0.3.954559732-release-arm64-v8a APK from here, or you can skip this if you want to download the supported version directly from Morphe
To use this feature, your smartphone needs to run Android 10 or later. Here are the full requirements:
- Android 10+ (Android 12+ recommended)
- Requires Sideloading enabled
Download the Morphe app for Android. It lets you patch your apps. For those who are unaware, patching is basically modifying the app and adding features that don’t exist.
Step 1: Download the Morphe app on your Android phone. Visit the official Morphe GitHub page and tap Download. Or download directly from the official Morphe site
Step 2: Once downloaded, install the app.
Step 3: Open the Morphe app and tap on Sources.
Step 4: Tap on the Plus icon, paste the following link in the Sources box, tap on Add this link, and tap on Add. https://github.com/jasonwu1994/Gboard-patches
Step 5: Wait for the source to load and tap on the Gboard app.
Step 6: Now tap on Yes, Help me find an APK, tap on Download APK, and download the app. Don’t install it.
Step 7: Now go back to the Morphe app, tap on Open APK file, and select the Gboard 18.0.3.954559732-release-arm64-v8a APK or later you downloaded above, and Morphe will start patching the app.
Step 8: Once patched, tap Install the app and allow Morphe to install the app on your device.
Step 9: Now open the patched Gboard and enable it. You need to set it as the default keyboard on some Android phones to use it, or you can go through the permission setup and switch to this keyboard later.
Step 10: Now open the patched Gboard and tap on Settings, scroll down, and tap on Patches.
Step 11: Tap on Advanced Voice Typing and enable the Enable Advanced Voice Typing option.
Step 12: Once enabled, go back to Voice Typing Settings and then select the Rambler feature.
Step 13: Now, to use the feature, you need to force stop the app. To do that, go to the patched Gboard app, long-press on it, tap on the i icon, then tap on the Force Stop option, and then confirm. These steps may vary depending on your smartphone brand and Android version.
Step 14: Now open any app where you can type, bring up patched Gboard, tap on the microphone icon, and start using Rambler.
This is how you can enable the Google Pixel Rambler feature on a supported Android smartphone without root. Since it is a manual process, I have included details step by step to help you understand.

FAQs on Using Google Rambler on Non-Pixel Phones
1. Is it safe to use a patched version of Gboard with my Google account?
Yes, it is safe to install if you follow my steps exactly and only use the resources I included in this guide. For safety, I also highly recommend checking the app before installing using Google Play Protect or using third-party antivirus scanner tools like VirusTotal.
2. Will Rambler continue working after Gboard or Android gets updated?
Yes, since you are using a separate Gboard patched version, updating the original Gmail app won’t affect this patched version. However, the patched version also needs to be updated in case Google blocks access to the Rambler feature for other devices.
3. Can I switch back to the official Gboard later without losing my keyboard settings?
You won’t lose any settings; you can simply switch back to the original Gboard if you want to anytime.

Google Rambler currently supports Arabic, English, French, German, Hindi, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, and a few other Indian languages,

Yes, the Google Pixel Rambler feature uses cloud processing to fix sentences; however, Google says this data is not saved, stored, or shared and is deleted immediately after the processed text is delivered.

Harry Brook: England white-ball captain relishing working with mentor of Kevin Pietersen's calibre
Harry Brook says Kevin Pietersen's mentorship and masterclasses are already bearing fruit for England as they look to take momentum from unbeaten T20 series in three ODIs against Sri Lanka; watch first ODI live from midday this Tuesday on Sky Sports Cricket
Monday 21 September 2026 13:55, UK
Captain Harry Brook says leaning on a mentor of Kevin Pietersen's calibre will only help the continued upward trajectory of England's white-ball sides.
Pietersen, regarded as one of the greatest batters of the 21st century, has been brought into the England white-ball set-up in a mentoring role by head coach Brendon McCullum in the build-up to next year's 50-over World Cup.
Brook shed light on the impact Pietersen was already having on the squad, both on and off the field, with the team's approach to playing spin already addressed in a masterclass from the former England captain.

"KP has been very good," Brook told a press conference. "He's enjoying the role, he's enjoying himself.
"He's been good to have around, little chats here and there. Away from the game, sat having a coffee and a chat about how he sees the game and how he thinks it should be played.
"He was a hero to many of us growing up, so it's good to have a man of his calibre in our side."
On the masterclass, Brook added: "A lot of it was about picking the length of spin. That is key to facing spin and being able to rotate strike as well as possible.
"In ODI cricket that's an area we probably need to improve as a side. It can make a massive difference to winning games of cricket.
"He [Pietersen] was a hell of a player against spin, alongside [Joe] Root and [Marcus] Trescothick. They were very good players at playing spin, so it's about picking their brains and asking them what worked for them and putting that into your game."
'Higher-octane cricket'
England, fresh from a 3-0 series sweep over Sri Lanka that lifted them to the top of the T20 world rankings, face Sri Lanka again in their first ODI since teaming up with Pietersen.
The three-match series starts in Durham on Tuesday, live on Sky Sports, and Brook has challenged England to maintain their momentum.
"We can take a hell of a lot of confidence from being unbeaten in the T20s," Brook said.
"Going into this ODI series we want more of the same. We're trying to play a higher-octane style of cricket and put them [the opposition] under pressure with bat and ball.
"We want to be one of the fittest sides in the world. To do that, we've got to work hard on and off the field.
"We are trending in the right direction. There are a few touches here and there which we can improve."
Brook - better than Pietersen?
Brook was hailed as an "absolute freak" by Ben Stokes as he tonked a 42-ball hundred, England's joint-second-fastest in T20Is, to pave the way for a 119-run victory in the T20 series opener against Sri Lanka in Southampton.
The swashbuckling innings was played in front of England legend Pietersen, and commented on by Stokes, who took to social media to say that, in his opinion, the Yorkshireman's ability outstrips that of Pietersen.
Asked to comment on Stokes' assessment, Brook said: "They are his opinions. I'm just trying to stay in the moment and in the present as much as possible.

England have made three changes to the side which secured a 2-1 ODI series victory over India with a 27-run victory at Lord's on July 19.
Tom Banton replaces Jacob Bethell at the top order, Jamie Overton has been deployed as an all-rounder role in Sam Curran's absence, while Rehan Ahmed replaces the injured Adil Rashid.

Three arrested in South Africa over one of nine women's bodies found
- Published
Three suspects have been detained in South Africa in connection with the murder of a woman in an area east of Johannesburg – the last of nine recent cases in that region that has shone a spotlight on the level of violence against women in the country.
Under pressure to solve the spate of murders which has involved victims' bodies being dumped on a roadside, police have described the arrests of the three – a man and two women - as a "breakthrough".
Referring to all nine cases, acting police chief Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane said her officers were "working tirelessly to bring those responsible to justice".
The three suspects are due in court on Monday morning.
Their case relates to the death of Jabulile Ntimba, whose half-naked body was found wrapped in a sheet in Dawn Park last Thursday.
Several of the recent victims were discovered partially clothed and with injuries, but police have stressed that they have not established whether all the deaths are connected or whether a serial killer is responsible.

Shares of ecommerce major Meesho surged as much as 9.3% during the intraday trading after brokerage UBS maintained its ‘Buy’ rating on the stock and raised its target price to ₹260 from ₹210. The stock touched an intraday high of ₹239.45 on the BSE. It was trading 8.9% higher at ₹238.55 at 11:25 IST. At the current price, UBS’ revised target implies a further upside of around 9%. Meesho’s market capitalisation stood at ₹1.10 Lakh Cr (around $11.5 Bn). The brokerage raised its net merchandise value (NMV) estimates for Meesho for FY29-FY31 by 7%-18%, along with a similar increase in its contribution profit projections. It also increased its EBITDA estimates for the period by 20%-40%. UBS attributed its higher NMV projections to the continued expansion of Meesho’s buyer and seller ecosystems, along with the rapid growth in SKUs and logistics partners. Meesho’s annual transacting sellers jumped 81% YoY to 10.4 Lakh in Q1 FY27, while its annual transacting users rose 29% to 27.4 Cr. The ecommerce platform’s NMV increased 34% YoY to ₹11,614 Cr during the quarter. The brokerage expects Meesho’s earnings to grow faster than NMV over the medium term as the company improves advertising monetisation and its logistics economics. In Q1 FY27, Meesho’s contribution margin expanded to 4.6% of NMV from 4% in the preceding quarter. Its adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to ₹178.2 Cr from ₹230.1 Cr in the year-ago period. The company also narrowed its consolidated net loss by 54% YoY to ₹132.8 Cr during the quarter, while operating revenue surged 48% to ₹3,707 Cr. Meesho listed on the bourses in December last year. At its current price, the stock is trading nearly 115% above its IPO issue price of ₹111 and about 6% below its 52-week high of ₹254.65.

iPhones and Macs are like two peas in a pod. Apple’s hardware synergy means you can launch iPhone apps right from the macOS desktop, respond to texts without picking up your iPhone, and even copy text on one platform and paste it on the other. That kind of seamless connectivity does not natively exist for Android phone owners at the operating system level.
Google’s trying to change that with Googlebooks, a new class of laptop. First teased in May, the company finally shared more details about the new OS at a media-only event in New York City last week. Like with Android, hardware manufacturers can make their own Googlebooks, provided they hit specific standards set by Google.
Today marks the launch of five new computers that comply with the Googlebooks standard, one each from HP, Dell, Lenovo, Acer, and Asus. These machines are powered by either Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X Elite chip or Intel’s Core Ultra 3 (MediaTek also supports the Googlebook platform with its new Dimensity CX C10 Max chip, but none of the new laptops use the chip yet).
Preorders open today, and the machines hit store shelves on October 4, starting at $899. Every purchase includes a full year of Google AI Pro service with 5 terabytes of storage.
Here are the new laptops, all of which are clamshells except the Acer, which is a 2-in-1 machine:
- Acer Googlebook 14 ($899)
- Dell XPS Googlebook ($1,199)
- HP Googlebook 14 ($1,299)
- Lenovo Googlebook 15 ($1,299)
- Asus Googlebook 14 ($1,299)
Some of the standards Google has set include using “premium materials,” like aluminum, magnesium, or carbon fiber, to make them lightweight. They need at least 16 GB of RAM, deliver more than 45 tera operations per second (TOPS), a touchscreen (LCD or OLED), a backlit keyboard, a haptic trackpad, Dolby Atmos speakers, studio-quality microphones with noise cancellation, and at least 14 hours of battery life. Googlebooks will receive 10 years of software updates.
They must feature the Glowbar—the signature LED strip on the laptop’s exterior that identifies the machine as a Googlebook. It’s a callback to the glowbar Google used on its original Chromebook Pixel. (Speaking of which, Google hasn’t shared whether it’s making its own Googlebook under its Made by Google Pixel hardware division.) Developers can access the Glowbar to customize the lights to specific actions in their apps, and there’s also an Easter egg app consumers can unlock to customize the light color and animation themselves. Like HiLight introduced on the latest Pixel phones, the Glowbar will illuminate when you talk to Gemini.
“There’s a lot the laptop gets right, but much of it was designed decades ago, before mobile devices were invented,” Sameer Samat, president of the Android ecosystem, said at the event. “Reinventing laptops is a multi-year endeavor. Our first step is to focus on the Android community because today there isn’t a laptop that is designed to seamlessly work with your Android phone.”
Googlebook merges Android’s mobile-first operating system with ChromeOS, the OS powering Chromebooks. Google says Chromebooks aren’t going anywhere and will continue to serve schools and act as the budget-friendly option for consumers. While the Googlebook interface feels like a blown-up version of Android, it’s not just an Android-powered desktop. Rather, it’s a distinct OS optimized for x86 and ARM chip architectures.
What’s particularly interesting is how Android apps work on the device. They’re categorized in three ways. When you set up your Googlebook with your Android phone, important data flows seamlessly to the laptop, including Wi-Fi networks, passwords, settings, messages, contacts, and photos. Not all of your phone apps will automatically be installed, though, as Google deems some apps as “better on the web," like Facebook. (You can still install the Facebook app if you want and get the mobile-shaped experience.)
The next tier of Android app is “Optimized for Desktop.” These apps take advantage of the bigger screens with better layouts and a little more functionality. The final tier is “Made for Desktop,” like the desktop versions of Chrome. Google says around 20 or so apps are either optimized for desktop or made for the desktop so far, including CapCut, Adobe Photoshop, Notability, and Fantastical. As the platform grows, Google expects more developers will target Android’s “Made for Desktop” tier and bring their desktop-grade apps from Windows and macOS to Googlebook.
People want to play games on their laptops, and so Google says you’ll be able to access more than 20,000 titles on the Play Store, many of which support cross-device play between mobile, tablets, and laptops. Google says around 50 of the 100 top titles are optimized for keyboard, trackpad, and touchscreen. But since you can’t download AAA games for Googlebooks (yet), especially without a discrete GPU, Google is offering 1 year of Nvidia’s GeForce Now game streaming service, which is optimized for the platform.
New Frontiers
Googlebook is an opportunity for Google to bring artificial intelligence to the forefront of the laptop computing experience, which is why many of the core new features are AI-powered. For example, similar to Android 17, you can generate your own desktop widgets with simple prompts to Gemini.
Magic Pointer is the marquee Gemini feature. Wiggle the mouse pointer over anything, and a Gemini overlay will suggest contextual actions. For example, if you wiggle over an event someone invited you to, you’ll get a prompt to automatically “Create an event” and have it added to your Google Calendar with one tap. Or if you’re wondering what breed of dog you’re looking at (whether it’s a video or photo), wiggle and ask Gemini, “What’s the breed?” If you’re wondering whether an email is a phishing attempt, wiggle over it and ask Gemini.
AI companies are also heavily focused on voice-to-text as the future of computing, which is why Google is injecting its Rambler feature natively into Googlebook. It debuted on the latest Google Pixel 11 smartphones and is a potent AI-powered voice dictation engine that transcribes whatever you say. It intelligently cuts your “ums” and “uhs,” and even knows when you make a mistake and restate something, keeping the parts it believes you want to convey. You can ask it to format sentences in a particular tone, include bullets or emoji, and even mix in different languages. You can call up Rambler with Google’s Quick Insert key, a key found on Googlebook keyboards and newer Chromebook keyboards. Rambler works in any text field.
The rest of the platform leans heavily into Android smartphone continuity. In the Files app, context-aware search lets you find photos by simply typing “dog” instead of the file name—and it searches files on your phone just as easily as local storage. Meanwhile, “Continue on” hands off ongoing tasks so apps open on your laptop right where you left off on mobile, and an app-casting feature lets you stream phone-only apps like DoorDash directly to the desktop.
What if you have an iPhone? Google offers a new “Link to iOS” app that lets users access messages and some notifications on the desktop, but cross-platform limitations mean you can’t enjoy the same breadth of features. Then again, iPhone owners will probably stick to Macs. At least Android now has something comparable.

On August 17, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) announced its revamped social media team, appointing Deepak Mhaskey as the national social media convenor, and Priti Gandhi, Shivanand Dwivedi, Alok Bhatt and Arun Yadav as co-convenors.
While curiosity grew as to who these newly appointed individuals were and their past work and association with the party, social media users were quick to notice that immediately after the announcement, Gandhi, Dwivedi and Yadav made their X accounts private and there was no trace of Bhatt on the internet.
While all the other IT cell members are back to being active on X, albeit after deleting hundreds of thousands of old posts, Alok Bhatt is the only one in the group whose X handle remains inaccessible or ‘protected’ even a month after the new team was announced.
The only remnants of Bhatt’s online presence are the now-disabled X account, screenshots from his X posts and some articles in Right-wing outlets like OpIndia, Organiser and Swarajya.
Alt News found that in the past, Bhatt had been called out for controversial tweets several times. In archived screenshots of his posts from the past, the BJP functionary can be seen using sexist, Islamophobic, and derogatory language, some of which can be seen below:
Who is Alok Bhatt?
Bhatt, who claims to hail from Dehradun, has worn many hats over the course of his career. According to his LinkedIn profile, he graduated from Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University (HNBGU) in Uttarakhand and went on to work with several organisations, including NIIT University, where he served as financial controller until April 2010.
In 2010, he founded Nature Connect Outdoors — an education and adventure non-profit organisation that deals in outdoor education and skill development, including treks, camping, and rafting expeditions. According to the website’s bio, Bhatt had “shunned his corporate career” to follow his passion, which culminated in the formation of the NGO. The organisation is still functional.
According to details available on Zauba Corp, Bhatt is a Chartered Accountant (CA) and the partner of a firm of CAs called RSAC & CO LLP, incorporated in May 2021.
Bhatt has also served as the economic adviser to former Uttarakhand chief minister Trivendra Singh Rawat. However, it’s not clear when he was appointed and when exactly his tenure ended. He wrote an article for Firstpost defending the ministry of housing and urban affairs over the controversial Central Vista project. The author bio designated him as ‘Economic Advisor’ to Rawat.
In 2020, after a district officer’s press release promoting inter-caste and interfaith marriages drew criticism from social media users, Bhatt had reportedly tweeted: “No one from the government has spoken in support of promoting interfaith marriages. No one in the BJP government in their wildest dreams will support anything that is made out here.”
We sent an email and called up Bhatt several times to know more from him, but he did not respond.
Long-standing Association With BJP
Bhatt’s X handle, @alok_bhatt, was followed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. In fact, Modi quote-tweeted one of Bhatt’s posts in 2024, where he urged people to watch the film Sabarmati Report.
Bhatt was also invited to PM Modi’s swearing-in ceremony in the past. In 2024, Right-wing influencer Vikas Pandey shared an image with Bhatt alongside former BJP spokesperson Nupur Sharma, member of the economic advisory council to the PM, Sanjeev Sanyal, and others, with the caption “First swearing in”.

The Pamphlet-Savitr Analytics-Alok Bhatt Connection
In 2022, Bhatt took on a directorial role at Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation, a company that was incorporated in April 26 that year, with Bhatt and Ashish Nautiyal initially named as directors. According to documents filed with the Union ministry of corporate affairs (MCA), Bhatt holds 9,500 shares, or 95 per cent of the company, while Nautiyal holds the remaining 500 shares, or 5 per cent.
Interestingly, Nautiyal is also the founding editor of the Right-wing media outlet, The Pamphlet.
Savitr Analytics has no website or online presence. We went through its financial records filed with the MCA for the financial years 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25, and found that it was registered as a Section 8 company, i.e., a non-profit. In the 2024-25 financial year, its total revenue from operations was Rs 2.7 crore.
The organisation’s revenue across all three years comes from ‘sale of services’, and the rows for ‘Grants or donations received (relevant for Sec 8 companies)’, present in the 2022-23 and 2023-24 filings, are left blank in 2022-23 and 2023-24. In 2024-25, the row does not exist.
Under ‘Corporate Information’, they state ‘Research and awareness about Indian culture and heritage…’, ‘Promotion of commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity, and environmental protection…’ and ‘Advancement of education, learning, and skills development…’ as their activities.
There was a category called ‘professional expenses’ in the 2022-23 filing that was later relabeled as ‘content production expenses’. Rs. 41,48,600 was spent in the first year, Rs. 95,36,600 (filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the second year, and Rs. 1,38,53,200 (also filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the third year.
Next, we found that an individual named Ridhika Aggarwal stated on LinkedIn that she worked as a content writer for Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation until August 2023. We went through her X timeline (linked to her LinkedIn profile) and found that she wrote at least three articles for The Pamphlet during her tenure at Savitr. None of the articles are currently available on the website.
Ridhika is also listed as a non-official member of a steering committee formed by the Union ministry of environment, forest and climate change in 2023.
The Pamphlet, previously known as The Indian Affairs, posted for the first time on Facebook in April 2022, which is the same time when Savitr Analytics was incorporated.

आज ही के दिन साल 2019 में लोकसभा चुनाव का रिजल्ट भी आया था और प्रधानमंत्री… pic.twitter.com/6lAVSW3twN
— V Ashish Nautiyal (@ashu_nauty) May 15, 2024
The Pamphlet claims to “cut through the noise of the modern information ecosystem by offering readers and viewers clarity, depth and perspective on issues that shape India and the world.” Its reports have seem to be echoing pro-BJP narratives. An August 11 video report, for instance, was captioned: “Questions raised in the public domain regarding the credentials of two CJP leaders, Abhijeet Dipke and Saurav Das, have brought up several serious concerns”. It questioned Dipke’s Boston University degree, academic timeline and funding, as well as Das’ property, tenancy, rent, police verification, and electoral records.
During the CJP protests, another report took a swipe at Mohammed Junaid, who had been feeding protesters, with the reporter noting that “such bhaijaans were also seen” at the protest sites in Shaheen Bagh and Farmers’ stir. Thumbnails of these reports carried AI-generated visuals of individuals critical of the Union government, their faces distorted through AI to portray them in a negative light. This is a tactic common across Right-wing outlets and social media troll handles.
More recently, the outlet, alongside Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, Law Beat, The Jaipur Dialogues and The Sunday Guardian, was summoned by the Delhi high court over a Rs 2 crore privacy suit by Cockroach Janta Party spokesperson Saurav Das, who alleged that they had disclosed his home address and other personal details online. The case will be heard on September 14.
The video below depicts a time when the outlet was still called The Indian Affairs, and Nautiyal (in striped shirt) can be seen with his colleagues alongside educator Pawan Gupta.

— The Pamphlet (@Pamphlet_in) July 22, 2022
Nautiyal’s last video with The Pamphlet was uploaded in December 2024. In June 2025, Nautiyal was pictured with the OpIndia team. His first video for OpIndia, an interview with Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Dhami, came a month later, in July 2025.
Nautiyal is now the multimedia & digital head and editor at OpIndia, and is no longer listed as a director of Savitr on the MCA website.
It is worth noting that The Pamphlet’s website does not disclose any parent company, ownership, editorial team, funding details or board of directors. Its ‘About Us’ page offers only a description of what it does, while calling itself ‘an independent digital media platform’. The only publicly mentioned funding source we could find was YouTube memberships of The Pamphlet costing Rs. 119 to Rs. 3199 per month.
Nautiyal is not the only link between Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet. An individual named Shiv Kumar Mishra was appointed the director of Savitr Analytics in April 2023. In March 2023, Mishra was announced as the CEO of The Pamphlet.
Please welcome @shivkmishr, Founder & CEO, The Pamphlet https://t.co/U53aK62Fzo
— The Pamphlet (@Pamphlet_in) March 14, 2023
In other words, two of the three directors of Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation have held senior positions at The Pamphlet. And in both cases, the appointments to Savitr and The Pamphlet came in close succession. This raises the question of whether the two entities are formally linked.
We also found that The Pamphlet had an office space from its inception in Dehradun, and it is evident from a photo posted by Nautiyal that it began with a team of at least 20 people. Bhatt, the reader would remember, also claims to be from Dehradun.
While all of this points to a connection between Bhatt and The Pamphlet, there appears to be a concerted effort to keep that relationship under wraps. Hence, we tried to dig more.
Is Bhatt Linked to The Pamphlet? We Asked The Pamphlet
We sent an email to The Pamphlet on September 3 asking them about the relationship between Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet, and whether Alok Bhatt was connected to The Pamphlet, given that he holds a 95% stake in Savitr Analytics, a company whose other directors have held senior positions at The Pamphlet. We also asked them about their funding sources, since nothing is mentioned on the website.
In reply, they asked us to send our queries to another email ID of The Pamphlet and also to Alok Bhatt, Nirwa Mehta, Ashish Nautiyal and Shiv Mishra. Interestingly, they provided us with the email IDs and phone numbers of each of these individuals. This, in itself, might be considered an indicator of some sort of link between The Pamphlet and Bhatt. It is unlikely for an organisation to provide the direct contact details of someone with whom it has no professional association.
We then sent our queries to all of them.
Nautiyal responded to us saying that his reporting manager, OpIndia editor Nupur J Sharma, “suggested” him “not to give (you) any quotes or information as a matter of policy of not engaging with entities that don’t act in good faith”. A day later, he took to X to let the world know that a woman from Alt News “with a Hindu-sounding name” had approached him with some questions.
Pamphlet editor Nirwa Mehta sent us a 1,071-word response, but did not answer any of our questions. Instead, she sent a detailed set of reciprocal questions concerning Alt News’ funding transparency, the outside associations of its founders and editor, and grants received by individuals associated with Alt News, both currently and in the past. She offered to answer Alt News’ questions in writing once Alt News answered hers first.
It is worth noting that The Pamphlet published a video on Alt News on August 16, 2026, without seeking a response from the organisation.
This correspondent responded to Mehta, stating that questions concerning Alt News’ funding should be directed to its editor, while questions concerning any of the founders’ personal assignments should be directed to the person concerned. We also reminded her that a so-called expose on Alt News’ founders had been published by The Pamphlet without either of the concerned persons being approached for a response — a violation of basic journalistic ethics.
In her final response, Mehta did not address the question of ethics. Instead, in a demand that many may find bizarre, she asked this correspondent, “as a responsible employee”, to take her questions to the Alt News directors.
At this point, we felt there was no point continuing the conversation.
We will update our article if The Pamphlet answers Alt News’ questions on whether Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet are connected in any way, and whether Alok Bhatt, BJP’s new IT cell member who continues to remain away from X, holds a position at The Pamphlet.
Social Media Posts Answer the Question
The connection between The Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt is one of internet’s worst kept secrets, it seems. We found several instances on social media where well-known faces from the Right-wing ecosystem tagged Alok Bhatt alongside members of The Pamphlet team — whether to thank them for invitations to Delhi Shabdotsav 2026, where The Pamphlet Panchayat featured on the itinerary, or in connection with other events involving the organisation.
On January 5, 2026, Right-wing influencer Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, who was recently criticised for comparing Newslaundry journalists to prostitutes, thanked The Pamphlet team — including its editor Nirwa Mehta, anchor Shreya Arora, and Bhatt — for inviting him to speak at The Pamphlet Panchayat.
Responding to Iyer-Mitra, Nirwa Mehta and another The Pamphlet employee, Pratibha, thanked him for being a part of the session. The exchange is significant because it can be seen as an acknowledgement by the Pamphlet editor and another employee of Bhatt being a part of the organisation.
Delhi Shabdotsav 2026 was a three-day cultural and literary festival held from January 2 to January 4, 2026, organised by Suruchi Prakashan with the support of the department of art, culture and languages of the Delhi government. The Pamphlet was the digital partner at the event and hosted ‘The Pamphlet Panchayat’ at the fest. The Pamphlet team held and moderated several discussions over the three days, including those with Sanjeev Newar, Vijay Patel, and Subhi Vishwakarma. The subjects of the discussions ranged from ‘Love Jihad: factsheet’ to ‘Bharat’s Hostile Neighbourhood & Need to Regain Shatrubodh’.
We went through the images posted on Shabdotsav’s website and found that Bhatt was present at the event.
The link between Alok Bhatt and The Pamphlet becomes more apparent in another conversation on X in which Iyer-Mitra directly addressed Mehta as Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt’s ‘staff’. Iyer jokingly rebuked Mehta for liking a certain kind of car. Tagging Bhatt, he wrote, “Do @Pamphlet_in and @alok_bhatt @shreya_arora22 approve of these disgusting and extremely hateful statements by their staff?” Mehta responded to Iyer-Mitra’s post, but did not object to the ‘staff’ reference.
On June 1, 2023, a little more than a year after The Pamphlet’s inception, one @saket71 posted a picture with Ashish Nautiyal, who was working at The Pamphlet then, and called him a ‘Media Mughal’. He later tagged Alok Bhatt and Shiv Mishra, praising them for “putting a great team together.”
Such a pleasure to meet the young stars of @Pamphlet_in , @RitikaChandola @himanshi__bisht and the whole team. Such a great young team, full of hope and dreams, and a visible sense of great camaraderie. Kudos to @alok_bhatt and @shivkmishr for putting a great team together. https://t.co/NnmHkA9rQO
— saket साकेत ಸಾಕೇತ್ 🇮🇳 (@saket71) June 1, 2023
Several people have congratulated Alok Bhatt at various points of time upon The Pamphlet reaching certain milestones.
To sum up, what raises serious questions about the BJP’s decision to name Bhatt as its social media co-convenor is not just his past social media conduct, but also the opacity surrounding his professional associations. One organisation he appears to be associated with, The Pamphlet, does not publicly disclose its ownership, editorial team, board or funding sources. Without any apparent source of funding, it starts off as a 20-member organization. Who pays their salary? How are establishment costs met? There are no answers. Again, another corporate entity closely linked to him, Savitr Analytics, has no website or public online presence despite reporting Rs 2.7 crore in operational revenue in 2025.
Things get murkier when one takes into account the desperate efforts by Bhatt’s associates to conceal his association with The Pamphlet, evident in the organisation’s refusal to answer direct questions regarding this.
In other words, a man linked to organisations with questionable records, and whose involvement with a pro-government outlet is abundantly visible in public, but markedly absent from the outlet’s own disclosures, has now been given a formal position in the BJP’s social media cell.

Tropical Storm Dujuan is skirting the coast of Japan and despite avoiding a direct landfall, is still expected to leave its mark. Dujuan briefly reached typhoon status on Friday before weakening to a tropical storm again on Sunday morning. But it is expected to restrengthen back to a typhoon by Tuesday morning. Sustained winds could reach 80mph (129km/h), with gusts approaching 100mph.
Although mainland Japan has avoided a direct hit, Dujuan’s track takes it across the Izu Islands, where evacuation warnings are in place. Heavy rain, flooding and landslide alerts are widespread, with high waves adding another threat to exposed coastal areas and islands.
Some exceptional rainfall totals are expected, with about 200mm (7.9in) possible along the southern coasts of the Chubu and Kanto regions in just 24 hours – roughly equivalent to the average rainfall for the entire month of September. The Tokyo metropolitan area is among the areas facing the heaviest rain, with some models suggesting nearly 90mm could fall within six hours on Monday evening. Further south, the Izu peninsula could receive more than 80mm in just three hours – 38% of the month’s usual rainfall in a single evening. Dujuan is expected to continue north-eastwards before dissipating in the north-west Pacific later this week.
The Atlantic hurricane season remains unusually quiet, despite Tropical Storm Fay developing south-west of the Azores over the weekend. Fay is not expected to strengthen further, extending the record for the latest first hurricane to form in a hurricane season during the satellite era. The previous date record was 11 September, set in 2002 with Hurricane Gustav and equalled in 2013 with Hurricane Humberto.
South-west Europe may get one last taste of summer with a blast of heat this week. Temperatures across Spain and Portugal will rise significantly above the monthly norm, to the low to mid 30s celsius. Even in north-west Spain, in Santiago de Compostela highs could reach about 35C (95F) on Tuesday, about 12C above the typical daytime high. Heading into the weekend, warmth will spread into central Europe, but most likely with less intensity than earlier in the week across the Iberian peninsula.

Brazilian serial killer lived in the woods and was nicknamed "mosquito"
A man who Brazilian authorities say killed 16 people lived in the woods to avoid capture and was nicknamed “mosquito” by locals because of his frail build, the Brazilian police investigator responsible for his arrest said Monday
SAO PAULO -- A man who Brazilian authorities say killed 16 people lived in the woods to avoid capture and was nicknamed “mosquito” by locals because of his frail build, the Brazilian police investigator responsible for his arrest said Monday.
Douglas Garcia, the investigator who led the two-day pursuit for 33-year-old Jorlan Lopes da Silva that ended on Sep. 13, told The Associated Press that the suspect used to hide in the thick bush in his own makeshift camps. The killings linked to da Silva occurred within the last three months in the isolated region of Mulungu in Brazil’s northeastern state of Paraiba.
“That allowed him to evade capture for years,” Garcia said. “Jorlan lived mostly in the woods, that’s why it was so hard to find him and link him to crimes that didn’t seem to be connected at first.”
Garcia said police finally saw the link between da Silva and other crimes after he shot an 18-year-old dead in a public square. The investigator said the serial killer claims he has only attacked criminals, but evidence collected thus far shows that was not the case.
Garcia also said da Silva is providing evidence he committed more crimes than those he is being prosecuted for but added he cannot discuss further details as some investigations continue and others are being reopened.
The investigator said the identity of the victims and details about their deaths are being kept confidential so the prosecution can do its work.
Da Silva was captured wearing a black dress with white stripes, a wig and painted nails. He was carrying a baby that authorities confirmed was not related to him, but they did not provide any other details.
“This is a very different person, he said he killed for the first time at age 13,” Garcia said. “We caught him because he wasn’t able to reach his tent in the woods, so he, out of desperation, got that disguise, took that baby that is not his and was ultimately arrested,” Garcia said.
Police said at the time that da Silva was a member of a criminal gang that has killed dozens of people in the region. He denies any affiliation with local gangs and told investigators upon his arrest that he was “in a personal war.”
The region of Mulungu, where the recent killings took place, lies 2,500 kilometers (1,553 miles) north of Rio de Janeiro.

Is AI supercharging software engineers or reducing them to mindless button-pushers? A tech professional's viral post has sparked a fierce online debate after he described his AI-driven workplace as a “soul-sucking” environment devoid of critical thinking. An anonymous software engineer with the handle “v0xium” revealed that their new role at an undisclosed company revolves entirely around Claude Code. According to the techie, the AI tool now generates everything from product specifications and tests to tickets and reports. "Nobody knows anything here," v0xium wrote on Sunday, amassing nearly 6.2 million views as of Tuesday morning. “People are working 12 to 13 hours a day just to press enter.” The techie also claimed employees face intense pressure to ship products at maximum speed, leaving them with little to no time to review the AI's output or understand the underlying code. “Nobody is thinking anymore,” he wrote. Following the massive response to his initial post, v0xium took to X to share an extended, philosophical thread about the existential dread currently gripping the developer community. Acknowledging advice from peers telling him to just use LLMs, collect his paycheck, and be happy, he argued that humans inevitably need to find meaning in their work. Because quitting is not an option due to financial obligations, he advised developers to find their purpose outside of working hours, even if free time is scarce. He warned of a bleak future for traditional software engineering, where developers face an ego-crushing reality: “An MBA can now come to you and say, 'Hey, I could have shipped that too. What have you done here?'” Beyond the workplace, he expressed deep concern about the future of intellectual curiosity, fearing that a generation of students relying entirely on AI to complete assignments will result in a workforce devoid of drive. While v0xium compared the current technological leap to the excitement of the space race, he sharply criticised the AI industry's persistent, negative messaging about job replacement. Instead of automating standard development tasks, he expressed a profound desire for artificial intelligence to focus on extending human life and curing diseases like cancer, which claimed his grandparents. “Software automation is fine, but most of our world can live without our CRUD apps,” he wrote. “What it cannot live without is new medicine and cures for new diseases.” He concluded his thoughts on the uncertain future of his profession, saying that tomorrow's professionals might be forced to merge the roles of engineering, design, and product management just to survive. Yet, despite the existential dread, he offered a final, defiant observation on his humanity: “At least no one is automating my consciousness yet.” The viral confession quickly caught the attention of prominent tech figures, sparking widespread concern over the evolving role of developers. Responding to the thread, tech billionaire Elon Musk simply wrote, “Yikes.” Venture capitalist and All-In Podcast co-host Chamath Palihapitiya offered a sharper critique, warning that companies are dangerously close to turning an entire generation of technical experts into people “pushing a button in front of casino slot machines.” Palihapitiya emphasised that the true utility of AI tools shouldn't be limited to speed. “The value of automated software is not making the software faster,” he argued. “It is understanding your intention and making the software BETTER.” GitLab CEO Bill Staples observed a fundamental shift in the development process, noting that “the human has become the orchestration layer for the machines.” Software development has emerged as the first major breakthrough for workplace artificial intelligence, with tools from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google now seamlessly generating code, debugging programs, and executing complex assignments. While some developers argued that AI eliminates tedious tasks and allows them to focus on core building, others fear a looming shift in their professional agency, according to a Business Insider report. Many, according to the report, worry about being reduced to merely overseeing, correcting, and validating machine-generated output, stripping away the fundamental problem-solving essence of their jobs. v0xium told Business Insider that the root of the problem lies in corporate leadership's obsession with churning out features. Management, he explained, often prioritises sprint cycles and pull requests as the ultimate metrics of success, regardless of whether the shipped features actually benefit the end user. "Writing code was never the bottleneck; it was the systems around it," he said. This relentless drive creates immense pressure to automate every stage of development, from product-requirement documents and system designs to user interfaces and backend architecture. “If everything is automated, what remains? Human meat proxies,” v0xium said, utilising an industry slang term for employees who simply pass along AI outputs without critical analysis. The viral debate mirrors broader anxieties sweeping the global tech sector. Business Insider quoted Deedy Das, a partner at Menlo Ventures, saying that some engineers are facing an "identity crisis bordering on depression" as experienced workers are increasingly forced to review a relentless flood of AI-generated code. Liu Shengyu, an AI developer at DeepSeek, also expressed concern that artificial intelligence could soon surpass his own specialised coding abilities, leaving him to merely steer AI agents rather than write the code himself, the news outlet said. Can't treat AI as ‘magic wand’ v0xium warned that corporate leaders cannot treat artificial intelligence as a “magic wand” that can produce valuable products without human engineers who deeply understand the underlying code, architecture, and users. Developers, he stressed, need the space to solve complex problems. "If you take that away from us, there is nothing left," he told the publication. "Not even our soul. There will be no purpose." Does your iPhone's Safari browser privacy features actually make you safer?
Safari limits tracking by default, but private browsing still has limitations.
The iPhone's default Safari browser has gained a reputation for being private, especially as an alternative to Chrome for those who don't want to turn over their entire life history to Google. According to the Safari info page, the browser blocks third-party cookies by default, uses machine learning to limit cross-site tracking, hides your IP address from known trackers and removes identifying info from certain URLs. In 2019, Apple published a white paper covering the full range of Safari's privacy capabilities if you're interested in the details.
All these features are important because advertising and data-broker networks (and by extension, the FBI) are itching to gobble up your private data. Tracking info often follows you throughout unrelated sites, searches, purchases and profile visits. Safari helps by cutting most of these data leeches off at the knees, limiting the data shared with those networks and making it more difficult for advertisers to build an infrastructure based on your behavior.
However, "private" doesn't place Safari on the same pedestal as a quality VPN. Websites can still see info that's required to serve the page you're on, including a general idea of your location. Safari's defaults mean the average iPhone user is unknowingly handing over less data, but the browser is far from an impenetrable shield.
What Safari actually protects
Privacy and security are distinct concepts, though they're closely related. Privacy focuses on how your personal info is collected and used, while security refers to ways your data is protected from attack. Insecure data cannot be private, but a secure website can have poor privacy practices. Thus, we should consider features of Safari that cover both areas.
Safari's strongest privacy tools tackle address tracking as well as account security and unsafe website behavior. Its cross-site tracking protections try to stop advertisers and third parties from recognizing you as you move from site to site. Private Browsing adds a few layers, including blocking trackers, masking your IP address from known trackers and automatically removing some tracking info from links.
Safari also supports passkeys, which let you sign in with Face ID or Touch ID instead of a traditional password. Passkeys are phishing-resistant by design because creating one is tied to a certain website; they won't work on a fake lookalike page. Apple Pay is also integrated into Safari, so you can avoid entering your card numbers and authenticate with Face ID to use your saved cards stored privately in Apple Wallet.
But for all the good Safari does, it still has limits (as all browsers do). While it will warn you about dangerous sites, it can't verify that every page you visit is legitimate and won't stop you from entering your credentials on a convincing phishing site. It will warn you about poor passwords, and while Apple Intelligence in iOS 27 will be able to automatically set stronger passwords for you, this feature isn't out yet.
Private browsing doesn't hide your activities from your ISP or sites you're logged into, and anti-tracking tools reduce data collection but fall short of stopping websites from collecting data you submit directly. Safari can't protect you from what you decide to trust.
Safari vs. Chrome and Brave on iPhone
On an iPhone, the privacy differences between browsers can be smaller than their marketing suggests. Apple requires third-party browsers on iOS devices to use Safari's WebKit rendering engine (outside of the EU), so Chrome, Firefox and Brave can't use the same browser engines on iPhone as they do on desktop. However, there are still feature differences; PrivacyTests.org has an overview if you'd like to dive into a full comparison.
Brave is a worthwhile alternative for those seeking a stronger content blocker. Its iPhone app promotes tracker and ad blocking, as well as the privacy-focused Brave Search that doesn't collect any data about you. This is in contrast to Safari using Google by default. Brave also offers an optional VPN/firewall subscription, if that's something you're interested in.
One of Safari's advantages is that its protections are built-in and enabled by default. Apple frequently compare this to Chrome's, which are not. However, Chrome has many of the same protections; it's just a matter of turning them on. The question isn't really whether Safari is perfectly private, as no browser is. The two most pertinent points are whether the browser's default options increase your privacy and if privacy-enhancing options are available at all.
For most iPhone owners, Safari is a solid option. There's value in using the browser designed by the same company who made your phone and the OS it runs, especially when it doesn't require fiddling with settings to be privacy-respecting. If you want more control, however, you can always add content blockers or opt for Brave. No matter which browser you use, never assume it will protect against every scam or questionable decision.

Months after seemingly giving up on Destiny 2, Bungie now says it’s planning to restore vaulted content in the game like campaigns, destinations, and raids. The decision reverses the Destiny Content Vault that Bungie created six years ago, controversially removing older content from Destiny 2 that players had paid to access.
Bungie says it’s ‘not done with Destiny’ and will bring back vaulted content
Bungie is reversing its controversial content vault that saw Destiny 2 content removed six years ago.
“We understand that removing these experiences had a lasting impact on player trust and enjoyment of Destiny,” admits Bungie. “We cannot change the decision we made, but we can acknowledge its impact and do the work to make it right by restoring these important parts of Destiny’s history.“
All Destiny 2 players will get access to the vaulted content, but it’s not a simple switch of a button for Bungie. The developer made big changes to Destiny 2 with the Beyond Light expansion, meaning it has to go back and update lighting, encounters, combatants, and other underlying systems for this older content. “That work will take time, but it is necessary to ensure returning content meets the stability and gameplay standards of Destiny 2 today,” says Bungie.
The decision to return this content to Destiny 2 comes just weeks after a “Sunrise” Destiny 2 offline preservation mod appeared. The mod lets players access older areas in Destiny 2 that had been vaulted, but not the exact campaigns and missions that players had experienced previously.
Bungie now says its own restoration project is the “first step to lay the foundation for how we reforge into new stories and games that you all deserve.” Could that be a Destiny 3 sequel? There’s no mention of such a project, despite fans desperately pleading for a successor to Destiny 2 in multiple high-profile Twitch streams in recent weeks. Bungie is only committing to building a “stronger long-term future for Destiny” right now.
Alongside the Destiny 2 efforts, Bungie is also admitting that Marathon, its extraction shooter, didn’t “reach as many players as we had hoped, and we also know and understand that the game needs to evolve.” That means Marathon will expand deeper into a survival experience. The changes are a little vague right now, but it sounds like Marathon really needs to change and attract more players if it’s to be a sustainable project for Bungie.

Snapdeal parent AceVector has set a price band of ₹30-₹32 per equity share for its IPO, valuing the company at up to ₹1,741.4 Cr ($181.7 Mn) at the upper end.
The IPO comprises a fresh issue of shares worth ₹287 Cr and an offer for sale of up to 4.16 Cr shares. At ₹32 per share, the size of the IPO is ₹420 Cr.
The IPO will open for public subscription on Friday (September 25), following anchor bidding on Thursday (September 24). It will close on September 29. AceVector’s shares are expected to list on the BSE and NSE on October 5.
AceVector reduced the fresh issue by ₹13 Cr from the ₹300 Cr proposed in its UDRHP after raising the same amount through a pre-IPO placement. It also cut the OFS component by 34.9% from the earlier proposed 6.39 Cr shares.
SoftBank’s Starfish I Pte Ltd, AceVector’s largest shareholder and part of its promoter group, will sell up to 2.76 Cr shares through the OFS. At the upper end of the price band, the stake sale will fetch Starfish up to ₹88.3 Cr.

US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said Iranian airlines could "effectively be shut out of global operations" from Wednesday and threatened foreign companies providing services to Tehran’s aviation sector with secondary sanctions.
Bessent on Monday said, “on September 23, all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world”.
“If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system,” Bessent said, according to Al Jazeera.
The warning comes as the Trump administration expands its sanctions campaign aimed at restricting Iran’s access to international financial and commercial networks.
Earlier this month, the US treasury department imposed sanctions on additional Iranian airlines as well as companies outside Iran accused of supporting Tehran’s aviation sector.
Iran’s aviation industry has already faced years of US sanctions, limiting Iranian carriers’ ability to acquire new aircraft and access spare parts and maintenance services.
The latest measures are part of a broader US sanctions regime targeting Iran’s economy, including its energy, shipping, technology, gold and digital-asset sectors. 
Secondary sanctions can subject foreign companies doing business with sanctioned Iranian entities to restrictions on access to the US financial system.
Bessent’s comments came a day after talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, ahead of a planned meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
China is a key economic partner and diplomatic supporter of Iran, making Beijing’s cooperation significant to Washington’s efforts to restrict Tehran’s access to international finance.
According to Al Jazeera, Bessent said Chinese officials had been “very engaged” in discussions over the US pressure campaign. He also said Washington was holding positive talks with Chinese financial authorities, including People’s Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng, on compliance with US sanctions targeting Iran.

Messi in Argentina squad for farewell friendly
- Published
Argentina have named Lionel Messi in their squad for a friendly against Benin in October in a match which is set to be the forward's farewell to international football.
Messi announced his retirement from Argentina duty in August in the wake of his country's defeat by Spain in the 2026 World Cup final and after saying he was considering his future in football following the death of his father, Jorge.
The 39-year-old, who captained Argentina when they won the 2022 World Cup, said the decision to stop playing for La Albiceleste hurt him "deeply" but that he had "given it my all" and had "nothing left to give".
Messi, an eight-time Ballon d'Or winner who currently plays for Inter Miami, is Argentina's all-time leading scorer and most-capped player, having scored 125 goals in 207 appearances.
"We made the decision to invite the best player in the world, the symbol of our national team, our captain, Lionel Andres Messi, so that he can have the farewell he truly deserves on 6 October here in Argentina," said Argentine FA president Claudio Tapia.
River Plate's Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires, which has an 85,000 capacity, will host the game against Benin.
Argentina's 2022 World Cup winners have also been invited to the match, which Tapia said would be an "unforgettable" occasion.
