Realistically, there aren’t a ton of things on a Mac that can use all that bandwidth, especially since Apple doesn’t support external GPUs. But you do need a Thunderbolt 5 Mac to daisy-chain multiple computers together to form a compute cluster, so if that’s something you’re interested in, keep it in mind when you buy—maybe you’re buying multiple desktops, or maybe you already have an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro you’d like to test the feature with.
The only real gripe with this design continues to be its bottom-rear-mounted power button; apparently, complaints about this are being sent to the same trash can Apple has always used for complaints about the Magic Mouse’s bottom-mounted charging port. It doesn’t come up often in everyday use if you just let your Mac go to sleep rather than shutting it down. But the positioning problem does really call attention to itself when you pair a TouchID-equipped external keyboard with the mini, since it requires a quick double-tap of the Mac’s power button before the sensor will work.
Meet the M6
Apple’s first M6-series chip is making its debut in the humble Mac mini, and the chip looks like the biggest upgrade Apple’s lower-end chip has gotten since the M4 generation added extra efficiency cores.
The headliner is the presence of two of Apple’s so-called “Super” cores, Apple’s nomenclature for P-cores that are even faster than its typical P-cores. Those are added on top of four P-cores and six E-cores for a total of 12 CPU cores. M4 and M5 both had 10 CPU cores. In the M4, these were split between four regular P-cores and six E-cores, whereas the M5 split them between four super cores and six E-cores (the M5’s cores were referred to as P-cores when it launched but were rebranded later when the M5 Pro and Max came out). The M1, M2, and M3 generations all used four P-cores and four E-cores.
The M6 has fewer super cores than the M5 but the same number of E-cores and four additional P-cores. While they’re apparently no longer “super,” the P-cores still perform well enough to ensure that the M6’s multi-core performance is better than M5’s overall.

Apple has mixed super cores with both other kinds of cores before, but this is its first chip to include all three kinds at once. To get around the awkwardness this might create at the CPU scheduler level, the built-in powermetrics tool suggests that Apple is still treating the M6 like a chip with just two types of cores. The six E-cores are all gathered together in one cluster, and the two Super cores and the four P-cores are all lumped together into a second six-core cluster called the “PS cluster.”
Powermetrics also reports that both the P- and S-cores have the same peak and minimum clock speeds, unlike in the M5 Pro and M5 Max where they’re different clusters with different clock speeds (both P- and S-cores in M6 range from 1.44 GHz to 4.79 GHz). The sysctl utility also suggests they share the same 20MB pool of L2 cache, up from 16MB for the 4-core Super cluster in the M5 (the E-core cluster has a bit more L2 cache, too, 8MB up from 6MB in the M5). The Super cores do have more L1 instruction and data cache, so they are definitely still different cores, and there are likely other differences that we can’t detect using software-level tools. But if you were wondering how macOS was going to treat a chip with three different kinds of CPU cores at a software level, the answer is “to act like it still has two different kinds of cores.”

The M6 gets additional GPU cores for the first time since the M2, increasing the count from 10 cores to 12. These cores include improved versions of the integrated neural accelerators Apple introduced in the M5-series GPU for speeding up AI and machine-learning workloads like ray-tracing and MetalFX upscaling. A “Dual 16-core Neural Engine” also bumps the number of Neural Engine cores from 16 to 32. Saying you have 2×16 of something strikes me as a roundabout way of saying you have 32 of something, but I suppose the end result is the same either way.
One small wrinkle in the M6 variants the Mac mini uses: The basic 16GB Mac mini offers 153 GB/s of memory bandwidth, the same amount as the M5. The 24GB and 32GB versions offer 170 GB/s, an 11 percent increase that should marginally improve graphics performance and the speed of any local AI models you run on this machine. Our review unit is the 24GB version.
What of the M6 Pro, M6 Max, or M6 Ultra? If the rumors are true, the M6 could end up being a lonely chip.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple isn’t planning a full M6 chip generation and that it could skip directly to M7 branding for the Pro, Max, and Ultra chips. That would be a first for the company, which skipped shipping an M4 Ultra but has otherwise shipped a baseline, Pro, and Max-series chip in each generation so far.
But it makes sense for a couple of reasons. The first is that most of the M6’s gains can be attributed to its extra CPU and GPU cores relative to the M5, and the M5 Pro, M5 Max, and M5 Ultra all obviously still have more of both kinds of cores than the M6 does. The second is that it’s still pretty early for TSMC’s 2 nm process, following three generations where Apple used versions of TSMC’s 3 nm process, and Apple is probably fighting with every other fabless chipmaker on Earth to reserve capacity. Apple could be sticking with smaller, simpler 2 nm chips for now and saving its bigger and more complex chips for later, when capacity will be higher, yields will be better, and costs may be lower.
Performance
The new mini re-uses the launch strategy for last year’s Mac Studios, which used an M4 Max in the base model and an M3 Ultra in the top-tier configurations. The basic Mac mini uses the brand-new M6, while the semi-professional Mac mini tier gets the M5 Pro that we saw in MacBook Pros back in the spring.
This means the M6 mini has newer tech than the more-expensive M5 Pro mini—and marginally better single-core CPU performance, too. The M6’s single-core is roughly 8 to 10 percent faster than the M5 family’s in our benchmarks; graphics performance is also up by roughly 10 percent. In multi-core CPU benchmarks, the M6’s performance is roughly 20 percent faster than the M5.
But for heavy multi-core performance, having more cores is still more important than using the newest cores. The M5 Max (which uses the same 18-core CPU block as the M5 Pro, so it’s a decent stand-in) is still generally 60 or 70 percent faster than the M6 in our multi-core benchmarks.
If you’re comparing the last-generation mini to this one, the upgrades over the M4 are pretty substantial. Single-core CPU performance improves by between 20 and 30 percent in most tests, while both graphics performance and multi-core CPU performance are up by between 50 and 80 percent—and occasionally even more, in some tests. The M6 does nearly as well as the M4 Pro in the Blender benchmark and beats the M5 by around 40 percent, again suggesting that this benchmark in particular is benefiting from the GPU cores’ built-in Neural Accelerators.
Usually at this point we would talk about the chip’s estimated power consumption using the powermetrics tool, a built-in utility that gives clock speed and power consumption data for the CPU and GPU cores in Macs. This is a software-based reporting tool, which makes it imperfect for comparisons between chip generations. But it does at least give us some vague estimate of Apple’s power efficiency.
For the M6, powermetrics doesn’t actually report CPU power levels. It appears in the tool’s logs, but the value is always “0.” I’ve asked Apple whether this is a bug or an intentional behavior change (it still works fine for M5-generation chips), and I’ll update this if I get a response.
About that price
The $599 M4 Mac mini was a tiny, affordable desktop computer with as much speed and memory as most people need for general-purpose computing. You could quibble with the 256GB base storage, but it was still the most usable the basic Mac mini had ever been.
The M6 mini’s $899 starting price sets us way back. That’s a $300 increase in just under two years for a computer that has a faster chip in it but otherwise shares the key specs and most of the capabilities.
One could argue that this merely resets Mac mini pricing back to where it was circa 2020. A base M1 Mac mini cost $699 to start, and upgrading to 16GB of RAM added another $200. It just feels like a big step back, given how great the M4 mini was.
If you need a desktop computer right now for anything from basic browsing to less-intensive local AI models, this is still Apple’s most affordable computer (chatbots and image generation should run pretty well on it; more intensive coding-centric models will be a bit squeezed for RAM and memory bandwidth, even at 32GB). And even the $599 M4 mini was undercut by the kind of lowest-common-denominator cheap mini PCs you could get on Amazon. It’s just hard to swallow the current price, given how much better it was not all that long ago.
The good
An impressively fast and quiet little computer that can fill roles from “entry-level desktop” to “midrange coding and video editing rig.”
M6 is a big step up for Apple’s entry-level chip, with more CPU and GPU cores and other improvements.
Large improvements over the M4 mini, thanks to a two-generation silicon jump.
The bad
Zero upgradability, aside from what you can add with external accessories. What you buy is what you have until you buy the next thing.
256GB of storage in the base model is low, especially if you want to play games or run any kind of AI models locally.
Power button on the bottom is mildly inconvenient on the occasions you have to interact with it.
M6 version can’t be daisy-chained together with Thunderbolt 5 to join a compute cluster.
The ugly
The memory crisis means we can’t have nice things unless we’re willing to pay out the nose for them.
Andrew is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica, with a focus on consumer tech including computer hardware and in-depth reviews of operating systems like Windows and macOS. Andrew lives in Philadelphia and co-hosts a weekly book podcast called Overdue.

Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping up a record ₹41,248 Cr from the public markets. The surge was driven by a combination of macroeconomic tailwinds and regulatory support. While robust GDP growth projections helped revive investor appetite, SEBI’s reforms played a key role. Measures such as simplified DRHP filings reduced red tape, while more flexible ESOP rules allowed founders to retain meaningful ownership. Retail investors also fuelled the frenzy as demat accounts crossed the 20 Cr mark. The OFS component dominated public issues last year, providing liquidity to the early backers of the new-age tech companies. Post-listing performance also followed the usual curve, with investors rewarding companies that prioritised profits, sustainable growth and governance over hype. “Besides the readiness that startups showed in their unit economics, there is also an increase in the founders committing to their businesses for next couple of decades and grow their businesses by adding adjacent profit pools – something that the public markets reward handsomely,” said Ashish Kumar, cofounder and general partner at Fundamentum Partnership. Building on the momentum, thirteen new-age tech companies have already made their D-Street debut so far this year. Of these, ESDS Software Solution, Klassroom, RentoMojo, SEDEMAC, Kissht, LEAP India and Shiprocket made a bumper debut on the bourses. Nevertheless, the IPO pipeline remains strong. Twenty four startups have already filed their DRHPs with SEBI, while over 25 are in various stages of finalising their IPO plans. Unicorns like OYO, Razorpay and Zetwerk alone could raise over ₹34,000 Cr in 2026, making it one of the biggest years for startup IPOs. However, recalibration is likely to define 2026 as investors are expected to prioritise strong fundamentals, profitability and low cash burn when backing new-age tech companies. “IPO-bound startups in 2026 will be increasingly defined by their ability to demonstrate predictable cash flows, sustainable unit economics, and operational discipline rather than headline growth alone. Public market investors will place greater emphasis on governance, capital efficiency and long-term value creation, favouring companies that balance scale with financial prudence,” Orios Venture Partners’ managing partner Rehan Yar Khan told Inc42. There are other challenges as well. Average retail subscription levels are moderating, while foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are pulling back in droves, reflecting caution amid geopolitical tensions and muted secondary market performance. The ongoing conflict in West Asia has further complicated the situation. Yet, the overall outlook remains bullish for new-age tech IPOs. Maturing business models, deeper domestic capital pools and an evolving regulatory framework favouring transparency position India as a leading startup IPO hub. Fifty years ago, a young director named Barbara Kopple came out with her first film, a documentary she thought would be little seen.
“When I started making the film, I thought, ‘Oh, my parents will see it and their friends and maybe a museum will show it,’” she recalls.
That film was Harlan County U.S.A., about a long running strike at a coal mine in southeast Kentucky, and it was immediately hailed as brilliant, earning Kopple an Academy Award. She would earn a second Oscar for her 1991 documentary American Dream, about a strike at a Hormel Foods plant in Minnesota.
Kopple has made many other documentaries in intervening years – on actor Gregory Peck, singer Sharon Jones, and country band the Chicks (formerly the Dixie Chicks), among others. But she returns to the theme for which she is best known – working people in America — in her new documentary Union Town. It just held its U.S. premiere at the Camden International Film Festival in Maine after bowing at the Venice Film Festival earlier in September.
Watch on Deadline
Union Town follows the battle for better wages and working conditions on three fronts in New York City — at UPS, at Amazon, and among “deliveristas” – that is, people who work for apps like DoorDash making food runs for customers.
“I think that they [labor organizers] have a big fight on their hands, but I think that they’re road warriors and I feel an awful lot of hope,” Kopple tells Deadline in an interview at the Camden Opera House, where Union Town screened. “Each time they win something, it’s glorious. It’s wonderful. And they get a little closer and a little closer. And what else can you do? You have to keep fighting… Looking at the people that they work with who can hardly make a living or people who die in the plants because there’s no air conditioning [in summer] or no heat in the winter, it’s just a very human thing to do, so you can’t stop.”
In the past four decades, union participation in America has dropped by about half. “[But] they’re still there. They’re still there,” Kopple says of unions. “And if you don’t have them, you don’t have anything.”
She points to Antonio Rosario, a veteran of a 1997 strike at UPS who serves as the Teamsters lead union organizer for Amazon workers in the northeast. At one moment in the film, Rosario is with his young sons at the dinner table and holds a bundle of sticks in his hands to illustrate the importance of worker solidarity.
“Tony is trying to show them the difference that if you have a lot of people together, it takes too much to break it,” Kopple explains. “And if you just have one stick, you can break it. And that’s what it is. It’s people who have your back. It’s people who will help you and it gives you a sense of strength that you can change.”
Of the three groups seen in the documentary, deliveristas face the worst conditions and pay – they work year-round in every kind of weather, driving their bikes through snow in winter, for instance. Kopple documents the case of Victor Hidalgo, a 24-year-old man who was working for a pharmacy delivery company in 2024 when a New York Fire Department vehicle hit his bicycle, killing him. At a Q&A following the U.S. premiere, Kopple said Hidalgo’s aunt urged her to put him in the documentary.
“She said, ‘I don’t want anyone to ever forget Victor,’” Kopple recounted. “’Please come and film the funeral. Please come and let people know that these things really happen.’”
Deliveristas rely on tips as a major source of income, but customers often don’t give them much (one deliverista recalls a person opening his hand to deposit a tip and placing in his palm a piece of candy). What’s worse, the tips they receive through the app may not go to them; in 2025 DoorDash reached a nearly $17 million settlement in New York after being accused of effectively taking workers’ tips. (Per the New York Attorney General’s office, “Customers were misled into believing their tips would directly benefit Dashers. Instead, DoorDash would keep the tips meant for Dashers and take it out of their guaranteed pay. DoorDash would guarantee pay to a delivery worker, and then only actually pay them whatever the tip did not cover.”).
“What it does if people get to see this film is maybe they’ll give big tips. Maybe they’ll talk to the people who deliver or at least understand them,” Kopple says. “Ever since UPS got their contract, every time I see a UPS truck, I stop and I talk to the driver and I say, ‘So how’s your contract? How’s work?’ And they’re looking at me like, ‘Who’s this crazy person?’ But it’s wonderful to do it… [It shows] somebody cares. Somebody’s out there who cares about them. They’re not invisible.”
Autlook is handling worldwide film sales for Union Town. The 2024 documentary Union, about the successful effort to organize workers at an Amazon facility in Staten Island, NY, struggled to find U.S. distribution (it was clear Prime Video wouldn’t touch it). That film by Stephen Maing and Brett Story is now streaming through Criterion.
Kopple says it’s “too soon to tell” about potential distribution of Union Town. “This was the third time the film has ever shown, and I had just finished it maybe two weeks before Venice. So, it’s totally at the beginning. I mean, I hope it gets great distribution and gets shown far and wide.”

Tilbury LNG facility in Delta, B.C. gets greenlight for expansion
The province says the project could generate 100 permanent jobs
The federal government has approved expansion of the Tilbury LNG facility in Delta, B.C., saying potential adverse effects are justified by the project's benefits.
Monday's approval under the "one project, one review" principle came immediately after the B.C. government issued an environmental assessment certificate to FortisBC for the project on Tilbury Island in the Fraser River.
The province says the project could generate 6,200 full-time-equivalent years of employment during construction and 100 permanent jobs, and contribute up to $1.7 billion to provincial GDP during construction.
Federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin says in a statement the project shows how to "create jobs and grow the economy while protecting the environment and advancing reconciliation."
The project involves adding a large new storage tank and equipment to produce up to 7,700 tonnes of liquefied natural gas per day.
But it has faced opposition from within the B.C. government, with Kelly Greene, minister of emergency management and climate readiness, saying in July she was "disappointed" by FortisBC's decision to move forward with the project, citing safety concerns.
"For months, I have listened to safety concerns from people in my community. I raised those issues with government at every opportunity. I am disappointed with FortisBC's decision, as I know many of those I represent will be," she said at the time.
Greene said her opposition had remained unchanged since before she was elected to the legislature, while B.C. NDP Premier David Eby said his government has a "big tent," which allowed Greene to criticize the plan.
Federal Energy Minister Tim Hodgson called the approval "a step forward in our mission to get major nation-building projects built faster."
"Today's approval of the Tilbury Phase 2 LNG expansion project will power [B.C.] Ferries with cleaner fuel, strengthen Canada's energy security and create economic opportunities for British Columbians," he said on social media on Monday.
The B.C. government had touted the expansion as helping meet rising demand for LNG at the Port of Vancouver and improving access to fuel for vessels that travel the coast and across the Pacific.
The province said in a statement on Monday that the environmental assessment certificate included "18 legally binding conditions related to air quality, wildlife protection, greenhouse-gas reduction, health and emergency planning, and ongoing monitoring of impacts to First Nations."
It said the Environmental Assessment Office sought consensus with 12 Indigenous nations, while 13 other Indigenous groups were informed of key milestones.
The assessment process was initiated in February 2020, but the province said it was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic, and FortisBC submitted a revised application in February 2026.

The Manipur Police arrested two persons, including a 40-year-old woman, from Thoubal district’s Lilong on September 14 in connection with the seizure of addiction-causing pharmaceutical drugs. The police found in their possession 50 boxes containing 15,000 capsules of “Tramadol Hydrochloride Tramanil”, weighing about 7 kg.
Also Read: Highest prevalence of opioid use disorders in eastern parts of India: UNODC report
The consignment, allegedly for illegal distribution to specific clients, was seized almost a month after a youth died at a drug rehabilitation centre in the State’s capital, Imphal. He had reportedly been injecting crushed tablets of Tapentadol, an opioid analgesic thrice as potent as Tramadol.
These incidents and the admission of another Tapentadol user at the drug rehabilitation centre with a serious infection due to injections confirmed what anti-narcotic officials and counsellors suspected — drug addicts were shifting to opioid analgesics available as prescription pain management medication from heroin and other narcotic substances made costlier by the ongoing ethnic conflict in Manipur.
“We are investigating to ascertain the source and intended destination of the Tramadol capsules and to determine the extent of involvement of the arrested duo in the possession or distribution of the pharmaceutical drug,” a Manipur police officer said.
The police and drug enforcement agencies in Manipur said data on seizures of opioid analgesics sold or ferried illegally in the State were not immediately available. They, however, said the price factor could have dictated the shift from methamphetamine and heroin, locally known as No. 4.
High prices
The prices of narcotic substances increased sharply after Manipur spiralled into seemingly unending violence in May 2023. According to reports in the local media, a vial of heroin, for instance, costs almost ₹5,000. A strip of Tramadol or Tapentadol costs between ₹40 and ₹400 depending on strength, brand, and manufacturer.
“Tramadol and Tapentadol are painkilling compounds derived from opium alkaloids. Taken for pain relief, they cause a sense of well-being, but can develop dependence if these are taken continuously for a few weeks,” Krishanu Krori, a Guwahati-based medicine specialist, told The Hindu.
“Addicts increase the dosage through injections after typically starting with 50-100 mg. Apart from a sense of euphoria, they develop disinterest in daily activities, withdrawal from family and society, and a craving for violence,” he said.
Counsellors in Manipur said pharmacists should strictly observe prescription requirements and health authorities should monitor emerging patterns of Tramadol and Tapentadol misuse. Hospitals and rehabilitation centres also need updated guidance on dependence, withdrawal, and complications associated with its misuse and injection, they said.
Opioid analgesics have become a worry for enforcement agencies beyond India’s northeastern region too. In August, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) unearthed an organised network involved in the clandestine manufacture, concealment, and illegal export of such drugs, a scheduled psychotropic substance, to African countries.
The seized items included 1 lakh Tramadol Hydrochloride tablets, 1 lakh Tapentadol tablets, machinery, and raw materials. The DRI sleuths arrested three key members of the syndicate during the operation at the Mumbai Air Cargo Complex.

These drones could cover up to 98 percent of the world's oceans by 2028
New ocean-sensing drones are being built to withstand the deepest depths of the ocean.
More than 70 percent of our planet is covered by the ocean, but the vast majority of it remains unexplored — an increasingly urgent blind spot as climate change raises water temperatures and. Autonomous underwater drone floats could soon close that gap, with a growing fleet set to cover more than 98 percent of ocean volume by 2028.
Exploring new depths
Today, the vast majority of ocean data is generated by members of the Argo Program — an international collaboration launched in 1999 that deploys 4,000 data-collection floats worldwide. The majority of Argo drones (like the one pictured above) descend between 2,000 and 4,000 meters into the ocean, but 10 percent of ocean warming occurs below these depths, marking a major gap in data collection.
This year, Ifremer — the French state ocean agency — reported its two Deep-6000 prototypes had completed five dives of 6,000 meters (nearly 20,000 feet) between January 11 and February 2 of this year, collecting crucial data on the abyssal zone. These successful missions make France the third country in the world, following China and the United States, to develop Argo floats capable of reaching these depths.
Ifremer said that by 2028, 30 more deep-sea floats will join the existing Argo-led international fleet of 4,000 devices, allowing researchers to explore more than 98 percent of the ocean.
The US currently operates more than 100 deep-sea floats and China operates more than thirty.
How do the dives work?
More than 90 percent of the ocean is considered deep ocean, reaching 200 meters (656 feet) deep or more — and of the entire ocean, only five percent has been explored. The lack of research on the deepest ocean areas — or abyssal zones — is largely due to technical constraints. At these depths, the ocean puts an enormous amount of pressure on machinery — approximately one atmosphere for every 10 meters of depth.That means at 6,000 meters, the pressure is approximately 600 times greater than that at sea level.
"The main challenge was to design a system that could withstand the pressures of the deep sea, be self-sufficient in terms of energy to remain operational for seven years, and keep costs under control," Xavier André, head of profiler technology development at Ifremer, said in a press release.
To accommodate for the massive amounts of pressure, Ifremer constructed the hulls of its Deep-6000 prototypes with composite materials other than pure titanium. At 88 pounds, the devices weigh approximately twice as much as a typical Argo float, allowing it to better withstand the intense pressure.
The float missions for these Argo devices run on ten-day cycles: the float is dropped from a boat, descending to a "drift" depth where it stays for nine days, then further descending to a "profile" depth for approximately three hours. The float then ascends back to the surface, where it sends data it has collected to a satellite. This process is repeated until its battery dies — usually around 150 cycles over three to five years.
What information do the drones collect?
The floats collect information on water salinity, temperature, oxygen and pressure to help scientists at weather and climate centers better understand how the ocean is behaving as climate change warms the waters. Argo data can be used to improve forecasts of major climate phenomena like monsoons, ocean warming, sea level rise and ocean circulation. The 4,000 floats that exist globally produce more than 100,000 temperature and salinity profiles per year, and all Argo data is free online to access and use.
Virginie Thierry, a physical oceanographer at Ifremer, said in a press release that the new Deep-6000 floats will allow the French organization to track ocean warming all the way through abyssal depths.
"We will also be able to obtain information on deep ocean circulation," she said, "which contributes to the storage of climate signals such as heat and carbon in the deep ocean, and refine ocean prediction models. Argo is an example of truly remarkable international cooperation, with more than 60 countries contributing to it."

It's unclear whether the Trump administration would follow through on any plans to demolish the Kennedy Center. Snopes reached out to the White House for comment and awaits a reply.
In September 2026, after the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts announced it would close its doors due to financial difficulties and the need for renovations, an image circulated online that social media users claimed (archived) showed U.S. President Donald Trump viewing a large, illustrated printout about the demolition of the Washington, D.C. landmark.
For example, the Instagram page Occupy Democrats posted images of Trump and the printout, writing, "BREAKING: A sharp-eyed photographer unearths Trump's plan to DESTROY the Kennedy Center – catching him staring at a placard that says 'Kennedy Center Demolished' through the window of his plane!"
The images and claims about what they showed also circulated on Facebook (archived), Threads (archived), X (archived), Bluesky (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers wrote in, asking about the authenticity of the images.
Several social media posts correctly credited images of Trump looking at the printout to the Agence France-Presse photographer Brendan Smialowski. One photo, published by Getty Images on Sept. 16, showed Trump viewing a printout with lettering at the top that read "dy Center DEMOLISH." Another image showed the start of the printout read "Kennedy." Getty Images and AFP are both reputable photo repositories and trusted sources.
As such, we rate claims that Trump viewed a printout about the demolition of the Kennedy Center true.
We contacted the White House Press Office to ask what the printout showed and whether Trump planned to demolish the Kennedy Center and await a reply.
Photos circulated amid tensions surrounding Kennedy Center name
Getty Images wrote that Smialowski took the photos of Trump looking at the "Kennedy Center" printout through a plane window after the president landed at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, on Sept. 16.
Earlier the same day, C-SPAN aired video footage of Trump telling reporters in North Carolina that his administration should be recognized for its work fixing and subsidizing the Kennedy Center, which he claimed had lost "hundreds of millions of dollars" before he stepped in to help.
The president added (time code 06:01): "I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition because frankly if we don't do that it's going to close, it'll end up being ripped down." He was likely referring to fundraising for the center's renovation work.
The day before, on Sept. 15, a federal judge ordered that the Kennedy Center Board of Trustees, which Trump heads, could not "install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing." Judge Christopher R. Cooper wrote the order as part of a lawsuit brought by U.S. Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat, who sued Trump in Dec. 2025 to stop the renaming of the Kennedy Center after Trump.
That same day, Trump announced on Truth Social that the Kennedy Center's board had voted to close the building to carry out "Renovation and Reconstruction" work. However, he wrote, that work would not be carried out unless and until courts allowed "the Board's approved name."
The board voted in December 2025 to rename the Kennedy Center to the "Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts" or "Trump Kennedy Center." Cooper blocked this change in May 2026 and ordered the center to remove Trump's name from public view. The center appeared to comply with this order in June 2026, erecting scaffolding to cover Trump's name on the building facade.
Court ordered 30-day notice period for demolition work
It was unclear at the time of this writing whether the "Kennedy Center DEMOLISH" printout Trump viewed on Sept. 16 was related to his remarks about the center being "ripped down" without "recognition" for his administration, or to what degree it represented the administration's plans for the center.
According to court documents filed in a separate lawsuit against the Kennedy Center Board of Trustees that sought to stop "demolition, new construction, major reconstruction, major renovation, or major aesthetic transformation" of the Kennedy Center without congressional approval, lawyers for the board said the Center's position in August 2026 was that "the building will not be demolished and that no new structure will be constructed."
Lawyers for the Kennedy Center's Board of Trustees pledged to tell plaintiffs and the court in that case if the center's position changed.
Following the publication of Smialowski's images, Cooper ordered defendants in the Beatty case, which included Trump and the Kennedy Center Board of Trustees, to give "more than 30 days notice" if the center changed its position that the building would not be demolished or have a new structure added.
Neither Trump nor the Kennedy Center Board of Trustees, who were defendants in both lawsuits, had given such notice of by the time of this writing.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether a forklift repeatedly hit the Kennedy Center pillars on Sept. 16, 2026, and whether the Trump administration cut down the center's weeping willows.

The victims were walking as part of a padyatra to the shrine for the annual Bhadarvi Poonam fair, which attracts lakhs of devotees from across Gujarat.
One person was killed and 11 others injured after a speeding Scorpio hit a group of people near Dolgarh Patiya on the Himmatnagar-Idar highway late on Monday evening, police said.

Seven to eight of the injured were pilgrims walking towards Ambaji as part of a padyatra for the annual Bhadarvi Poonam fair, while the others were volunteers at the seva camp and local residents of Talod taluka, according to Gohil. Gaza children return to in-person schools for first time in 3 years
The move is a fragile milestone; the conflict with Israel has killed around 22,000 youngsters and over 770 education workers
Hundreds of thousands of children in Gaza have returned to in-person teaching for the first time in nearly three years, albeit in damaged or makeshift school buildings and tents, and with uniforms, notebooks and pens unaffordable for many families.
The United Nations Children’s Fund (Unicef) says 98 per cent of schools in Gaza were either destroyed or damaged during the war, and Gaza education officials say about 660,000 students have been deprived of in-person learning and regular participation in education.
The reopening on Saturday was a fragile milestone for Gaza after a conflict that has killed around 22,000 students and more than 770 education workers, including 532 teachers, according to Ibrahim Ramadan, director of education for East Khan Younis.

Aviation regulators turn to AI to help manage the nation's airspace
WASHINGTON — The federal agency in charge of air traffic control is turning to artificial intelligence to help manage the nation's airspace.
The Federal Aviation Administration officially launched its ambitious $875-million-dollar software overhaul on Monday, announcing the rollout would begin at three major airports that serve the Washington, D.C. region.
The new system is known as Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, or SMART for short.
"By fundamentally reshaping how we manage our airspace and preventing problems before they happen, SMART will slash those frustrating delays, reduce stress on air traffic controllers, and lower travel prices," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement.
The long-awaited rollout, however, was upstaged by an equipment outage that snarled air traffic at major airports on the East Coast.
The FAA said the problems began with a blown circuit at its air traffic control facility in Philadelphia, which also handles traffic at Newark Liberty International Airport. Aviation officials tried to switch to a backup line, but found it had been accidentally cut by an Amtrak construction crew in New Jersey, Duffy said in a social media post.
The cut fiber optic line caused a telecom outage and forced the FAA to pause flights in the Northeast, including at John F. Kennedy and LaGuardia Airports in New York City.
FAA administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters the equipment failure underscored the need to replace outdated infrastructure. The new software is part of a broader $12.5 billion push to modernize the nation's air traffic control system.
Regulators and airlines hope the AI-enhanced tool will make flying more efficient, though critics warn that it won't solve bigger problems with the air traffic control system.
FAA and DOT leaders emphasize that the new technology is not intended as a replacement for human air traffic controllers. They describe it as a tool that's supposed to make controllers' jobs easier by reducing congestion and conflicts in the air before they happen.
"The way we manage traffic today is chaotic and we can do better," said FAA administrator Bryan Bedford during a Senate hearing earlier this year. "We need to manage that at the FAA, rather than rely on commercial airlines to simply schedule however they want."
FAA leaders say the SMART system will help optimize the nation's airspace by considering all planned airline flights, as well as weather, wind, and other variables, and tweaking those flight schedules to reduce congestion.
The FAA tapped a relatively small company called Air Space Intelligence to build the system. The company has previously made AI-enhanced software for dispatchers at Alaska Airlines and other carriers, but this project presents a significantly bigger and higher-profile test.
Skeptics question whether the SMART system will be the game-changer FAA leaders have promised.
"It won't replace humans. It'll be another tool in the toolbox," said Dave Riley, a former air traffic controller who retired in 2020 after more than 20 years at the FAA. "But of course, when you call it AI, it gets a lot of attention."
Riley downplayed concerns of the AI tool going rogue because human air traffic controllers will still be in charge of keeping planes safely separated.
"The fears of AI killing us all in the next 10 years, I don't think this platform is going to be about that," he said.
But Riley doubts the tool will do much to solve the bigger problems in the air traffic control system — particularly the staffing shortage. The FAA is still thousands of certified air traffic controllers short of full staffing, forcing many controllers to work mandatory overtime and grueling schedules.
The National Air Traffic Controllers Association, the union that represents controllers, distanced itself from the new system.
"NATCA has not been involved in the design, testing, or implementation of SMART and therefore cannot speak to its effect on the air traffic control workforce at this time," the union said in a statement.
Airlines for America, the trade association that represents the major airlines in Washington, praised the FAA's push to modernize the nation's flight management tools.
"Its potential to strengthen safety, increase capacity and improve efficiency will have a direct positive effect on American travelers," the group said in a statement. "We're just in the initial stages, but it's one of the most exciting and bold initiatives taken on by the FAA in decades."

In September 2026, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said his agency was investigating claims that Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota married her brother to commit immigration fraud.
In the past, U.S. President Donald Trump and other Republicans have also amplified the claim, which has circulated since 2016.
Mullin said in a video interview (archived), "We know that she married her brother to try to bring him into the United States" and that federal officials were investigating alleged "illegal activity."
Snopes has previously reported on this claim about Omar marrying her brother and concluded it was unfounded, meaning there's no credible evidence supporting it. In 2016, Omar became the first Somali American elected to the Minnesota state House of Representatives. As a young immigrant with progressive politics, Omar has been targeted by numerous unfounded rumors about her religion and family.
Snopes sent a list of questions to Omar's spokesperson at the time we first investigated this claim but did not receive responses.
As we previously reported, the origins of the rumor surrounding Omar's relationship with her brother are unclear. The claim first appeared on an online Somali community discussion forum called SomaliSpot and was then picked up by Powerline, a conservative blog. An August 2016 blog post stated:
A reader has written us to point out that the Somali website Somalispot posted information suggesting Omar's involvement in marriage and immigration fraud. The post notes that Omar married Ahmed Hirsi in 2002. Hirsi is the father of Omar's three children. Omar is depicted with Hirsi and their children on Omar's campaign website here.
The post further notes that Omar married her brother Ahmed Nur Said Elmi in 2009, implying that the latter marriage assisted his entry into the United States. Her brother was a British citizen. "As soon as Ilhan Omar married him," the post continues, "he started university at her [a]lma mater North Dakota State University where he graduated in 2012. Shortly thereafter, he moved to Minneapolis where he was living in a public housing complex and was later evicted. He then returned to the United Kingdom where he now lives."
Snopes sent questions to Powerline blogger Scott Johnson in 2019, who did not provide any substantive evidence supporting the claim.
Omar denied the rumor in a 2016 statement, calling that marriage "a difficult part of my personal history that I did not consider relevant in the context of a political campaign." Her full statement can be found below:
In 2002, when I was 19 years old, Ahmed Hirsi (whose name before he received citizenship was Ahmed Aden), the father of my children and love of my life, and I, applied for a marriage license, but we never finalized the application and thus were never legally married. In 2008, we decided to end our relationship in our faith tradition after reaching an impasse in our life together.
I entered into a relationship with a British citizen, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, and married him legally in 2009. Our relationship ended in 2011 and we divorced in our faith tradition. After that, he moved home to England. I have yet to legally divorce Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, but am in the process of doing so. Insinuations that Ahmed Nur Said Elmi is my brother are absurd and offensive.
Since 2011, I am happy to say that I have reconciled with Ahmed Hirsi, we have married in our faith tradition and are raising our family together. Like all families, we have had our ups and downs but we are proud to have come through it together.
In 2002, Omar and Hirsi reportedly applied for a marriage license. The couple married in an Islamic ceremony but never completed the process for a civil marriage, according to Hirsi. By 2008, Hirsi and Omar had separated (per Islamic custom). After that relationship ended, Omar had a civil marriage with Elmi in 2009. When that relationship ended, Elmi moved to England and they divorced per Islamic practice in 2011, but without receiving a legal divorce.
Omar later reconciled with Hirsi and remarried in an Islamic ceremony. In 2017, Omar formally petitioned for divorce from Elmi, and legally wed Hirsi in 2018. Hirsi and Omar legally divorced in 2019.
Snopes found no credible evidence that Elmi and Omar were siblings in a fraudulent marriage.
According to Omar, she and her family fled the Somalian civil war in 1991. They moved to the U.S. in 1995 after residing for four years in a Kenyan refugee camp. Omar's mother had died, so her father and grandfather raised her and her siblings. In 2018, Omar showed a reporter from the Minneapolis Star Tribune photos of documents from her family's entry into the U.S. after fleeing the civil war. She did not provide the reporter with copies of these papers but showed that they listed her father and showed her as the youngest of seven children. There was no one named Ahmed Nur Said Elmi listed in the documents.
We previously noted that Omar and her siblings all arrived in U.S. with refugee statuses. Omar was a minor when she became a naturalized U.S. citizen. How one sibling could end up with a completely different immigration status from the others remains unexplained by the claims.
According to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services policy, immigrants can apply for permanent residency status (opening the pathway to naturalization) if they are siblings of a U.S. citizen, or if they are married to a U.S. citizen. Any sibling of Omar's would not have to marry her in order to secure a path to citizenship.
Additionally, if Elmi desperately wanted U.S. citizenship, he would not have immediately returned to England after his split with Omar.
Snopes has covered numerous claims about Omar, including the rumor that her father participated in war crimes or genocide, and the false claim that Omar said al-Qaida made her "proud."
Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

Here is a story that on the face of it seems so wildly unlikely it can only be true. Indeed, the very concept of a romantic documentary sounds almost oxymoronic, an indication of how much nonfiction films have become synonymous with grim histories full of suffering and injustice. Let’s hope this sweet work, directed by Orlando von Einsiedel (who’s made his share of hardcore, suffering-intensive docs including Oscar-winning short The White Helmets) launches a new trend in nonfiction film-making for stuff that makes you happy-cry.
The basic meet-cute happened in 1975, when PK (played by Chirag Lobo in the film’s extensive re-enactments) met Lotta (Mina Dale) in Delhi. He was a poor street artist, a Dalit, the lowest possible caste, once called Untouchables. The real PK Mahanandia appears on screen to explain how he had left his rural village for Delhi in order to get away from all that caste hierarchy. When he met Lotta he pretty much knew he’d met the woman of his dreams because he’d been carrying a horoscope his father had commissioned for him when he was a baby that prophesised he’d fall in love with a woman whose family owned a jungle. Lotta, a backpacker from Sweden, hailed from a clan back home that owned a forest, so that was good enough for PK to believe he’d met his fate. After a chaste holiday romance bloomed between these two crazy kids, she went back to Sweden and he decided to bicycle the 6,000 miles all the way there from India to prove his love.
As we hear the now elderly young lovers describe what they were thinking at the time, we watch Lobo and Dale act out the journey, with poor PK getting into a few scrapes that set him back a few steps as he plods his way westward. Some of the most touching interludes are the interactions he has with strangers along the way that seem incredibly naturalistic and semi-improvised. Cynics might quibble that one can’t help wondering what darker parts of the story have been left out, and note that the actors chosen to play the lovers are a few notches more conventionally beautiful than the actual people – but every love story has its soft focus, flaw-concealing fudges so we’ll let it slide here.

The leaders of France and Canada have pledged closer ties to grapple with rising geopolitical tensions, climate change and the erosion of democratic values, after they met in a French territory off Canada’s Atlantic coast.
The two leaders’ visit to Saint-Pierre and Miquelon – the first by a French president since 2014 and the first by a Canadian prime minister – came just weeks after Donald Trump posted an image showing the islands, as well as all of Canada and other countries in North America, covered by the US flag.
Ottawa has been seeking closer ties with the EU amid an increasingly acrimonious trade war with the US.
“Our societies are being shaken by new storms: the upheavals, caused by climate change, the erosion of democratic norms, and new threats to our sovereignty,” Canada’s Mark Carney said in a statement alongside France’s Emmanuel Macron on Sunday. “The time has come to strengthen our ties.”
Macron added that the two allies agreed to forge closer ties in sectors ranging from space and climate to energy.
“We both believe in democracy, the rule of law, respect for international law, respect for free and fair trade, science as the basis for our decisions, and the strategic autonomy that we defend,” the French president said.
Diplomats said the visit by Macron, who was en route to the annual UN general assembly of world leaders, had a symbolic weight following Trump’s social media post.
The image Trump shared showed the US flag draped over a map of the US, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, and was labelled “United States of America”. It included Saint-Pierre and Miquelon and French Caribbean territories.
Responding to questions on Trump’s post, Macron dismissed any notion that the territories could not be French and said he did not need to reaffirm that point every day just because “people have strange ideas or say strange things”.
For France, Saint-Pierre and Miquelon is strategically important due to its location on the doorstep of the US and the Arctic.
The territory also occupies a key place in France’s cooperation with Canada, including over energy.
Macron, whose government is facing increased pressure at home over rising fuel prices, said the talks had opened the door for bilateral discussions aimed at sealing concrete deals. 
Paris hopes Canada will broaden its exports of liquefied natural gas to Europe rather than primarily to Asia.
“Canadian liquefied natural gas projects can help. They are important for Europe,” Macron said.
The two leaders also discussed Canada’s relationship with the EU after the bloc proposed that Ottawa become its first associate member, something Macron said France supported.
Trump threatened the EU with “serious tariffs” and a halt to trade after the proposal – an idea he derided as “laughable”.
Any move towards deeper integration is likely to face hurdles. More than a decade after the EU and Canada agreed to the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, and nine years after its provisional application began, several EU member states have yet to ratify the accord, including France.

For a long time, sleep research has treated the cerebral cortex as a passive follower reacting to signals from the deep brain. “Usually, sleep is associated with being controlled by subcortical regions,” said Geoffrey Terral, a neuroscientist at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York.
The cortex is where the slow rhythms of deep sleep can be seen, but researchers assumed the signals that triggered them originated elsewhere. In a recent Nature study, Terral and Renata Batista-Brito, who runs the lab, report a population of cortical cells that challenges that assumption.
These cortical cells make up only around one percent of the cortex’s inhibitory neurons, and switching them on in a mouse puts the animal to sleep. “What our work shows is that the cortex can not only see this rhythm but also initiate it by itself, and this is sufficient to promote sleep,” Terral said.
The 1 percent
The cells are called Sst-Chodl neurons, after two genes that are active in them. Long-range inhibitory neurons marked by the activity of these genes have been known for some time, based on studies in monkeys, but researchers couldn’t figure out how to manipulate them using these genes. Aiming at either one of these genes captures a huge, heterogeneous family of different neurons. “A single gene is not able to target these cells,” Batista-Brito said.
Inhibitory neurons account for about a fifth of all cortical neurons, so Sst-Chodl cells amount to roughly one neuron in a thousand in the cortex. “If you’re not really specific, the contaminants are going to be much more dominant than the specific cells,” Batista-Brito said.
Building a strategy that labels a cell only when both genes are on took her team years.
“Going after these cells was really a high-risk project because the likelihood of seeing anything with 0.1 percent of neurons in the cortex is really low,” Batista-Brito said. “I wrote a bunch of grants on these projects that were always rejected because it was too high-risk.”
Her first look at the anatomy of Sst-Chodl neurons proved the risk worth taking. “At first, I saw two or three cell bodies in the whole brain,” Batista-Brito told Ars. “Despite that, there was massive, massive arborization all over the visual cortex, like I never saw with any other neuron.”
That “massive arborization” is a tree-like branching that connects neurons to other parts of the brain, making them part of a wider communication network. It was also very unusual, as inhibitory neurons are almost always local. They receive inputs from different, sometimes distant regions in the brain and exert control over their immediate surroundings—their own small patch.
“Sst-Chodl neurons are kind of the opposite,” Batista-Brito said. “They are receiving inputs that are quite precise, but then they are broadcasting that information everywhere.”
A single Sst-Chodl cell branches out to the entire visual cortex, then sends axons to the areas of the brain responsible for touch, hearing, spatial memory, navigation, and voluntary movements.
The quiet hours
To see when the cells fire, the team imaged them with while tracking the mice’s pupil size, muscle tone, facial movement, running, and cortical electrical activity at the same time. Ninety-five out of 111 imaged cells lit up during slow-wave sleep and quiet, motionless wakefulness, and fell silent during running and REM sleep.
During slow-wave sleep, the cortex alternates between UP states of vigorous firing and DOWN states of near-silence; the Sst-Chodl neurons broke this pattern. “Their activity is even higher at the termination of the UP state,” Terral said. “Once all the other neurons start to decrease their activity, those neurons start to increase it even more.”
They also skip the rebound that other cells show coming out of a DOWN state. “Those cells behave totally differently to any other cells we can measure around that transition,” Terral said.
To really understand what they do, the team made the SSt-Chodl neurons fire on command using optogenetics, which involves inserting the gene for a light-activated ion channel that can stimulate the nerve cells to fire.
The long reach
Optogenetic stimulation of the Sst-Chodl cells in the visual cortex drove delta power—the slowest, highest-amplitude brain waves measured during deep, restorative sleep—up across every layer. It also tightened spike timing and made DOWN states more frequent and longer. But overall firing barely changed.
“Those neurons are not changing so much the firing rate,” Terral said. “They change just the coordination—whether the neurons fire together or not.”
Normally, driving a population at a given frequency entrains the network at that frequency. Here, it didn’t matter.
“If we did a flat stimulus, or delta, or 20 hertz, or 60 hertz, you still induced the same kind of oscillation,” Batista-Brito said. “There’s something about the intrinsic properties of these cells that, once they trigger, they go on this one frequency.”
She emphasized that we don’t currently know how they do this.
The reach of these neurons also proved unusually long. “Their cell bodies were in the visual cortex, but they could regulate the activity of most of the neurons we were recording,” Terral said.
Direct inhibitory currents appeared in a third of cells two millimeters out, and stimulating the visual cortex had measurable effects as far as frontal motor areas.
In the final step, the team focused on behavioral experiments. They checked if stimulating the Sst-Chodl neurons would put the mice to sleep. It did.
A sleep switch
Activating the cells across the cortex of freely moving mice increased slow-wave and REM sleep, cut the time taken to fall asleep, and sent the animals into their nests during the day. Then the team tried it during the dark phase, when nocturnal mice are mostly awake.
“We could have them sleep more during the time that they are awake than they usually sleep during the day,” Batista-Brito said. “I never thought this experiment was going to work. We are manipulating one percent of inhibitory neurons with local injections, so we are hitting only a fraction of those cells. And we could see an effect that was really quite striking.”
That effect, Batista-Brito argues, points toward the idea that these neurons might be the cortex’s sensors of sleep pressure, something first proposed by Thomas Kilduff, the director of the SRI International’s Center for Neuroscience and co-author of the study.
Sleep, Batista-Brito explains comes in two flavors: the circadian sort that follows the light and homeostatic sleep, the accumulated fatigue that eventually makes us sleep whether we want to or not. Kilduff, Batista-Brito said, showed that after sleep deprivation, these are the most active cells in the cortex.
One question Batist-Brito and her colleagues still don’t have the answer to, though, is what activates these cells.
What flips the switch?
“One caveat of our work is that it was done in the visual cortex,” Batista-Brito said.
The findings about the coordinating role of the Sst-Chodl neurons, the team claims, should generalize to different brain regions, but the actual wiring may not. Batista-Brito’s lab is now repeating the anatomy part of their work in the prefrontal cortex. Their prediction is that there we’ll see inputs from other areas, such as the hypothalamus and the thalamus, and that will be what triggers the network for sleep specifically.
The cells are conserved from salamanders to humans, which is why the paper argues they could be an entry point into the sleep disruption running through so many psychiatric illnesses.
The team is now focused on three remaining questions: what activates these cells, whether they actually sense sleep pressure, and why they drive delta power.

Wigan Warriors have been there, done that, and got the T-shirt when it comes to making it to the Betfred Super League Grand Final and so their routine is set as they hunt down the treble in 2026.
Wigan have already added two trophies to their cabinet this season having won the Challenge Cup and League Leaders' Shield, with the Grand Final just one step away.
To get there, they need to beat Wakefield in the semi-finals on Saturday September 26, live on Sky Sports after Daryl Powell's side defeated Leigh in the eliminators.

Matt Peet lost a first final as head coach of Wigan at Old Trafford in 2025 against Hull KR, but has already made sure that such heartbreak was fuel to achieve more.
But now, with success firmly in their sights once again, Wigan will keep looking forward while being rooted in the present and ensuring they are firmly focused on the semi-finals.
"We have been through this experience a few times now, learned some lessons, and it is exciting," Peet told Sky Sports.
"It is not a case of that everything we did last year was wrong, some things we got right, we just weren't good enough on the evening.
"We will do what is right for this year's team for this moment on their journey and our journey.
"It is more about looking forward than back."
If Wigan were to win the Grand Final, it would mark Peet's 10th trophy since taking over as head coach of his hometown club in 2022, success coming under him at a staggering speed.
However, those statistics are of no importance to him and the most important trophy is always the one next in your sights.
"It is not about that, the next one is always the one," he added.
"We just want to play well in the semi-finals. Not thinking too much about Old Trafford or the trophy or talking about that.
"We know we are going to be up against a very determined and capable team in the semi-finals who have just had a fantastic win.
"They will be battle-hardened and confident so we just have to concern ourselves with that."
O'Neill: Ready to right heartbreak of 2025
2025 was a particularly unique year for Wigan under Peet. They made finals but did not win them as Hull KR swept every honour available.
They also fell to a tough 24-6 loss in the Grand Final, which saw Brad O'Neill sent to the sin-bin for a dangerous tackle.
O'Neill has been one of Wigan's standout performers across 2026, being named in the Super League Dream Team, and would love to right that wrong.
Indeed, he feels they have put themselves in the best possible position to do exactly that.
"I feel like going away together pre the semi-final when we get the week off is a great opportunity to get some work in but also a good time to bond as well and get away and fresh. Just to enjoy each other's company," O'Neill told Sky Sports.
"We have done it for the last few years and everyone seems to like it.
"I feel like it would mean a lot. Last year was a tough one to take at Old Trafford for myself personally and for the club.
"To put those wrongs right would mean a lot to us all.
"We have given ourselves the best opportunity to do it, we just have to commit now and get through this semi-final first."

Richard Marles says the Department of Defence is examining how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for the US from Australia were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong.
The acting prime minister said “very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end” will be reviewed, however, he claimed the technology parts were not “sensitive”, as first reported by Politico over the weekend.
The parts, which were being transported by another unknown third party on behalf of manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, still remain unaccounted for months later following their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong.
The last known location of the fighter jet components – in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China – has sparked concern that some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed.
“We are examining [Australia’s involvement], but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program, and through the US’s prime contractor, Lockheed,” Marles said on Tuesday.
“My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here, or sensitive parts.
“Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Politico reported sources said the “sensitive” shipment contained on of the jet’s canopies, which reportedly contains stealth technology.
The Guardian has contacted the Pentagon.
While many details have not yet been revealed, Michael Shoebridge, a director for Strategic Analysis Australia who has worked in intelligence agencies, said there were two reasons why China, or another adversary, would want F-35 parts – to reverse engineer them, or to learn how to better exploit and attack them.
Shoebridge added the shipment’s pitstop in Hong Kong was “such an unexpectedly stupid thing” for the manufacturer or Australia to do.
“This is an act of incredible ineptitude and stupidity, and so it’s more the Chinese taking advantage of an incredible stroke of luck brought to them by the stupidity of the people involved,” he said.
Last week, the US State Department announced that the Trump administration would continue with the sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia, despite reported concerns from the US intelligence community that China could obtain some of the stealth technology.
Australia was one of the early development partners in the F-35. The program spreads the development, supply, management and sustainment of the fighter jets across different countries.
More than 70 Australian companies have production and sustainment contracts with the F-35 program. In excess of 700 of the fighter jet’s “critical pieces” are manufactured in Victoria alone, according to the state government. Australia also hosts a regional distribution hub for F-35 parts in New South Wales.
Australian companies involved in the program’s supply chain have been awarded contracts valued at over $5.2bn, as of September 2025.
Shoebridge said the missing shipment of parts could mean the whole multibillion-dollar fleet is vulnerable to adversaries.
“They’re all now carrying the risk of whatever vulnerabilities this has brought to the to the aircraft,” he said.
“So it’s not just a US-Australia issue. It’s every operator of the F3-5 program [that] has an interest in understanding what happened and what was potentially exposed.”

The story uses screenshots and not the actual viral video in view of its sensitive nature.
A 12-second long video is going viral on social media where a woman is seen bathing in river water while wearing a bikini.
The video was posted on September 15 by X user Barkha Trehan, who describes herself as ‘Activist | Voice Of Men | President, Purush Aayog’. She wrote, “Location : Haridwar. Madam: My Body My Choice. Your take ??” The video garnered over 1 million views. (Archive)
In her X bio, Trehan identifies herself as a “men’s rights activist” and the “president of Purush Aayog”. She also claims to be a TEDx speaker and a “Hindu entrepreneur”; she apparently also “directed a documentary titled The Curse of Manhood”.
Media outlet News 18 Hindi published a report with screenshots from the video pointing out that it had angered social media users. (Archive)
This same video was posted by content creator Piyali Banerjee, where she questioned the “basic decency” and “knowledge of clothing” of the woman.
Other social media users also shared the same video with similar captions, questing the woman for wearing a bikini in Haridwar, with misogynistic comments about her character.
The video is also viral on Instagram.
Fact Check
To verify its authenticity, we ran a reverse image search on a few keyframes from the viral clip. This search led us to a reel posted on Instagram on August 18. The 21-second long reel was uploaded by an account named ‘ishika_pandit’. It showed the same woman bathing at the same spot, but wearing completely different clothes.
This video matched the background of the viral clip with the steel railing on the river and the foundations of a bridge clearly visible in the background. The woman’s hand gestures also mirror the viral video, and the same two men are visible in both videos.
Based on these similarities, it can be concluded that the video uploaded on August 18 is the original footage. The woman in the original video is seen wearing a yellow suit, and not a bikini. Thus, the viral clip is a doctored version of the original video, manipulating the attire of the woman.
Some social media users highlighted the possibility of the viral clip being an AI-generated deepfake, claiming that the woman’s clothes had been purposely changed from a suit to a bikini. (Archive)

Taking a safe bet here that most of you who have heard of Louise Joy Brown have not heard at all of Jean Purdy, or her role in the birth of Baby Brown. Louise Brown was the first baby born of an IVF procedure on July 25, 1978. But this might not have been a joyful story, but for Jean Purdy.
Like all the heroines in this column, Jean Marian Purdy, a clinical embryologist and a critical part of the development of in vitro fertilisation, remained uncredited for a long while. Born in Cambridge, U.K., she went to work with physiologist Robert Edwards and gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe at the Physiological Laboratory in Cambridge. They were working on a high-risk experiment and taking medical science where it had never been before – who would have thought babies could be created in test tubes before the trio managed to show that it is possible.
Purdy trained as a nurse in Addenbrooke Hopsital in Cambridge, and joined Edwards in 1968 as a research nurse and quickly became indispensable to the team. Going back to study the records later, scientists established that it was Purdy who managed the laboratory, prepared and tested culture media, and recorded and organised the data of the early IVF work in the lab. Besides this, the records also put her at the centre of patient care, in this case, supporting women who volunteered their eggs and wombs at a time when public sentiment was entirely against it.
Purdy was the first to recognise and describe the formation of the early human blastocyst – the cluster of cells that forms five or six days after a sperm fertilises an egg, in the culture, a key milestone in pre-implantation development. It represents the early stage of embryonic development, where the embryo implants itself into the wall of the uterus to establish a pregnancy. Purdy was the first to see the embryonic cells successfully dividing in the lab, soon these cells would go on to become on 25 July 1978, she was the first to see the embryonic cells that would become Louise Brown. This moment is significant, because it was the first indication that their pioneering technique had worked.
That was not all; between 1970 and 1985, until her death, she co-authored 26 academic papers with Edwards and others in leading journals, including Nature, documenting methods, outcomes and sophistication that made IVF safe and more reliable.
After NHS funding for IVF was withdrawn following early successes, Purdy helped establish the world’s first dedicated IVF clinic, Bourn Hall Clinic near Cambridge in 1980, and served as its technical director. Again, she helped standardise medical protocols for IVF and scale up treatment, overseeing the birth of more than 500 IVF babies before her death from cancer at just 39 years, in 1985.
In their article The Oldham Notebooks: an analysis of the development of IVF 1969–1978. V. The role of Jean Purdy reassessed, archived in PubMed, Martin H. Johnson and Kay Elder, look at her body of work in early fertility care. The authors pored over the Oldham Notebooks - 21 handwritten laboratory notebooks and loose records kept primarily by Purdy between 1969 and 1978. They concluded that: “Purdy’s interests were clearly focused on the research and development aspects, especially those exploring viable embryo development and improved transfer procedures. For example, in a film made in 1980 (Williams, 1980), she talks about a modification to the transfer cannula that she was trying. Thus, whilst Edwards provided the ideas and the intellectual stimulation and Steptoe the authoritative clinical skills, it is arguable that without Purdy’s systematic approach and dedicated contributions, the project at Oldham may have faltered.”
Despite all this, centuries of sexism weighing in on the scientific community, a classic example of the Matilda Effect, her role was minimised in public memory for decades. Even though Edwards and other colleagues objected to it, Purdy’s name was omitted from a commemorative plaque installed at Oldham Hopsitals, associated with IVF’s breakthrough. Correspondence from Edwards archived at Cambridge later described Purdy as “crucial” to their work, underscoring how her erasure contradicted the team’s own view of her importance. In fact, Edwards’ own records state his growing confidence in her and her essentiality in the team: Purdy was “being ‘particularly good with the patients’, and her ‘cooperation had become crucial. It was no longer just Patrick and me. We had become a threesome’.
However, only Edwards was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for IVF. While recognition for the work that Purdy did, has grown only recently, thanks in good measure to the research of Johnson and Elder, some things cannot be corrected any more. Now, some museums and clinics cite Purdy as the first clinical embryologist, and other institutions have begun naming awards and exhibitions after her. Sidelined again, this time, though her collaborators acknowledged her work, Purdy’s contributions were callously and credit consistently denied.
Though belated, it’s now time to undo the wrongs. It is time to say her name! Say Jean Purdy, shout it out from the rooftops!
