Flights resume after ground stops at major U.S. airports, including New York's JFK and LaGuardia
Thousands of flights were cancelled or delayed because of the telecommunications issue
The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration resolved a telecommunications problem late in the afternoon that had snarled thousands of flights across the country, with incoming flights halted for hours at major East Coast airports.
The issue started around 9:45 a.m. ET when workers accidentally cut a telecom line in New Jersey used by the FAA. This forced a halt to incoming flights at major airports, on a day when 130 world leaders and dozens of ministers were arriving in New York for the annual high-level meeting of the United Nations General Assembly.
The FAA stopped arrivals at all three major New York-area airports as well as Philadelphia and Boston, and two smaller airports in the New York region. The problems were not fully resolved for eight hours.
Prime Minister Mark Carney was among the leaders whose flights were affected. His office said his planned flight into New York this evening was delayed, meaning he would not make it to a scheduled event. He is expected to arrive in the city later Monday night.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on X late in the afternoon that telecom lines had been repaired and normal operations throughout the Northeast were resuming. He said it would take time to resolve existing delays and urged passengers to check the status of flights for which they were waiting.
Fewer than a dozen flights were affected at Toronto's Pearson International Airport as a result of the ground stop in the U.S.
Officials at Pearson and at Montreal's Trudeau International Airport said they were continuing to monitor the situation, and encouraged passengers flying to or from the U.S. to contact their airlines directly for updated information.
FlightAware, a flight-tracking website, said about 7,000 flights were delayed or cancelled, including 1,400 flights at the three major New York-area airports.
More than half of all flights were cancelled at Newark, a major United Airlines hub. United said it issued a travel waiver to help impacted passengers.
The issue also forced the diversion of more than 100 flights to other airports.
Flights at Philadelphia had resumed by late in the afternoon after a second ground stop was lifted. Reagan Washington National Airport also halted flights for more than an hour because of volume issues.
A ground stop at Boston, which stopped accepting flights because of spillover volume, was also lifted.

PATNA: Allegations by girl students of a government school in Nawada that their headmaster entered their washroom and touched them inappropriately have raised serious questions over the safety of minors inside educational institutions, coming a day after a Class X student was allegedly molested on a road in Jamui.
The back-to-back incidents have triggered outrage, with Congress leader Pawan Khera on Tuesday questioning the safety and dignity of women and girls in Bihar.
In a video shared by Khera on social media, the girls are seen crying and alleging that the headmaster entered their washroom, picked them up and made them sit on his lap. The students, accompanied by their parents, had staged a protest on the school campus on September 18. Following the allegations, the headmaster was arrested under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act.
The Nawada incident allegedly took place a day before the Jamui episode, in which a Class X student was allegedly sexually harassed on the road by a group of men. Her friend was also physically assaulted. A video of the incident, which went viral on social media, showed the girls pleading with the accused to spare them as the alleged harassment continued.
The incidents have brought the safety of minor girls into sharp focus, with concerns being raised over their vulnerability both in public spaces and within schools, where they are expected to be protected.
Targeting the BJP government in Bihar, Khera said the two incidents reflected an “utterly unacceptable standard of safety and dignity for women and girls”.
“The BJP in Bihar must paint its face black,” he wrote on X, referring to the alleged harassment in Jamui and the accusations against the school headmaster in Nawada.
The two cases have intensified scrutiny of safeguards for school-going girls and women in public spaces, as well as the need for accountability in cases of alleged sexual harassment.

Moral policing can be done in decent, elegant fashion: Bihar Minister's shocker
Bihar minister Shreyasi Singh drew criticism after saying moral policing could be done more decently while condemning the harassment of a boy and a girl in Jamui.
Bihar Minister and Jamui MLA Shreyasi Singh on Tuesday sparked a massive controversy with her remarks that “moral policing can be done in a more decent and elegant fashion”, while condemning the harassment of a boy and a girl in Jamui district.
“Moral policing can be done in a more decent and elegant fashion. But the way they mishandled and mistreated the boy and girl together is absolutely not tolerable,” Singh, a former sports shooter, and a BJP leader, told India Today TV.
Her remarks came after a viral video surfaced showing the boy and the girl being confronted and harassed by a group of people on a roadside in Jamui district a few days ago, triggering nationwide outrage.
When asked to clarify her remarks, Singh said people could have an opinion about how others chose to live their lives, but there were better ways to express such views.
“You can have an opinion about how somebody chooses to live their life and what they want to do with it. Maybe there is a better way to do it. But the way they have treated them is absolutely not tolerable. The videos that have come are shocking,” she said.
She said she was unable to understand how members of the local community could treat the minors in such a manner.
“How can you treat a boy and a girl of the society that you are living in? They must have known that the boy and girl are kids from Jammu. I can't fathom the fact that they were treated this badly by locals,” Singh said.
The minister also said she would ensure that there were no loopholes for those responsible to escape accountability.
“To help curb this (crime), I am going to ensure from my side that there is absolutely no loophole for them to get out. This incident needs to set a precedent for the future,” she said.

Jenee Gragston dropped to the ground and held on to the grass as if it could save her life. She yelled to her family members to get down. She later told me that she didn’t know where the bullets were coming from, but she knew they were close. When the firing stopped, the cries began. She could hear her 4-year-old nephew howling: “Get it off me! Get it off me!” She wasn’t close enough to see what had happened, but it looked like he had blood on his chest. A teenage boy was lying near the child. The teenager “never screamed or anything,” she said. “I can still see all of it.”
It was a Saturday afternoon, mid-August in Lexington, Kentucky. Hundreds of people had gathered in Charles Young Park to celebrate what’s called East End Day—a combination of family reunions, live music, and lots of food. I grew up going to festivals in that park, though I lived on the west side of town, in the Charlotte Court housing projects.
Kentucky isn’t the most dangerous place in America, but it’s up there, with the 14th-highest rate of gun deaths. Twelve years ago, my uncle was murdered in Lexington. Three years ago, my sister’s husband was shot and killed there. I worry about my brother, who still lives there. He had gotten himself off the streets for a while, but is now back living in the city. Lexington had recently seen a hard-won drop in gun deaths—last year was the fourth straight year of declines in gun violence among young people. This spring and summer set a record of 190 straight days without a homicide. Then came the East End Day shooting, which killed that teenager, 16-year-old Di’Zhon Robertson, and wounded four others—including the 4-year-old, who was shot in the leg. The next weekend, another person was killed. The weekend after that, four separate shootings left two more dead.
Gragston was selling Polish sausages in the park. She’d paid more than $300 for the grill, $300 for the sausages, more than $1,000 in fees, $75 for the booth. Business was good; some people returned for seconds. Her husband, her kids, and other family members had come to help her set up her tent. Her 4-year-old nephew was handing customers sodas and water bottles. On the basketball court nearby, Devine Carama was talking with a group of young people. Carama is the director of ONE Lexington, a city-funded program that tries to prevent gun violence by mentoring at-risk boys. He, too, threw himself down when he heard gunfire. “I almost got shot that day,” he told me. Two people near him were hit—a man and his girlfriend. Carama and others tried to bandage the man’s leg; he told me he could see a glimmer of bullet or bone through the blood.
A day later, 18-year-old Jametrius Griffin turned himself in and was charged with murder. According to court testimony, Griffin’s younger brother had gotten into an argument; punches were thrown, and the younger brother fell or was pushed. When Griffin saw that, he yanked out a gun and started firing.
For the past three years, Robertson had participated in ONE Lexington’s summer youth program, which offers workshops on building emotional and social skills, as well as college-campus visits. “He wasn’t a street kid,” Carama said. Griffin’s younger brother was in ONE Lexington, too—in its school mentoring program. The organization had also helped Griffin get a job at UPS. The group’s work seemed to be making a difference. And then a fight left one young man dead, one wounded, and one in prison.
In many ways, Lexington feels like a small town, where everyone knows everyone. I went to middle school with Griffin’s lawyer, Daniel Whitley, who has a big reputation locally for representing people accused of murder—and for winning their cases. The week after the shooting, I spoke with Whitley and with Griffin’s mother, Jay-Me Baxter, on a video call.
“A bunch of bullshit” was how Baxter described the park shooting, “because everybody’s friends and everybody’s family.” She said her youngest son told her he had been bullied by Di’Zhon Robertson and others. The day after the shooting, she made the same argument in a video she posted on Facebook that outraged many in the community. She suggested that her older son had had no choice and said she didn’t care “who makes it home as long as mine do.” (I tried to reach Robertson’s mother through family members to see if she would talk with me about what happened to her son; her sister replied that the family didn’t want to relive it. But friends and family members described the teenager as quiet, observant, and “very respectful.”)
“I’m like, Shit, I know Di’Zhon’s mama,’” Baxter told me—the other mother was close friends with her own sister. Baxter said she had had a conversation with her about the beef between the boys, and assumed the issue had been settled. Griffin loved football, and he had started college at Kentucky State University. “But you know them kids,” she said. “They be doing stuff in silence.” Her son must have been simmering with fury.
I knew Baxter’s family growing up—she’s a year older than me, and they, too, lived in the Charlotte Court housing projects. She didn’t remember me, but she knew my brother. Her mother was white, and had nine children. Baxter, the third-oldest, is half Black, like her younger siblings. But the oldest two are white. Her mother used to cry, Baxter told me, because “the white kids didn’t ever live with us.” In our majority-Black neighborhood, a white mother with mixed-race kids stood out. Baxter remembers people throwing rocks through their windows and a lot of name-calling—“white bitch.” Her family was poorer than many others, but people in the neighborhood assumed that she was privileged, and tormented her for it. “That white mama, man,” she said. “You know what I’m saying?”
That kind of bullying is part of the pain of being impoverished. You feel so low, you desperately want to make someone else feel lower.
Baxter is a single mother, and Griffin is the oldest of her five children. Like my own mother, she lost custody of her kids because of drugs—she signed over her parental rights to her mom. She told me the story as if she was discussing a character in a book: “Jay-Me got in trouble. Jay-Me started using drugs, cocaine specifically.” Like my mother, Baxter was a victim of sexual abuse. She grew up watching her mother “get beat by men. I done been touched by men, and I never told my mama until a couple months before she died.”
It took Baxter seven years to stop using drugs and get her kids back. Those kids needed her, yet she kept choosing drugs over them, she said, as her voice cracked and tears hit her cheeks. “That hurts, because I can’t believe I did that.” I’ve heard those same words from my own mother and watched her cry for the same reason.
Before Baxter signed over her rights, she said, she asked her mother to promise that what she’d experienced as a little girl wouldn’t happen to her kids. She wanted to break the cycle of violence, poverty, and dysfunction that is the inheritance of so many children. “I’m not a gun mama,” Baxter told me, but she believes in “stepping in the street” to fight. “I’ve been fighting all my life,” she said.
Backgrounds like these are so common in Whitley’s line of work that he seemed to tune out our conversation. At one point on the video call, we heard the sound of snoring. Baxter joked about it: “Listen to him. My lawyer tiiiiiired.” We continued talking for a few more minutes and never heard from him again. “Night night, Daniel,” she said before we hung up. He called me back later, apologized for not saying goodbye, and said he hadn’t been asleep.
Despite the pity I felt for Baxter and her family, I felt more for those shot by her son, and their families.
Di’Zhon Robertson’s uncle Tyrone Johnson officiated his funeral, and told me that the church was full of people “struggling with their emotions.” I was told by attendees that the teenager’s grieving mother had to be pulled off the coffin. Damon Williams Jr., a 14-year-old wounded in the shooting, was hit in the thigh. He had been planning on joining his middle school’s football team this season. Lakeisha Martin was shot in the stomach and the sternum. East End Day, her older brother Isaiah Barron told me, “is a day for our community that we look forward to every year.” Martin was in the hospital for 21 days and will be unable to work for months.
The day of the shooting, Jenee Gragston rushed to the hospital as her nephew went into surgery. She told me the police said she should leave her tent, and could return later to retrieve everything. But when her husband went back to the park, almost everything was gone. The cooler with the meat. The grill, the propane tank, even her prescription eyeglasses. Other tents had been robbed as well. Gragston told me that she was grateful her nephew was okay, but that she would never go to one of the park festivals again.
Lexington is trying hard to reduce this kind of gun violence. Mayor Linda Gorton told me the city has handed out free gun locks and offered to buy back guns from residents, among other interventions. Through ONE Lexington, it offers groceries, hotel stays, and educational funds to people affected by gun violence. The city relocated a family whose house had been shot up, Gorton said. Still, she conceded, “there are times when we cannot control every human being’s behavior.”
It doesn’t help that Kentucky has such lax gun laws. Just this year, state legislators dropped the age required to carry a concealed firearm from 21 to 18. When I was growing up in Lexington, gun violence was even worse. Whenever you have a community of young men who feel powerless and disrespected, who have been raised to protect themselves and their families from perceived threats, and who believe words can’t save them but a gun might, then death will follow. The story of what happened in Lexington this summer is particularly tragic because so many had worked so long and so carefully to make a difference. But a gun changes everything in a moment.
Carama, of ONE Lexington, told me he has more friends who are dead than alive. He, too, said that “a lot of it is out of our control,” and that there’s only so much someone from outside a young person’s family can do. You can monitor a kid all you like, but if he has a gun, “you got a split second to react.” Ultimately, he said, “you can’t prevent everything. It’s just not possible.”
In Jay-Me Baxter’s account, she tried, in her way, to intervene. “The mamas grew up together,” she told me. “This could’ve been prevented.” But it wasn’t.

Indian nationals travelling to Malaysia have been warned against using the country's 30-day visa-free entry facility to look for employment. The High Commission of India in Kuala Lumpur said it had observed a “noticeable increase” in Indian nationals entering Malaysia through the visa-free route to seek jobs. In an advisory posted on X on Tuesday, the mission said some travellers were being misled by “unscrupulous agents” making false employment promises. The warning comes as Malaysia continues to allow Indian passport holders visa-free entry for up to 30 days. Malaysia's official immigration information says the exemption remains in place until December 31, 2026. The High Commission said the 30-day facility is intended for tourism and social visits and does not permit employment. Indian nationals travelling to Malaysia for work must instead have the required employment documentation, including a valid work permit or Visa With Reference (VDR). The Malaysian Immigration Department also states that a Visa With Reference is used for purposes including work, subject to the required approval. The Indian mission warned that people attempting to use the tourist facility to find employment could face overstaying, illegal status, exploitation, detention and legal action. The High Commission separately advises Indian workers planning legal employment in Malaysia to travel with a valid Malaysian visa and employment-related documents. The mission has also advised genuine tourists to carry documents that can be verified by Malaysian immigration authorities. These include a confirmed return ticket, hotel booking and a passport valid for at least six months. Indian passport holders must also submit the Malaysia Digital Arrival Card (MDAC) online three days before arrival. Malaysia's official guidance lists the same requirements for Indian travellers entering under the visa waiver. The High Commission's advisory follows previous instances in which Indian travellers faced entry-related issues in Malaysia over suspected job-seeking, inadequate accommodation proof, insufficient funds or missing return tickets. The mission's latest warning specifically highlights the risks of relying on agents promising employment and travelling under a facility that does not authorise work. For Indians travelling to Malaysia for employment, the High Commission's existing guidance recommends having the appropriate visa, employment contract and employer details before departure. Trump planning sanctions against International Criminal Court over Netanyahu arrest warrant: report
Punitive sanctions on the court are expected to cripple its ability to carry out its work prosecuting war crimes
Donald Trump is reportedly preparing sanctions against the International Criminal Court after the global tribunal issued an arrest warrant for Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Sweeping sanctions could prohibit the court from carrying out transactions in dollars, cutting it off from the global financial system and drastically undermining its work, according to the Wall Street Journal.
The Trump administration has made no secret of its disdain for the court, which prosecutes war crimes and genocide worldwide. U.S. officials want the court to drop its arrest warrants against Israeli leaders as well as a past probe into American troops in Afghanistan.
American officials told the WSJ the move could be finalised as soon as this week, during or just after the United Nations General Assembly in New York, which Netanyahu is expected to attend.
The ICC issued arrest warrants for the Israeli premier in 2024 over alleged war crimes. President Trump has said Netanyahu will not be arrested if he visits the United States, which is not a member of the ICC.
Sanctions against the court have already been drawn up, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters, although the exact timing of an announcement remained unclear.
According to Israeli media, Netanyahu is still expected to fly in for the UN General Assembly later this week, but has cut his visit short and plans to leave immediately after delivering a speech.
The prime minister will fly to New York on the day of his address on Thursday, missing a planned diplomatic visit to Texas, according to i24News. It was unclear whether he would still meet with Secretary of state Marco Rubio, the outlet reported.
Rubio in July announced a campaign to isolate the court, calling on other countries to withdraw from the tribunal. Washington has imposed sanctions on some ICC judges and prosecutors already but has held off from sanctioning the court itself.
Last year, Trump accused the court of “illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel.”
An executive order issued at the time put visa and financial sanctions on people working on ICC probes of US citizens or allies.
Any entity-wide sanctions imposed by the U.S. Treasury would prohibit U.S. citizens and companies from providing funds, goods, or services to the court without a license from the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). Banks often over-comply with such U.S. sanctions because they depend on access to the American financial system.
Among the court’s operations that could be affected by sanctions against the entire organization are the purchasing of IT services and insurance, the hiring of investigators and conducting everyday financial transactions, such as paying dozens of American employees, the ICC's registrar and president have warned.
Trump's opposition to the court goes back to his first term. It surfaced again with a plan to penalize ICC officials, an idea developed in November 2024 when Trump was reelected and the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza conflict.
The ICC was established in 2002 by the international community to prosecute war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. It asserts jurisdiction only if a member state is unable or unwilling to prosecute atrocities itself. The United States has never been a member.

Ready-to-heat meals are convenient, quick, and easy to prepare. Never frozen. Proteins in particular are surprisingly well textured. Can be prepped in an air fryer to good effect. Free consult with a dietitian.
TIRED
Meals are still too reliant on microwaves. Reheated meals have inherent limitations, especially with texture. Many meals lean on fat and sodium for flavor.
Like many children of the West Coast, I am a sucker for teriyaki salmon—a Japanese classic that slid easily into the menu of funny little bento shacks owned by former surfers named Dan or Dave.
And so maybe I was a prime target for a teriyaki salmon and “forbidden rice” meal from Factor, HelloFresh’s ready-to-heat meal delivery service. Factor preps and cooks its meals freshly in a commissary kitchen and then, through the magic of modified atmosphere packaging, Factor ships this meal in the mail without the indignity of freezing. All I have to do after that is heat it up.
What surprised me is how good the salmon tasted, even after being reheated. After air-frying my meal with the sauce drizzled on top, the salmon remained flaky and mild, without rubber or mush. The rice was al dente, lightly crisped. I’ve tested nearly every meal delivery service in existence, and one of the most interesting developments in food tech over the past decade has been the rise of the fully prepared, ready-to-heat meal that’s actually palatable.
With Factor, HelloFresh’s ready-to-heat meal delivery service, I’ve witnessed this process in real time. Over the six years since the meal kit giant acquired Chicago-founded Factor (previously Factor 75), Factor’s meals have evolved from their roots as essentially protein pills in TV dinner form to something much more sophisticated. It’s also expanded to include flatbread pizzas and frankly delicious smoothies and juice blends.
Not every meal tasted as good as that salmon, of course. And at around $13–17 a serving for dinner, Factor is more expensive than scratch cooking but less expensive than delivery. The cost is comparable, perhaps, to the ready-to-heat meal boxes you might find in your local supermarket deli section, except delivered to your door. Factor also tends to offer steep discounts for the first week or month.
After testing four different deliveries of Factor meals over the past two years, here’s my experience.
Factor by the Numbers
Specs
Cost per meal
$13—17 per serving (usually closer to $14), plus $10+ shipping
Meal plan options
Choose anywhere from four to 24 meals a week
Lowest-cost plan at full price
$70 for four meals, not including shipping
Size of weekly menu
100+ meal options, plus juices, smoothies, protein shakes, breakfasts, and desserts
Gluten-free meals?
Most meals made without gluten, but not in a certified gluten-free facility
Plant-based meals?
About a dozen vegetarian or vegan meal options
Other dietary plans or restrictions
Meal filters include high protein, low calorie, low carb, low sodium, and keto
Prep time
A few minutes in the microwave (or less than 10 minutes in an air fryer)
How Factor Works and Who It’s For
Like all prepared meal delivery services, Factor is a lot like ordering a week’s worth of meals from a restaurant—in this case, one of HelloFresh’s regional kitchens. Factor’s website will ask you a few questions about your preferences, ranging from allergens to whether you’re looking to up your protein levels or lose weight.
Then you’ll be asked to choose the number of meals you want to order a week—and the day you want them delivered. In general, the more meals you order per week, the less they cost. Most fall in a modest 600-calorie range. The following week, a box arrives at your door with your chosen selection of meals, plus some ice packs.
Factor’s selling point over other ready-to-heat meal kits has always been twofold. One is that its meals are friendly to keto and other versions of high-protein and carb-conscious diets, which goes back to the company’s founding 15 years ago by a fitness-obsessed MMA fighter. The other is that its microwaveable meals have never been frozen, leaving open the possibility for actual texture in one’s meal—a light crispness to the green beans, say, or the grill char and soft give of a medium-rare filet mignon.
Meals can include classic Midwestern meats and twos, but also barramundi filets topped with a “Niçoise” olive topping, Caribbean-spiced chicken thighs, and the occasional premium-priced filet mignon with truffle butter. More than half of meals contain 30 grams or more of protein, and more than half are no-gluten-added, usually with rice or potato sides. (Though take note that Factor is not prepared in a fully gluten-free facility.)
In the past couple years, Factor has also branched out to add more fresh ingredients and even baked goods. There are calzones now. Flatbread pizzas. Mixable salads and warmable soups, each available as a dinner option. But there’s also a world of market add-ons, including smoothies, protein shakes, and downright terrific juice blends.
How Does Factor Taste?
Over the past two years, I’ve tried about three dozen Factor meals, ranging from breakfast pancakes to meals involving steaks, shrimp, and pork chops. The results, after reheating in an oven, air fryer, or microwave, are not quite the same as a fresh-cooked meal, including meal kits you prepare yourself using HelloFresh’s other services. Any meal that looks like it might be mushy probably is. But proteins in particular fare quite well, whether shrimp or fish or pork chops.
Heated, frozen, then reheated chicken breast tends to have the character of wet chalk. But a never-frozen chicken breast from Factor had the texture of … wait for it … chicken breast. Shrimp is plump. And the tenderness, juiciness, and blessed pinkness of a truffled medium-rare filet mignon slab from Factor was nothing short of startling after I steamed it in the microwave, according to Factor’s instructions.
But the results are even better when I ignore Factor’s instructions and cook for eight minutes at 340 degrees Fahrenheit in an air fryer, specifically the Ninja Crispi (7/10, WIRED Recommends) that allows me to put wet ingredients below the crisper plate, and proteins or potatoes atop the crisper. This leads to light browning on a pork chop, but especially much better crispness on green beans or carrots or potato sides. When left to my own devices, this is kinda the only way I want to heat a prepared meal, and I will continue to lobby for Factor to add air fryer instructions.
But while Factor fares better than most prepared meals I’ve tested, it hasn’t solved every issue inherent in ready-made delivery meals. Some of the gluten-free dishes, and anything that looks like a hash or ragu, can struggle with texture. For every crisp green bean or air-fryer-charred broccoli, there’s slightly gummy pasta or limp zucchini. As a rule of thumb, it’s best to steer toward dishes with rice and potato as starches.
Meals can also lean a bit too hard on sodium, especially an otherwise nicely browned calzone filled with meatballs and mozzarella. But most meals still didn’t edge much over a third of the daily recommended sodium intake, and for those watching their diet, Factor does offer an unusual perk: a free 20-minute consult with a dietitian. I took advantage of this with HelloFresh’s sister plan, Green Chef, and got surprisingly helpful advice on fiber and protein needs.
Juice Worth the Squeeze
But for a moment, I’d like to talk about juice.
One of the most delicious things I’ve ever tasted was a sweetly coral-colored elixir poured from a chilled glass carafe at a Georgian bakery in Northeast Philadelphia. The drink was, according to my server, nothing special: a proprietary blend of juices made from fresh strawberries and other “delicious fruits.” I’ve been chasing that high ever since—but am usually sorely disappointed by the tepid, stale bottles that clog the fridge case at your average natural grocer.
I’ve often resorted to juicing fruits myself, which takes some effort and cleanup. But I was genuinely surprised to get some of that same fix from Factor, via the company’s add-on six-juice variety pack. Dang if a vibrant cucumber-apple-pineapple “gut greens” juice blend from Factor didn’t put supermarket juice blends to shame: a mix of tropical brightness, apple sweetness, savory spinach, and a prickle but not a stab wound of mint and ginger.
A Green Supreme smoothie fared equally well, and I also enjoyed an apple-kale-wheatgrass bottle to a shocking degree—again for its balance of savor, sweetness, and brightness. Some of the juice flavors leaned a little too hard into turmeric, and the option of 2-ounce ginger-turmeric-lemon wellness shots seemed a little silly. But in all, fresher-than-expected juice delivery is a boon, available for around $3 per 12-ounce bottle in the multi-packs—better than at many health food stores.
Tacked onto an eight-meal plan, those juices and smoothies can make Factor feel like a downright wholesome option for breakfast and a work lunch. If a microwave meal will always be graded on a curve, the trade-off is ease: a full meal with meat and sides that arrives premade at your door, awaiting a turn in the air fryer.

Mum's viral barefoot race sparks debate over India's education crisis
- Published
Despite having no training, or even a pair of running shoes, Ramabai Ranveer sprinted barefoot to victory in her first-ever race in August.
The 47-year-old widow had entered a 3km (1.86-mile) community run with a single goal: winning the prize money to help pay for her two daughters' education.
When she crossed the finish line first, Ramabai from Maharashtra in western India was delighted. The 3,000-rupee ($31; £23) prize would help her buy books and study materials for her daughters.
It was not much money. It would not come close to covering the cost of higher education in India, or even a course at the coaching centre where one of her daughters is preparing for a government recruitment examination.
But videos of her barefoot run spread rapidly on social media and in newspapers, striking a nerve as India's education system faces unusual scrutiny.
"Is it glory or a source of shame for us as a society?" one social media user remarked.
Soon, a woman who had never imagined becoming a runner was being held up as a symbol of something much bigger: the extraordinary lengths some Indian families go to in the hope that education will give their children a better life.
For Ramabai, the decision to run was simple.
"My elder daughter came to me early in the morning and said, 'Mummy, I want to take part in a running race'," she told BBC News Marathi from her home in Beed district.
"I asked her where it was and she said it was nearby. She told me that if she won the prize money, it would help with her education."
Her younger daughter, Arati, lives in Nanded and was struggling to afford books.
"I couldn't send her money to buy books and because of that she didn't speak to me on the phone for eight days," Ramabai said. "So I decided I had to run and win the race."
When her slippers kept slipping off, she removed them, gathered her sari and ran barefoot, pulling ahead to win the women's 30-60 category.
Her elder daughter, Pooja, also won a prize after finishing second in her age group. But she reserved her praise for her mother, describing her as courageous.
Ramabai has been the family's sole provider since her husband died in 2012.
"I did whatever work I could find," she said. "I picked soybeans and chickpeas in other people's fields. I also collected turmeric, processed it and sold it."
She left school when she was 13. Her daughters, she says, should have the opportunities she never had.
"I believe that as long as I am alive, I should do everything I can to give my daughters a good education."
That aspiration is shared by millions of Indian families. But getting a child through the education system and into a secure career can involve years of preparation, intense competition and, for many families, considerable expense.
One of Ramabai's daughters is preparing for police recruitment and the other for the civil services - two fiercely competitive routes into the security and social status associated with a coveted and secure government job.
Millions of young Indians spend years preparing for such examinations, often paying for coaching and study materials. But faith in the system has been shaken by repeated allegations of question-paper leaks and other irregularities.
The controversies have fed a wider sense of frustration among young Indians over education, jobs and the increasingly uncertain promise of a secure future. That frustration has also fuelled student-led protests and youth movements demanding changes to India's education system.
For families such as Ramabai's, education is something they make sacrifices for every day.
After her husband's death, she took whatever work she could find. She now cooks at the coaching centre where one of her daughters prepares for police recruitment.
Ramabai's run also drew the attention of authorities. Earlier this month, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant directed local officials to provide her with financial assistance of 50,000 rupees.
But Sukhadeo Thorat, a former chairman of the University Grants Commission, says the family's story points to broader structural challenges.
"If a woman is compelled to struggle so hard for her daughters' education, it shows that government education schemes are not reaching people adequately," he said. "Both the central and state governments run a variety of schemes. The problem is that implementation remains weak."
For Ramabai, though, the debate is secondary. What matters most is ensuring her daughters have a better future.
"I don't want them to go through the hardships I have faced," she said. "I don't want them to struggle through mud or travel under the scorching sun and rain. Whatever I have suffered, I don't want my daughters to suffer the same."

Merz vows to keep coalition together for Germany's 'democratic future'
- Published
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz says he will keep his ruling coalition together for the sake of his country's "democratic future", following resounding defeats for his party in two state elections.
"We are determined to live up to the historic challenges our country is facing," Merz said, referring to the coalition between his Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).
Merz's position has come under mounting pressure after Sunday's election results. In the north-eastern Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the most votes, with the CDU failing to reach the threshold to even enter the state parliament.
Meanwhile in Berlin, the CDU came second to the hard-left Die Linke party, with the AfD also making significant gains.
Speaking at the news conference on Monday, Merz described the result in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern as "a heavy blow".
"This election is a profound turning point. It is a dramatic, unprecedented result for the CDU in Germany," he said.
He however pushed back against the idea that his low popularity ratings were behind the election defeats.
"The reasons for these election results go far beyond my own person," he insisted.
Merz is under mounting pressure after months of poor approval ratings, and there have been rumours he could be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap.
Asked earlier on Monday how long Merz has left in office, the AfD's co-leader Alice Weidel told the BBC: "Pretty soon, he's going to leave."
The two local elections took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won a major victory.

Inter-state gang behind Sagar spurious liquor tragedy: MP Police
Fake liquor was manufactured at Chandu Raja’s house in Tatarwara and distributed it in neighbouring villages
An inter-state fake liquor gang sourced raw material from Delhi, then manufactured and sold adulterated alcohol that killed at least 20 people in Madhya Pradesh’s Sagar district earlier this month, police said, adding that one of the makers died after drinking the spurious product himself.
The probe revealed that Dinesh Shivhare, a resident of Morena, manufactured the spurious liquor – branded “Sagar Gold” -- and was later hospitalised after drinking it. He died from alcohol poisoning after gang members got him hurriedly discharged from the hospital, fearing discovery.
Police seized machines used to produce bottles, sealing equipment, 11,050 empty bottles, raw capsules for plastic bottles, and other materials during raids conducted across the state.
So far, police have named 52 people as suspects in the case, arresting 37. The primary suspects, Manish Lodhi and Siddharth Kushwaha are yet to be arrested.
“On September 6, police received reports of deaths in villages under Banda police station due to spurious liquor consumption. Separate cases were registered and the main accused Ravi Lakhera and Karni Sena leader Chandrabhan alias Chandu Raja were arrested,” Anurag Sujania, Sagar superintendent of police, said.
“In the interrogation, the accused revealed a wide network. Ravi Lakhera, who was released on bail in a fake liquor manufacturing case in Lalitpur just 15 days ago, confessed that he, along with Manish Lodhi alias Yashwant Thakur, and Ashish Sahu, planned to manufacture and supply fake liquor under the cover of licensed contracts,” Sujania said.

“Another accused, Chandu Raja alias Chandrabhan, admitted to partnerships with licensed contractors Siddharth Kushwaha and Manish Lodhi to facilitate illegal sales through licensed shops. Further investigation showed that Shivanjay Rajput and Rohit Patel connected Chandu Raja with Dinesh Shivhare of Morena, who brought raw materials including industrial spirit from Delhi and bottle wrappers from Gwalior,” said the SP.
Fake liquor was manufactured at Chandu Raja’s house in Tatarwara and distributed it in neighbouring villages.
“Chandu Raja gave consent to Dinesh Shivhare and his team to make fake liquor in village Tatarwara, so that more profit could be earned. The liquid used for making liquor had come to Sagar by transport. Chandu Raja sold the boxes of the liquor through his associates under the guise of licensed shop to the commission agents of nearby villages of Tatarwara village Nauraj, Gugra, Chhapri, Jagthar, Bamurabheda, Patan and surrounding villages,” Sujania said.
“After tasting this fake adulterated liquor, accused Dinesh Shivhare and associate Deva alias Devendra Jatav became serious,” said the officer.
Shivhare was admitted to a private hospital in Bhopal by the other suspects on September 5. Next day, his condition deteriorated excessively and accused realised the liquor had turned toxic. So (even) in serious condition, they got him discharged from the hospital and sent him to Morena. He died on the way. And Deva alias Devendra Jatav lost his eyesight.
A police team arrested a bottle supplier, Pankaj Rai, and, acting on his information, raided the factory operating in Rai Colony in Gwalior.
In investigations conducted by a separate police team, the owner of RN Chemical, Anup Giri, who sent chemicals from Delhi to Sagar, was taken into custody and on questioning, confessed that he had sent five plastic drums of industrial spirit/thinner from Delhi to Sagar by transport. Giri has been arrested.

Easy for anyone to use. Consistently perfect prints. Enclosed chamber for temperature control. New tool-free nozzle-swap feature. AMS add-on makes multicolor printing a breeze.
TIRED
Speed causes a lot of shaking—needs a very stable surface to sit on. Filament waste disposal makes a mess. Fumes from high-temperature filaments are still very intense.
Does the average consumer actually need a 3D printer? Isn’t it just for people who want to sell fidgets at the flea market, design obscure brackets in CAD, or print groups of Warhammer figurines?
Yes, they do, and no, it isn’t.
Photograph: Kat Merck
In my four weeks of testing the Bambu Lab P2S Combo, I have printed a sponge holder for my kitchen sink; caps and parts for my hydroponic gardens; various clips and hangers; a Mason jar lid organizer; a shovel; a couple of funny signs; plant pot coasters; a shoehorn; truck bed tie-downs; a pair of earrings; and, of course, a Benchy—every piece perfectly smooth and looking like it was purchased from a store. Owning a 3D printer is like having an Amazon fulfillment center right in your house.
While I'm no stranger to 3D printing—I owned the open-frame Bambu Lab A1 before I started testing 3D printers—I have never used a machine as easy to operate as the P2S. In fact, when we reviewed Bambu Lab’s P2S predecessor, the popular and bestselling P1S, earlier this year, tester Brad Bourque declared it the easiest-to-use 3D printer he’d ever tried, claiming its lack of complicated steps and futzing has changed the way he thinks about 3D printing.
The P2S builds on the already excellent P1S design with a new 5-inch color touchscreen, tool-free nozzle swapping, a beefed-up 1080p 30-frames-per-second camera with improved AI failure detection, and a redesigned airflow system. I wasn’t exactly in love with the latter, but one complaint for a system with thousands of failure points is more than enough to earn the P2S a solid A-grade.
Detail of identical pigeon figurine printed on white Bambu Lab PLA: A1 on left, P2S on right.
Photograph: Kat Merck
Photograph: Kat Merck
It Really Is That Easy
If you own another brand of mid- or lower-tier 3D printer, any Bambu Lab machine will already feel like an upgrade. Much like an iPhone, any Bambu Lab printer will work seamlessly right out of the box, with easy-to-use software and intuitive design elements. With a little assembly, you’re ready to go.
The large touchscreen allows you to perform many functions and troubleshooting right on the machine. These printers are easy for even the most clueless newbie to use and understand—so much so that some call the company “the Apple of 3D printing.” (Even better, the company’s free, flagship Bambu Studio software is open source.)
What makes both the P1S and P2S worth the upgrade from the A1 is the enclosed chamber that provides environmental control for acrylonitrile filaments like ASA and ABS, which require high temperatures to melt and are notoriously prone to warping. In the P2S, Bambu Lab incorporates a new airflow system that switches modes depending on the filament—it pulls in cooler air for more easily melted PLA, or retains air (and therefore heat) for ASA and ABS.
However, I did notice that when printing in ASA (note that the P2S comes with only a rough-textured build plate; I had to buy the smooth $30 engineering plate separately), the resulting fumes were overwhelming—I had to close the door, open the windows, and turn on an air purifier. There is a carbon filter in the back of the device, but during high-heat prints, the airflow is supposed to circulate inside the unit; instead, it seemed to leak out around the door and other cracks.
Video: Kat Merck
Fumes are emitted from all 3D printers, so this is not really a flaw on the company’s part, just an indication that the redesigned airflow system has room for improvement. Make sure you keep the printer in a room with a door that can close if you’re printing with any kind of impact-modified plastics. Bambu Lab’s helpful Wiki also offers a 3D-printable exhaust kit that can redirect fumes outside.
And speaking of locations, you will also want to ensure the 15 x 16 x 19-inch P2S is on a very firm surface—perhaps even on the ground. At 600 mm per second, the nozzle moves vigorously, which will shake whatever it’s on. I was using a low wooden table, but since I found myself using the printer near-daily, the shaking eventually loosened the table’s leg joints, resulting in multiple X-Y axis error messages on the machine. Research showed this to be a somewhat common issue, almost always resolved by finding a firmer surface.
I was not able to test the AI failure detection, as none of my 30-plus prints failed (aside from a couple of mismeasurements on my end), but I did have occasion to view through the 1080p camera—if you download the free Bambu Handy app, it will store a little time-lapse video of your object being printed, which is fascinating to watch.
In Living Color
The “Combo” in the name refers to the Automatic Material System (AMS) that sits on top of the printer. (You can also buy it separately at $299.) It holds four spools of filament that auto-feed to your project—a game changer if you’re printing something with multiple colors. Without it, a multicolor print would necessitate stopping the print, removing the spool of filament, and installing a new one on the side. For the P2S, the AMS also has the ability to dry the filament—this removes any absorbed ambient moisture that would create steam when heated and mess up your print.
The AMS add-on allows for seamless multicolor prints.
Photograph: Kat Merck
I tested the P2S on the West Coast in late summer, when the humidity was very low, so my filament stayed below 40 percent relative humidity, according to the built-in hygrometer—it didn’t need drying. However, if you live in a humid region, springing for the AMS will be a massive time-saver.
With the P1S, if you needed to swap out a different nozzle, it was something of an ordeal—you basically have to unplug everything and take apart the assembly with screws. On the P2S, the front of the nozzle head is magnetic and pops right off—simply unclip the old nozzle and clip in the new one. Another massive improvement if you find yourself swapping nozzles often.
The P1S’s automatic nozzle cleaning function that “poops” filament blobs out the back of the machine is still in effect on the P2S. I’d been warned, but I was still surprised to see the amount of detritus it left on the floor, especially during multi-color prints. I highly recommend that a “poop chute” or collection basket be one of your first prints. (And there are plenty of fun designs for using the waste filament blobs once they’ve accumulated, from creative games to a “poop Atlas” filament waste world map.)
Do You Really Need One?
Yes, unless you need a dual-nozzle printer or a commercial-grade unit that can also laser cut and engrave—features this printer doesn’t offer. The ability to print and customize useful household and garage objects, art projects, and toys easily and quickly—with minimal fuss—makes the P2S worth every penny. This is doubly so if you have some basic engineering skills, as importing files into Bambu Studio is a cinch.
Bambu Lab-brand filaments start at about $15 a roll with spool. Note that we flagged some app inconsistencies when using non-Bambu filaments with the P1S, but I did not have any non-Bambu filaments on hand to test in the P2S, so I can’t vouch for whether this issue has been fixed.
While the P2S may well be overkill if you only want to print the occasional fidget or figurine, if you regularly find yourself in need of some annoyingly specific organizer, replacement cap, or bracket, this machine could well pay for itself over time in both convenience and material costs.

A survivor from a prison cell in Nigeria where 37 suspected illegal goldminers died while in the custody of a paramilitary group this week has recounted his panic and struggle for breath, as police on Friday fired teargas at people protesting against the deaths.
Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) – a paramilitary group that works with police – initially blamed the deaths in Minna, the state capital of the mineral-rich state of Niger, on a disease outbreak.
However, an intelligence report seen by Agence France-Presse said preliminary information suggested that overcrowding and inadequate ventilation were responsible.
Dauda Shehu, a survivor from the cell, told journalists at a hospital on Friday: “We were jam-packed in the cell, no ventilation for us to breathe well. All of a sudden we realised that we could not breathe and we were all scampering for where to get fresh air, we even appealed to them several times, banged the cell door, but they refused to answer us.”
A video shared online showed the bodies of dozens of young men clad only in shorts, most of whom appeared to be teenagers, sprawled on the ground out in the open. Volunteers wearing gloves can be seen standing over the dead, while veiled women try to identify the bodies of their relatives. Voices shouting curses on those responsible can be heard in the background.
Protests over the deaths broke out on Thursday evening in Minna. On Friday dozens of young people, including miners and their relatives, gathered near the NSCDC’s office in the city. Police cordoned off the area and attempted to disperse the protesters by firing teargas.
A Reuters witness saw security forces fire live rounds as protesters – some armed with sticks, machetes and traditional hunting rifles – called for justice. Some protesters tried to set fire to government buildings in the Tunga neighbourhood. “We are not thieves – we are simply seeking a way to make a living by mining,” Yusuf Auwal, a miner who joined the protesters, told Reuters. At least one body lay on the streets. Soldiers and police officers patrolled Minna to try to restore order.
The NSCDC said the detainees had been held in raids on suspected illegal mines on 15 and 16 September in the Wushishi-Lukoto area west of Minna. Nigeria’s interior minister, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, ordered the immediate suspension of Niger state’s NSCDC commandant, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, pending the outcome of a full investigation.
Niger state, which is Nigeria’s largest and more than twice the size of Belgium, is rich in minerals and attracts thousands of artisanal miners, most lured by gold.
Police and the NSCDC did not initially provide a precise number of deaths but the state governor, Mohammed Umaru Bago, later confirmed 37 people had died.
“It’s so sad, it’s so tragic,” he said, adding an inquiry into the deaths had already started work. He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections due in January. The men were buried on Thursday, according to Islamic tradition, without any forensic investigations.
The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state is fuelling violence by criminal gangs, according to officials and experts. The gangs tax the miners and demand a cut from the extracted ore as a levy to allow them access to the pits.
Most of the illegally mined gold is smuggled to the United Arab Emirates, where it is laundered into the global supply chain in Europe, the US, Asia and South Africa, according to a 2024 Swissaid report.
Apart from gold, the state of Niger sits on deposits of other minerals including tantalite, copper and lithium, which are in strong demand for use in electric vehicles and clean energy technology.
Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

Quick Answer
OpenAI Codex can help beginners build Android apps with Expo and TypeScript using simple prompts. You can generate the app, preview it on your phone with Expo Go, fix errors, build an APK with EAS, and even add optional cloud sync using Supabase.
We recently shared a detailed guide on how to build Android apps using Google Antigravity. That approach is best for someone who wants an affordable way to build AI apps that work.
Current Google models in Antigravity offer way better rate limits than models from ChatGPT or Claude. However, Gemini isn’t the best for building advanced AI apps or if you want to include any other advanced features in your app.
For advanced apps, using Claude or ChatGPT Codex is the most reliable option. In this guide, you will learn how to build Android apps using Codex. OpenAI’s ChatGPT models in Codex are not free; you need a minimum ChatGPT Plus subscription to access top models. Also, the rate limits are very poor, which you can easily exhaust if you play with them for some time.
However, these models are way more powerful and currently among the leading frontier models. Also, thanks to the different connections, plugins, and MCP servers, the process of building Android apps using Codex is more convenient and takes fewer steps compared to Google Antigravity. In this guide, you will learn how to build Android apps using OpenAI Codex.
Table of Contents
Prerequisites
To build an Android app in Codex, you need:
- ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscription (which you can get from here)
- An Android app with Expo Go installed – Download the Expo Go app
- An Android phone
- A free account on supabase.com – Sign up here
- A free account on expo.dev
Once done, you can follow the process below to build Android apps using OpenAI Codex.
Set Up Codex
Step 1: First, download and install the ChatGPT app on your Mac or Windows. It is also available for Linux.
Step 2: Once installed, sign up with your ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscription account.
Step 3: Once done, switch to Codex.
Step 4: Now tap on New chat, and from here, tap on Choose Folder.
Step 5: Now, you can create a new folder or use the existing folder, which stores all your app files.
Create Your App
Step 1: Now, enter the following prompt. You can edit the prompt to include your own prompt. For this guide, I am building a simple Pomodoro app.
Build a simple Pomodoro timer app using Expo and TypeScript.
The app should let users start, pause, resume, reset, and skip Pomodoro sessions. Include focus, short break, and long break modes. Show the remaining time clearly, track completed focus sessions, and save the timer settings and session history locally using SQLite.
Create a clean, polished mobile UI that works well on Android. Do not create an Android build yet. First, implement the app, check for errors, and explain how I can preview it using Expo Go.
Step 2: Now, in the model selector, select GPT-5.6 Sol or GPT-6 Astra.
In this guide, we are building a simple Pomodoro timer application that keeps track of your focus and how much time you have been distracted.
The latest Codex GPT-6 Astra model is very good at frontend development. Even if you haven’t included reference images of the app UI, since it is a simple app, it can generate a very reliable UI based on the prompt.
However, if you want something unique that is personalized to yourself, I highly recommend submitting UI references. It will generate exactly what you are looking for, including the font options that you used while designing the app. You can use Google Stitch to generate UI.
Design the UI With Google Stitch (Optional)
You can use Google Stitch for designing the UI. It is very similar to Figma, but more AI-focused: it lets you generate UI through AI prompts and also lets you customize with basic tools.
We created a detailed course on how you can create UI designs using Google Stitch, with 12+ videos guiding you through all the core features of Google Stitch.
If you want to quickly create UI designs using Google Stitch, you can go to stitch.withgoogle.com and follow these steps:
Step 1: Paste your prompt (for whatever your app is) into the prompt area.
Step 2: Wait for Google Stitch to generate your UI designs.
Step 3: Tap on the prototype icon at the top to check the preview.
Step 4: Export and save it as a zip file.
Step 5: To upload the references to the Codex file in the entry box, after entering the prompt, you can click on the plus icon and select Files and folders. From here, you can attach the UI reference images (Remember you need to extract the folder).
You can attach up to 10 images, which is more than enough for a basic or even a medium-level app with all those screens.
Preview the App on Your Phone
Step 1: Wait for Codex to generate the full design in the Expo app, and then you can enter the prompt so that it can show you a preview of the app. You can install the Expo Go app on your Android phone. Open the app and scan the QR code generated by Codex after following these steps.
Step 2: Carefully review everything and ensure that everything works.
Step 3: Once finished, enter this prompt to preview the app on your mobile. If it asks you to run the terminal code, you can ask GPT to run the code for you.
GPT models are often known for lying: even though something isn’t finished, it confidently mentions that it has finished or fixed the issue. I highly recommend you verify each and every output.
Build the Android App
Once everything is ready, you can build the Android app. Since we are using Expo, the free version only allows you a limited number of builds, and afterward, you need to wait for a set time to build it into an Android app.

npx eas-cli@latest login
Step 3: Now sign in to your account using your username and password. This is a one-time process. Every time you want to build an Android app, you can just ask Codex to use this account to build it.

Add Cloud Sync With Supabase
You can follow a similar process if you want cloud sync. To access your app data on other devices, you need to upload it to the cloud. To do that, you can use a free Supabase database and connect your app to the Supabase backend so it can store your data. Supabase offers three projects for free.
Here is how to connect your app to Supabase. This is completely optional and only recommended if you want your app data to be cloud-synced and need to use the app on other devices. Otherwise, the current app you built uses local SQLite, which stays on your device unless you delete it.
For Supabase, you can directly install the Supabase extension or use an MCP server. To do that:
Step 1: Create a free account on Supabase.
Step 2: Create a new project.

Thousands of patients in India are diagnosed with melanoma, a type of skin cancer, each year. While melanoma is far less common here than in Western populations, it is far from rare and the way it presents in our patient population makes it uniquely difficult to detect early. Too many patients come to us when the disease is already advanced, precisely at a time when treatment options have never been more powerful or more personalised. This contrast between available therapies and the stage at which patients are diagnosed defines one of the most pressing challenges in melanoma care in India today.
Why melanoma gets missed
The warning signs most people associate with skin cancer come from research developed for fairer-skinned populations, where melanoma tends to appear on sun-exposed areas as an irregular or darkening mole. That picture does not reflect what clinicians see in India.
Melanoma here, most commonly presents on the soles of the feet or beneath the nails, sites that are rarely examined and even more rarely associated with cancer. This condition is called acral lentiginous melanoma, a subtype that accounts for 35 to 60% of cases in dark-skinned individuals. Such lesions are frequently mistaken for bruises, fungal infections, or diabetic ulcers, and by the time a biopsy is taken, the disease has often progressed.
Mucosal melanomas, a rare type of cancer that starts in the mucous membranes, are highly aggressive with a very low chance of recovery and produce few early warning signs. Most are diagnosed only after spread has occurred.
Any pigmented lesion that changes or persists, wherever it appears on the body, deserves investigation rather than reassurance.
A decade of transformation
When I began my oncology career, managing advanced melanoma meant offering patients limited and rarely durable options. That has fortunately changed significantly.
The foundational shift came from James Allison and Tasuku Honjo, whose discoveries on CTLA-4 and PD-1 earned them the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Their research established the principle of immune-checkpoint blockade: rather than attacking a tumour directly, we can sometimes release the biological brakes that stop the patient’s own immune system from doing so. The results can be extraordinary. Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter was diagnosed at 91 with melanoma that had spread to his liver and brain. Surgical resection of liver disease, stereotactic radiation for the brain, and immunotherapy with the checkpoint inhibitor pembrolizumab produced a durable remission, and he lived to 100.
Precision medicine has reshaped the approach in parallel. Some melanomas carry specific mutations, particularly in the BRAF pathway, that can be directly targeted with molecularly designed therapies. This is where next-generation sequencing, or NGS, becomes critical. In simple terms, it reads the genetic blueprint of a patient’s tumour and identifies the alterations that should guide treatment, turning what was once a single clinical decision into a detailed, individualised process.
The melanoma story is not over; it is only becoming more exciting. TIL therapy takes tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes, expands them in the laboratory, and reinfuses them in far greater numbers, a step toward truly personalised cellular treatment. In August 2026, intismeran, a personalised mRNA vaccine built from the patient’s own tumour sequence, was combined with pembrolizumab in high-risk melanoma patients after surgery. The results were striking: a significant reduction in recurrence compared with pembrolizumab alone, making it the first positive late-stage trial of a personalised mRNA cancer vaccine, though survival data remain pending.
What still needs to change
All of these advances deliver their best results when treatment begins early. The more sophisticated our therapies become, the more clearly we see that they work best before the disease has spread. In India, awareness and referral gaps continue to push diagnosis toward advanced stages.
Recalibrating public health messaging to reflect how melanoma actually presents in Indian patients is a start. Faster pathways from primary care to specialist centres matter equally. More fundamentally, India needs a national melanoma registry, stronger epidemiological and genomic data, more clinical trials in Indian patients, and deeper international collaboration. The advances of the past decade are genuinely extraordinary. Whether they reach the patients who need them comes down to one thing: a diagnosis early enough to act on.
(Prof. Jyoti Bajpai is director – medical precision immuno-oncology, Apollo Hospitals, Mumbai & Western Zone. drjyoti_ba@apollohospitals.com)

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.
Link: WHO appreciates the signing of these milestone agreements

Hallgrimsson accused of 'ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity'
- Published
The Israel FA has accused Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity" in comments made last week.
During his squad announcement for the upcoming Nations League games which include two fixtures against Israel on 27 September and 4 October, Hallgrimsson said: "We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide. We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel," when the subject of keeping his players focused on the games was raised.
On Monday, Israel's football body hit back on those comments on social media, saying: "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way.
"Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."
The Football Association of Ireland has not responded to the Israel FA's comments, with a protest also taking place at the Republic of Ireland team's hotel on Monday evening as pressure to boycott the fixtures continues to build.
The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians.
Israel has regularly denied committing genocide or war crimes and has said its actions in Gaza have been justified as a means of self-defence.
Irish sportspeople urge boycott of Israel games
More than 160 Irish sportspeople have signed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine Group to urge a boycott of the games against Israel.
The Republic of Ireland are due to play Israel on 27 September in Hungary before the reverse fixture in Serbia on 4 October.
The letter states that the FAI, Uefa and the Irish government should have intervened before this stage, but there is still time to "show the power of sport to unite".
Sportspeople such as Olympian Ciara Mageean, former Republic of Ireland footballer Louise Quinn, ex-Ireland rugby fly-half Tony Ward - who boycotted an Irish rugby tour of South Africa - and boxers Tyrone McKenna and Eric Donovan have signed the letter.
Also included in the 160 plus names are GAA's Padraig O'Hora, Joe Brolly, Colm O'Rourke, Michael Darragh Macauley, Philly McMahon, Valerie Mulcahy and Rena Buckley, as well as para-athlete Alan Dineen and ultimate frisbee's Stephen Jones, who both boycotted fixtures against Israel earlier this year.
"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter states.
"Putting on the Irish jersey and representing your country means something. But the Ireland we want represented is the one that remembers its roots in anti-colonial and anti-imperial resistance, which Irish sport played a large part of.
"This moment symbolises something deeper, it is bigger than sport. But in a way this IS sport.
"Not playing the game would be the most sporting thing you could do. Through your leadership and courage, it would show the power of sport to unite, remind us of the shared values that connect us all, and have an impact far beyond the game."
- Uefa rejected request to keep Republic of Ireland and Israel separate - FAI 
  - Published3 days ago
- Republic of Ireland braced for testing Nations League 
  - Published16 hours ago
- Hallgrimsson spoke to players individually about Israel games 
  - Published4 days ago
In July, the FAI's General Assembly endorsed a motion for the Republic of Ireland to go ahead with their upcoming Nations League fixtures against Israel with 75 votes to 32 against and three abstentions from the 114 delegates.
The FAI had previously said boycotting the games would cause "significant and lasting harm" to Irish football as well as leading to a potential loss of 10.3m euros (£9m).
The fixture has caused much controversy with Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson adding that he spoke to players in his squad individually about the prospect of facing Israel, and "none of us feel comfortable playing in these games".
The Nations League games mark the Republic of Ireland's first competitive action since their World Cup play-off semi-final heartbreak against the Czech Republic in March.
Since the penalty shootout loss in Prague, they have played four friendlies, beating Grenada and Qatar and drawing with North Macedonia and Canada.

A former police officer claims he killed two men in self-defence and began cleaning up the crime scene because he was “understandably panicked”, a Sydney court has heard.
Beau Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of fatally shooting 26-year-old Jesse Baird and his partner, Luke Davies, 29, with a police service weapon at Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
The prosecution has argued the former police officer developed an “infatuation” with Baird which manifested in “compulsive” behaviour and escalated after Baird ended their brief relationship in 2023. It’s alleged Lamarre-Condon began planning to murder him in early 2024.
Kourtnee Baird said her brother had confided in her regarding Lamarre-Condon the last time she saw him alive.
“Jesse said that he was fearful he was a NSW police officer,” she told the court on Tuesday.
“He had access to a weapon, a gun, and [Jesse] said he would go on his phone and block contacts from Jesse’s male friends.”
When her brother was on his way home from the gym, he would receive messages from Lamarre-Condon that said, “you looked really good at the gym tonight”, Kourtnee Baird told the court.
Sometimes when her brother went for coffee or a meal, Lamarre-Condon would send him messages saying he looked nice in what he was wearing.
Asked if her brother felt he was being followed, Kourtnee Baird replied: “Very much so.”
Jesse was “very erratic, very shocked and just would explain how crazy some of the things [Lamarre-Condon] was doing were,” his sister said.
Lamarre-Condon’s lawyer, John Stratton SC, told the jury on Tuesday that the policeman had been acting in “self-defence” when he shot Baird.
The morning the couple were killed, Lamarre-Condon entered Baird’s home wearing a motorcycle helmet and disguised as an UberEats driver.
This way, he would not be recognised while picking up his belongings, Stratton said.
He had a key he was given by Baird and had a gun on him because, according to his “training”, he was not allowed to leave a weapon in a car where it might be stolen, the jury was told.
Because Baird did not recognise Lamarre-Condon, a struggle ensued during which the 26-year-old was killed, the defence barrister said.
The officer’s gun was flung across the room and Davies picked it up, Stratton told the court. Lamarre-Condon then grabbed Davies by the arm and pushed the gun towards him.
In the struggle that followed, Davies pulled the trigger and shot himself, the court was told.
“What he did was self-defence,” Stratton said.
After the shootings, Lamarre-Condon immediately began to clean up the crime scene.
This was because he was “understandably panicked”, the defence lawyer said.
“He was a police officer and he knew this looked bad,” Stratton told the court.
“These were the actions of a man who panicked considerably, who knew the gravity of the situation he was in, knew how it would be perceived and was overawed by it.”
Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC alleged Lamarre-Condon entered Baird’s house with a stolen key before shooting him twice and shooting Davies through a bedroom door.
Audio of the three shots was played to the courtroom: the first two coming in quick succession before the third, 51 seconds later. Baird and Davies’ loved ones wiped away tears as they listened in court.
Lamarre-Condon later told a friend he had killed two people, the prosecution said.
According to Hatfield, when the friend asked if he was joking, Lamarre-Condon responded: “I wish I was, I don’t feel like it was me … I feel like I need some help, this job has fucked me up.”
Asked how he did it, Lamarre-Condon allegedly said “with a gun”, made a hand gesture and said “pew pew”.
The police officer later bought a second surfboard bag – days after he had bought the first, the jury was told.
He returned to Baird’s home that afternoon before one of Baird’s housemates came home.
“She did notice the two surfboard bags which, at this stage, were in the back courtyard,” Hatfield told the court.
“She will tell you what she thought was rust [was] seeping out from the bags,” Hatfield told the court.
“She took a photo and sent it to her housemate but didn’t realise at the time that the bags contained two bodies.”
A photo of outdoor furniture with a pool of blood was shown to the court on Tuesday.
On the night of the alleged murders, Lamarre-Condon moved the bodies from the Paddington terrace to a hired van, the crown said.
A day later, posing as Baird and using the dead man’s phone, Lamarre-Condon texted his Paddington housemates’ group chat claiming Baird was going on a road trip to Perth, the jury was told.
Lamarre-Condon then messaged one of his own friends, who was living in Perth, and told her he was going to send her a phone by express post.
He said he needed her to turn it on in Western Australia before throwing it into the ocean, the court heard.
Lamarre-Condon subsequently made an unsuccessful attempt to sink the two bodies in a dam near Goulburn, before moving them to a fence line near a monastery in Bungonia, the prosecutor told the court. They were found eight days later.
Jesse’s mother, Helen Baird, told the court about the first time she had met her son’s partner, Luke, a month before they were killed.
“It was early days but they were both smitten with each other,” she said on Tuesday.
A few weeks later, her son sent a photo of himself with Davies at a Pink concert. Her voice broke as she said “underneath [the photo] it said ‘Luke’s my boyfriend’”.
“I sent a big love heart and said ‘I’m so happy for you’,” Helen Baird told the jury.
The trial before justice Natalie Adams continues.

- In September 2026, a claim circulated online that big box retailer Walmart once created special lapel pins for its employees to commemorate the 9/11 attacks.
- The rumor stems from posts on social media that include alleged photos of the pin, which features a frowning version of Walmart's Smiley mascot with a teardrop on its yellow face, along with a banner that reads, "September 11, 2001."
