In September 2026, a claim circulated online that big box retailer Walmart once created special lapel pins for its employees to commemorate the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. The claim gained steam online as people discussed the 25th anniversary of 9/11. 
Social media posts and Reddit threads include alleged photos of the pin, which features a frowning version of Walmart's "Smiley" mascot with a teardrop on its yellow face, along with a banner that reads, "September 11, 2001." One Facebook user wrote:
After 9/11, Walmart reportedly gave employees commemorative pins featuring its famous yellow smiley face transformed into a frown with a single tear. Surviving examples have become unusual pieces of early 2000s memorabilia, though documentation about exactly when and how Walmart distributed them is limited.
Walmart does have a history of issuing collectible pins to its employees. Examples of purported Walmart 9/11 commemorative pins have been put up for sale 
Snopes contacted the retailer to ask if the company created it. We also reached out to an eBay seller specializing in Walmart pins, including the 9/11 design in question, to ask for more details about it and where it was acquired. We will update this article if we receive a response.
Snopes found the pin listed for sale by eBay seller UpNorth Mercantile. One listing that was deactivated on Aug. 31, 2026, showed the pin retailing for $14.99. It appeared there had been a quantity of 30 available that either sold out or were unlisted by the seller.
The same seller showed two live auctions for the pin with bids of more than $100 each, as of this writing. UpNorth Mercantile's eBay store showed dozens of collectible Walmart pins for sale, including the alleged 9/11 pin and other variations of Walmart's smiley face logo.
Smiley was first introduced in 1990, according to Walmart's own timeline. It became the mascot for the brand's signature "Rollback" price-cut promotions in 1996, then was sidelined in 2006 due to a trademark war. In 2016, Walmart's then-chief marketing officer Tony Rogers proclaimed the return of Smiley.
He said, "We first introduced Smiley in 1990 and, since then, he has been a widely recognized symbol for low prices. In fact, nearly 70% of our customers still associate Smiley with savings at Walmart even though he's been behind the scenes for the past decade."
Walmart lightly documents its employee lapel pin culture on the corporate website, which says:
Lapel pins may be small, but they hold big meaning! We use them to celebrate and commemorate. They show off our goals and our wins. They honor hometowns and heroes. Pins are our love language, our very own cultural currency.
The website describes an annual event called Associates Week, scheduled around the time of the company's shareholders conference, as a "pin lover's paradise." According to Walmart, Associates Week brings together employees from across the globe, during which "pin trading becomes a common language."
One of the Reddit threads featuring the 9/11 pin appeared in the r/WalmartEmployees subreddit, where current and former workers discuss working for the company.
A search within the subreddit for conversations about employee pins yielded a wide variety of results, showing the prevalence of pin culture at the corporation. Users posted images of the 9/11 pin by itself or of one attached to a jacket.
(Pangram)
Snopes ran images of the pin through Pangram, an artificial intelligence detection service, including those taken from the various social media posts and eBay listings.
All versions came back with results that declared no generative AI was used to create the images. It's important to note that such tools are not always reliable. None of the pictures we checked showed any signs of being AI-generated.
In sum, it appears that photos of the lapel pin in question are authentic and specimens of the pin itself are available for purchase on eBay as of this writing, but it was not possible to verify that it was an official offering from Walmart's own line of employee pins, as online posts claimed.

Amid a bull run for Lenskart, early investor Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA) today offloaded 3.5 Cr shares of the company via its holding entity Platinum Jasmine A 2018 Trust. The investor raked in ₹2,390.6 Cr via the bulk deal, valuing each share at ₹683.02. This is slightly higher than the stock’s closing price for the day. This is the second time when ADIA has offloaded its stake in the eyewear giant in recent months. Earlier, in June, ADIA pared 4 Cr shares in a block deal worth ₹1,960 Cr. The company’s shares have rallied significantly since then. For comparison, the June block deal valued a share at ₹490, about 40% lower than today’s closing price. At the end of the June quarter, ADIA’s Platinum Jasmine A 2018 Trust held 16.98 Cr shares or 9.77% stake in the company. Hence, the shares offloaded today represent slightly over 20% of the shares held by ADIA, or just around 2% of the company’s total equity. Lenskart’s shares have rallied 51.3% on a year-to-date basis, providing its early investors a fertile ground to register gains. Investors like SoftBank, Temasek and Alpha Wave have offloaded stake in droves in the company over the past few months. Most recently, BNP Paribas, Societe Generale and US-based hedge fund Millennium Management offloaded shares worth ₹2,670.2 Cr via multiple bulk deals on September 1. Lenskart touched an all-time high of ₹725 on September 18 (Friday). The shares made their public market debut at ₹390 apiece on the BSE in November 2025. The bull run comes amid multiple positive brokerage notes after the eyewear major’s strong Q1 FY27 performance. Jefferies raised its target price to ₹680 from ₹600, while Macquarie increased its target to ₹675 from ₹625. The bullish outlook followed a 273% YoY jump in Lenskart’s consolidated net profit to ₹228.4 Cr in Q1 FY27, from ₹61.2 Cr a year earlier. Its operating revenue also grew 43% YoY and 8% QoQ to ₹2,714.2 Cr. However, shares of Lenskart closed today’s trading session 3.3% lower at ₹683.85 on the NSE.

Games-South Korea team condemn Asian Games organisers over logistical 'shortcomings'
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept 22 : South Korea's Chef de Mission Lee Sang-hyun criticized Asian Games organisers on Tuesday for logistical failures that had inconvenienced athletes and said concrete measures must be taken to ensure the problems are not repeated.
Lee told Reuters his delegation had requested a meeting with senior Games officials and wanted a formal apology "at a higher level" after South Korean athletes were affected by transport and accommodation issues at the event in Japan.
"I hope the organising committee and the OCA (Olympic Council of Asia) will give these issues greater attention," he said at Korea House, the team's hospitality hub in Nagoya.
"More than simply apologising, I believe it is important for them to come up with concrete measures to prevent these problems from happening again and put those measures into practice.
"However, they have not yet provided us with any concrete plans for how they intend to improve things going forward."
The OCA, which governs the quadrennial Asian Games, did not provide immediate comment.
To reduce costs, local organisers have accommodated athletes and officials in a mix of hotels, temporary wooden containers and a cruise ship rather than build a traditional Games village.
South Korea moved their men's basketball team out of their container units at Garden Pier and into hotels because they said the beds were too short and after one of the units flooded during heavy rain.
Lee said the containers were "extremely cramped" for the basketball players and that administrative confusion on the cruise ship over bookings and room assignments had inconvenienced athletes.
"So our delegation has been making a great deal of effort to find alternative accommodations outside the official facilities," he added.
"I believe those efforts have helped create a better environment for our athletes to perform, and in the case of the men’s basketball team, they contributed to the team’s gold-medal victory."
The men's team had to cancel a training session hours before their final against Japan because their shuttle bus did not show up.
"It was understandably very unsettling for the players," Lee said. "And because it was such an important final - and especially because they were playing Japan, the host country - it made the situation all the more significant."
COST-CUTTING
Transport issues have affected other South Korean athletes including the men's football team, the defending Asian Games champions, and Lee put the problems down to cost-cutting.
"In placing greater emphasis on these priorities, I think the Aichi-Nagoya Games have experienced some shortcomings in terms of administration," he said.
The South Korean men's hockey team were also upset when the North Korea's national anthem was played instead of their own before their 5-0 win over Bangladesh.
Lee believed the incident had a "significant negative impact" on the players and confirmed Games officials had visited the team to apologise.
Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games Deputy Secretary General Takaaki Omi told reporters on Tuesday the anthem mix-up was a serious mistake but said accommodation and transport arrangements had generally been functioning properly.
The bus that failed to turn up for the basketball team was a case of human error, he added.
"While I would like to apologise to the athletes and team officials for the areas where we have been unable to respond as flexibly as we should have, we will proceed by prioritising the competitions above all else going forward," he said.

How the race they said women couldn't run took centre stage
- Published
For 32 years, the women's 800m was absent from the Olympics, with its competitors deemed too frail. Now, it is one of the most hotly anticipated events on the track.
This extraordinary story starts at the 1928 Olympic Games, which represented a huge - if temporary - step forward for women's sports.
The Amsterdam Games were the first to allow women to compete in track and field events. Five women's events were added to the programme - the 100m, high jump, discus, 400m hurdles and, controversially at the time, 800m.
The progress, however, was temporary.
German athlete Karoline Lina Radke, external became the first woman to win Olympic gold in the 800m - but she would also be the last for another 32 years.
The event was removed from the Games after reports - later proven to be false - claimed competitors suffered extreme exhaustion after the race, and the International Olympic Committee decided women were too frail to compete, external over the two-lap distance.
Fast forward almost 100 years and the event now gets headline status at major events.
In recent times, it's been the battle between Britain's Olympic 800m champion Keely Hodgkinson and the Swiss European champion Audrey Werro that has captivated fans.
So how did the 800m become the 'one to watch'? BBC Sport spoke to the women who helped shape the race to find out.
'You don't realise what you've done'
It was the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, and Ann Brightwell (nee Packer) had just crossed the finish line of the women's 800m to take gold - and set a new world record.
In doing so, Brightwell became the first British woman to win an Olympic gold on the track, in a time of two minutes 01.1 seconds.
She told BBC Sport: "My husband, who was my fiance then, said to me, 'you don't realise what you've done'.
"I didn't give it a thought at the time… but now I realise I played a very small part in women running longer distances."
But the controversy hadn't completely gone away. Brightwell knew all about the claims that had seen women unable to compete for 32 years after the 800m was removed from the Olympics.
Brightwell adds: "Men weren't happy about women competing in these very high profile events…we were considered too frail and too delicate.
"And they took it upon themselves to make it look really bad. They were saying women were collapsing on the way round. But it was all a lie."
After 1928, women's middle-distance shrunk into the shadows for the next few decades.
The 800m was finally reintroduced to the Olympic programme in 1960 and, four years later, the then-22-year-old Brightwell went to her first Olympics, fitting training around her job as a teacher.
"Many people in my era either had to take unpaid leave or resign, or they got sacked because they were trying to juggle their sports with their career," she said.
"My school was very tolerant towards what I was doing, so I was fortunate."
Going out for a run around the local streets or countryside - which seems so commonplace today - was unusual in the era Brightwell was competing.
"If I just felt like an easy run, I would run around my village, around the streets… people commented on it or tooted their horns. And it was funny looking back, but it never troubled me," the now 84-year-old told BBC Sport.
Brightwell's 800m time of 2:01.1 stood for almost three years, before Australian Judy Pollock broke that with a new time of 2:01 flat in 1967.
The next target was to go under two minutes.
Breaking 'sub-two' - and a stubborn world record
"Records are great and medals are the best, but when you break a barrier it's a fantastic feeling," said Christina Boxer-Cahill (nee Boxer).
It was at the 1979 European Cup final in Turin that Boxer-Cahill looked up at the clock and realised she'd gone under two minutes.
She added: "I knew this would probably be my last chance, because there were other girls in Britain trying to do it."
In 1971, Germany's Hildegard Falck, external had become the first woman to break the two-minute barrier.
Eight years later, it was the 22-year-old Boxer-Cahill who became the first British woman to do so, in a time of one minute 59.05 seconds.
"It's a bit like when Roger Bannister broke four minutes for the mile. Once he'd done it everybody did it because you see what's possible," Boxer-Cahill, who is now 69 years old, told BBC Sport.
"I just think I'm so fortunate that I was in a sport where everybody accepted that you have men and women's races in the Olympics."
From 1971 to 1983, the women's 800m world record would be broken six times.
But the 1983 record stands to this day.
It belongs to Czech athlete Jarmila Kratochvilova, who ran a time of one minute 53.28 seconds at a meeting in Munich.
Kratochvilova's record has been questioned, with claims it was assisted by her country's doping regime that existed at the time, something she has strenuously denied.
In 2017, European Athletics proposed wiping out records set before 2005 - sending a strong signal that records set before then were disputable.
Several Soviet satellite states - including East Germany - are known to have been operating state-sponsored doping programmes throughout the 1980s.
At the 1988 Seoul Olympics, Boxer-Cahill finished fourth in the 1500m, behind a Russian athlete who was later banned for doping.
Boxer-Cahill said: "I was running during that Eastern Bloc era when, you know, they've looked back and some of the performances, there's sort of a cloud over it.
"I'd just have loved to have been on that rostrum. I wish the Eastern Bloc system hadn't been there, but that's what it was.
"Politics in sport, when you're the performer, it frustrates you. But if you get too frustrated, all it's going to do is upset your own performance."
Women's 800m 'stronger than ever'
"We've got not just two but several girls who are running under two minutes every time they turn out," Brightwell told BBC Sport.
"It's stronger than it's ever been."
Kratochvilova's 43-year-old record is looking increasingly precarious.
The 800m European champion Werro has come closest, running a time just 0.42 seconds shy of the record at the Zurich Diamond League.
Keely Hodgkinson, the current 800m indoor world record holder, told BBC Sport earlier this year that she's never felt closer to breaking the outdoor record.
She said: "I really do believe we can break it, but a lot of things have got to come together."
Hodgkinson is one of six athletes competing in the 800m at Athlos, the all-female athletics event taking place in London, on Friday.
"I do think the [800m] world record will go in the next year or two, and hopefully this season, because we're on a real high, aren't we?" Boxer-Cahill told BBC Sport.
"If it happens towards the end of the season, 2026 [would be] the year of women's 800m running."

Addiction clinics around the country are seeing a growing number of cases related to gas station products made from the kratom leaf and its derivatives.
At the telehealth addiction clinic Boulder Care, for example, people who report using kratom products constituted 3% of all new patients in September 2025. By July 2026, that number was 8%, and in August, it jumped to 14%.
“That really is quite an explosion,” said Ayesha Appa, the company’s head of medical affairs.
Kratom has been sold in the U.S. for decades, historically as a powder made from the dried leaf that’s native to Southeast Asia. People tout it for its mood- and energy-boosting powers, as well as pain relief.
Even for these lower-strength products, there’s a risk for physical dependence. But most of these Boulder patients report using newer, more potent products with highly concentrated levels of 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH, a compound that’s found in the kratom leaf only in trace amounts. Unlike the more dominant alkaloid in the kratom leaf, 7-OH acts directly on the brain’s opioid receptors, meaning it can have stronger, more opioid-like effects, including sedation and euphoria.
The Food and Drug Administration recently flagged 7-OH products as an emerging opioid threat, while the Drug Enforcement Administration proposed an effective ban on 7-OH above a certain threshold. That law has yet to be finalized, but numerous states have enacted similar restrictions. Appa theorized that laws revoking access to the products may be leading people to experience withdrawal.
“I think we’re really seeing and feeling what happens when people lose access and need to seek care in unprecedented numbers,” Appa said.
Even before local bans were put into place, other clinicians noticed similar trends.
Last year, there was typically no more than a single patient per week being admitted for kratom use at two inpatient clinics run by the Recovery Centers of America in Massachusetts, said Myles Jen Kin, a medical director for the group. The withdrawal was mild, requiring “comfort meds” only. But these days, those same two clinics see anywhere from 10 to 20 people per week who are either completely dependent on kratom or 7-OH, or those products are part of a larger substance use problem, Jen Kin said. And the severity of the withdrawal seems to be increasing with the prevalence. “We’re basically treating it as if it’s fentanyl or oxycodone or heroin,” Jen Kin said.
With limited research available, clinicians at addiction treatment centers are on the frontlines treating patients going through withdrawal from these products.
“Having kratom [patients] without any research, it’s just another day for us. It’s how we deal with addiction in general,” said Jen Kin. “It’s just sadly the truth in our country.”
Who uses these products?
Clinicians say they’re seeing two broad categories of people seeking treatment for kratom or 7-OH dependence: those who are completely new to drug use and treatment, and others who are more experienced, and perhaps have been in treatment before.
People who take kratom do so for a number of reasons: to boost energy, ease anxiety, or to quiet chronic pain. Others have used the products as a way to self-manage withdrawal and recovery from other substances, like opioids or alcohol. They might purposefully escalate to 7-OH products, or take them incidentally.
Kratom has traditionally been sold in the U.S. as a powder, pill, or tea, while newer products also appear in the form of gummies and liquid shots. 7-OH is often misleadingly marketed as kratom, and all types of products have been found to be contaminated with other compounds not listed on the packaging, as well as additives like caffeine, kava, or CBD.
Federal survey data indicates that from 2019 to 2023, the number of people who have tried kratom products in their lifetime rose from around 4 million to 5 million. In the last decade, reports to U.S. poison centers regarding kratom exposure increased from 258 to 3,434 overall, including a sharp rise in 2025. (Kratom doesn’t appear to be acutely lethal in the way a drug like fentanyl is, as 79% of related deaths reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in the last decade involved other substances, mainly other opioids.)
“The common story I get from a lot of these clients is that they didn’t know really what it was,” said Phil Smyth, executive director of Milestone Treatment Center, which has three clinics across New Jersey, Virginia, and Texas. He’s also seen an increase in patients who need medical assistance to detox from 7-OH products, many of whom began taking them to reduce some sort of pain.
Dependence seems to build fast. “People find themselves needing to take more sooner, and tolerance can really build quickly, and people can experience incredibly severe opioid withdrawal while buying something marketed as wellness,” Appa said.
Steve Klein, a physician at Caron Treatment Centers in Pennsylvania, said that kratom and 7-OH usage tends to be pretty benign at the start. Patients may see these products sold “over the counter” and think: “How bad could it be?” That eventually leads some newer drug users down what Klein calls a “potency rabbit hole.” He’s also seen patients who were in remission from opioid use disorders try kratom and then quickly spiral. By the time they’re checking into residential care at Caron, they’re normally using pretty high doses of 7-OH, Klein said.
How treatment centers are responding
Existing research on kratom has found withdrawal to be generally mild, but users, clinicians, and advocates say the experience can be as taxing as opioid withdrawal. “That’s what we see with kratom — that fight-or-flight phenomenon of agitation, sweating, anxiety, diarrhea,” said Ken Jin. People may not realize they’re dependent on the products, but then begin to feel irritable and unable to sleep or eat without them, Smyth from Milestone said.
Early case reports show that medications for opioid use disorder including buprenorphine alone and in combination with naloxone can help to manage kratom use disorders. Methadone has also been shown to have potential.
Last month, nearly a third of Boulder Care’s new patients starting on buprenorphine reported currently using kratom or 7-OH.
Still, testimonies from treatment centers may represent a sort of sampling bias, according to Katherine Hill, an epidemiology Ph.D. candidate at Yale School of Public Health who has studied kratom. People who may be more easily self-managing kratom or 7-OH discontinuation wouldn’t show up at a treatment center.
Until more data is available, anecdotes abound. There are Reddit forums online dedicated to discussions about quitting kratom and quitting 7-OH. There, people swap tips and recount their own, personal experiments with tapering off the products and trying to replace them with new ones. The kratom channel has been around for more than a decade, while the one dedicated to 7-OH was created in 2024.
“Well I finally gave in and went to rehab,” someone wrote on the 7-OH forum last month in between detox and being transferred to inpatient care. “For the first time in a very long time I can see a light at the end of the tunnel even though I just stepped into hell.”

It has become increasingly common for AI firms to announce that their latest and most capable models engaged in unauthorized real-world hacking. Google, which has been slow to release frontier Gemini models in recent months, has been absent from the “rogue AI” conversation until now. Following a Wall Street Journal report, Google has confirmed that Gemini models hacked three companies during a May 2026 test, but the nature of the intrusion isn’t as troubling (or impressive) as previous AI hacks.
The hack took place during a test conducted by cybersecurity firm Irregular. A collection of Gemini models were taking part in a “capture the flag” exercise intended to test the AI’s cybersecurity capabilities in a closed environment. The AI was instructed to retrieve information from a fake company (which shared a name with a real company) within this environment. Irregular was not supposed to allow the model to operate outside its servers, but due to a misconfiguration, Gemini was able to access the Internet.
When Gemini started snooping around the web, it targeted real infrastructure instead of the fakes. For one of the three hacks, Gemini simply guessed passwords until it accessed a company’s online services. In the other two instances, Gemini searched public software repositories until it found login credentials for companies that had been accidentally included.
In all three test runs, Google’s models reportedly stopped after realizing they had accessed a real company’s servers. At that point, Irregular changed its configuration to prevent the AI from accessing the Internet. Apparently, Irregular didn’t initially consider this event worthy of further investigation—it didn’t even tell Google about the hacks until July, following the news of other AI hacking incidents. After becoming aware of the event, Google notified the companies so they could (we hope) improve their password security.

Here's why Apple's Mac Studio has become so expensive
A big part of the story is soaring memory and storage prices, but other factors come into play as well.
If you want to run AI models locally or do high-end Hollywood VFX on Apple products, the Mac Studio is now your only solution. Equipped with a M5 Max or M5 Ultra processor, Apple's compact but powerful desktop delivers gobs of performance both alone and working in a cluster.
There's just one issue: the price. In 18 months since the last model, the M5 Max's base price has increased by $500 to $2,500, while the M5 Ultra starts at $5,500, up $1,500 from the M3 Ultra model. Those bumps go well beyond what's typical for Apple device upgrades. So why is that? A big part of the story is soaring memory and storage prices, but hedging and profit margins might come into play as well.
Who is the Mac Studio for?
There's no question that Apple's Mac Mini is a great desktop computer, offering a surprising amount of power in a shockingly small size. However, it tops out at an M5 Pro processor and 64GB of RAM, with 307 GB/s of memory bandwidth. That's enough for many demanding situations, but AI and content creation power users may need more.
Enter the Mac Studio. The "base" version (starting at $2,500) has an M5 Max processor with an 18-core GPU and 32-core GPU, and up to 128GB of unified memory, depending on the option chosen. That goes up to $5,899 for the 18-core CPU and 40-core GPU version with 128GB of RAM and 2TB storage. For AI or video editing pros, it's already capable of tasks "like running large language models and editing 8K video," as Apple says.
Then, there's the M5 Ultra model, squarely aimed at heavy AI power users. It uses an M5 Ultra processor that is two M5 Max processors joined together and supports up to 512GB of RAM. Its typical use case, Apple says, is to "store huge datasets entirely in local memory, increase the tokens-per-second speed and run huge LLMs with hundreds of billions of parameters entirely on device." Moreover, if budget permits, you can triple that performance by clustering four of those together via the high-speed Thunderbolt 5 ports. Demand for this kind of setup for AI reportedly caught Apple by surprise with the last model.
Video users will also be spoiled by the Mac Studio with an M5 Ultra chip. Filmmakers will be able to "color-grade uncompressed 8K footage in real time, VFX artists can render complex simulations... [and it can] simultaneously play up to 33 streams of 8K ProRes 422 at 30 fps."
That model starts at $5,500 with a 30-core CPU and 64-core GPU and 96GB of unified memory. If you really want to kit it out, though, you can get it with a 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU and 256GB of unified storage (512GB is coming next month). Memory bandwidth for that 256GB model tops out at 1.2TB/s, four times that of the Mac Mini.
With 2TB of storage, though, that option will run you $11,299. The Mac Studio M3 Ultra with the same configuration (the flagship 32-core CPU and 80-core GPU, 256GB of RAM and a 2TB SSD) retailed for $7,499 at launch, a cool $3,800 cheaper.
What on Earth happened?
The primary culprits for this massive price increase are the Mac Studio's large amount of high-end memory and storage, "RAMageddon" pricing, hedging and Apple's usual insistence on high profit margins. Apple said so itself when it first bumped MacBook prices back in June: "We've never seen component prices increase this much, this quickly. We've worked hard to absorb these costs and delay price increases for as long as possible, but the current environment has made that unsustainable."
Let's start with the RAM, or what Apple calls "unified memory," because it's shared between the CPU and GPU. With 1.2TB/s bandwidth when fully loaded with RAM, the Mac Studio M5 Ultra uses LPDDR5X memory. That RAM has a maximum throughput of 172GB/s, so Apple installs it right onto the M5 Ultra processor package to maximize speed, in a very wide bus (1,024 bits for the M5 Ultra model), to achieve the highest speeds. It's the fastest and most expensive memory available, other than high bandwidth memory (HBM) used for servers.
It's hard to say exactly how much the RAM makes up the price of a Mac Studio. Apple was reportedly paying around $6 per gigabyte for LPDDR5X memory earlier this year, but that price may be more like $10 or $11 now. Let's say its memory cost for the 256GB Mac Studio M5 Ultra is around $2,500-$2,800. It currently retails for far more than that, but Apple obviously has major buying power. That cost is still a big chunk, though.
Pricing for the NAND storage is also much higher, with Apple's cost is likely around $300 to $500 for 2TB worth based on the current market and high-end PCIe 5.0 memory it uses. Prices are reportedly around quadruple what memory cost when the previous Mac Studio came out, and double the price for storage.
That makes for an increase of about $2,200 to $2,400 at the high end. Rounding that up to account for other component increases, Apple's costs are around $2,400 to $2,600 more, based on those very rough estimates.
You may recall that I said the Mac Ultra with 256GB was $3,800 more expensive this year, so where does the rest of that price increase come in? Apple reportedly shoots for around 40 percent gross margins on its computer hardware, but the new Mac Ultra pricing is nearly 60 percent higher than the estimated cost increase. There are a couple of possible reasons. One is that Apple is hedging against even higher future RAM prices so it can limit Mac Studio M5 price changes later. Another is that Apple is using the memory shortage to lift margins for its flagship desktop Mac. Or maybe it's a little of column A, a little of column B.
Should I wait?
In my review of the Max Studio M5 Ultra, I said that Apple appeared to be targeting AI power users and developers more than ever. The nearly $4,000 price increase on this model for a midrange configuration means it's only affordable by companies or professionals doing high-end, high-paying work. For video or graphics pros, though, the Max Studio M5 Max is a better option at $3,100 to $3,600 for a decently equipped 48GB or 64GB configuration.
If you're thinking these prices might go down, I have bad news — it's rare for Apple to ever lower prices (the polishing cloth notwithstanding). Usually, the only time that happens is at the end of a product's cycle just before it's been replaced by a new version.
The Mac Studio M3 Ultra/M4 Max actually went up over time due to increasing memory prices, and that could easily happen again to the M5 Ultra/M5 Max through 2028 if RAM shortage projections are correct. Yes, they could go down if RAMageddon ends and memory becomes cheaper, but it's hard to say when or if that will happen. Apple has reportedly agreed to pay 30-40 percent higher prices for RAM and storage next year, so it feels safe to say that prices won't be dropping any time soon. In other words, if you need a Mac Studio and can pay for it, you might be better off to bite the bullet and buy one now rather than waiting.

There's always a danger in over-complicating products. Simple is so often best. The apocryphal story of NASA spending millions crafting a space pen while Soviet cosmonauts used a pencil is often cited as a prime example, even if it's actually not true. Perhaps it's not surprising that Dyson has got into hot water trying to reinvent the electric toothbrush.
The Chinese invented the first bristle toothbrush during the Ming dynasty. That concept muddled along quite nicely until 1937, when Tomlinson Moseley filed a patent for the earliest electric toothbrush. After more than 400 years, the Motodent marked the beginning of an evolutionary shift from manual brushing to powered oral care.
Having had considerable success reimagining established product categories such as stick vacuums and premium hair dryers—though not so much air-purifying headphones—the company earlier this month, with great fanfare, unveiled the next leap forward for teeth: the $499 Dyson CameraJet with a tiny camera to aim streams of rinsing fluid into the gaps between your teeth.
Others, like the Waterpik Sonic-Fusion 2.0, have already been daring (or foolhardy) enough to combine brushing and water flossing. However, Dyson upped the ante further by adding a macro-lens camera, allowing its “Gap Optical Targeting system,” trained on 470,000 dental images, to identify within 100 milliseconds precisely where to squirt fluid from the 12.5 milliliters of mouth rinse stored in its on-board reservoir.
It's taken Dyson six years, 38 patents, and an awful lot of money to make this camera-squirt-brush doohickey work. However, something has gone badly wrong with the CameraJet. So wrong that despite James Dyson globally launching the product at a Paris event mere weeks ago, you can no longer, as far as WIRED can ascertain, buy the CameraJet anywhere.
The CameraJet launched in US stores on September 8. Just a day later, reports began outlining the first user complaints of water in the battery compartment and failures within 30 seconds of use. Consumer Reports' own review unit stopped working less than 24 hours after unboxing. On September 11, French outlet Numerama reported that the French Dyson site and stores had reportedly stopped selling the toothbrush. By September 15, stores in the US, UK, and Singapore, where Dyson's headquarters now reside, had followed suit.
Despite the product disappearing from shelves and online stores, Liv Thomas, the company's head of Beauty Communications, insists to WIRED that the CameraJet hasn't been recalled. Instead, the gadget is “experiencing strong demand globally” and “shortages of supply as we are in the process of scaling up production." Units will reappear supposedly in “the coming weeks.” But what about the multiple reports of breakages, leaking, and battery failures in multiple countries?
“We have identified a single component issue affecting a small number of early batches,” Thomas says. “We have isolated those batches and are supporting affected customers.”
Thomas confirmed that Dyson would not answer questions on where—if anywhere—the Dyson CameraJet was still on sale worldwide. Nor would Dyson confirm when it stopped shipments of the product. Thomas also confirmed that Dyson refuses to detail what the faulty “single component” is, what problem it's causing for the CameraJet, or how many units have been affected globally. Dyson also refused to comment on why it had not issued a formal recall of these faulty early batches of the $500 device.
Dyson Reddit forums have lit up, with names such as “ScameraJet” being bandied around, along with one disgruntled buyer commenting: “Bought two of these and both of them have stopped working. Since I bought it in the UK and wasn’t planning to return it and have thrown the packaging away, I can’t even return them. Disappointed that they scammed so good. Unbelievable that it lasted just two weeks.”
Kyle Wiens, CEO of the repair company iFixit, feels the problem may well be leaking.
“This sounds like a waterproofing issue. Making products at scale with the tolerances required to waterproof are hard,” he says. “My guess without getting a chance to look at a failed unit is that we either have a tolerance issue where some parts aren't mating perfectly, or a failure in the adhesive curing process, either during manufacturing or in shipping.”
Wiens says this adhesive-curing failure can happen in such a way that a product can pass factory testing fine, but then heat or humidity (or both) during shipping causes a problem.
Adam Toner, founder and technical director of Ripcord Designs, a UK-based electronic design consultancy that has worked with multinational companies including Formula One Management and Panasonic, also thinks water is the CameraJet's problem.
“On a product like this, there just should never be any water ingress into the internals,” he says. “I don't have one in front of me, but I've seen a few videos and people explaining how you change the battery. Once you pull the battery off—which is where people say they're seeing water—it looks like there is probably access from that battery compartment into all of the internals of the device.”
The CameraJet not charging, overheating, or failing to start—all of that can be explained by water getting into the device, Toner says. He suspects the problem could be as benign as a faulty gasket or O-ring.
If water getting in does turn out to be an issue for the CameraJet, as these experts suggest, this begs the obvious question: How on earth has Dyson managed to spend six years developing a teched-up toothbrush, designed to be dunked in water every use, and that carries liquid around in it, yet fail to make it waterproof?
Wiens believes the CameraJet chaos could force a well-overdue rethink for Dyson.
“Clearly they didn't plan for this to happen," he says. "They should take this opportunity to invest in repairability. Making products easier to fix also makes them easier to rework when manufacturing defects occur. Dyson is way behind the industry on making repair parts and information available for their products. This should be a wake-up call for them to step up.”

Apple’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, could give the stagnant foldable market a much-needed push. It may not reinvent the category, but Apple’s reach, software focus, and mainstream appeal could make foldables far more popular.
September is here and so are the new iPhones. This year at Apple’s Surprise and Shine event, the Cupertino tech giant came with a number of changes, not just in terms of devices but in terms of management too. There was a new CEO – it was John Ternus’ first event as CEO – as well as new Apple Watches, AirPods and, of course, new iPhones too.
The Duo dominates the new iPhones
Even though Apple showcases a number of products during its September event, it is mainly the iPhones that the world waits for. And even in iPhones, it is usually the Pro and Pro Max iPhones that make the headlines (barring the odd occasion when the Air popped up). The plain iPhones are usually pushed to the sidelines and launched as the more “economical”, “affordable” iPhones whose price tags and generally minor upgrades in specs and design are the only things that get them any attention.
For the longest time, we have been feeling for the plain iPhones because they are quite capable and bring in big sales numbers (especially in markets like India, where they are bestsellers) and yet do not get the hype they deserve. Well, this time around, the iPhone Pro and the Pro Max got the taste of this bitter medicine. The two smartphones had to fold (pun intended) and give up all their headline space for the more expensive, exclusive, and most different iPhone since the inception of the original iPhone: the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable iPhone.
With the iPhone Duo, Apple has finally marked its official entry in the world of foldables. It comes with a starting price of Rs. 299,900 in India ($1,999 in the US), which has naturally inspired a tsunami of reinvented kidney jokes and all sorts of comparisons about all that you can buy for that price. It has also got many competing brands scoffing at Apple’s very late attempt at foldables, calling the Duo a “copy”. While some of the criticism and cynicism around the Duo is valid, we think a foldable phone from Apple is just what the foldable market needed to make foldables mainstream. Not because the Duo is an out-of-the-tech-world, never-seen-before, and extraordinary folding smartphone (hey, we haven’t reviewed it yet), but for much simpler reasons.
Ghost of foldables past: A story mainly of Samsung
Samsung is considered by many to be the modern foldable phone pioneer. It was the trailblazer that was responsible for actually bringing in foldable phones that not only landed on the tech moon but also managed to stick around for seven2 years – Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold arrived in 2019, followed by the Galaxy Z Flip in 2020. The brand did not really have a working blueprint that they could have used back then to have perfected their foldables and technology around it, but it enjoyed an early mover’s advantage in the segment and managed to create a very strong reputation for itself. They built a strong rapport with the consumers that none of the other brands could develop, even after launching just as good, just as powerful foldable smartphones.
Following Samsung’s start, many leading tech brands have been surfing the foldable wave for a while now. The OG flip phone master, Motorola; the Android originator Google; the flagship killer OnePlus; the Chinese Apple, Xiaomi; Vivo, Oppo, and others have created foldables with their own touches and twists. Huawei has gone one step further and has launched a tri-fold – a smartphone that folds twice. But even after all this effort, none of them could really be a standout foldable smartphone brand. Only Samsung did.
But in spite of Samsung’s consistency and the efforts of other brands, foldable smartphones have not become mainstream. They have never really made impressive numbers or become popular/common devices. Yes, most of them come with premium price tags, but even those that are relatively affordable – mostly flips or budget foldables (yes, there are some) – have not gained the kind of traction that had been expected. The foldable revolution that many had predicted seemed to have stalled, and apart from a few devices (mainly from Samsung), growth was largely limited.
Apple and the tech snowball effect… could it come to foldables?
Now Apple has stepped into the foldable ring, and while there are many contenders in it already, we think the Cupertino tech giant might get the buzz around foldables going. It has been quite a trend setter in the tech world, and is identified with premium innovation. Features, functions, and devices that existed long before Apple “reinvented” them suddenly became popular once they started shipping with an Apple logo and Apple’s own unique take on them. They not only became mainstream but also often became a common sight on products from other brands as well. Touchscreen phones, apps and app stores, music stores, portrait mode, notches (Dynamic Island), are just some of the products that Apple did not invent, but made a part of
everyday technology.
Of course, every time this happens, the Internet is flooded with techies pointing out how the particular feature or product has been around for years and how Apple is not really innovating or, rather, thinking differently (Apple’s very tagline). Despite all the chatter and gossip around this topic, somehow the feature picks up momentum, and soon enough the world gets interested in knowing how it works and then owning a device that lets them use it. This initiates a snowball effect of sorts, which leads to that feature or device becoming extremely popular.
We will keep it simple: quite often, it basically takes an Apple device or feature to grab mainstream attention. It happened with GUI, MP3 players, ultra-portable notebooks, touchscreen phones, tablets, TWS, smartwatches, and we think it could happen with foldables too. The Duo has the potential to put the seemingly jammed foldable wheels in motion.
It is important to remember that it is not like whatever Apple does just becomes a hit automatically. The brand has a loyal following, but it has released many features, devices, and functions that did not strike a chord with consumers and have faded away. The Apple Vision Pro, HomePod, iPhone Mini and iPhone Plus, the Touch Bar on the Mac…Apple’s failure list is quite long. It may be one of the most successful tech brands in history, but Apple is no tech Midas – there is no real guarantee that the iPhone Duo would be an absolute hit. The stakes are quite high for the Duo, especially given its price tag (which is even higher in India).
It has got the hype, but what would make the Duo click?
Unlike Samsung, Apple has not had to reinvent the foldable wheel. It has had time to read, research, develop, try, and make mistakes, and fix them all, even while observing the efforts of other tech brands. And while the Duo’s design and specs, and indeed, many of its features, are nothing we have not seen before, these are not areas where Apple differentiates itself from the regular crowd. The iPhone Duo needs to bring Apple’s attention to detail when it comes to user experience, and software tuned exactly to suit the needs and capabilities of the device it supports.
We have not yet had the pleasure (or pain) to experience the device but so far, from the looks and the videos on the Internet, we can tell you there are a few things we love about the iPhone Duo – the TouchID on the side (yes, we actually love it), the vertical tool bar for easy access, the matte display layer which makes the crease largely invisible, and yes, of course, the animation that blurs out the side/front screen when the phone is being opened or folded. But it’s not all pink skies and red roses. We are not very convinced by the asymmetrical shape of the device, the insanely high price tag, and, well, even the name. Duo? Really, Apple? We are also really curious about how Apple has worked on apps for the cover display as well as the inner ones.
But these are early days. The iPhone Duo is more than a month away, and we are sure Apple will fine-tune it even further before releasing it. In the meantime, we expect the kidney jokes to continue and even gather momentum, but on the flip side, curiosity will also grow, as we are sure more will be revealed about the device and its features and functions.
The iPhone Duo has generated more buzz about the foldables in a few months than other players in the field got in years, but it is all going to boil down to how well and how differently it works from other foldables. Given the interest levels around it, it might just prove to be the elixir that foldables need.

Dr. Reddy's Laboratories on Friday (September 18, 2026) entered into an exclusive distribution agreement with Takeda Pharmaceutical Company to promote and distribute its dengue vaccine, QDENGA, in India's private market for pediatric and adult vaccination.
Subject to local regulatory processes, the vaccine is expected to be available in the first half of 2027. The vaccine received marketing authorisation by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) in July 2026 for individuals aged 4-60 years, Dr. Reddy's said in a press release.
QDENGA, a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine, aims to strengthen dengue prevention and management by providing broad immune coverage across all four circulating dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4). Administered as a two-dose regimen given three months apart, it is India's first approved dengue vaccine, according to the release.
While Dr. Reddy's will exclusively manage private-market distribution, disease awareness, and healthcare professional engagement, Takeda will retain rights for the public market, legal ownership, and overall medical and brand oversight, it said.
"As the second-largest vaccine player in India, we believe the introduction of India's first approved dengue vaccine is an important development for the country's healthcare landscape," said M. V. Ramana, CEO, Global Generics, Dr. Reddy's Laboratories.
"Through our collaboration with Takeda, we look forward to making QDENGA available to eligible individuals and contributing to efforts aimed at addressing the country's dengue burden," Mr. Ramana said.
Dr. Mahender Nayak, Head of Intercontinental Markets, International Business Unit, Takeda, noted, "In parallel, our private-market collaboration with Dr. Reddy's will help enable timely private-market access for eligible individuals once QDENGA becomes available in India." Approved in 43 countries, QDENGA has seen over 32 million doses distributed globally.

The White House has a new helipad on the South Lawn.
President Donald Trump took off in Marine One from the helipad after an official ribbon-cutting ceremony on Monday.
Trump previously said the White House would receive the granite helipad, paid for by Sikorsky Aircraft — a subsidiary of Lockheed Martin — to support the new fleet of helicopters used as Marine One.
A Lockheed Martin spokesperson confirmed the contribution and told Business Insider it was being made to the National Park Service.
Trump previously said the permanent fixture would help protect the South Lawn's grass.
The newer helicopters from Sikorsky are about "two and a half times more powerful than the old ones," Trump said.
"When you land on the grass, it's not that the grass gets discolored. It gets ripped out," he said.
The helipad bears the White House seal and cost between $5 million and $6 million.
"Sikorsky is paying for it. You know why? Because they didn't tell us how powerful these helicopters were," Trump said. "And they felt a little bit guilty."
A Sikorsky spokesperson said that the new model for presidential transport — the VH-92A Patriot — delivers "increased performance and reduced maintenance costs and time over the current fleet of presidential helicopters."
A White House spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
Photos have shown the helipad being built amid other massive construction projects the administration is undertaking to transform the White House in line with Trump's vision.
The helipad faced at least one setback when Trump ordered contractors to redo portions of the work, resulting in crews having to dismantle the nearly 100-foot-wide granite seal that was already in progress, The Washington Post reported.
During construction, Marine One relied on the Ellipse, the park south of the White House, as its landing zone.
Below are photos tracing the history of presidential helicopter landings at the White House and the results of the new helipad.
Aviation pioneer James Ray landed an autogyro, an aircraft with a spinning rotor on top, on the White House South Lawn for the first time in 1931.
James Ray parked a Pitcairn-Cierva PCA-2 autogyro on the South Lawn as part of an award ceremony, according to the National Air and Space Museum. It was the first recorded instance of a rotary-wing aircraft landing on the lawn.
In 1957, President Dwight D. Eisenhower became the first US president to use helicopter transport from the White House lawn.
The first documented instance of Eisenhower boarding a helicopter from the South Lawn was on July 12, 1957, according to The History Channel.
The Marine Corps website states that helicopter transport helped turn a two-hour motorcade into a seven-minute helicopter ride.
Helicopter transport for the US president to and from the White House South Lawn later became standard operating procedure for short-distance travel.
The White House helicopter transport was named Marine One, a call sign for a Marine Corps aircraft carrying the president.
The fleet is operated by Marine Helicopter Squadron One, known as HMX-1 or the Nighthawks.
Marine One has become one of the most visible symbols of presidential travel, next to Air Force One.
Instead of a permanent helipad, White House personnel would place large landing disks on the South Lawn for Marine One helicopters.
The landing targets provide the aircraft with a stable contact point and could reduce turf damage.
The South Lawn is no match for the new Sikorsky aircraft.
In 2024, Lockheed Martin's Sikorsky formally delivered the VH-92A helicopter to the US Marine Corps to replace the older fleet of aircraft used for Marine One.
The government spent $5 billion on the new fleet.
Bloomberg previously reported in 2024 that issues with the VH-92A scorching the South Lawn have delayed the aircraft's ability to transport the president.
Trump says construction of the presidential helipad is underway.
Photos show that the grass on the South Lawn has been removed to make way for the construction of the permanent granite helipad.
"For 50 years, we've been landing helicopters on grass," Trump told reporters in July. "The grass is wet, soggy."
The helipad design features a 100-foot-wide presidential seal.
A massive granite presidential seal was set to be the centerpiece of Trump's helipad project.
The nearly 100-foot-wide design was taking shape on the South Lawn, intended to be embedded into the helipad surface, marking a highly visible presidential emblem at the heart of the landing zone.
The most eye-catching part of the White House helipad project is already being torn apart.
In early August, contractors were photographed removing the roughly 100-foot-wide granite presidential seal.
According to reporting by the Washington Post, the redesign came after Trump questioned the helipad's appearance and the South Lawn's slope.
It's unclear how much the revisions will add to the project's price tag.
Trump has repurposed the Ellipse until the helipad construction is completed
While construction continues on the White House's new helipad, Trump has temporarily shifted Marine One operations to the Ellipse, a park south of the White House.
The Washington Post reported that Trump has pushed to have the helipad finished before China's leader, Xi Jinping, is expected to visit later in September.
The helipad is only one of the construction projects the White House is going through under Trump 2.0.
Other renovation projects pursued under the second Trump administration include the demolition of the East Wing to make room for a 90,000 square-foot White House ballroom.
The project is estimated to cost $400 million.
The administration also hosted a UFC fight at the White House in June, temporarily turning the South Lawn into an arena.
By September, the granite presidential seal of the helipad was in full view.
The construction project began around June, according to The Washington Post.
On September 6, Trump announced in a Truth Social post that the helipad was completed.
Trump departed from the White House helipad after a ribbon-cutting ceremony
Trump boarded Marine One en route to New York following a ribbon-cutting ceremony on September 21.
Trump's remarks from the ceremony were largely drowned out by the helicopter and other background noises. Major TV networks also pulled coverage of the event after some news outlets were banned from the White House, making it nearly impossible to hear what Trump was saying.

Taylor Swift will have to find space for yet another award. MTV said Monday that the Queen of Pop Present will be the first recipient of its MTV VMA Artist Director Honors, set to be presented Sunday during the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards.
The inaugural prize celebrates a sustained and influential body of work from artists who have pushed creative boundaries and developed a clear directorial voice.
Swift has won Best Director at the VMAs four times and was nominated three other times. Among the untold number of accolades during her career, she is the only person to win the Album of the Year Grammy four times, most recently for Midnights in 2024, ande has 14 Grammy Awards overall on 58 nominations. She has racked up 11 consecutive No. 1 album since Fearless in 2008, along with topping the chart with four re-recorded LPs in 2021 and 2023, and has 15 No. 1 singles.
Her mammoth 2023-24 Eras Tour grossed more than 2.07 billion from nearly 150 shows around the world and spawned Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour, which became the top-grossing concert movie of all time with $180.8 worldwide.

CBS and MTV will simulcast the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards live at 7:30 p.m. ET/4:30 p.m. PT from the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles on September 27. The show also will stream live on Paramount+.

When a woman has difficulty conceiving or experiences repeated pregnancy loss, the focus often turns to the uterus, the quality of the embryos or ovarian reserve. However, hormones, too, can play an important role, and one hormone that deserves attention is prolactin.
Prolactin is produced by the pituitary gland and is best known for its role in breast milk production. Its levels naturally rise during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Outside these periods, however, persistently elevated prolactin, a condition known as hyperprolactinaemia, can interfere with normal reproductive function.
The symptoms are not always obvious. Some women may have irregular or absent periods, difficulty conceiving or an unexpected milky discharge from the breasts. Others may have no noticeable symptoms at all.
Prolactin and fertility
Reproductive hormones work as a closely connected system. Prolactin is part of this system, and when its levels remain elevated, it can interfere with the hormonal signals required for ovulation.
High prolactin can suppress the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone from the brain. This can subsequently affect Luteinising Hormone (LH) and Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH), which are involved in follicle development and ovulation. As a result, some women may ovulate irregularly or stop ovulating altogether. Their periods may become longer, unpredictable or absent, making conception more difficult.
Prolactin also interacts with reproductive hormones after ovulation. This is one reason why its possible role in the early stages of pregnancy has attracted clinical attention, although the relationship is more complex than simply linking one abnormal hormone level to pregnancy loss.
The link to repeated pregnancy loss
The relationship between elevated prolactin and recurrent pregnancy loss is documented in clinical literature but described with appropriate caution. A 2025 guideline published in the Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada found that elevated prolactin is associated with pregnancy loss and may contribute to luteal phase deficiency. The guideline recommends prolactin testing in women with recurrent pregnancy loss who also present with irregular periods or unexplained breast discharge.
The clinical nuance here is important. Hyperprolactinaemia is one contributing factor among several more established causes of recurrent pregnancy loss, such as chromosomal abnormalities in the embryo, uterine structural issues, antiphospholipid syndrome, and thyroid dysfunction. This does not reduce the clinical relevance of elevated prolactin, but it does mean that a single elevated test result should not be treated as the explanation before other causes have been assessed. The 2025 guideline is explicit on this: elevated prolactin should be confirmed through repeat testing before any treatment is initiated, and thyroid function should be checked first, as hypothyroidism can independently raise prolactin levels.
The connection with PMOS
Among women with PMOS, earlier known as PCOS, mildly elevated prolactin levels are occasionally found alongside the more typical hormonal pattern of the condition. Some research has found a mean hyperprolactinaemia prevalence of 11.9% in women with PMOS, though the range across studies is wide, reflecting how variable the relationship is across different populations and diagnostic thresholds. Hyperprolactinaemia is not considered a clinical manifestation of PMOS, and the two conditions are assessed and managed independently.
Why the elevation
The causes of elevated prolactin are varied. A benign, prolactin-secreting pituitary tumour called a prolactinoma is among the more significant causes and is identified through an MRI when prolactin levels are substantially elevated. Hypothyroidism, certain medications including antipsychotics and some antihypertensives, and occasionally stress or intensive exercise can also raise prolactin levels transiently. This is why repeat testing under standardised conditions such as fasting and avoiding physical stress before the blood draw, is important before a diagnosis of hyperprolactinaemia is established.
When true hyperprolactinaemia is confirmed, dopamine agonist medications such as cabergoline or bromocriptine are effective at normalising prolactin levels in most cases. Research has demonstrated successful restoration of ovulation and term pregnancy outcomes in women with hyperprolactinaemia following dopamine agonist therapy, including in cases involving pituitary tumours. The condition, when properly identified and treated, is one of the more manageable contributors to fertility challenges.
What women should know
For women experiencing recurrent pregnancy loss or difficulty conceiving, prolactin testing is a reasonable part of a comprehensive hormonal evaluation. The results need to be interpreted alongside thyroid function, ovarian reserve, and a full assessment of both partners, because the factors that influence reproductive outcomes are rarely operating in isolation.
(Dr. Prachi Benara is a fertility specialist at Birla Fertility and IVF, Gurgaon. prachi.benara@birlafertility.com)
